- Other Initiatives: - Multi-sectoral ‘Rural Prosperity and Resilience’ programme with states. - Mission for Aatmanirbharta in Pulses. - Prime Minister Dhan-Dhaanya Krishi Yojana (PMDKY, Budget 2025) - Target: - 100 districts with low productivity, moderate crop intensity, and below-average credit access. - Administered By: - Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare. - Benefits: - Enhance agricultural productivity. - Promote crop diversification and sustainable practices. - Develop post-harvest storage at panchayat/block levels. - Improve irrigation facilities. - Provide loans for short- and long-term needs. - Funding: - Converges existing schemes; inspired by NITI Aayog’s Aspirational Districts Programme. - Pillar 4A2: Agriculture - Output, MSP, Inflation, and Allied Sectors - Definition: - Agriculture encompasses the cultivation of crops, livestock rearing, and allied activities like fisheries and beekeeping, forming a critical sector of the Indian economy, contributing significantly to GDP, employment, and food security. - Context: - Indian agriculture faces challenges like low productivity, fragmented land holdings, and market inefficiencies, necessitating reforms in marketing, pricing, and infrastructure to enhance farmer incomes and ensure food security. - Significance for India: - As an agrarian economy, India aims to double farmers’ incomes, achieve self-reliance in food production, and control food inflation through initiatives like MSP, e-NAM, and PM-AASHA, aligning with Sustainable Development Goals and Atmanirbhar Bharat. - Agricultural Market Reforms - Definition: - Agricultural market reforms aim to enhance farmers’ access to markets, ensure remunerative prices, and reduce exploitation by intermediaries through regulated markets and digital platforms. - Agricultural Produce Market Committee (APMC) - Definition: - APMC is a state-level statutory body established under APMC Acts to regulate the first sale of agricultural produce at designated market yards (mandis), ensuring fair trade practices. - Historical Context: - Post-independence, APMC laws were enacted to protect farmers from exploitation by local moneylenders and traders who forcibly purchased produce at low prices. - Structure and Function: - APMCs operate mandis where farmers sell produce to licensed commission agents, ensuring regulated transactions but often limiting direct sales to consumers or corporates. - Challenges: - Cartelization: - Politically influential APMC trustees and commission agents form cartels, manipulating prices to deprive farmers of fair returns and engaging in hoarding, contributing to food inflation. - Poor Infrastructure: - Mandis charge multiple fees (entry, exit, etc.), but funds are often mismanaged, leading to inadequate cold storage, transport, and warehousing, resulting in wastage of perishables. - Lack of Integration: - APMC trustees often lack the vision to integrate with food processing industries, limiting value addition and market expansion for farmers’ produce. - Model APMC Act, 2003 - Definition: - The Model APMC Act, circulated by the Union Government, encourages states to reform archaic APMC laws to promote competition and direct marketing. - Key Provisions: - Allows private entrepreneurs and cooperatives to establish parallel markets, enabling direct sales to consumers. - Permits corporate companies to engage in contract farming, purchasing produce directly from farmgates, reducing dependency on APMC mandis. - Impact: - Aims to enhance market access, reduce middlemen’s influence, and provide farmers with better price realization. - Three Farm Laws (2020, Repealed 2021) - Overview: - Three farm laws were introduced in 2020 to reform agricultural marketing but were repealed in 2021 due to farmer protests. - Objectives: - Farmers’ Produce Trade and Commerce (Promotion and Facilitation) Act, 2020: - Allowed farmers to sell produce outside APMC mandis to buyers or organizations, promoting market freedom. - Farmers (Empowerment and Protection) Agreement on Price Assurance and Farm Services Act, 2020: - Facilitated contract farming through advance agreements between farmers and buyers, ensuring price assurance and protecting both parties. - Essential Commodities (Amendment) Act, 2020: - Relaxed stock limits for food processing companies to encourage investment and storage, reducing supply chain constraints. - Repeal Context: - Farmer organizations protested, citing risks of corporate exploitation and loss of APMC protections, leading to their repeal. Detailed analysis is covered in UPSC Mains syllabi. - Online Agricultural Marketing - e-National Agriculture Market (e-NAM) - Definition: - e-NAM, launched in 2016 by the Ministry of Agriculture under the Small Farmers’ Agribusiness Consortium (SFAC), is a pan-India electronic trading portal connecting over 580 APMC mandis for interstate and intrastate trade. - Features: - Central Sector Scheme, fully funded by the Union Government. - Provides free software and financial assistance (₹75 lakh per mandi) for infrastructure development. - Integrates Negotiable Warehousing Receipts (e-NWR) to facilitate trading of stored produce. - Benefits: - Reduces information asymmetry between buyers and sellers, enabling real-time price discovery based on demand and supply. - Enhances market access for farmers, allowing sales beyond local mandis, improving price realization. - Gramin Agricultural Markets (GrAMs) - Definition: - GrAMs, initiated in 2018 under the Ministry of Agriculture with NABARD funding, aim to upgrade ~22,000 rural haats into organized markets linked to e-NAM. - Features: - Owned by local bodies, state agricultural departments, cooperatives, or private entities, unlike the limited 580+ APMC mandis. - Budget 2018 announced infrastructure upgrades to enable direct sales from nearby haats, reducing transport costs to district-level mandis. - Benefits: - Improves market access for small farmers in rural areas, promoting inclusivity and reducing logistical barriers. - Agricultural Export Policy, 2018 - Definition: - Launched by the Ministry of Commerce, the policy aims to boost agricultural exports by improving market access and addressing supply chain inefficiencies. - Objectives: - Enhance export infrastructure, promote value-added products, and integrate farmers with global markets. - Detailed features are covered in UPSC Mains syllabi. - Farmers’ Income and Support - Situation Assessment Survey (SAS) - Definition: - Conducted by the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI) via the National Statistical Office (NSO), SAS assesses agricultural households’ income and socio-economic conditions. - Key Findings (2019, Published 2021): - Average monthly income of agricultural households increased from ₹6,426 (2014) to ₹10,218 (2019). - Highest Incomes: - Meghalaya (₹29,348), Punjab (₹26,701), Haryana (₹22,841). - Lowest Incomes: - Jharkhand (₹4,895), Odisha (₹5,112), West Bengal (₹6,762). - Land Fragmentation: - Average farm size reduced from 0.725 hectares (2003) to 0.512 hectares (2019), impacting productivity. - Income Support Challenges - NABARD’s All India Rural Financial Inclusion Survey: - Of ~21 crore rural households, ~10 crore are engaged in agriculture, but most struggle to earn ₹10,000/month due to low productivity and small land holdings. - Economic Survey 2018: - Climate change reduces farm incomes by 15-18% (irrigated farms) and 20-25% (unirrigated farms) due to higher temperatures and erratic rainfall. - Government Target: - Doubling farmers’ income by 2022-23 (from 2015-16 base) requires a 10% annual agricultural growth rate, but the sector struggles at ~5%, necessitating interventions like subsidies and income support. - PM-KISAN - Definition: - Pradhan Mantri Kisan Samman Nidhi, launched in 2018 by the Ministry of Agriculture, is a Central Sector Scheme providing income support to farmers. - Features: - Initially for small/marginal farmers (up to 2 hectares), extended in 2019 to all farmers regardless of land holding. - Provides ₹6,000/year in three ₹2,000 installments via Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) to eliminate middlemen. - Benefits over 11 crore farmers (Economic Survey 2023). - Benefits: - Ensures financial stability, reduces distress sales, and supports informed cropping decisions. - PM Kisan Maan Dhan Yojana - Definition: - A pension scheme for farmers, offering ₹3,000/month after age 60, with contributions of ₹55-200/month during working years. - Features: - On the farmer’s death, the spouse receives ₹1,500/month. - Covered in detail under Pillar 1D (Pension Schemes). - Minimum Support Prices (MSP) - Definition: - MSP is a government-announced price floor to ensure farmers receive remunerative prices for their produce, protecting them from market fluctuations. - Purpose: - Announced before sowing seasons for 23 crops (14 Kharif, 6 Rabi, 3 commercial, including sugarcane’s Fair and Remunerative Price - FRP). - Prevents distress sales and provides price signals to markets, ensuring prices are not drastically below MSP. - Covered Crops - Kharif Crops (14): - Paddy, Jowar, Bajra, Maize, Ragi, Arhar, Moong, Urad, Groundnut-in-shell, Soyabean, Sunflower, Sesamum, Nigerseed, Cotton. - Rabi Crops (6): - Wheat, Barley, Gram, Masur (Lentil), Rapeseed/Mustard, Safflower. - Commercial/Cash Crops (3): - Jute, Copra (coconut), Sugarcane (FRP). - Additional Notes: - MSP for Toria is based on Rapeseed/Mustard, and de-husked coconut MSP is based on Copra. - Sugarcane’s FRP is enforced on sugar mills, unlike direct government procurement for other crops. - MSP Computation - Process: - Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices (CACP) recommends MSP, approved by the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs (CCEA), chaired by the Prime Minister. - Formula (Post-Budget 2018): - MSP = (A2 + FL) x 1.5, where: - A2: - Actual costs (seeds, fertilizers, pesticides, hired labor, depreciation, fuel, etc.). - FL: - Imputed cost of unpaid family labor. - Ensures 50% profit over production costs. - Swaminathan Committee (2006): - Recommended C2 formula (including imputed rent on land and interest on capital), but not adopted due to high budgetary implications and fiscal deficit concerns. - Additional MSP Factors -
Factor Description
Cost of Production (A2 + FL) ensures 50% profit, forming the base for MSP.
Demand and Supply Higher MSP for crops like pulses to address shortages and encourage cultivation.
Domestic and International Price Trends E.g., higher MSP for soybeans if global prices rise, encouraging domestic production.
Inter-crop Price Parity Adjusts MSP to shift cultivation from water-intensive crops (rice) to millets or pulses.
Rational Resource Use Promotes sustainable crops like millets to conserve water and soil.
Consumer Impact Ensures MSP does not excessively raise consumer prices, preventing shortages of other crops.
Terms of Trade Balances agricultural and industrial price ratios to prevent labor shifts to other sectors.
- Benefits of MSP - Prevents distress sales by ensuring farmers can sell to government at MSP if private buyers offer lower prices. - Provides advance price information, aiding informed cropping decisions based on farm size, climate, and irrigation. - Acts as a market benchmark, ensuring prices are not significantly below MSP. - Limitations of MSP - Limited Reach: - Procurement is concentrated in big towns, with high transport costs for remote/tribal farmers. - Decentralized Procurement (DCP, 1997) allows states to procure wheat/rice, but penetration remains low. - Crop Bias: - Focus on cereals (rice, wheat), with limited procurement of pulses and oilseeds, reducing MSP’s effectiveness. - No MSP for Perishables: - Vegetables and fruits lack MSP, leaving farmers vulnerable to market fluctuations. - PM-AASHA - Definition: - Pradhan Mantri Annadata Aay Sanrakshan Abhiyan (2018), a Central Sector Scheme by the Ministry of Agriculture, addresses MSP limitations. - Components: - Price Support Scheme (PSS): - Central agencies procure pulses, oilseeds, and copra at MSP, expanding beyond cereals. - Price Deficiency Payment Scheme (PDPS): - Compensates farmers with the difference if private buyers pay below MSP for oilseeds. - Private Procurement Stockist Scheme (PPSS): - Engages private agencies to procure at MSP on behalf of the government. - 2024 Reforms: - Integrated PSS, Price Stabilization Fund (PSF), and Market Intervention Scheme (MIS) as sub-schemes under PM-AASHA for streamlined implementation. - Cotton Corporation of India (CCI) - Definition: - Established in 1970 under the Ministry of Textiles, CCI procures cotton at MSP when market prices fall below it. - Features: - No quantitative limits on procurement, ensuring all offered cotton is purchased. - Headquartered in Belapur, Navi Mumbai. - Food Corporation of India (FCI) Procurement - Definition: - FCI, along with CCI, Jute Corporation of India (JCI), NAFED, NCCF, CWC, and SFAC, procures crops at MSP under an open-ended procurement policy (no quantity limits). - Economic Cost: - Includes MSP, bonuses (if any), procurement incidentals (transport, labor, godown costs), and distribution costs for PDS, NFSA, and mid-day meal schemes. - Boss: - Ministry of Agriculture (procurement) and Ministry of Consumer Affairs (distribution). - Food Inflation - Definition: - Food inflation refers to the rise in prices of food commodities, impacting consumers, particularly middle-class families, due to supply-demand imbalances and market inefficiencies. - Causes: - Demand Side: - Growing middle class with higher disposable incomes increases demand for fruits, vegetables, and protein-rich foods. - Supply Side: - Poor monsoons, pests, and post-harvest losses due to inadequate cold storage and warehousing. - Hoarding by traders exacerbates shortages, driving up prices. - Key Commodities and Reasons (2022-24, Economic Survey) -
Commodity Reasons for Inflation
Milk Fodder shortage due to untimely rains, increased diesel prices raising transport costs.
Tomatoes Unseasonal heavy rains in Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana (April-September).
Wheat/Rice Excessive exports during the Ukraine war reduced local supply.
- Government Reforms - Milk: - Establish 100 fodder-centric Farmer Producer Organizations (FPOs) to enhance fodder availability. - Wheat/Rice: - Banned exports of wheat flour, maida, and semolina; increased rice export duty to 20% (later lifted in 2024). - Pulses: - Reduced customs duty and Agriculture Infrastructure Development Cess (AIDC) on imported pulses. - Edible Oils: - Lowered customs duty and AIDC on palm, soybean, and sunflower oils; imposed stock limits; directed companies to reduce prices by ₹15/liter under the Essential Commodities Act. - Soya Meal (Poultry/Fish Feed): - Declared as an essential commodity with stock limits to curb hoarding; allowed import of genetically modified soymeal (2021). - Chana: - Supplied to states at subsidized prices to stabilize markets. - Pulses Supply Shortage - Causes: - Preference for cereals and cash crops (e.g., sugarcane) due to higher MSP, reducing pulses’ cultivation area. - Pulses enrich soil nitrogen, promoting weed growth, which reduces yields. - Susceptibility to pests and fungal growth in humid storage conditions, causing ~25% post-harvest losses. - Solutions: - Reform MSP to incentivize pulses cultivation, especially in drought-prone areas, as they require less water. - Develop pest-resistant seed varieties, with a shift in research focus from cereals to pulses. - Cobweb Cycle - Definition: - The Cobweb Cycle, theorized by Nicholas Kaldor (1934), describes cyclical fluctuations in supply and prices due to farmers’ faulty expectations. - Mechanism: - High prices in one year lead farmers to overproduce the next, causing oversupply and price drops. Subsequent underproduction leads to shortages and price spikes. - Impact: - Economic Survey 2020 noted this cycle as a cause of price fluctuations in pulses, affecting market stability. - Vegetable Supply Issues - Causes: - Global Warming: - Heatwaves in April-May damage vegetable crops’ nascent buds, reducing yields. - Pests and Diseases: - Overuse of pesticides has led to pest immunity (e.g., whiteflies, red mites) in Maharashtra and South India, increasing crop losses. - Shift to Cereals: - High MSP for wheat/rice (2004-14) shifted cultivation away from vegetables and pulses. - Demonetization (2016): - Disrupted cash-based vegetable markets, reducing farmer prices and discouraging vegetable cultivation. - Price Wedge: - Large gaps between wholesale and retail prices due to high transaction costs, poor marketing infrastructure, and middlemen margins. - Weather Disruptions: - Heavy rains, floods, and cyclones (e.g., 2021 in Punjab, Haryana, HP) disrupt supply chains, causing shortages. - Farmer Protests: - Strikes in Maharashtra, UP, and MP led to destruction of produce (e.g., tomatoes, milk), exacerbating shortages. - Storage Issues: - Inadequate cold storage leads to 70% of tomatoes being grown in the Rabi season, causing shortages in other months if not stored properly. - Onion Inflation - Seasonality: - 70% of onions are grown in the Rabi season (December-January, harvested by May), making supply vulnerable to weather disruptions. - Causes of Shortage: - Late monsoons delay sowing; prolonged rains damage crops in major producers (Maharashtra, Karnataka, Telangana, Madhya Pradesh). - 2019: - Heavy rains (September-October) affected cutting and transportation, raising prices to ₹140/kg. - Government Reforms: - Export Ban (2019): - Commerce Ministry banned onion exports (except Andhra’s Krishnapuram onions, popular in Sri Lanka and ASEAN). - Imports: - MMTC Ltd. imported onions from Turkey and Egypt using the Price Stabilization Fund, supplied to state Food and Civil Supply Departments. - Stock Management: - Directed states to build buffer stocks, impose stock limits, and act against hoarding. - Long-Term Solutions: - Support farmer cooperatives for direct sales, enhance cold storage, and enforce anti-hoarding measures. - Economic Survey 2021 Recommendations: - Decentralize NAFED’s onion procurement (currently focused on Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat) to reduce weather-related risks. - Develop online monitoring systems for onion supply, similar to the eVIN vaccine network. - Promote dehydrated onions for longer shelf life and early sale of hydrated varieties to manage supply. - Storage and Transport Initiatives (2020) - Kisan Rail: - Indian Railways introduced refrigerated coaches to improve the national cold supply chain for perishables, milk, meat, and fish. - Challenge: - Railway Ministry reported funding shortages for the project. - Krishi Udaan: - Ministry of Civil Aviation facilitates flights on national and international routes to transport agricultural cargo, benefiting farmers in North-East and tribal districts by enabling premium sales of exotic produce. - Warehousing: - Encourages Warehousing Development and Regulatory Authority (WDRA), FCI, and Central Warehousing Corporation (CWC) to build more warehouses under the Ministry of Consumer Affairs to reduce post-harvest losses. - Food Inflation: Additional Government Initiatives - Price Stabilization Fund (2014) - Definition: - A Central Sector Scheme under the Ministry of Consumer Affairs, providing interest-free loans to FCI, NAFED, and other agencies to procure pulses and perishables for sale at reasonable prices. - Objective: - Stabilizes prices by increasing market supply during inflation. - Open Market Sale Scheme (OMSS) - Definition: - FCI sells surplus food grains in the open market during inflation to increase supply and moderate prices, complementing its PDS role. - Minimum Export Price (MEP) - Definition: - MEP sets a floor price below which commodities cannot be exported, used to curb exports during inflation to boost local supply. - Limitation: - Frequent MEP changes create uncertainty for export-oriented farmers, affecting cropping decisions. - Operation Greens (2018) - Definition: - A scheme under PM Kisan Sampada Yojana targeting Tomato, Onion, and Potato (TOP) to stabilize prices through supply chain improvements (covered under Agriculture Production and Processing). - Food Inflation: Edible Oils - Definition: - Edible oils (e.g., palm, soybean, mustard, groundnut, sesame, sunflower) are essential cooking mediums facing supply shortages in India due to inadequate domestic production and rising import costs, contributing to food inflation. - Causes of Shortage and Inflation: - Faulty MSP Policies: - Inadequate Minimum Support Prices for oilseeds discourage farmers, leading to low domestic production, forcing India to import ~60% of its edible oil requirements. - Rising Demand: - Increased consumption of fast food and junk food (e.g., wafers, fried snacks) among the younger generation drives demand for edible oils. - Global Supply Constraints: - La Niña climatic conditions reduce soybean oil production in Argentina and Brazil, key global suppliers, impacting availability for India. - China’s large-scale purchase of palm oil from Malaysia and Indonesia reduces the quantity available for India, increasing import costs. - Use of edible oils for biofuel production in the USA and Brazil further limits global supply for food purposes. - Supply Chain Disruptions: - The 2020 COVID-19 pandemic caused labor shortages and logistical constraints during lockdowns, disrupting edible oil supply chains and increasing prices. - Government Interventions (2021): - Reduced customs duty on imported palm oil to lower domestic prices. - Imposed stock limits under the Essential Commodities Act, 1955, to prevent hoarding by traders. - Criticism: - Critics argue that reducing import taxes does not effectively combat inflation due to persistent high demand and profiteering by sellers, which offsets price reductions. - National Mission on Edible Oils – Oil Palm (NMEO-OP, 2021) - Definition: - Launched by the Ministry of Agriculture, NMEO-OP is a centrally sponsored scheme to enhance domestic edible oil production, particularly palm oil, to achieve self-reliance and reduce import dependency. - Features: - Focuses on Northeast India and Andaman & Nicobar Islands for oil palm cultivation due to favorable climatic conditions. - States contribute funding alongside the central government. - Components: - Component 1: Price Assurance (DBT): - Farmers produce Fresh Fruit Bunches (FFBs) for crude palm oil (CPO) extraction by industries. - Government provides a Viability Price (VP) to farmers; if market prices fall below VP, the viability gap is paid via Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) to farmers’ bank accounts. - Component 2: Input Support and Training: - Subsidies for seeds, inputs, and training in modern techniques like half-moon terrace cultivation and bio-fencing (planting trees/shrubs to protect crops from cattle, wildlife, and winds). - Impact: - Aims to reduce India’s 98% import dependency on palm oil, lower the import bill, reduce current account deficit, and create income and employment opportunities for farmers. - Atmanirbhar Oil Seeds Abhiyan (2024) - Definition: - A scheme targeting increased production of oilseeds (mustard, groundnut, sesame, soybean, sunflower) to reduce import dependency and boost farmer incomes. - Features: - Develops high-yielding varieties, promotes modern farming techniques, strengthens market linkages, ensures procurement, and supports value addition and crop insurance. - Impact: - Enhances domestic oilseed production, aligns with self-reliance goals, and supports sustainable agricultural growth. - Food Inflation: Essential Commodities Act, 1955 (ECA) - Definition: - The ECA is a central legislation aimed at controlling the production, supply, and distribution of essential commodities (e.g., food grains, pulses, edible oils, sugar, fertilizers, seeds, medicines, petroleum products) to ensure affordability and availability during shortages or inflation. - Key Provisions: - Allows the government to impose stock limits and restrict movement of goods to prevent hoarding and black marketing. - Amendments and Repeal: - Essential Commodities (Amendment) Act, 2020: - Relaxed stock limits for food processing companies to encourage investment and reduce supply chain constraints. - Repealed in 2021 due to farmer protests fearing corporate exploitation and loss of APMC protections. - Impact: - Balances consumer affordability with producer incentives, though amendments faced resistance due to concerns over market deregulation. - Agro-Selling: Deflation (2017 Onwards) - Definition: - Agro-deflation refers to a decline in agricultural commodity prices, observed during the Modi government (2014 onwards), contrasting with high agricultural inflation during the UPA regime (2004-14). - Causes of Deflation: - Demonetization (2016): - Limits on cash transactions and fear of tracking by Income Tax/GST authorities reduced hoarding by traders, increasing market supply and lowering prices. - Global Market Dynamics: - Protectionism by the US/EU and falling international commodity prices reduced India’s agro-exports, increasing domestic supply and contributing to deflation. - RBI’s Hawkish Monetary Policy: - Tight monetary measures (e.g., higher interest rates) helped curb inflation by controlling money supply (detailed in Pillar 1A2). - Sugar Mills: Challenges - Definition: - Sugar mills face financial distress due to high sugarcane production and low global sugar prices, impacting their ability to pay farmers. - Fair and Remunerative Price (FRP): - The minimum price set by the Union government for sugarcane purchased by sugar mills, ensuring farmer income stability. - Some states set a higher State Advised Price (SAP), increasing mill obligations. - Cane Reservation Area: - Mills must procure sugarcane from farmers within a specified radius to protect local farmers from cheap imports from other states. - Challenges: - Bumper sugarcane production in India and Brazil increased global supply, lowering prices, but FRP was not reduced to maintain farmer incomes, doubling over 10 years. - Mills accumulate arrears (unpaid dues to farmers) due to financial strain. - Government Interventions: - Soft loans/cheap loans to sugar mills to clear farmer arrears. - 100% customs duty on imported sugar and 0% duty on sugar exports to boost domestic mill revenues. - Subsidies for sugar exporters to enhance competitiveness. - Sugar Subsidies and WTO Dispute - Issue: - In 2019, Australia, Brazil, and Guatemala complained to the WTO that India’s subsidies, soft loans, and tariff barriers led to excess sugar supply, depressing global prices and harming their local industries. - WTO Agreement on Agriculture (AoA): - Allows food subsidies for food security but not for export subsidies beyond this scope. - WTO Ruling (2021): - Ordered India to stop sugar export subsidies; India’s Commerce Ministry called the ruling “unacceptable” and planned to appeal. - Impact: - Highlights tensions between domestic farmer support and international trade obligations. - Agriculture Production and Processing: Other Schemes - Agriculture Infrastructure Fund (2020) - Definition: - A Central Sector Scheme by the Ministry of Agriculture to provide medium- to long-term loans for post-harvest infrastructure and community farming assets. - Beneficiaries: - Farmers, agricultural cooperatives, Farmer Producer Organizations (FPOs), Self-Help Groups (SHGs), agri-startups, and Public-Private Partnership (PPP) projects. - Features: - Loans worth ₹1 lakh crore provided by banks and NBFCs, with NABARD refinancing support. - Supports post-harvest management infrastructure (e.g., warehouses, cold storage) and community farming assets. - Offers 3% interest subvention and up to ₹2 crore credit guarantee via the Credit Guarantee Fund Trust for Micro and Small Enterprises (CGTMSE). - Valid for 10 years from 2020. - Impact: - Enhances storage and processing capabilities, reducing post-harvest losses and improving farmer incomes. - Bharat Campaign - Definition: - A campaign under the Agriculture Infrastructure Fund to train bankers and raise awareness for maximum loan disbursal and scheme promotion. - Features: - Encourages bankers to provide loans for agricultural infrastructure. - Full form: - Banks Heralding Accelerated Rural & Agriculture Transformation (not critical for UPSC). - Impact: - Strengthens financial support for agricultural infrastructure development. - Farmer Producer Company (FPC) - Definition: - FPCs are hybrid entities combining features of private limited companies (professional management) and cooperative societies (mutual benefits), enabling small farmers to pool resources. - Historical Context: - Introduced via the Companies Act, 1956 amendment in 2003 to counter predictions that small farms would disappear due to consolidation by large farmers. - Features: - Minimum 10 farmers can form an FPC; no upper limit. - Cannot become a public limited company (i.e., cannot invite public investment in shares/bonds). - Receives financial support and credit guarantees from the Ministry of Agriculture. - Impact: - Enhances collective bargaining power, market access, and economies of scale for small farmers. - Rashtriya Krishi Vikas Yojana (RKVY) & RAFTAAR (2017) - Definition: - RKVY, launched in 2007 by the Ministry of Agriculture, is a Core Scheme (partially funded by states) to promote agricultural development; rebranded as RKVY-RAFTAAR (Remunerative Approaches for Agriculture and Allied Sector Rejuvenation) in 2017. - Features: - Funds infrastructure creation (warehouses, cold storage, markets), training in modern techniques (e.g., mushroom cultivation, beekeeping, floriculture), and financial support for agri-enterprises. - Impact: - Enhances agricultural productivity, skill development, and entrepreneurship. - Green Revolution - Krishonnati Yojana (2017) - Definition: - An umbrella Core Scheme by the Ministry of Agriculture consolidating 11 previous schemes to promote sustainable agriculture and allied sectors. - Sub-Schemes: - Mission for Integrated Development of Horticulture (MIDH): - Promotes horticulture, including beekeeping; includes the Coordinated Programme on Horticulture Assessment and Management (CHAMAN) using remote sensing for production and disease assessment. - National Food Security Mission (NFSM): - Increases production of rice, wheat, pulses, millets, and commercial crops; includes sub-missions for nutri-cereals (e.g., jowar, bajra, ragi) and oilseeds (Yellow Revolution). - National Mission for Sustainable Agriculture (NMSA): - Promotes organic manures, bio-fertilizers, and rainfed area development. - National Bamboo Mission (NBM): - Augments farmer incomes through bamboo cultivation; amended Indian Forest Act, 1927, to exclude bamboo from the definition of trees. - Sub-Mission on Agriculture Extension (SMAE): - Enhances farmer training using electronic/print media and ICT tools. - National e-Governance Plan on Agriculture (NeGP-A): - Provides information on cropping methods and market prices. - Sub-Mission on Seeds and Planting Material (SMSP): - Promotes advanced seed production and quality certification. - Sub-Mission on Agricultural Mechanisation (SMAM): - Increases access to farm machinery via Custom Hiring Centres. - Sub-Mission on Plant Protection and Plant Quarantine (SMPPQ): - Minimizes crop damage from pests and invasive species. - Integrated Scheme on Agriculture Census, Economics and Statistics (ISACES): - Collects data for policy-making and research. - Integrated Scheme on Agricultural Cooperation (ISAC): - Supports cooperatives for marketing and processing. - Integrated Scheme on Agricultural Marketing (ISAM): - Develops online/offline marketing infrastructure. - Impact: - Comprehensive approach to modernize agriculture, enhance productivity, and ensure sustainability. - Food Processing: PM Kisan Sampada Yojana - Definition: - Launched by the Ministry of Food Processing Industries, PM Kisan Sampada Yojana is a Central Sector Scheme to develop food processing infrastructure, reducing wastage and enhancing farmer incomes. - Features: - Consolidates previous schemes like Mega Food Parks and Integrated Cold Chain. - Funds food processing parks, collection centers, and modernization of reefer vans (e.g., Patanjali Food and Herbal Park, Haridwar). - Operation Greens (2018): - Sub-scheme targeting Tomato, Onion, and Potato (T-O-P) for improved storage and transport to ensure year-round availability at affordable prices. - Atmanirbhar Expansion (2020): - Extended to all fruits and vegetables, offering 50% subsidy on transport from surplus to deficit areas and long-term subsidies for storage infrastructure. - Impact: - Reduces food wastage, improves farmer prices, and ensures affordable food for consumers. - Horticulture Cluster Development Programme (CDP) by NHB - Definition: - Managed by the National Horticulture Board (NHB, est. 1984, Gurugram), CDP is a Central Sector Scheme to develop horticulture clusters for enhanced production and market access. - Features: - Targets 9 lakh hectares, covering 10 lakh farmers across 55 clusters (e.g., apple in Shopian, J&K; mango in Lucknow, UP; grapes in Nashik, Maharashtra). - Impact: - Boosts horticulture exports and farmer incomes through targeted infrastructure and market linkages. - CDP-SURAKSHA (2024) - Definition: - A sub-scheme under CDP by NHB to provide instant subsidies for horticulture seed/planting material via E-Rupi vouchers. - Features: - Partner banks (HDFC, ICICI, SBI, Bank of Baroda) generate E-Rupi vouchers using NPCI technology. - Impact: - Enhances access to quality planting materials, improving productivity. - PM Formalization of Micro Food Processing Enterprises (PM-FME) - Definition: - A Central Sector Scheme to formalize unorganized micro food processing enterprises, FPOs, SHGs, and cooperatives. - Features: - Provides funding, training, and support for branding, marketing, and compliance with food safety standards. - Adopts a cluster-based approach (e.g., mango in UP, kesar in J&K, bamboo shoots in Northeast). - Promotes herbal cultivation and beekeeping. - Impact: - Enhances export potential, improves product quality, and supports rural entrepreneurship. - Agro-Allied Sectors: Animal Husbandry - Definition: - Animal husbandry involves livestock rearing, dairying, and poultry farming, contributing to employment, nutrition, and exports, employing over 8 crore farmers directly. - Constitutional Mandate: - Directive Principles of State Policy (Article 48) mandate modernizing animal husbandry, improving breeds, and prohibiting cow slaughter. - India’s Status (Economic Survey 2023): - World’s largest milk producer, third in egg production, eighth in meat production. - Increasing per capita availability of milk and eggs, though malnutrition persists in some states due to uneven distribution. - Livestock Census - Definition: - Conducted every 5 years by the Department of Animal Husbandry since 1919; the 20th Census (2018-19) reported India as having the world’s largest livestock population. -
Livestock Population (Million, 2018-19) Top States
Cattle 192.49 West Bengal, Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Bihar, Maharashtra
Goat 148.88 Rajasthan, West Bengal, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Madhya Pradesh
Buffalo 109.85 Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan, Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, Bihar
Sheep 74.26 Telangana, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu
Poultry 851.81 Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, West Bengal, Maharashtra
- 21st Livestock Census (2025): - Includes domesticated animals, poultry, and stray animals (e.g., cattle, buffalo, sheep, goats, pigs, camels, horses, dogs, elephants). - White Revolution - Definition: - The White Revolution refers to India’s dairy sector transformation, making it the world’s largest milk producer (20% of global production). - Historical Context: - Operation Flood (1970-1996), led by Verghese Kurien, established dairy cooperatives, increasing milk production. - Features: - Core Scheme under the Department of Animal Husbandry & Dairying, consolidating schemes like Dairy Entrepreneurship Development and National Livestock Mission. -
Component Description
Pashudhan Sanjivani Animal wellness program with an emergency helpline; issues Nakul Swasthya Patra (animal health card with UID).
e-Pashudhan Haat Online portal connecting farmers with breeders for indigenous bovine breeds.
MAITRIs Multipurpose AI Technicians delivering breeding inputs to farmers’ doorsteps.
E-Gopala App (2020) NDDB app providing cattle care, health, and diet information; integrates animal UID for buying/selling.
Gopal Ratna Award For farmers adopting 100% artificial insemination.
Rashtriya Gokul Mission Conserves indigenous bovine breeds (e.g., Gir, Sahiwal); funds Gokul Gram breeding centers.
National Kamdhenu Breeding Centre Two centers (Itarsi, MP; Chintaladevi, AP) for scientific breed conservation.
Rashtriya Kamdhenu Aayog (2019) Promotes cow productivity, welfare, and organic manure research; headquartered in New Delhi.
Dairy Sahakar (2021) Loans via NCDC for dairy sector infrastructure.
- Impact: - Per capita milk availability: 375 grams/day (varies from 71 grams in Assam to 1120 grams in Punjab). - Budget 2020: - Aims to eliminate Foot and Mouth Disease, Brucellosis (cattle), and PPR (sheep/goats) by 2025; uses MGNREGA for fodder farms. - Pashu Aushadhi Initiative (2025) - Definition: - A scheme to provide affordable generic veterinary medicines through cooperative societies and PM Kisan Samriddhi Kendras. - Features: - Includes ethno-veterinary medicines (e.g., garlic/turmeric formulations for animal fever). - Similar to Jan Aushadhi Kendras for human generic medicines. - Impact: - Reduces treatment costs, improving livestock health and farmer profitability. - Challenges in Dairy Sector - Excess Milk Supply: - Post-2017 global milk surplus crashed prices, leading private dairies to cut procurement rates, causing farmer distress and protests (e.g., milk spilling on highways). - Slaughter Restrictions: - Socio-political restrictions on selling old, non-milking animals to slaughterhouses hinder farmers’ ability to buy new livestock, impacting the leather industry. - COVID-19 Impact (2020): - Lockdowns reduced demand (tea shops, restaurants closed), forcing farmers to sell to cooperatives unable to pay due to slow business. - Fodder Shortage (2022): - Inflation in fodder prices increased milk production costs, contributing to milk price inflation. - Cow Welfare Cess - Definition: - A state-level cess (e.g., Punjab, Chandigarh, Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan) on liquor, electricity, etc., to fund cow welfare initiatives. - Impact: - Supports cow protection and welfare programs, aligning with cultural and political priorities. - Small Ruminants (Economic Survey 2019) - Definition: - Sheep and goats, known as small ruminants, are resilient livestock with high survival rates under drought conditions compared to bovines (cattle, buffalo, mithun, yak). - Advantages: - Survive on shrubs/trees, have higher reproduction rates, and face no vigilante issues, enabling frequent sales. - Boost incomes for small, marginal, and women farmers. - Impact: - Promotes sustainable livestock rearing in resource-scarce regions. - Atmanirbhar Dairy Cooperatives - Definition: - Initiatives to support dairy cooperatives post-COVID-19 lockdown to address reduced milk sales. - Features: - 2% loan interest subvention for working capital; additional 2% for timely repayments (total 4%). - Dairy Processing and Infrastructure Development Fund (DIDF): - 2.5% interest subsidy for new milk processing/chilling facilities. - National Animal Disease Control: - 100% vaccination for Foot and Mouth Disease and Brucellosis. - Animal Husbandry Infrastructure Development Fund: - 3% loan interest subsidy and 25% credit guarantee. - Impact: - Strengthens dairy cooperatives, enhances disease control, and improves infrastructure. - Amul Golden Jubilee (2023-24) - Definition: - Marks 50 years of the Gujarat Cooperative Milk Marketing Federation (GCMMF), known as Amul, founded in 1973 by Verghese Kurien, the “Father of the White Revolution.” - Significance: - Amul is the world’s 8th largest dairy, contributing significantly to India’s dairy sector growth. - Agro-Allied Sectors: Fisheries – Blue Revolution - Definition: - The Blue Revolution focuses on increasing fish production and aquaculture to enhance employment, income, exports, and food security, with India as the second-largest fish producer globally. - Context: - Inland fisheries dominate production; frozen shrimp is India’s largest seafood export. - Pradhan Mantri Matsya Sampada Yojana (PMMSY, 2020) - Definition: - An umbrella scheme by the Ministry of Fisheries, Animal Husbandry & Dairying to modernize fisheries infrastructure and boost production. - Features: - Combines Central Sector (fully Union-funded) and Centrally Sponsored (state-funded) sub-schemes, worth over ₹20,000 crore. - Supports Sagar Mitra youth extension workers for training fishermen, loans/insurance for fishing vessels, inland aquaculture, seaweed cultivation, and quality control labs. - Develops fishing harbors, post-harvest infrastructure, and marketing support. - Valid for 5 years from 2020. - Budget 2024 Updates: - Targets increasing aquaculture productivity from 3 to 5 tons per hectare. - Aims to double exports to ₹1 lakh crore and generate 55 lakh jobs. - Plans to establish five integrated aqua parks. - Impact: - Enhances fisheries exports, creates jobs, and ensures compliance with global health standards. - PM Matsya Kisan Samridhi Sah-Yojana (2024) - Definition: - A Central Sector sub-scheme under PMMSY to support micro and small fisheries enterprises. - Features: - Investment of over ₹6,000 crore (2023-27) for enterprise registration, loans, insurance, and performance grants for quality control. - Impact: - Formalizes unorganized fisheries, improving access to finance and markets. - Shaphari Certification (MPEDA, 2021) - Definition: - A certification by the Marine Products Exports Development Authority (MPEDA) ensuring aquaculture products (e.g., shrimp, fish) are free of harmful chemicals, aligning with UN FAO guidelines. - Impact: - Enhances export quality and compliance with US/EU sanitary standards. - Fish Capture Devices (Economic Survey 2025) - Definition: - Technologies to enhance aquaculture productivity and sustainability. -
Device Description
Cages Netted enclosures in lakes/rivers allowing water flow while containing fish.
Pens Netted enclosures in natural water bodies restricting fish to specific areas.
Raceways Narrow channels with continuous water flow for oxygen supply and waste removal.
Recirculating Aquaculture Systems (RAS) Tanks with water filtration and reuse for efficient fish farming.
Biofloc Systems Use microorganisms to convert waste into protein-rich feed in the water.
- Sweet Revolution (Honey/Beekeeping) - Definition: - The Sweet Revolution promotes beekeeping to boost farmer incomes and support food processing, chemical, and pharmaceutical industries. - Initiatives: - Honey Mission (2017) by Khadi and Village Industries Commission (KVIC). - National Beekeeping & Honey Mission (NBHM, 2020) by the Ministry of Agriculture. - Impact: - Generates income from honey, beeswax, and bee venom; enhances pollination for crops. - Agricultural Research, Education, and Extension - Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR) - Definition: - Established in 1929, ICAR is an autonomous body under the Ministry of Agriculture, overseeing agricultural research, education, and extension services. - Features: - Operates over 690 Krishi Vigyan Kendras (KVKs) for last-mile connectivity, helping farmers adopt modern technologies. - Impact: - Drives innovation in farming practices, improving productivity and sustainability. - Agriculture Census - Definition: - Conducted every 5 years since 1970 by the Ministry of Agriculture with NSSO, assessing land holdings, cropping patterns, and agricultural inputs. - Features: - Delayed in 2020 due to COVID-19; 2021-22 census phase-1 expected completion by December 2023. - Agricultural year (July-June) differs from financial year (April-March). - Impact: - Provides data for policy-making and resource allocation. - Digital Crop Survey System (2024) - Definition: - A GPS-enabled mobile app system by the Ministry of Agriculture to replace manual crop surveys, reducing delays and errors. - Features: - Census covers entire population/area; surveys sample a subset (e.g., 10%). - Impact: - Enhances accuracy and efficiency in agricultural data collection. - Global Cooperation: Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) - Definition: - Established in 1945 (HQ: Rome, Italy), FAO is a UN agency promoting global food security and agricultural development. - Features: - Publishes the Food Price Index (FPI) monitoring inflation in cereals, oilseeds, dairy, meat, and sugar. - Celebrates World Milk Day (June 1) since 2001, with 2021 theme “Sustainability in the Dairy Sector.” - International Year for Millets (2023) - Definition: - Declared by the UN General Assembly to promote millets globally, led by India, which accounts for 80% of Asia’s and 20% of global millet production. - Features: - Millets are Kharif crops, grown in rainfed conditions, requiring less water and inputs. - Notified as nutri-cereals in 2018 under NFSM for nutritional support. - Budget 2023 funds the Indian Institute of Millet Research, Hyderabad (ICAR). - Impact: - India’s millet yield (1239 kg/ha) exceeds the global average (1229 kg/ha), supporting food security and climate resilience. - MAHARISHI (2023) - Definition: - Millet and Other Ancient Grains International Research Initiative, launched at the G20 Summit 2023 (Agricultural Chief Scientists meeting). - Features: - HQ at Indian Institute of Millets Research, Hyderabad, for R&D and awareness. - Impact: - Promotes global millet research and adoption. - MIIRA (2023) - Definition: - Millet International Initiative for Research and Awareness, proposed by India with G20 support for global millet R&D. - Impact: - Enhances international collaboration in millet innovation. - 1st Global Symposium on Farmers’ Rights (2023) - Definition: - Organized by FAO and the Indian Ministry of Agriculture in New Delhi to protect farmers’ rights against seed companies (e.g., PepsiCo’s potato seed disputes). - Impact: - Strengthens farmer protections in intellectual property disputes. - Other International Years - 2024: - Camelids (camel species). - 2025: - Quantum Science-Tech, Cooperatives, Glaciers’ Preservation, Peace and Trust. - SAARC Food Bank (2007) - Definition: - Established by SAARC countries to provide food (wheat/rice) during emergencies. - Features: - Stocks managed by national agencies (e.g., FCI in India); no central HQ. - Impact: - Enhances regional food security. - Agricultural Market Information System (AMIS, 2011) - Definition: - Established in Rome, Italy, AMIS tracks food prices and coordinates with FAO, OECD, and World Bank to ensure global food supply stability. - Features: - G20 Summit 2023 noted rising fertilizer prices post-Russia-Ukraine war, using AMIS to address supply issues. - Impact: - Supports global food price stability and supply chain coordination. - International Rice Research Institute (IRRI, 1960) - Definition: - Based in Los Baños, Philippines, IRRI reduces poverty and hunger through rice science, funded by Ford, Rockefeller, and the Philippine government. - Impact: - Enhances rice productivity and food security in Asia. - International Grains Council (IGC) - Definition: - Based in London, IGC promotes cooperation in wheat and coarse grain trade; India is an exporting member since 2003. - Impact: - Facilitates India’s grain exports and global market integration. - Global Awards and Famous Scientists - World Food Prize - Definition: - Known as the “Nobel Prize in Agriculture,” awarded annually by the World Food Foundation (HQ: Iowa, USA) on World Food Day (October 16). - Notable Recipients: - 2023: - Dr. Swati Nayak (IRRI, India), nicknamed “Bihana Didi” for seed research. - 2024: - Dr. Geoffrey Hawtin and Dr. Cary Fowler (USA/UK) for crop biodiversity. - Norman Borlaug (USA, 1914-2009) - Contributions: - Father of the global Green Revolution; developed dwarf wheat varieties (Sonora-64, Lerma Rojo-64) in Mexico, earning the Nobel Peace Prize (1970). - M.S. Swaminathan (India, 1925-2023) - Contributions: - Father of India’s Green Revolution; modified wheat varieties using gamma rays, improving yields from 1.5 to 4.5 tonnes/ha (trials in Jaunti, Delhi, 1965). - Awards: - Padma Shri, Padma Bhushan, Padma Vibhushan, Ramon Magsaysay, World Food Prize. - Pillar 4B1-i: Manufacturing & Services - Industrial Policy and LPG Reforms - Definition: - Industrial policy outlines government strategies to promote manufacturing and services, aiming to enhance economic growth, employment, and global competitiveness, with LPG (Liberalization, Privatization, Globalization) reforms marking a pivotal shift in India’s industrial landscape since 1991. - Context: - India’s industrial policies have evolved from public sector-led heavy industries (1948-1991) to market-driven approaches post-LPG, focusing on innovation, infrastructure, and ease of doing business to align with global trends like the 4th Industrial Revolution. - Significance for India: - Manufacturing and services contribute significantly to GDP and employment, with policies like Make in India and Startup India aiming to position India as a global manufacturing hub, foster innovation, and create jobs, addressing challenges like skill gaps and industrial sickness. - Liberalization, Privatization, and Globalization (LPG) - Definition: - LPG reforms, initiated in 1991 during the Balance of Payments (BoP) crisis under PM Narasimha Rao and FM Manmohan Singh, aimed to deregulate industries, reduce government control, and integrate India into the global economy. - Historical Context (1948-1991): - 1948 Industrial Policy Resolution (Shyama Prasad Mukherjee): - Focused on public sector-led heavy industries (e.g., oil, mining, steel, chemicals). - PM Nehru’s vision emphasized employment generation, self-reliance, and raw material supply for consumer goods industries. - 1956 Industrial Policy Resolution: - Reinforced public sector dominance, reserving key industries for government control. - Liberalization - Definition: - Withdrawal of government controls and regulations to enhance industrial efficiency and competitiveness. - Pre-1991: - Mandatory licensing for private industrial activities. - Production quotas (e.g., limits on telephones, scooters) enforced by government inspectors. - Resulted in delays, corruption, and lack of ease of doing business. - Post-LPG Reforms: - Abolished production quotas and inspector raj. - Licensing limited to specific sectors: - Alcoholic drinks - Tobacco products - Electronic aerospace and defense equipment - Industrial explosives (gunpowder, nitrocellulose, matchsticks) - Hazardous chemicals (hydrocyanic acid, phosgene, isocyanates) - Industrial Entrepreneur Memorandum (IEM): - Simplified process for entrepreneurs to register with the Commerce Ministry for data collection, except in public sector-reserved industries. - Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs): - Granted operational freedom via MoUs and Navratna/Maharatna status, reducing ministerial interference. - Small Scale Industries (SSI/MSME): - Pre-1991: - Reserved sectors (e.g., pickles, mustard oil, glass bangles) restricted big corporates. - Post-2015: - Reservation list eliminated, allowing broader private participation. - Privatization - Definition: - Transfer of ownership or operations from public to private sector, either by allowing private entry into reserved sectors or reducing government shareholding in CPSEs below 50% (disinvestment). - Pre-1991: - Many sectors (e.g., banking, insurance, aviation) reserved exclusively for public sector, leading to low competition and innovation. - Nationalization of private industries in national interest (e.g., banks, insurance). - Post-LPG Reforms: - Private sector allowed in banking, insurance, aviation, telecom, etc. - Stopped nationalization practices. - Reserved sectors limited to: - Atomic Energy - Railways (partially opened to private train operators post-2020) - Globalization - Definition: - Integration of economies through free flow of goods, services, labor, capital, technology, and ideas. - Pre-1991: - Inward-looking economy with import substitution policies. - High tariff and non-tariff barriers, leading to smuggling issues. - Strict controls on currency convertibility and foreign investment. - Post-LPG Reforms: - Joined WTO, relaxed tariff/non-tariff barriers. - Eased norms for foreign companies and investments, enhancing global market access. - Beyond LPG: Towards 4th Industrial Revolution - Definition: - The 4th Industrial Revolution (4IR) optimizes computerization using cloud computing, AI, and IoT, enabling smart factories with cyber-physical systems for efficient resource use. - Global Context: - Originated as a buzzword at the 2016 World Economic Forum (WEF) Davos Summit. - Countries like Germany, France, China, and the USA have government-funded 4IR programs. - India’s Initiatives: - 2017: - Commerce Ministry’s AI taskforce (Dr. V. Kamakoti) for economic transformation. - 2018: - Defense Ministry’s AI taskforce (N. Chandrasekharan, Tata Sons) for national security. - 2018 Budget: - ₹100 crore for Department of Science & Technology’s mission on cyber-physical systems. - 2019 Budget: - National Programme on Artificial Intelligence by NITI Aayog. - Global Partnership on Artificial Intelligence (GPAI, 2020) - Definition: - A multi-stakeholder initiative to bridge AI theory and practice through cutting-edge research. - Features: - Founding members: - India, US, UK, EU, Australia, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, Mexico, New Zealand, South Korea, Singapore. - Secretariat: - Paris, France, hosted by OECD. - Annual Summits: - 2021 (Paris), 2022 (Tokyo), 2023 (New Delhi), 2024 (Serbia). - Budget 2023: - Three Centers of Excellence for AI in agriculture, health, and sustainable cities. - AI Kosha & AI Compute Portal (2025) - Boss: - Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY). - Features: - AI Compute Portal: - Provides access to 10,000+ GPUs for startups, researchers, and companies. - AI Kosha: - Tools to transform AI-related ideas into impactful solutions. - Impact: - Enhances AI innovation and accessibility for Indian stakeholders. - New Industrial Policy - Context: - Last industrial policy in 1991; new policy formulated since 2017, awaiting cabinet approval (2024). - Focus Areas: - Technology & Innovation: - Incentives for AI, IoT, robotics. - Manufacturing & MSME: - Support for small-scale industries. - Ease of Doing Business: Simplified regulations. - Infrastructure & Investment: - Enhanced connectivity. - Trade & Fiscal Policy: Export promotion. - Skills & Employability: - Workforce training for 4IR. - Samarth Udyog Bharat 4.0 - Boss: - Ministry of Heavy Industries, Department of Heavy Industries. - Objective: - Prepare Indian manufacturing for 4IR by 2025 through awareness, demo centers, training, industry-academia networking, and international cooperation. - Related Initiatives: - National Capital Goods Policy (2016): Boosts domestic production of textile, mining, and printing machinery. - 2023: - India’s first Centre for 4IR (C4IR) in Hyderabad, focusing on healthcare and life sciences, with WEF support. - Industry 5.0 - Definition: - Complements 4IR by focusing on societal value, worker well-being, human-robot collaboration (cobots), and sustainable resource use. - Comparison: -
AspectIndustry 4.0Industry 5.0
FocusEconomic value, efficiency, productivitySocietal value, worker well-being
AutomationRobot-centricHuman-robot collaboration
SustainabilityIgnoredMindful resource consumption
- Circular Economy - Definition: - An alternative to the linear economy (make, use, dispose), circular economy maximizes resource use, extracts value, and regenerates waste. - Origin: - 2019: - NITI Aayog proposed circular economy for resource efficiency in India. - Impact: - EU: - Expected savings of €600 billion, 580,000 jobs, and 450 million tonnes CO2 reduction by 2030. - India: - Potential to generate 1.4 crore jobs in 5-7 years. - Circular Economy: Business Models - Shifted to Mains (not covered here as per instructions). - Right to Repair Portal (2022) - Boss: - Ministry of Consumer Affairs. - Features: - Companies must upload repair manuals for consumer products (mobile phones, electronics, durables, automobiles, farming equipment). - Enables self-repair or third-party repair, reducing e-waste and promoting circular economy. - Impact: - Enhances consumer empowerment, environmental conservation, and aligns with global practices (e.g., Europe). - India Plastics Pact (IPP, 2021) - Boss: - WWF-India and Confederation of Indian Industry (CII). - Features: - Indian companies commit to circular economy practices for plastic products, focusing on reduce, reuse, recycle. - Impact: - Reduces plastic waste and promotes sustainable production. - Mission LiFE (Lifestyle for Environment) - Origin: - 2021: - PM Modi introduced at UNFCCC COP26, Glasgow. - 2022: - Launched at Statue of Unity, Gujarat. - Features: - Promotes sustainable lifestyles (e.g., avoiding plastic bags/straws, turning off idle appliances/engines). - Emphasizes reduce, reuse, recycle principles. - Impact: - Encourages environmentally conscious behavior to support circular economy goals. - National Manufacturing Policy (NMP, 2011) - Boss: - Commerce Ministry, DPIIT. - Targets: - Increase manufacturing’s GDP share to 25% by 2022. - Create 100 million jobs. - Features: - Promotes ease of doing business, skill upgradation, innovation funding, and green technologies. - Establishes National Investment and Manufacturing Zones (NIMZ). - NIMZ (National Investment and Manufacturing Zones) - Definition: - Industrial townships with SEZs, industrial parks, warehousing zones, and export-oriented units. - Features: - Tax incentives and relaxed FDI norms. - Infrastructure support (rail, road, energy, communication, schools, hospitals). - Relaxed labor laws (e.g., night shifts for women, flexible hiring-firing). - Self-governing under Article 243(Q-c), exempt from traditional municipal norms. - Examples: - Ahmedabad-Dholera (Gujarat), Dadri-Noida-Ghaziabad (UP), Manesar-Bawal (Haryana). - Industrial Information System (IIS, 2017): - GIS-enabled database for industrial areas, aiding entrepreneurs with data on raw materials and transport hubs. - Industrial Corridors - Boss: - Commerce Ministry, National Industrial Corridor Development and Implementation Trust (NICDIT). - Features: - Funds industrial areas, townships, warehousing, rental factories, social infrastructure (schools, hospitals), and connectivity (roads, railways, airports, pipelines). - Notable Corridors: - Delhi Mumbai Industrial Corridor (DMIC, 2006): Covers UP, Haryana, Rajasthan, MP, Gujarat, Maharashtra; 49% NICDIT, 26% JICA, rest Indian PSUs. - Others: - Amritsar-Kolkata, Chennai-Bengaluru, Bengaluru-Mumbai, Vizag-Chennai, East Coast (Kolkata-Chennai), Odisha Economic Corridor. - Defence Parks: - Pallakad (Kerala, 2017), Tamil Nadu, Uttar Pradesh (2018). - NICDP: 12 Industrial Nodes/Cities/Parks - Boss: - Commerce Ministry. - Budget 2024: - Announced 12 new industrial nodes in Khurpia (Uttarakhand), Rajpura-Patiala (Punjab), Dighi (Maharashtra), Palakkad (Kerala), Agra, Prayagraj (UP), Gaya (Bihar), Zaheerabad (Telangana), Orvakal, Kopparthy (AP), Jodhpur-Pali (Rajasthan). - Impact: - Catalysts for achieving $2 trillion export target by 2030. - Staple Thesis: Natural Resources in Economic Growth - Theory: - By Harold Innis and W.A. Mackintosh, posits economic growth depends on natural resource abundance (e.g., Canada: wood, coal; Saudi Arabia: oil). - India’s Context: - Economic Survey: - India lacks abundant natural resources, necessitating focus on low-skill manufacturing via Make in India. - Make in India: Overview - Boss: - Commerce Ministry, DPIIT. - Objective: - Position India as a global hub for manufacturing, design, and innovation across 27 sectors. - Features: - Relaxed FDI norms. - Fostering R&D and innovation. - Building infrastructure (roads, railways, ports). - Simplifying factory, labor, and tax laws. - Enhancing skill development. - Key Sectors and Initiatives: -

- Challenges: - Most sectors require skilled labor, while India has a large unskilled workforce, necessitating focus on education and skill development (e.g., Skill India). - Make in India 2.0 - Launch: - 2022 (Phase 1.0: 2014). - Targets: - ₹3 lakh crore investment in 5 years. - 60 lakh jobs. - Sectors: - 15 Manufacturing: - Aerospace, automotive, pharma, biotech, capital goods, textiles, chemicals, electronics, leather, food processing, gems, shipping, railways, construction, renewable energy. - 12 Services: - IT & ITeS, tourism, medical travel, logistics, accounting, audiovisual, legal, communication, construction engineering, environmental, financial, education. - 24 sub-sectors (not detailed in raw text but implied as extensions of the above). - Impact: - Enhances investment and job creation, building on Phase 1.0’s foundation. - Assemble in India - Definition: - Economic Survey (2020, Vol1Ch5) proposed shifting from Make in India to Assemble in India, focusing on integrating India into global value chains (GVCs) for network products. - Network Products - Definition: - Products (e.g., computers, TVs, mobiles, road vehicles) manufactured across GVCs by MNCs (Apple, Samsung, Nike), designed in high-wage countries (US/EU/Japan) and assembled in low-wage countries (e.g., China). - Example: - iPhone: - LCD (South Korea), processor (Taiwan), WiFi chip (Malaysia), assembled by Foxconn in China. - 2020: - Foxconn started iPhone 11 assembly in Chennai due to US-China trade war. - Benefits of Assemble in India - Job Creation: - 2025: - 4 crore jobs. - 2030: - 8 crore jobs. - Export Share: - 2025: - Increase India’s global export share to 3.5%. - 2030: - Increase to 6%. - Impact: - Leverages semi-skilled labor, boosting employment and export competitiveness. - Production Linked Incentive (PLI) Scheme - Definition: - Provides 4-6% subsidies on incremental sales of goods manufactured in India (base year: 2019-20; some companies can choose 2020-21). - Exception: - Drone industry receives 20% subsidy. - Validity: - Stopped accepting new applications in March 2025. - PLI 1.0: 13 Sectors -

- PLI 2.0 for IT Hardware (2023) - Boss: - MeitY. - Products: - Laptops, tablets, all-in-one PCs, servers, semiconductors, integrated chips. - Benefits: - 5% incentive on incremental sales of IT hardware made in India. - Tenure: - 6 years from registration. - PLI 1.0 IT manufacturers automatically upgraded to PLI 2.0. - PLI Scheme: Benefits - Reduces imports, increases exports, boosts jobs and GDP. - Economic Survey 2023: - India’s global export share (2.2% in 2021) to improve. - Mobile Sector: - ₹10 lakh crore GDP contribution, 60% export share, 2 lakh direct jobs, 6 lakh indirect jobs. - Automobiles: - 7.5 lakh jobs. - Drones: - 10,000 jobs. - Encourages MNCs (Foxconn, Wistron, Pegatron) to shift from China to India (e.g., Tata’s acquisition of Wistron’s Bengaluru factory for iPhone production). - PLI Lapsed (March 2025) - Reasons for Lapse: - Improved pharma and mobile manufacturing but failed to raise manufacturing’s GDP share from 17% to 25%. - Many firms did not start production or meet targets. - Indian steel, textiles, solar panels uncompetitive against Chinese firms globally. - Industrialists cite bureaucratic delays in subsidy release. - Electric Vehicles: FAME & PMP Schemes - Covered in Pillar #5 (Infrastructure - Transport). - Balance Sheet Deleveraging (Economic Survey 2023) - Definition: - Reducing corporate debt through loan repayment, restructuring, asset sales, or profit increases. - Progress: - Reforms (IBC Code, Bad Bank, ECLGS, PLI) facilitated deleveraging. - Indicators: - Interest Coverage Ratio: - Improved from 3 (2020) to 5 (2022). - Debt to Equity Ratio: - Reduced from 0.8 (2020) to 0.4 (2022). - Startup India (2016) - Boss: - Commerce Ministry, DPIIT. - Definition (2019): - Companies not older than 10 years, with turnover < ₹100 crore, working on innovative goods/services. - Features: - 3-year exemption from income and corporation tax. - Self-certification for EPFO and ESIC compliance. - Relaxed public procurement norms (e.g., no experience/turnover requirements). - Simplified exit norms under I&B Code (90-day liquidation). - Fund of Funds for Startups (FFS): Provides capital to startup schemes. - Support for industry-academia partnerships, incubation, patent filing (low/zero fees). - Foreign Venture Capital Investors (FVCI): Relaxed TDS and currency convertibility norms. - Startup India Seed Fund Scheme (SISFS, 2021): Financial aid to 3600 startups over 4 years. - Prarambh Summit (2021): - Commerce Ministry + BIMSTEC countries for startup collaboration. - Unicorn Company - Definition: - Privately held startup valued at $1 billion or more (not listed on stock exchanges). - Origin: - Coined by Aileen Lee (2013). - Examples: - Swiggy, Byju’s, Unacademy. - Data (Jan 2022): - India (80+), China (300+), USA (400+). - Network Effect & Related Concepts - Network Effect: - A product/service becomes more valuable as more people use it (e.g., social media platforms attract more advertisers with larger user bases). - Metcalfe’s Law: - Similar to network effect, applied to telecom networks (value grows with user connections). - Free Riders: - Users benefiting from services without payment (e.g., using Starbucks’ Wi-Fi without buying coffee; tax evaders using public infrastructure). - National Policy on Electronics (NPE, 2019) - Boss: - MeitY. - Objective: - Make India a global hub for Electronics System Design and Manufacturing (ESDM). - Features: - Tax benefits, subsidies for R&D, and skill development in 5G, IoT, AI, machine learning, VR, drones, robotics, medical electronics, automotive electronics, and defense electronics. - Sovereign Patent Fund (SPF): - Government buys patents/IPR to enable MSMEs to use them without heavy royalties. - Targets (2025): - Produce 100 crore mobile handsets, export 60 crore units. - Create 1 crore jobs. - Achieve $1 trillion digital economy (Economic Survey 2023). - Electronics Development Fund (EDF, 2015) - Boss: - MeitY, managed via Canara Bank’s CANBANK Venture Capital Funds Ltd. - Features: - Fund of Funds model, investing in SEBI-registered venture capital funds for electronics startups. - Design Linked Incentive (DLI) for Semiconductors - Boss: - MeitY, implemented by C-DAC. - Features: - 4-6% subsidy for Indian companies designing semiconductors, ICs, chipsets to reduce reliance on Taiwan. - National Digital Communications Policy (2018) - Boss: - Ministry of Communications, Dept of Telecom. - Status: - Outdated for 2025-26 prelims, compressed in notes. - National Policy on Software Products (2019) - Boss: - MeitY. - Targets (2025): - 10,000 startups, 35 lakh jobs, 10% of India’s GDP. - Electronics & Startups: Notable Schemes/Portals (2022) -

- Quantum Technology (2020) - Definition: - Quantum computers use qubits, leveraging quantum mechanics for faster processing (e.g., Google’s Sycamore: 200 seconds vs. 10,000 years for conventional supercomputers). - Applications: - Computing, communications, cybersecurity. - Budget 2020: - National Mission on Quantum Technologies (5 years). - Related: - 5G, public data (Pillar #5: Communication Infrastructure). - Startup Criticism/Challenges - Shifted to Mains (not covered here as per instructions). - Startup Shutdown: Exit of Sick Industries - Definition: - Sick industries have accumulated losses exceeding net worth (assets minus liabilities). - Causes: - Internal: - Mismanagement, low worker morale, strikes. - External: - Rising energy/raw material costs, falling demand. - Historical Context: - 1985: - Sick Industrial Companies Act (PM Rajiv Gandhi) created BIFR (Finance Ministry) to revive or shut down sick industries. - Issues: - Slow decision-making, prolonged government support, termed “Chakravyuh challenge” by Economic Surveys. - Post-2016 (PM Modi): - Repealed Sick Industrial Companies Act; cases transferred to National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT). - Process: - Wilful/incapable defaulters: - Liquidation under SARFAESI Act. - Others: - Insolvency Professional (IP) creates resolution plan within specified days; if unacceptable, liquidation follows. - Voluntary shutdown: - Startups can liquidate within 90 days under I&B Code, enhancing ease of doing business. - Pillar 4B1-ii: Manufacturing & Services - Intellectual Property Rights - Definition: - Intellectual Property Rights (IPRs) are legal rights protecting creations of the mind, such as inventions, literary/artistic works, designs, symbols, and names, governed by WTO’s TRIPS Agreement (1995), covering Copyright, Trademarks, Geographical Indications, Industrial Designs, Patents, Integrated Circuits, and Trade Secrets. - Global Authority: - World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO), a UN specialized agency (HQ: Geneva, Switzerland), oversees global IPR standards and initiatives. - WIPO - Key Functions - Global Innovation Index (GII): - Ranks countries based on innovation performance across seven pillars: knowledge/technology outputs, market sophistication, human capital/research, institutions, business sophistication, infrastructure, and creative outputs. - Marrakesh Treaty (2013): - Mandates nations to enhance accessibility of copyrighted books for visually challenged individuals. - India was the first to ratify, launching Sugamya Pustakalaya e-library for visually impaired, in collaboration with Daisy Forum of India (NGO) and Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), under the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment’s Divyangjan Department. - IPR - Indian Laws -

- IPR - Copyright Related Bodies - Copyright Office - Boss: - Commerce Ministry (DPIIT), earlier Education Ministry. - Nature: - Statutory, quasi-judicial, full-time. - Function: - Registration of copyrights through the Registrar of Copyright. - Copyright Board - Nature: - Statutory, quasi-judicial, part-time. - Functions: - Resolves disputes related to copyright registration and fixes royalty rates for music, books, etc. - Intellectual Property Appellate Board (IPAB) - Established: - 2003, to hear appeals under Trademark Act, GI Act, Patent Act, and Copyright Act. - Abolished: - 2021, due to delays in delivering justice; appeals now filed in High Courts. - Copyright Act - Automatic Existence - Copyright exists automatically upon creation of a work, requiring no formal registration. - Registration with Copyright Office is advisable to establish ownership in legal disputes (e.g., piracy cases). - Copyright Act - Covered Works - Original literary, software, musical, and artistic works. - Cinematographic films. - Sound recordings. -
Type of WorkExamples
Literary WorkPamphlets, brochures, novels, books, poems, song lyrics, computer programs
Artistic WorkDrawings, paintings, sculptures, architectural/technical drawings, maps, logos
Dramatic WorkDance, mime, screenplay, music, sound recordings, cinematographic films

- IPR - Patents: What Cannot Be Patented - Frivolous inventions (e.g., schoolbag, laptop bag). - Inventions harmful to public order, morality, humans, animals, plants, or environment (e.g., stone-pelting machine). - Atomic energy-related inventions. - Mere discovery of scientific principles, abstract theories, or natural substances (living/non-living). - Plant/seed varieties and their biological production processes. - Animal breeding or medical treatments for humans/animals. - New forms of known substances without enhanced efficacy. - Mere rearrangement/duplication of known devices. - Aggregation of component properties (e.g., lemon + sugar + water = juice). - Mathematical formulas, business methods, game methods (e.g., Dhoni’s helicopter shot). - Computer programs or information presentation. - Integrated circuits (protected under Semiconductor Integrated Circuits Layout-Design Act). - Literary, dramatic, musical, artistic works, or cinema/TV shows (protected under Copyright Act). - Traditional knowledge (e.g., Ayurvedic information). - Patent: Discovery vs. Invention -
AspectDiscoveryInvention
DefinitionHighlighting an existing phenomenonCreating something novel/unique
ExampleNewton discovering gravityBell inventing the telephone
PatentableNoYes
- IPR: Biopiracy & Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (TKDL) - Biopiracy: - Exploitation of traditional knowledge or genetic material without consent of local communities (e.g., neem oil for skin diseases, turmeric for wound healing). - TKDL (2001): - Boss: - CSIR (Science Ministry) and AYUSH Ministry. - Objective: - Prevent biopiracy by documenting traditional knowledge. - Features: - Digital database of over 3 lakh Indian traditional medicines/techniques (Ayurveda, Unani, Siddha, Sowa Rigpa, Yoga) in five languages (English, German, French, Japanese, Spanish) for patent examiners. - Impact: - Helped revoke/ban over 200 biopiracy-related patents. - IPR - Patents: Compulsory Licensing - Definition: - Government can use, manufacture, import, or sell a patented invention without the patent holder’s consent in public interest, permitted under WTO’s TRIPS Agreement. - Example (2012): - Anticancer drug Nexavar (Bayer Pharma, Germany) was priced at ₹2.5 lakh per 120 tablets. - Indian government issued compulsory license to NATCO to produce it at ₹8,880 per 120 tablets, with 6% royalty to Bayer. - Concerns: - US and EU oppose compulsory licensing, citing losses to their MNCs due to low prices and royalties. - Patent Pools - Definition: - Voluntary agreements among patent holders to pool patents, managed by a third party, licensing production to others at low cost and distributing royalties. - Context: - Proposed by Costa Rica and other developing nations for COVID-19 drugs/vaccines. - Opposition: - Pharma MNCs (US, UK) resist due to reduced monopoly and profits. - TRIPS Waiver Demand by India & South Africa - Proposal (2020): - India and South Africa sought a TRIPS waiver for COVID-19 drugs, vaccines, diagnostics, PPE, and medical technologies to enable production in developing nations. - Outcome: - Approved at 2022 WTO Geneva Summit, allowing third-world countries to use patented technologies without penalties at WIPO/WTO. - IPR - Evergreening of Patents - Definition: - Extending patent life beyond 20 years by slightly modifying the original invention to file a new patent, an unethical practice prohibited under Indian Patent Act (Section 3(d)). - Examples: - 2013: - Novartis’ blood cancer drug Glivec patent expired; Supreme Court rejected their new patent application, allowing Indian companies to produce generic versions at lower costs. - 2023: - Similar case with Johnson & Johnson’s TB drug Bedaquiline. - IPR - Utility Patents - Definition: - Recognize minor/superficial improvements to existing products (e.g., adding a speaker to a microwave to announce food readiness). - Status: - Commerce Ministry opposes amending Patent Act to allow utility patents, citing risks of exacerbating evergreening. - IPR - National IPR Policy (2016) - Boss: - Commerce Ministry. - Motto: - Creative India; Innovative India. - Features: - Shifted Copyright Office and IPAB from Education Ministry to Commerce Ministry (DPIIT). - Conducts IPR awareness for industry, police, customs, and judiciary to combat counterfeiting/piracy. - Offers new IPR courses in higher education, reduces patent fees for startups and grassroots innovators. - IPR - Digital India FutureLABS (2024) - Boss: - MeitY, implemented by C-DAC. - Objective: - Foster collaboration between government labs, startups, and large companies in mobile, IT, electronics, and automobiles. - IPR - Interim Budget 2024 - Allocates ₹1 lakh crore fund for R&D, offering 50-year interest-free loans to the private sector to scale up research and innovation. - ADITI Scheme (2024) - Boss: - Ministry of Defence, Department of Defence Production, under iDEX framework. - Features: - Up to ₹25 crore grants for startups’ R&D in defence technology. - Related Schemes: - Defence India Startup Challenge (DISC), iDEX Prime, iDEX Internship. - Budget 2025 - Startup/IPR/Manufacturing - Fund of Funds: - ₹10,000 crore for startups. - Atal Tinkering Labs: - 50,000 labs in government schools. - Focus Product Scheme: - Footwear & Leather, Toy Sector, Food Processing. - R&D Observations (Economic Survey 2025) - India ranks 6th globally in patent filings. - Gross Expenditure on R&D (GERD): ₹1,27,381 crore (2020), 0.64% of GDP. - Private sector R&D contribution: 36% in India vs. >70% in China, Japan, South Korea, USA. - Issue: - Indian companies rely on “jugaad” mentality, underinvesting in R&D despite subsidies and tax benefits. - IPR - Notable Schemes -
