- Pillar 4B1-iii: Sectors of Economy - Ease of Doing Business (EoDB) - Definition: - Ease of Doing Business (EoDB) measures how conducive a country’s regulatory environment is to starting and operating a business, assessed through various parameters like registration, taxation, and contract enforcement. - Sectors: Ease of Doing Business Report - World Bank’s Doing Business Index (Discontinued 2020): - Measured business ease based on 10 parameters (e.g., registering property, getting electricity, paying taxes) using a simple average. - Discontinued in August 2020 due to allegations of data manipulation, particularly regarding China’s rank. - World Bank’s B-READY (Business-Ready) Index (2026) - Replacement for the Doing Business Index. - India’s B-READY report to be published in 2026. - Commerce Ministry (DPIIT) coordinates with World Bank for data collection. - EoDB - Indian States: BRAP Ranking - Boss: - Commerce Ministry (DPIIT) with World Bank. - Parameters: - Access to information, single window system, labour, environment, etc. - 2024 Rankings: - Top: - Kerala, Andhra Pradesh, Gujarat, Rajasthan, Tripura, Uttar Pradesh. - Worst: - Arunachal Pradesh, Telangana, Punjab, Puducherry. - EoDB - Economic Freedom of the World - Boss: - Fraser Institute, Canada. - Measures individuals’ ability to make economic decisions (e.g., starting a business, accessing loans, government regulations). - Note: - Low-profile report, not critical for memorization. - EoDB: Budget-2023 Announcements - Vivad se Vishwas I – Relief for MSMEs - Context: - MSMEs failing to complete government/CPSE contracts during COVID (Feb 19, 2020 - Mar 31, 2022) had bid security/earnest money/performance security forfeited. - Budget-2023: - 95% of forfeited amount to be refunded to MSMEs. - Vivad se Vishwas II – Settling Contractual Disputes - Context: - Contractual disputes (e.g., NHAI/ONGC penalties on contractors) pending in courts. - Budget-2023: - Offers voluntary out-of-court settlement via arbitrator/mediator, targeting 500 cases worth ₹1 trillion. - PAN Card as Common Business Identifier - Objective: - Use PAN as a unified identifier for businesses across platforms (e.g., GSTIN, LIN, CIN, Udyam number). - Benefits: - Simplifies login/registration on government portals. - Enhances tax authorities’ ability to detect fraud/tax evasion. - Aids bankers in assessing financial capacity for loans. - Unified Filing Process - Context: - Companies submit multiple compliance documents to various ministries (Labour, Corporate Affairs, Commerce, MSME). - Budget-2023: - Proposes a common portal for unified filing to reduce time/effort. - EoDB for MSME: GSTN gets AA Status - Account Aggregator (AA): - NBFC that collects/provides financial data with client consent. - RBI granted AA status to GST Network (GSTN). - Benefit: - MSMEs can share GST tax data to secure loans more easily from banks/NBFCs. - One-Stop Solution for Identity and Address Updating - Context: - Personal data stored across multiple government platforms (e.g., driving license, property tax, scholarship portals). - Budget-2023: - Proposes a single portal using Aadhaar and DigiLocker for updates. - DigiLocker: - MeitY’s app/portal (2015) for storing documents (e.g., marksheets, licenses). - Training of Civil Servants in Mission Karmayogi - Mission Karmayogi (2020): - Ministry of Personnel’s training/skill development program for civil servants. - iGOT Karmayogi: - Online training portal for Union/State/UT civil servants. - Budget-2023: - Training to make civil servants more citizen- and business-friendly. - EoDB 2.0 in Budget-2022 - EoDB 1.0: - Removed ~1,500 laws and 25,000 compliances. - EoDB 2.0 Focus: - Trust-based governance. - Digitization of manual processes. - Integration of Central and State systems via IT bridges. - Citizen-centric services. - Removal of overlapping compliances. - Crowdsourcing suggestions for reforms. - Pro-Business vs Pro-Crony (Economic Survey 2020, Vol 1, Ch 3) - Crony Capitalism: - Business success driven by political-business nexus rather than hard work or innovation. - Economic Harm: - Leads to rent-seeking, high prices, and reduced wealth creation as profits are used for debauchery or further cronyism rather than R&D. - Cronyism: - David Ricardo & Rent Seeking - Example: - Mobile company pays bribes for spectrum/license, raising consumer prices to recover costs, profits, and bribes. - Other Examples: - High coal-based electricity prices, toll fees, private hospital/school fees. - Ricardo’s Term: - Rent-seeking behavior, extracting abnormal profits at public expense without contributing to wealth creation. - Enforcing Contracts Portal (2021-June) - Boss: - Department of Justice (Ministry of Law). - Features: - Provides case statistics for commercial/civil courts in Delhi, Mumbai, Bengaluru, Kolkata. - Offers access to commercial laws for reference. - International Arbitration Centre @GIFT City (Budget-2022) - Arbitration: - Out-of-court dispute resolution using an impartial third party. - Context: - Foreign companies vs. Indian entities currently use arbitration centers in Singapore, Netherlands, etc. - Budget-2022: - Establishes an International Arbitration Centre in GIFT City for timely dispute resolution under international jurisprudence. - Transparency International - Corruption Perceptions Index - Boss: - Transparency International (1993, HQ: Berlin, Germany), a global anti-corruption NGO. - 2021 Rankings: - #1 (Denmark, Finland), #180 (South Sudan), India #85. - India’s Rank Trend: - 2018 (86), 2019 (80), 2020 (86), 2021 (85), 2024 (93/180). - Recommendations: - Address conflicts of interest and preferential treatment. - Regulate electoral financing and election integrity. - Control lobbying activities. - EoDB - Labour Reforms - Context: - Multiple Central labour laws (e.g., Minimum Wages Act 1948, Payment of Wages Act 1936, Payment of Bonus Act 1965, Equal Remuneration Act 1976) require extensive compliance and inspections, hindering EoDB. - Second National Labour Commission (2002): Recommended consolidating laws into four Labour Codes. - Labour Codes (2020): -

- Pre-Code Reforms: - Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act, 2017: - Applies to factories, mines, plantations, shops. - Maternity leave: - 26 weeks (1st/2nd child), 12 weeks (3rd child onwards or adoption/surrogacy). - Creche required for 50+ workers; minimum 4 daily visits allowed for mothers. - Option for work-from-home post-maternity leave. - Written notification of rights to female workers. - Payment of Wages (Amendment) Act, 2017: - Allows salary payment via cheque/NEFT, reducing cash transactions. - Child Labour (Prohibition) Amendment Act, 2016: - Bans employment of children under 14, except in TV/cinema/sports (not circus) or non-hazardous family enterprises after school hours. - Adolescents (14-18) allowed in non-hazardous work. - Criticism: - Removal of certain occupations (e.g., chemical mixing, battery recycling) from hazardous list may lead to adolescent exploitation. - Apprentices (Amendment) Act, 2014: - Relaxes 1961 Act’s strict rules (e.g., stipend, holidays, overtime set by employer, not government). - Violations result in fines, not jail. - Maternity Leave for Construction Workers (2024) - Boss: - Ministries of Road Transport and Highways, Housing and Urban Affairs. - Provisions: -
ScenarioMaternity Leave Duration

More than two children12 weeks
Adoption12 weeks

- Additional facilities: - Latrines, urinals, washing areas, creches, accommodation. - Digital wage payments mandated. - Fixed Term Employment (2018) - Removed from 2025-26 syllabus as outdated. - Minimum Wages - Definition (ILO): - Minimum remuneration an employer is legally required to pay, expressed per day/hour. - Origin: - Concept dates to Arthashastra (2nd Century BCE); British-era Payment of Wages Act 1936 ensured timely payments but lacked minimum wage provisions. - Constitutional Mandate (DPSP): - Article 43: - Secure living wage and decent standard of life. - Article 39: - Adequate livelihood, equal pay for equal work for men and women. - Minimum Wage Reform: Anoop Satpathy Committee (2019) - Boss: - Labour Ministry. - Objective: - Determine methodology for fixing national minimum wage (detailed recommendations in Mains Handout). - Minimum Wages - Code on Wages 2019 - Objective: - Merges Minimum Wages Act 1948, Payment of Wages Act 1936, Payment of Bonus Act 1965, Equal Remuneration Act 1976. - Domains: -
DomainSectors CoveredFeatures
Union GovernmentAir transport, railways, ports, mines, oil fields, telecom, banking, insurance, Central Government jobs, CPSEs, autonomous bodiesCentral Advisory Body sets floor wages based on minimum living standards
State GovernmentsAll other sectorsState Advisory Boards ensure minimum wages ≥ floor wages
- Update Frequency: - Revised every 5 years or less. - Salient Features - Overtime Pay: - Minimum 2x normal wages for extra hours. - Payment Frequency: - Daily, weekly, fortnightly, or monthly via cash, cheque, or e-transfer. - Deductions: - Allowed for penalties, absence, rent, loans. - Right to Bonus: - 8.33% of wages or ₹100 (higher) for workers earning <3x specified amount, capped at 20% of annual wages. - Gender Discrimination: - Prohibited; equal pay for equal work. - Penalty: - Up to 3 months jail, ₹1 lakh fine. - Status: - Passed by Parliament, but implementation delayed due to COVID (rules and minimum wages pending notification). - EoDB - Factories Act Reforms - Factories Act 1881: - Focused on child labour prevention. - Factories Act 1948: Regulates worker safety, health, welfare. - Definition: - Premises with manufacturing using power and 10+ workers (or 20+ without power) in the last 12 months. - Requirements: - Washrooms, drinking water, spittoons, creches, etc. - Restrictions: - No women in night shifts or near dangerous machinery; mandatory inspections with risk of arrests for violations. - Factories (Amendment) Bill, 2014 - Proposals: - Redefines factory (20+ workers) to exempt smaller units. - Allows women in night shifts and near machinery with safety measures. - Replaces arrests with fines for minor violations. - Status: - Pending in Parliament; states like Rajasthan amended state laws (labour in Concurrent List). - EoDB - Industrial Disputes Act 1947, 2010 - Provisions: - Factories with 100+ workers require state government approval for retrenchment. - Advance notice needed for changes in work hours, holidays; workers can complain to Labour Ministry. - Issues: - Hinders EoDB by restricting adoption of labour-saving technologies or emergency work hour increases. - Reforms: - 2010 Amendment: - Technical relaxations by Union. - State Reforms: - Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh relaxed norms to attract investment (labour in Concurrent List). - Economic Survey 2019: - Rajasthan progressed in employment and investment; inflexible states (West Bengal, Bihar, Kerala) lag in jobs, capital, and wages due to low productivity. - Jan Vishwas (Amendment of Provisions) Bill, 2022 - Amends 42 Acts to reduce compliance and decriminalize offenses. - Examples: -

- Notable Laws Amended: - Press and Registration of Books Act 1867, Boilers Act 1923, Indian Forest Act 1927, Indian Post Office Act 1898, Environment (Protection) Act 1986, Public Liability Insurance Act 1991, Information Technology Act 2000, Patents Act 1970. - Budget-2025 on EoDB - Jan Vishwas Bill 2.0: Decriminalize 100+ provisions. - High-Level Committee for Regulatory Reforms: Review non-financial sector regulations, certifications, licenses. - Speedy approval for company mergers. - Investment Friendliness Index for States. - EoDB - Shram Suvidha Portal (2014) - Boss: - Labour Ministry. - Features: - Labour inspectors upload reports within 48 hours, reducing bribery and record tampering. - Online registration/payment for ESIC/EPFO. - Compliance document uploads for labour/factory acts. - Samadhan Portal: - Handles industrial disputes between workers, trade unions, and industrialists. - EoDB - Corona: Suspension of Labour Laws - Context: - States like UP, Gujarat, MP suspended labour laws for 3 years (or 1,000 days for new factories). - Provisions: - Small factories exempt from inspections. - Increased work hours without clear overtime wage guidelines. - Implications (Trade Union Concerns): - Reduced investment in worker safety/amenities (washrooms, creches). - Forced extra hours without adequate overtime/bonus. - Arbitrary hiring/firing without recourse due to suspended laws. - Undermines EPFO, ESIC, bonus, job/social security rights. - Corona Suspension Labour Laws: Union Says No - Constitutional Context: - Labour in Concurrent List (7th Schedule). - Article 254(1): - Parliament’s laws prevail over state laws. - Article 254(2): - State law amendments require President’s assent (guided by PM). - Union Response: - Rejected state suspensions (e.g., UP’s 3-year, MP’s 1,000-day suspensions). - Inter-State Migrant Workmen Act, 1979: Union may enforce to protect migrant workers if needed. - Inter-State Migrant Workmen Act, 1979 - Contractor Obligations: - Regular wage payments. - Equal pay for equal work (gender-neutral). - Suitable work conditions. - Residential accommodation. - Free medical facilities. - Protective clothing. - Reporting fatal accidents to government. - Banking as Public Utility Service - Industrial Disputes Act: - Statutory right to strike, except for government employees and public utility services (e.g., electricity, telecom). - Implications of Strikes in Public Utility: - Deemed illegal; workers can be dismissed or required to pay compensation. - 2020-April: - Banking declared a public utility service to prevent strike-related delays in MSME loans and economic revival. - EoDB - Building Homes & Running Shops - Model Shops & Establishments Bill, 2016 - Boss: - Union Government (circulated to States/UTs). - Subject: - State List; each state has its own Shops and Establishments Act for wages, hours, holidays. - Features: - Allows 24/7, 365-day shop/mall operations. - Permits women in night shifts with safety measures. - Adoption: - Gujarat adopted in 2019 with modifications. - Benefits: - EoDB, overtime pay, increased employment (day/night shifts). - Real Estate Regulation & Development Act (RERA), 2016 - Boss: - Ministry of Housing and Urban Poverty Alleviation. - Subject: - Land (State List), but contracts (Concurrent List). - Features: - Establishes State-level Real Estate Regulatory Authorities (RERAs) and Appellate Tribunals. - Mandatory project registration on RERA website (includes facilities like fire systems, sewage plants). - No advertisements or payments before registration. - Real estate agents must register with RERAs. - Project details published online for buyer verification/complaints. - Separate bank account for buyer payments. - Builder liable for interest on buyer’s loans if project delayed; RERA can order refunds or project completion. - Free repairs for defects within 5 years. - Penalties: - Up to 3 years jail + fines. - Benefits: - Online registration reduces bribery. - Enhances consumer protection. - Separate accounts curb tax evasion and malpractices (e.g., selling same property twice). - Challenges: - Increased compliance costs may raise home prices. - Pre-RERA projects face legal loopholes for justice. - Some states (non-BJP) lack RERA chairpersons/websites. - Real Estate GRETI Index - Boss: - JLL and LaSalle (foreign companies). - India’s Rank: - 31st out of 89 countries (2024). - Pillar 4B2-i: Sectors of Economy - Manufacturing, Textile, MSME - Sectors of Economy - Manufacturing, Textile & MSME - Overview: - Focuses on key sectors contributing to India's economy, with emphasis on textiles and Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs). - Textiles Ministry - Organizations: - CPSEs: - Cotton Corporation of India, Jute Corporation of India, National Textile Corporation Ltd. - Attached Offices: - Development Commissioners for Handloom and Handicrafts. - Statutory Bodies: - National Jute Board, Central Silk Board, National Institute of Fashion Technology (NIFT). - Others: - Autonomous bodies, export promotion councils, research associations, advisory boards for apparel, textile, wool, silk, carpet. - Industry Significance (ES25): - Indian textile industry: - 2nd largest manufacturer and exporter globally. - Employment: - 4.5 crore direct jobs, 6 crore in allied sectors. - Contribution: - 11% of India’s manufacturing GDP. - Rankings: - #2 in cotton, silk, man-made fiber production; #6 in textile/apparel exports. - Textile Ministry - Notable Schemes/Initiatives - Jute Packaging Material (JPM) Act, 1987: - Mandates 100% foodgrains and 20% sugar be packed in jute bags to support jute industry against plastic competition. - Technical Textiles: - Includes fishing nets, bulletproof jackets, surgical gowns, parachutes. - Applications: - Automobile, aerospace, architecture, occupational therapy, sports, apparel. - Budget-2020: - National Technical Textiles Mission (2020-21 to 2023-24) to reduce $16 billion import dependency. - Project India Size: - Develops India-specific size charts for shoes, shirts, pants, replacing UK/US standards. - India Handloom Brand Logo (2015): - Certifies handmade products (e.g., saris, bedsheets) for quality, zero defects, eco-friendliness, and traditional design. - Application: - Online via Textile Ministry’s Development Commissioner for Handloom. - Pehchan Cards (2016): - Aadhaar-linked cards for handicraft artisans to access scheme benefits. - e-Cocoon App: - Mobile app for quality certification in silkworm seed sector. - E-Dhaga App & BunkarMitra Helpline: - Advises weavers on business operations. - PM Mega Investment Textiles Parks (PM-MITRA, Budget-2021): - Seven parks with 30% Union subsidy, 1,000-acre land from states. - Locations: - Virudhunagar (TN), Warangal (TS), Kalaburagi (KA), Amravati (MH), Navsari (GJ), Dhar (MP), Lucknow (UP). - 5F Formula: - Farm → Fiber → Factory → Fashion → Foreign Export. - Central Sector Schemes (100% Union-funded): - National Handloom Development Programme: Weavers Mudra Scheme (interest subvention, credit guarantee for loans). - Amended Technology Upgradation Funds Scheme (ATUFS): Funds for machinery upgrades (also Power Tex for powerlooms). - Ambedkar Hasthshilp Vikas Yojana & Handloom Weaver Comprehensive Welfare Scheme (HWCWS): Training, skill development, marketing support. - Pradhan Mantri Paridhan Rojgar Protsahan Yojana (2016): Textile Ministry pays employer’s EPFO contribution for 3 years to boost formal jobs. - Samarth Scheme (2017): - Capacity building via training by MSDE-hired institutes, funded by Textile Ministry. - Rebate of State and Central Taxes and Levies (RoSCTL, 2019): Input Tax Credit for textile/garment exporters until March 31, 2024 (similar to RODTEP, Pillar 3A). - Kasturi Cotton Bharat (2022) - Boss: - Textile Ministry, Cotton Corporation of India, trade bodies, industry. - Features: - Certifies high-quality Indian cotton with brand logo. - Uses blockchain and QR codes for supply chain monitoring. - Textile Problems (ES25) - Complex, non-localized value chain (e.g., cotton from Gujarat/MP/Andhra to Tamil Nadu for yarn, then Maharashtra/Gujarat for fabric). - Export competition from China, Vietnam. - Trade barriers: - US tariffs, EU’s climate/deforestation rules (Ref: Pillar 3C). - Man-Made Fibers (MMF): - India produces <10% of global output, facing competition from Vietnam, China, Taiwan. - Leather Industry - Tamil Nadu (ES25) - Tamil Nadu excels in leather and non-leather footwear, employing 2 lakh people. - Hosts: - Central Leather Research Institute, Council for Leather Exports, Footwear Design and Development Institute. - Manufacturing & Services - MSME Ministry - Organizations: - Government Company: - National Small Industries Corporation Limited (NSIC), an NBFC under RBI, founded 1955, HQ: Delhi, aids MSME loan access. - Attached Office: - Development Commissioner (MSME). - Statutory Bodies: - Khadi & Village Industries Commission (KVIC), Coir Board. - MSME - Truckload of Schemes/Initiatives - PM’s Employment Generation Programme (PMEGP, 2008) - Boss: - MSME Ministry via KVIC (Central Sector Scheme, 100% Union-funded). - Beneficiary: - Std. 8 pass individuals/SHGs starting new non-farm micro-enterprises. - Funding: - Entrepreneur (5-10%), KVIC (15-35%), rest via bank loans (credit-linked subsidy). - Criteria: - Varies by rural/urban area, General/SC/ST/Women/PH/Minorities/Ex-Servicemen/North East. - Public Procurement Order (2012) - Mandates Central Ministries/Departments/Govt Companies to procure: - 25% of goods/services from Micro and Small Enterprises (MSEs). - 3% of 25% from women-owned MSEs. - 4% of 25% from SC/ST-owned MSEs. - Preferences: - Local suppliers, minimum 50% local content (Make in India). - Monitoring: - MSME-Sambandh web portal. - Legal Basis: - MSME Development Act, 2006. - Public Procurement - GeM Portal - Government e-Marketplace: - Online portal for Union/State/PRIs/PSUs to buy goods/services (e.g., stationery). - Boss: - Commerce Ministry’s not-for-profit GeM Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV). - Benefits: - Transparency, efficiency, cost savings vs. traditional tendering. - SWAYATT Initiative: - Promotes startups, women, youth entrepreneurs via GeM. - ES22: - Highlights GeM’s significance (Ch. 02, Fiscal Development, p. 73). - One District One Product (ODOP, 2021) - Boss: - Commerce Ministry with Union/State support. - Objective: - Transform each district into an export hub by promoting products with export potential (e.g., Jaipur’s Blue Pottery). - Support: - Marketing, branding, logistics, infrastructure, incubation, training, R&D. - MSME - Atma-Nirbhar Funding/Schemes (2020, Corona) - Loans: - MUDRA: - 2% interest subvention on Shishu Loans (Ref: Pillar 1D3). - Non-NPA/NPA Borrowers: - Emergency Credit Line Guarantee Scheme (ECLGS) / Guaranteed Emergency Credit Line (GECL). - Subordinate Debt for stressed MSMEs. - Equity: - Infusion via Fund of Funds. - Procurement Protection: - Foreign companies excluded from tenders up to ₹200 crore. - Swavalamban Challenge Fund: - Supports non-profits, educational institutes, social startups for entrepreneurship, financial inclusion, green tech (Boss: SIDBI, UK-based org). - Ubharte Sitaare Programme (USP, 2021-Aug) - Boss: - EXIM Bank, SIDBI (Alternative Investment Fund, Ref: Pillar 1B1). - Objective: - Supports export-oriented MSMEs with debt, equity, and technological assistance. - PM Vishwakarma Scheme (2023-Sep) - Ref: - Pillar 1D (Financial Inclusion). - MSME Ministry - Miscellaneous Initiatives - ASPIRE (2015) - A Scheme for Promoting Innovation, Rural Industry, and Entrepreneurship. - Boss: - MSME Ministry (Central Sector Scheme, 100% Union-funded). - Features: - Sets up business incubators and startup funds for agro-based industries. - Solar Charkha Mission (2018) - Boss: - MSME Ministry via KVIC (Central Sector Scheme). - Features: - Establishes solar charkha clusters in rural areas with loan subsidies, training, awareness. - Gramodyog Vikas Yojana - Boss: - MSME Ministry via KVIC. - Objective: - Develop village industries. - Pilot (2020-June): - Agarbatti manufacturing with automatic machines for artisans. - MSME Ministry - Portals/Helplines - UAM/Udyam Assist Portal (2015): - Online registration for MSMEs via Udyog Aadhaar Memorandum (UAM) using Aadhaar. - Replaces Entrepreneurs’ Memorandum; provides unique Udyog Aadhaar ID. - Benefits: - Access to MSME schemes; retail/wholesale traders eligible for Priority Sector Lending (Ref: Pillar 1A2). - CHAMPIONS Web Portal (2020-May): - Handles MSME complaints/grievances and scheme support. - Hub (Delhi) and Spoke (field offices, state govts) model. - MSME Samadhaan: - Enforces MSME Act 2006; State Micro and Small Enterprise Facilitation Councils (MSEFC) address delayed payments by government buyers. - Online complaint filing for delayed payments; Budget-2022 mandates 75% payment within 10 days with bill tracking. - MSME-Sampark: - Connects MSME Technology Centre trainees/students to recruiters. - Udyam Sangam/Samvad: - Workshops, conventions, melas organized by MSME Ministry, usually in Delhi. - Udyami Mitra Yojana: - Toll-free helpline for first-generation entrepreneurs. - Udyami Bharat (2022): - Seminar/workshop launched by PM in Delhi. - MSME - Funds for Development - India Inclusive Innovation Fund: Promotes grassroots innovations. - SFURTI (Scheme of Fund for Regeneration of Traditional Industries): Sets up clusters for Khadi, Coir, Handicraft. - CGTMSE (Credit Guarantee Fund Trust for Micro and Small Enterprises): Funded by MSME Ministry, SIDBI; provides collateral-free loans (Ref: Pillar 1D). - RAMP (World Bank): - Supports MSMEs via IBRD funding. - ES23/ES25 Data: - Registered Units (2023): - 1.32 crore (1.27 crore Micro). - Jobs (2024): - 23.24 crore individuals. - Exports: - Over ₹9 lakh crore. - Pillar 4B2-ii: Sectors of Economy - Services - Service Sector - Overview: - The service sector is a critical component of India's economy, contributing significantly to GDP and employment. - Service Sector - 3/4/5 Level Classification - Tertiary: - Trade/commerce, transport, communication, banking, finance, real estate. - Quaternary: - (1) Information/data-based, (2) Research and Development (R&D)-based. - Quinary: - Specialists, consultants, decision-makers, policy formulators focusing on creation, rearrangement, and interpretation of ideas, data, and new technologies (gold-collar professions). - MBA Terms: Outsourcing vs. Home-Shoring - Outsourcing: - Contracting work to an external agency to improve efficiency and reduce costs (e.g., Apple phones made by Tata, US bank call centers in Bengaluru). - Home-Shoring: - Employees work from home instead of company offices to save on office maintenance costs (e.g., Infosys employees coding from home). - MBA Terms: BPO vs. KPO - Business Process Outsourcing (BPO): Basic tasks like customer support, data entry. - Knowledge Process Outsourcing (KPO): Advanced tasks like VFX for Hollywood, legal/pharma writing, online SAT coaching by Indian professionals. - Service Sector Data (ES25) - Global GDP: - 62% from services. - Indian GDP: - FY14 (50.6%), FY25 (55%). - Global Service Exports (2023): #1 USA (13%), #7 India (4.3%). - Employment: - 30% of Indian workers. - States like Meghalaya, Uttarakhand, Mizoram: >33% GSDP from trade, repair, hotels, restaurants (tourism-driven). - Servicification of Industrial Sector (ES25) - Services enhance manufacturing value addition (e.g., clinical trials for pharmaceuticals, fashion design for garments, online support for cars/laptops). - Subscription-based models (e.g., Maruti Suzuki’s car ownership) integrate services into products. - Service Sector - Public Administration (ES25) - Public administration (government services) contributes to GDP. - Rich/industrialized states: - Low % GDP from public administration due to high industrialization. - Poor/North-Eastern states: - Higher % GDP from public administration due to low industrialization. - ES25 (Ch. 8, p. 237): Detailed analysis, low prelims utility. - Economy of India - Threats/Challenges - Definition: - Economy based on intangible assets like workers’ knowledge, IPR (e.g., space, pharma, IT, e-learning). - Challenges: - Competition from China in space, pharma, IT. - Philippines, Indonesia offering English-proficient graduates in IT, engineering to MNCs. - Space sector growth driven by ISRO support, but electronics/hardware lacks similar backing. - Pharma: - Private sector-driven but insufficient R&D investment (ES25). - Brain drain of talent since the 1970s. - Service Sector Recommendations (ES25) - Detailed in Mains lecture (not covered here). - Sunrise Sector (Budget-2022) - Definition: - New sectors with rapid growth potential. - Sectors: - AI, geospatial systems, drones, semiconductors, space, genomics, pharmaceuticals, green energy, clean mobility. - Objective: - Government support to foster growth. - Service Sector - E-Commerce - E-Commerce vs. E-Business - E-Commerce: - Buying/selling via digital platforms (subset of E-Business). - E-Business: - Broader, includes e-commerce, production, supply chain, management, product development, HR, finance. - E-Commerce Transaction Types - B2B: - Business-to-business (e.g., Infosys developing SBI’s e-banking website). - B2G: - Business-to-government (e.g., Infosys developing GST portal). - B2C: - Business-to-consumer (e.g., Amazon selling to individuals). - C2B: - Consumer-to-business (e.g., warranty claims on Dell’s website). - C2C: - Consumer-to-consumer (e.g., selling used goods on OLX, reporting traffic on Google Maps). - E-Commerce Challenges - Anti-competitive practices: - Exclusive partnerships (e.g., Flipkart/Amazon restricting Xiaomi/Oppo sales to their platforms). - Marketplace model issues: - E-commerce giants (e.g., Amazon’s Cloudtail) offer deep discounts, harming other online/offline merchants. - Investigation: - Competition Commission of India (CCI, Corporate Affairs Ministry) probing Amazon/Flipkart (2021); legal battles ongoing. - E-Commerce Term: Predatory Pricing - Definition: - Selling products at unrealistically low prices to eliminate competitors. - Issue (2024-Aug): - Commerce Minister accused e-commerce platforms of predatory pricing, harming 10 million retail stores (electronics, apparel). - E-Commerce Rules (2019-Feb) - Boss: - Consumer Affairs Ministry (under Consumer Protection Act, 2019). - Rules: - Ban on exclusive agreements (e.g., Flipkart cannot restrict Xiaomi sales to its platform). - Stricter norms on cashbacks, discounts, and shell companies selling at deep discounts. - Mandatory disclosure: - Expiry date, country of origin, return/refund policies, seller address, customer care, ratings. - Consumer-friendly rules; logical reasoning for MCQs (e.g., banning fake reviews is correct). - Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020 - Fall-back liability: - E-commerce platforms (e.g., Amazon) liable if suppliers fail to deliver, causing consumer loss. - Country of origin identification for goods. - Fair opportunity for domestic sellers via product suggestions. - Ban on dictating commission rates (to avoid misuse of dominant position). - No sharing of customer data without consent. - Criticism Against E-Commerce Rules - Foreign companies: - Rules push “Make in India” via Consumer Protection Act, argue competitive domestic products don’t need such measures. - Overlap: - Consumer Protection Authority encroaching on CCI’s domain. - Data rules: - Should be under Personal Data Protection Bill, not Consumer Protection Act. - Open Network for Digital Commerce (ONDC) - Boss: - Commerce Ministry’s DPIIT (non-profit, 2021). - Objective: - Digital platform to connect buyers/sellers, using open-source protocol to prevent exploitation by e-commerce giants. - Comparison: - Platform fees: - Swiggy/Zomato (25-40%) vs. ONDC (2-10%). - Example: - McDonald’s burger ₹250 (Swiggy) vs. ₹200 (ONDC). - Benefits: - Ends duopoly (Amazon-Flipkart, Ola-Uber, Swiggy-Zomato), product-agnostic (allows food, taxi bookings). - Analogy: - UPI/BHIM reduced seller fees (Paytm) and product prices; ONDC does similar for e-commerce. - ONDC Observations (ES25) - Transactions: - >14 million across 1,100+ cities (Nov 2024). - Sellers: - 7 lakh+ active. - Saarthi App: - AI-driven (with Bhashini) for buyer-side app creation. - Affordable onions in NCR region. - E-Commerce Rules vs. ONDC - E-Commerce Rules (Consumer Affairs): Focus on buyer protection, some seller safeguards. - ONDC (Commerce): - Protects both buyers and sellers. - Issue: - No merger of initiatives (suggestions to PM). - Q-Commerce (Quick Commerce) - Delivery: - 15 minutes to 1 hour (vs. 1-3 days for e-commerce). - Examples: - Dunzo, Swiggy Instamart, Blinkit, Zepto (vs. Amazon, Flipkart). - E-Commerce: Anti-Fake Review Framework (BIS) - Boss: - Bureau of Indian Standards (Consumer Affairs Ministry). - Guideline: - Indian Standard (IS) 19000:2022 to combat fake reviews. - Measures: - Verify/ban fake reviewers (via email/OTP), penalize merchants paying for fake reviews. - Voluntary framework, not legally binding. - E-Commerce: Google App Store Anti-Trust (CCI Order) - Issue: - Google mandated pre-installation of Play Store with Android, charging 15-30% commission, creating a monopoly. - CCI (2022): - Fined Google $161 million (₹1,337.76 crore). - Appeals: - Google lost at NCLAT and Supreme Court. - Mergers & Acquisitions (M&A) - CCI Threshold - Issues: - Data misuse, cartelization, monopoly from M&As (e.g., Sun Pharma-Ranbaxy, Tata-Vistara/Air India). - Competition Act 2002 (Amended 2023): - CCI approval needed if: - Deal value >₹2,000 crore. - Target company has substantial business operations in India. - Retail Trade - Itinerant Retailers & Cheap Jacks - Itinerant Traders: - No fixed place, move with wares (e.g., peddlers, hawkers). - Cheap Jacks: - Itinerant with temporary shops (e.g., watch/shoe repair, street-side salons). - Manufacturing - Bodies for Quality Standards - Consumer Affairs Ministry - Statutory - BIS (1986) - Bureau of Indian Standards: Apex regulator for standardization, quality certification. - Certifies ISI mark for goods (e.g., helmets, gas stoves) meeting standards. - Nodal for ISO standards, WTO’s Technical Barriers to Trade (TBT) agreement (Ref: Pillar 3B). - BIS & Gold-Silver Hallmarking - Certifies purity of gold (14, 18, 22 carat) and silver. - Mandatory since June 2021 (previously voluntary since 2000). - Exemptions: - Jewelers with turnover <₹40 lakh. - Benefits: - Assures gold quality, enables tax authorities to monitor trade for tax evasion. - BIS Certificate for Mitticool Refrigerator (2022) - Developed by Mansukh Bhai Prajapati (Gujarat), uses evaporative cooling (clay-based, no electricity). - BIS Standard (IS 17693:2022): Specifies clay type, dimensions, temperature. - Supports 6/17 UN SDGs (e.g., no poverty, zero hunger, clean energy). - Power Ministry - Statutory - BEE (2001-02) - Bureau of Energy Efficiency (Energy Conservation Act, 2001). - Star Labeling: - Mandatory for ACs, refrigerators, tubelights, TVs, geysers, inverters, LED lamps; voluntary for computers, LPG stoves, fans. - Chiller Star Labeling: - For commercial HVAC systems. - RAISE Program: - Improves AC quality/efficiency (EESL, USAID joint initiative). - Health Ministry - Statutory - FSSAI (2006) - Food Safety and Standards Authority of India: Sets scientific standards for food manufacture, storage, distribution, sale, import. - Repealed Prevention of Food Adulteration Act 1954, other food-related laws. - Labeling: - Green circle (vegetarian), brown circle (non-vegetarian/egg). - Bans: - Recycled plastic/newspaper for food packing, calcium carbide/acetylene for fruit ripening (ethylene permitted). - Limits: - Trans Fatty Acids <2% (2022), no mustard oil blending (2021, due to dropsy/allergy risks). - MSG Issue: - Banned in Maggi noodles (lead/MSG), later lifted by High Court. - Food Safety Mitra (2019): Trained youth assist food businesses with FSSAI compliance. - Food Safety Index: - Compares states. - AGMARK: - Agro Ministry’s certification for agricultural commodities (wool, cotton, meat). - Commerce Ministry - Non-Statutory - QCI (1997) - Quality Council of India: Non-profit, funded by Commerce Ministry, CII, FICCI, ASSOCHAM. - Supports industries with ISI, ISO, OHSAS, KAIZEN certifications. - Zero Defect and Zero Effect (ZED) certification for MSMEs. - Commerce Ministry - Non-Statutory - NPC (1958) - National Productivity Council: - Autonomous, under DPIIT. - Services: - Research, consultancy in industrial engineering, agri-business, quality, HR management. - President: - Commerce Minister. - One Nation, One Standard Scheme (2019) - Boss: - BIS. - Objective: - Standard-setting organizations (e.g., FSSAI, BEE) align with WTO’s TBT Code of Good Practice, get SDO label from BIS. - First SDO: - Railway Ministry’s RDSO (2021, Lucknow). - Benefits: - Transparency, openness, impartiality, effectiveness. - PARAKH Laboratory Network (2021) - Boss: - DPIIT. - Online portal: - Directory/GPS of approved labs for ISI, hallmarking, FSSAI certifications. - OIML Certificate for Weighing Machine Makers - OIML: - International Organization of Legal Metrology (HQ: Paris, 1996). - India (2023): - 13th member, enables domestic testing for weighing/measurement devices. - Consumer Protection Act, 2019 - Nodal: - Consumer Affairs, Food and Public Distribution Ministry. - Replaces Consumer Protection Act, 1986. - Consumer Protection Act - Consumer Courts - Consumer Disputes Redressal Commissions (CDRCs): - District: - Up to ₹50 lakh. - State: - ₹50 lakh to ₹2 crore. - National: - >₹2 crore. - E-Daakhil Portal (2020): - Online complaint filing. - Appeal: - District → State → National → Supreme Court. - Consumer Protection Act - Other Bodies - Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA): Headed by Union Minister, with DG-led investigation wing; can launch class actions, order recalls/refunds. - Consumer Protection Councils: - Advisory bodies for awareness. - Consumer Protection Act - Features - Product Liability: - Companies liable for injury, damage, or death from defective goods/services. - Unfair Contracts: - Excessive deposits, unilateral terminations penalized. - E-Filing: - Complaints via electronic means, video conferencing hearings. - Penalties: - Up to ₹50 lakh fine, 5 years jail; ₹50,000 fine for frivolous complaints. - Celebrity Ads: - Misleading ads lead to bans, financial penalties. - Mediation: - ADR mechanism, no appeal against mediation settlements. - Stricter rules for e-commerce (Ref: Pillar 3A), adulteration, spurious goods. - Social Media Influencers - CCPA Rules (2023) - Mandatory disclosure of cash/gift-based promotions. - Penalties: - ₹50 lakh fine, ad ban up to 6 years. - UPSC Toppers - CCPA Rules (2023) - DoPT enforces Central Civil Services (Conduct) Rules, 1964: Prohibits government servants from engaging in trade/business. - Consumer Protection - Banking Customers - RBI Initiatives: - Integrated Ombudsman Scheme (One Nation, One Ombudsman). - Centralised Receipt and Processing Centre (Chandigarh) for physical complaints. - Consumer Protection - Dark Patterns - Definition: - Manipulative e-commerce practices (e.g., drip pricing, disguised ads, bait-and-switch, false urgency). - CCPA issued guidelines to curb these. - Consumer Protection - Drip Pricing - Definition: - Partial price advertised, additional charges (e.g., shipping, platform fees) revealed at checkout. - Example: - Shoes ₹4,700 + ₹300 hidden fees = ₹5,000. - Consumer Affairs Ministry warned against this (May 2024). - Consumer Protection - Spam Protection in USA - CAN-SPAM Act (2003): - Regulates commercial emails for products/services. - Mains Questions - Focus: - 4th Industrial Revolution, Make in India, manufacturing improvement, LPG reforms’ impact. - Covered in separate Mains-QEP course, not Raftaar (PCB) Prelims. - Pillar 4C: Economic Planning, NITI Aayog, and Statistical Systems - Definition: - Economic planning is the process through which a government identifies socio-economic challenges such as poverty, inequality, low agricultural productivity, and inadequate industrial or infrastructural development, setting strategic goals and policies to address them, ensuring sustainable growth and equitable resource distribution. - Context: - India’s economic planning has evolved from centralized, Soviet-inspired models to a more decentralized, cooperative framework under NITI Aayog, emphasizing innovation, inclusivity, and data-driven governance to align with global economic trends and national development goals. - Significance for India: - Economic planning drives India’s vision of becoming a developed nation by 2047, fostering cooperative federalism, sustainable development, and robust statistical systems to enhance policy effectiveness and global credibility. - Economic Systems - Definition: - An economic system is a structured mechanism through which a society organizes the production, distribution, and consumption of goods and services, shaped by ownership structures, resource allocation, and decision-making processes. - Types of Economic Systems: -
Economic System Capitalism Mixed Economies Socialism
Ownership of Industries Private sector dominates. Few industries reserved for public sector; rest by private sector. Public sector/government/collective ownership; no private property.
Production Decisions Market forces (supply and demand) decide what to produce (e.g., more bikes or books). Essential goods/services by public sector; others by private sector. Government decides what and how much to produce.
Production Methods Cheaper mode (labor or capital) chosen by private entities. Public sector: government decides; private sector: entrepreneurs decide. Preference for labor-intensive methods.
Distribution Only consumers who can afford goods/services can purchase them. Essential goods: government may fix prices (e.g., NPPA for stents); others: market-driven. Government distributes via subsidies/rationing shops.
- Global Context: - Most nations, including India and the USA, operate mixed economic systems. China, officially socialist, functions as a mixed economy in practice. Pure socialist systems (e.g., North Korea, Cuba) face economic hardships. Communism, a branch of socialism, often involves totalitarian governance with single-party control. - Anarcho-Capitalism and Libertarianism - Libertarianism: - Emphasizes individual liberty with minimal government intervention, prioritizing personal and economic freedom. - Anarchism: - Advocates a society without government or rulers, relying on voluntary cooperation. - Anarcho-Capitalism: - Concept by Murray Rothbard (1950s, USA), advocating complete privatization of all functions, including police and judiciary, replaced by private arbitrators. -
Aspect Capitalism Anarcho-Capitalism
Government Role Controls law, order, contracts, judiciary. All functions, including police and judiciary, privatized.
Trade and Taxes Taxes on imports; protects local industries. No taxes on imports; free trade prioritizes cheap goods.
- Relevance: - Gained attention due to Argentina’s President Javier Milei advocating anarcho-capitalism, highlighting debates on government roles in economic systems. - Closed vs. Open Economy -
Closed Economy Open Economy
No imports, exports, or economic relations with other countries (e.g., North Korea). Engages in imports, exports, FDI, and FPI with global markets (e.g., India).
- Significance: - Closed economies aim for self-sufficiency (autarky) but face resource constraints. Open economies leverage global trade for growth, as seen in India’s liberalization post-1991. - Great Reset Initiative by World Economic Forum (WEF) - Concept: - Proposed by WEF founder Klaus Schwab, it calls for a “reset” of capitalism to create a new social contract emphasizing equality in health, finance, energy, and education. - Context: - Revived post-COVID-19 due to its impact on vulnerable populations, highlighting the need for inclusive economic models. - Relevance: - Aligns with global discussions on sustainable and equitable growth, influencing India’s policy focus on inclusive development. - Miscellaneous Economic Terms - Washington Consensus (1980s): - A set of economic policy recommendations by IMF, World Bank, and U.S. Treasury for developing nations, focusing on liberalization, privatization, and reduced government control, similar to India’s LPG reforms. - Reaganomics (1980s): - Policies under U.S. President Reagan, emphasizing reduced government spending, tax cuts for businesses, and deregulation to stimulate economic growth. - Thatcheromics (1980s): - Policies under UK PM Margaret Thatcher, focusing on privatization of public enterprises and reducing government control to enhance market efficiency. - Autarky: - An economic system of self-sufficiency with minimal global trade, akin to a closed economy (e.g., North Korea). - Adam Smith’s Invisible Hand: - Refers to the self-regulating nature of markets, where individual self-interest drives efficient resource allocation through supply and demand. - Economic Planning - Definition: - Economic planning involves a government preparing a roadmap to address socio-economic issues like poverty, inequality, and underdevelopment by setting goals, allocating resources, and implementing policies. - Types of Economic Planning: -
Type Description
Totalitarian vs. Democratic Totalitarian: Centralized control (e.g., USSR, North Korea). Democratic: Participatory, as in India post-independence.
Centralized vs. Decentralized Centralized: Top-down planning (e.g., USSR). Decentralized: Local participation, as in India after 73rd and 74th Amendments.
Inducement vs. Direction Inducement: Incentives like subsidies guide actions. Direction: Central authority sets mandatory targets.
Indicative vs. Imperative Indicative: Flexible guidelines with public/private consultation (e.g., India, France). Imperative: Rigid state control (e.g., USSR).
Financial vs. Physical Financial: Resource allocation in monetary terms. Physical: Allocation in terms of labor, materials, machinery.
Timeframe-Based Operational (up to 1 year), Tactical (3-7 years), Strategic/Perspective (10+ years).
- Economic Planning Before Independence - Key Plans: - Hind Swaraj (1909, Gandhi): - Advocated minimal wants, self-reliance, and small-scale production (khadi, cottage industries), opposing industrialization. - Planned Economy for India (1934, M. Visvesvaraya): - Proposed a 10-year plan focusing on industrial development, authored by the engineer and Bharat Ratna recipient. - Congress Plan (1938, Nehru): - Proposed a National Planning Commission, stalled due to World War II. - Bombay Plan (1944): - A 15-year investment plan by industrialists like JRD Tata and GD Birla, emphasizing industrial growth. - Gandhian Plan (1944, Sriman Narayan Agrawal): - Focused on agricultural and rural economy with a decentralized approach. - People’s Plan (1945, MN Roy): - Socialist-leaning, advocating state-controlled resource distribution and agricultural mechanization. - Sarvodaya Plan (1950, Jayprakash Narayan): - Based on Vinoba Bhave’s philosophy, prioritizing agriculture and cottage industries. - Economic Planning After Independence - Establishment: - Inspired by the Soviet model, PM Nehru established the Planning Commission in March 1950 to draft Five-Year Plans (FYPs). - National Development Council (NDC, 1952) approved FYPs, comprising PM, CMs, and others. - Planning Commission dissolved in 2014 by PM Modi, replaced by NITI Aayog in January 2015. - Five-Year Plans (FYPs): -
Plan Period Theme/Model/Target Outcome
1st 1951-56 Harrod-Domar Model; focus on agriculture, irrigation, power. Successful: Exceeded GDP growth target.
2nd 1956-61 P.C. Mahalanobis Model; socialist pattern, rapid industrialization, heavy industries. Successful: Achieved GDP growth target.
3rd 1961-66 Sukhmoy Chakraborty & John Sandy Model (Gadgil Yojana); economic independence. Failed: Due to droughts, wars with Pakistan and China.
Plan Holiday 1966-69 Annual plans due to 3rd FYP failure. -
4th 1969-74 Ashok Rudra & Alon Manney Model; growth with stability, self-reliance; “Garibi Hatao” slogan. Failed: Due to Bangladeshi refugee crisis, drought.
5th 1974-79 C. Subramaniam, later D.P. Dhar; agriculture prioritized; poverty removal, self-reliance. Terminated in 1978 under Morarji Desai.
Rolling Plan 1978-80 Morarji Desai’s annual progress evaluation. -
6th 1980-85 Poverty removal via IRDP, NREP, TRYSEM schemes. Moderate success.
7th 1985-90 Pranab Mukherjee Model; focus on employment, private sector priority. Moderate success.
Annual Plans 1990-92 Due to political instability. -
8th 1992-97 John W. Miller Model; LPG reforms under PV Narasimha Rao; focus on employment, education, health. Successful: Exceeded GDP growth target.
9th 1997-02 Growth with social justice, equity; 7 Basic Minimum Services; indicative planning. Failed: Due to Asian Financial Crisis.
10th 2002-07 Target 8% GDP growth, double per capita income, reduce poverty to 15%. Failed: Targets not achieved.
11th 2007-12 C. Rangarajan; faster, inclusive growth; 9% GDP growth, 70 million jobs. Failed: Due to US subprime crisis.
12th 2012-17 Faster, inclusive, sustainable growth; 9% GDP, 4% agriculture, 10% manufacturing; 50 million jobs. Failed: Due to global slowdown.
- Planning Commission: Limitations - Centralized Approach: - Top-down planning ignored state-specific needs, reducing flexibility. - Bureaucratic Inefficiency: - Slow decision-making and rigid targets hindered adaptability. - Limited Private Sector Role: - Nehruvian socialist bias restricted private sector participation. - Inadequate Monitoring: - Weak focus on implementation and outcome evaluation. - Financial Dependence: - States relied heavily on central funds, undermining cooperative federalism. - Planning Commission vs. NITI Aayog: Structure -
Aspect Planning Commission NITI Aayog
Establishment 1950-2014 2015 onwards
Chairman Prime Minister Prime Minister
Vice Chairman Cabinet Minister rank (e.g., Montek Singh Ahluwalia). Arvind Panagariya (2015-17), Rajiv Kumar (2017-22), Suman K Bery (2022-present).
CEO Member-Secretary (IAS). Secretary-level bureaucrat (e.g., Parameswaran Iyer).
Ex-Officio Members Finance Minister, Planning Minister. Up to 4 Union Ministers (Home, Defense, Finance, Agriculture).
Full-Time Members 4-7, Minister of State rank. Economists, scientists (e.g., Arvind Virmani, Ramesh Chand, V.K. Saraswat, Vinod Kumar Paul).
Special Invitees None. Union Ministers (e.g., Transport, Health); list dynamic.
Part-Time Members None. Tech experts (none as of July 2024).
Governing Council National Development Council (PM, CMs, UT Lieutenant Governors). PM, CMs, UT Lieutenant Governors; promotes cooperative federalism.
Regional Councils None. Ad hoc councils for regional issues (e.g., irrigation, Naxalism).
- Planning Commission vs. NITI Aayog: Functions -
Planning Commission NITI Aayog
Drafted Five-Year Plans; allocated funds for centrally sponsored schemes and state plans using Gadgil-Mukherjee formula. Drafts Three-Year Action Agenda, Seven-Year Strategy, Fifteen-Year Vision (2017-32); Strategy for New India @ 75 (2017-23). No fund allocation; Finance Commission/Ministry handles this.
Focused on plan implementation. Serves as a think tank; designs policies, monitors schemes via dashboards (e.g., SDG India Index, School Education Quality Index).
- NITI Aayog: Notable Initiatives - Darpan Portal (2017): - NGOs register for unique IDs to access government grants for schemes. - Aspirational Districts Programme (2018): - Transforms 115 backward districts across 49 KPIs (health, education, infrastructure); monitored via “Champions of Change” portal. - Strategic Disinvestment: - Recommended disinvestment of loss-making CPSEs (e.g., Air India, Pawan Hans). - POSHAN Abhiyaan: - Aims for malnutrition-free India by 2022, focusing on women and children; led by NITI Vice-Chairman. - Policy and Legislative Support: - Frames policies on energy, minerals; model acts for agricultural land leasing, livestock selling. - Agricultural Reforms: - Revamped MSP via price deficiency payments (PM-AASHA) and fertilizer subsidies through DBT. - Sustainable Development Goals (SDG): - Developed SDG India Index to track 17 SDG goals; promotes methanol/biofuel economy. - GIRG Dashboard: - Monitors India’s performance on global indices (e.g., UNDP’s Multidimensional Poverty Index). - Output Outcome Monitoring Framework: - Enhances monitoring of government scheme implementation. - Seminars and Innovation: - Organizes workshops, conferences; runs Atal Innovation Mission (AIM) with grants for incubators and Mentor India program. - State Support Mission (2022): - Funds state-level think tanks (State Institutions of Transformation) to design policies and ensure effective scheme implementation by 2047. - Prime Minister’s Economic Advisory Council (PM-EAC) - Establishment: - Non-constitutional, non-statutory body formed in the 2000s to advise the PM on economic issues; reconstituted in 2017 post-demonetization and GST. - Composition: - Chaired by Bibek Debroy (died 2024); includes 7 full/part-time members; supported by NITI Aayog. - Recommendations: - GST Council-like body for public expenditure. - Reduce GST slabs and direct taxes to boost economic growth. - PRAGATI - Overview: - Pro-Active Governance and Timely Implementation (2015), a PMO web platform for monitoring scheme implementation and addressing public grievances (e.g., tax refunds, EPFO claims). - Mechanism: - PM conducts monthly video conferences with Union ministries and state chief secretaries. - Other Related Organizations - eSamikSha (2014): - Cabinet Secretariat portal to monitor decisions/follow-ups post-PM meetings, ensuring timely action by officials. - Project Monitoring Group (PMG, 2013): - Fast-tracks approvals for public, private, and PPP projects via the e-Nivesh Monitor portal. - Investment Commission (2004-09): - Chaired by Ratan Tata; recommended investment-friendly policies; revival considered in 2016 but faded. - CPGRAMS (2007): - Centralized Public Grievance Redress and Monitoring System under DARPG; allows citizens to file complaints against central ministries for corruption, delays, etc., via portal and “My Grievance” app. - Apex/Independent Offices - Offices not under any ministry: - President’s Secretariat, Cabinet Secretariat (includes RAW), Prime Minister’s Office (includes NSA), NITI Aayog, Department of Atomic Energy, Department of Space, National Security Council Secretariat. - Statistical Systems - Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI): - Headed by Secretary & Chief Statistician of India (Indian Statistical Service officer). - Components: - National Statistical Office (NSO): - Formed in 2019 by merging Central Statistics Office (CSO) and National Sample Survey Office (NSSO). - CSO: - Computes GDP, GSDP, IIP, ASI, CPI, and Economic Census (6th in 2013). - NSSO: - Collects data on socio-economic indicators, rural-urban prices, and ASI. - Plans for a National-Level Data Warehouse for centralized statistical data and big data analytics. - Programme Implementation Wing: - MPLADS (1993): - MPs suggest development works worth ₹5 crore annually per constituency. - Twenty Point Programme (2006): Monitors schemes for poverty alleviation, employment, health, etc. - Infrastructure and project monitoring. - National Statistical Commission (NSC) - Establishment: - Set up in 2005 via Cabinet resolution, based on C. Rangarajan Committee recommendations; non-constitutional, non-statutory. - Structure: - Part-time chairman, 4 part-time members, NITI CEO as ex-officio member; Chief Statistician serves as Secretary. - Functions: - Sets standards for data collection and publication; coordinates among agencies; replaced NSSO’s Governing Council. - Controversy (2019): - Two members resigned, citing government sidelining; alleged suppression of 2017-18 Employment Survey showing job losses post-demonetization/GST. - Implications: - Data manipulation risks undermining confidence in India’s statistical systems, affecting IMF voting rights and credit ratings by agencies like S&P, Moody’s, and Fitch. - Standing Committee on Statistics (SCoS) - Establishment: - Formed as SCES in 2019; renamed SCoS in 2023; dissolved in September 2024. - Role: - Advised on survey methodologies and results; chaired by Pronab Sen. - Dissolution: - Official reason: - Replaced by Steering Committee for National Sample Surveys. - Unofficial reason: - Pronab Sen’s criticism of delayed population census. - Mahalanobis National Award - Overview: - Awarded by MoSPI for outstanding contributions to statistics; named after P.C. Mahalanobis, father of Indian statistics and architect of 2nd FYP. - Recipient: - C. Rangarajan (2020), former RBI governor. - Pillar 4C2: Indicators → Unemployment - Disclaimer on Data Consistency - Data on employment/unemployment may vary across sources (e.g., PLFS, Economic Survey) due to revisions by the government and selective reporting. Focus on trends rather than specific figures for exams, as cross-referencing all data is impractical. - International Labour Organization (ILO) - Established: - 1919, under Treaty of Versailles, post-World War I. - Status: - UN specialized agency, headquartered in Geneva, Switzerland. - Key Report: - World Employment and Social Outlook. - ILO Core Conventions - India ratified 6 out of 8 core conventions: -
Convention Ratified by India
Forced Labour Convention Yes
Abolition of Forced Labour Convention Yes
Equal Remuneration Convention Yes
Discrimination (Employment and Occupation) Convention Yes
Freedom of Association and Protection of Right to Organize Not yet
Right to Organise and Collective Bargaining Convention Not yet
Minimum Age Convention Yes
Worst Forms of Child Labour Convention Yes
- Wage Theories - Subsistence Wage Theory (Adam Smith) - Wages should cover basic needs (food, shelter, family expenses). - Mechanism: - If wages rise above subsistence, more workers enter, increasing labor supply, pushing wages back to subsistence level. - If wages fall below subsistence, fewer workers participate, reducing supply, pushing wages up to subsistence level. - Natural Wage Theory (David Ricardo) - Also known as the Iron Law of Wages. - Real wages tend toward the minimum required to sustain workers’ lives, similar to Smith’s theory but with nuanced economic adjustments. - Miscellaneous Wage Theories -
Theory Description
Residual-Claimant Theory Wages are what remains after paying rent, interest, and profits to other factors of production (land, loans, investors).
Bargaining Theory Wages determined through negotiations between workers, employers, and trade unions.
Marginal Productivity Theory Wages depend on the value a worker adds to the company, based on their productivity.
- Occupational Structure of Indian Workers -
Sector 2017–18 Share (%) 2023–24 Share (%)
Agriculture 44.1 46.1
Manufacturing 12.1 11.4
Services 31.1 29.7
Total 87.3 87.2
- Note: - Total is less than 100% as sectors like mining, construction, and utilities are excluded. - Unemployment: Involuntary Types - Voluntary Unemployment: - Individuals choose not to work, seeking higher wages or preferring not to work. - Involuntary Unemployment: - Individuals willing to work at prevailing wages but unable to find jobs due to external factors. - Major Types and Reasons - Causes: - Slow economic growth vs. rapid population growth. - Defective education system and lack of employable skills. - Insufficient banking, transport, and communication infrastructure. - Social discrimination (e.g., against SC/ST, women, physically handicapped). - Types: -
Type Features
Cyclical Occurs during economic downturns (recession/depression); mass layoffs (e.g., Maruti laid off 3000 workers in 2019 due to low car sales).
Frictional Transitional unemployment when individuals search for new jobs.
Disguised Workers appear employed but contribute zero marginal productivity (e.g., excess workers in farming).
Seasonal Jobs tied to specific seasons (e.g., agriculture, tourism, sugar mills).
Underemployment Workers employed below their qualifications/salary potential (e.g., M.Com as delivery boy).
Technological Job losses due to automation (e.g., handloom workers vs. textile machines). WEF (2018) predicts 75 million jobs lost by 2025, but 133 million new jobs in tech-related fields.
Structural Mismatch between workers’ skills and job requirements (e.g., C++ programmer in a Python-demand market).
Natural Rate of Unemployment (NRU) Sum of frictional and structural unemployment; baseline unemployment in a healthy economy.
Non-Accelerating Inflation Rate of Unemployment (NAIRU) Refer to Pillar 4E (Inflation and Phillips Curve).
- Employment-Related Terms in News - Baumol’s Cost Disease Theory (1965) - By William J. Baumol and William G. Bowen. - Wages rise in certain sectors (e.g., doctors, professors in USA; farm laborers in Punjab/Haryana) despite no increase in productivity, due to labor shortages (e.g., MGNREGA reducing farm labor supply). - Moonlighting - Undertaking additional jobs alongside primary employment. - Issue: - Companies like Wipro and Infosys have terminated employees for moonlighting due to risks of leaking trade secrets, software codes, or client lists. - Unemployment: NSO Survey Types -
Aspect Quinquennial Employment and Unemployment Surveys Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS)
Frequency Every 5 years (1972–2011/12; discontinued). Annual, since 2017; includes workers aged 15+.
Households Surveyed Non-agriculture workers in rural/urban areas. All sectors (agriculture, non-agriculture) in rural/urban areas.
- PLFS Details: - Annual Reports: - Report #1 (2019-May): - July 2017–June 2018. - Report #6 (2023-Oct): - July 2022–June 2023. - Quarterly Bulletins: - Released for specific periods (e.g., Q2 2020: August 2021). - Note: - Quarterly data has low cost-benefit for exam preparation. - Indicators: Unemployment Rate (UR) - Definition: - Percentage of involuntarily unemployed individuals in the labor force. - Formula: - UR = (Number of involuntarily unemployed / Labor force) × 100. - Example: - 2018 UR = (3 crore unemployed / 51.8 crore labor force) × 100 = 5.8%. - Measurement Approaches: -
Approach Criteria
Current Weekly Status (CWS) Unemployed if no work for even 1 hour in a week.
Current Daily Status (CDS) Unemployed if no work for even 1 hour in a day within a week.
Usual Status (US) Employed if worked at least 30 days in 365 days; otherwise, unemployed. Subdivided into Principal Activity Status (PS) and Subsidiary Economic Activity Status (SS). Official reports prioritize US.
- PLFS 2017–18: - UR = 6.0% (Usual Status), highest in 45 years.' - Economic Survey Insights: - High UR: - Arunachal Pradesh, Kerala, Manipur, Bihar. - Low UR: - Gujarat, Karnataka, West Bengal, Sikkim. - UR highest among urban youth (20%), lowest among illiterates (1.1%). - Worker Population Ratio (WPR) - Definition: - Percentage of employed persons in the total population. - Formula: - WPR = (Number of employed persons / Total population) × 100. - Labour Force Participation Rate (LFPR) - Definition: - Percentage of persons in the labor force (working or seeking/available for work) in the population. - Formula: - LFPR = [(Number of employed + Number of involuntarily unemployed) / Total population] × 100. - 2017: - All-India LFPR = 37% (male + female, rural + urban). - Female LFPR: -
Year All-India Female LFPR (%) Rural Female LFPR (%)

- Insights: - Sikkim has the highest female LFPR (56.9%). - Urban female LFPR is lower than rural due to women pursuing higher education or staying home as housewives. - Over 75% of rural female workers are in agriculture. - Female LFPR is significantly lower than male LFPR. - Economic Survey 2025 (ES25) Reasons for Female LFPR Increase: - Rising rural women participation. - Better capture of unpaid female work in PLFS. - Government schemes promoting women’s employment (see Pillar 6D). - Why Female LFPR Declined (2004–2018) - From 45% (2004) to 23% (2017): - Increased pursuit of higher education, delaying job market entry. - Rising rural male incomes, leading women to take domestic roles. - Mechanization in agriculture/animal husbandry reducing female labor demand. - Declining textile/leather exports due to US/EU protectionism. - Slowdown in real estate, reducing construction jobs for women. - Cultural and patriarchal norms limiting women’s mobility. - Lack of computer/English skills for emerging startup jobs. - NSO Time Use Survey (2019): Women spend 7.5 hours on unpaid domestic/caregiving tasks vs. 5.7 hours on paid work. - Solutions to Improve LFPR - Invest in childcare/daycare, paid parental leave, family-friendly workplaces, elderly care facilities. - Ensure equal pay, career progression, and social security (EPFO/ESIC) for women. - Government schemes for women’s skill development and entrepreneurship (see Pillar 6: HRD). - Augmented Female LFPR - Definition: - Regular Female LFPR + unpaid women workers (e.g., domestic duties, collecting vegetables/firewood for household use). - Issue: - PLFS excludes unpaid domestic work, underrepresenting female labor force participation. - ES25 Unemployment Data -

- Requirement: - India needs to generate 78.5 lakh non-farm jobs annually until 2030. - Salaries of Indian Workers (ES25) - Profit vs. Salary Trends - Average salary: - ₹15,885 (FY19) to ₹20,702 (FY24), a 30% increase. - Company profits: - Increased 300% (4x) in the same period. - Issue: - FY24 profits rose 22%, but new hiring only 1.5%, with mass layoffs prevalent. - Japanese Model for High Salaries - Japan’s social contract: - Consumers overpay for goods/services; companies invest in R&D, infrastructure, and decent wages; government supports with tax-funded infrastructure. - India’s Issue: - Consumers overpay, but companies underinvest in R&D/wages, limiting job and salary growth. - Worker Types by NSO -
Type Description Trends (PLFS)
Self-Employed Work for themselves, charging fees (e.g., own-account workers, business owners, unpaid family laborers). Increased due to gig economy growth.
Wage/Salaried Employees Work for an employer with fixed wages; year-round jobs. Decreased post-COVID-19.
Casual Workers Short-term, daily/monthly wage workers (e.g., ragpickers, construction workers). Male: Stable proportion; Female: Declined post-COVID-19 (e.g., lockdown layoffs).

- Unorganized Sector - Definition: - Firms not registered under laws like Shop Establishment Act, Factory Act, or Companies Act; workers lack social security (EPFO/ESIC). - Features: - Casual/seasonal work, irregular payments, no trade union protection. - Legislation: - Unorganized Sector Workers’ Social Security Act, 2008, provides life/disability cover, health/maternity benefits, and old-age protection. - Formalization: - Increasing proportion of formal workers indicates job formalization. - Informal Workers - Definition: - Workers not in formal records/contracts, even in organized sectors (e.g., drivers, security guards in companies like Reliance). - Sectors with High Informal Workers: Construction (>80%), mining (>30%), transport/hotels/restaurants (>10%). - Issues: - Lack minimum wages, EPFO/ESIC benefits; vulnerable to economic shocks (e.g., 60 lakh migrant workers fled cities during COVID-19 via Shramik Special trains, May–August 2020). - Unorganized Workers: E-Shram Portal (2021) - Overview: - National database by Ministry of Labour & Employment for ~38 crore unorganized workers (e.g., construction workers, street vendors, domestic workers). - Features: - Free registration; issues e-Shram card with Universal Account Number (UAN). - Benefits: - ₹1 lakh for partial disability, ₹2 lakh for accidental death; access to social security schemes. - ES23 Data: - 28 crore registered; highest from UP (29%), Bihar (10%), West Bengal (9%); sectors: agriculture (52%), domestic workers (9.8%), construction (9.1%). - Gig Workers & Two-Sided Market - Definition: - Temporary workers outside traditional employer-employee setups (e.g., delivery boys, app-based taxi drivers, freelancers). - Data: - 7.5 million gig workers (2020–21), projected to reach 20 million in 8 years. - Two-Sided Market: - Buyers and sellers interact via platforms (e.g., Amazon, Ola, Uber). - Decisions of one group (e.g., customer ratings) affect the other (e.g., delivery boy’s payment). - Characteristics: - Workers classified as independent contractors, not employees, depriving them of EPFO/ESIC benefits. - Short-term, temporary contracts; payment based on piece rate, ratings, or profit share. - Code on Social Security 2020 aims to address social security gaps. - Formal Temporary Flexi Workers - Definition: - Temporary workers hired through staffing companies (e.g., TeamLease supplying cleaners to Infosys). - Features: - Staffing companies handle wages, social security; 1% of Indian workforce (vs. 2.2% in Europe); mostly aged 21–30, earning ₹20,000–22,000 in low-skill jobs (e.g., data operations, sales). - AI & Job Loss: Engel’s Pause - Concept: - During Britain’s Industrial Revolution, technological advancements initially did not benefit workers (Engel’s Pause). - ILO: - 75 million jobs at risk from AI by 2025. - ES25 Recommendations: - Reskill workers for tech-related jobs. - Establish Stewarding Institutions for ethical AI research. - Avoid high taxes on AI company profits to prevent reduced R&D or company relocation, which could exacerbate job losses. - Job Elasticities vs. AI-Induced Job Loss -
Sector AI Job Loss Risk Reason
Teachers High AI-based tutors may replace ineffective teachers, though regulations (e.g., UGC/NEP) can mandate minimum teacher hiring.
Telecom Workers High Oligopolistic market (e.g., Jio, Airtel) allows companies to collude, lay off workers, and maintain high prices.
Financial Sector Low Requires salesmen, auditors, and analysts to oversee AI-driven processes.
Medical Sector Low Nurses and doctors remain essential.
Retail/Wholesale Low Salesmen, laborers, and transporters still needed.

focuses on broader employment trends. - Pillar 4D: Indicators → GDP - Gross Domestic Product (GDP) - Definition: - Market value of all final goods and services produced within a country’s domestic territory in a specified period (usually one year). - Domestic Territory: - Includes political frontiers, territorial waters, ships, aircraft, fishing vessels operated by residents, and embassies/consulates abroad (per NIOS). - GDP Potential: - Maximum output a country can produce using available labor and capital at a constant innovation rate. - GDP Gap: - Difference between potential GDP and real GDP. - GDP Calculation Method #1 → Expenditure Approach - Formula: - GDP = C + I + G + (X – M) - Consumption (C) - Includes: - Purchase of new cars, mobiles, computers (Indian or imported), notional rent of self-occupied houses. - Excludes: - Second-hand goods (only new goods made in India counted), new house construction (counted in Investment). - Investments (I) - Includes: - Tangible assets (new houses, land, buildings, factories, trucks, machinery), intangible assets (IPR, patents, software), raw materials, intermediate goods, wages for production, unsold inventory. - Excludes: - Savings in banks, shares, bonds (counted as capital given to entrepreneurs). - Government Purchases (G) - Includes: - Salaries, procurement of computers, stationery, vehicles, etc. - Excludes: - Scholarships, subsidies, transfer payments (counted in private consumption). - Exports minus Imports (X – M) - Exports added: - Foreigners buying Indian-made goods/services contribute to India’s GDP. - Imports subtracted: - Indian consumption of foreign goods not made in India. - Result: - GDP at Current Market Price; adjusted with inflation (base year 2011) for GDP at Constant Market Price. - GDP Calculation Method → Expenditure (NSO Real Life) - NSO Formula (2022-23, Approx): - Private Final Consumption Expenditure (PFCE): ₹164 lakh crore - Gross Fixed Capital Formation (GFCF) + Change in Stocks (CIS): ₹79 lakh crore - Government Final Consumption Expenditure (GFCE): ₹28 lakh crore - Net Export of Goods & Services: (–)₹12 lakh crore - Discrepancies: - ₹6 lakh crore - Total GDP @ Current Market Price: >₹270 lakh crore - Total GDP @ Constant Market Price (2011): ~₹159 lakh crore - Growth Rate Calculation: - 2021-22: - ₹149 lakh crore - 2022-23: - ₹159 lakh crore - Growth Rate: - [(159 – 149) / 149] × 100 = ~7% - GDP Growth Rate (2011 Base Year, Real/Constant Market Price) - ES25 Projection for 2025-26: 6.3–6.8% - CIGXM Components (ES25) - Data not provided in raw text; typically includes PFCE (~60%), GFCF (~30%), GFCE (~10%), and net exports (varies). - GDP Calculation Method → Production/GVA - Gross Value Added (GVA): Value of final goods minus intermediate goods. - Example: -

- GVA = Total value added (₹1 + ₹4 + ₹5 = ₹10 lakh) or (Final – Intermediate = ₹16 – ₹6 = ₹10 lakh). - GVA at Basic Price: Excludes taxes and subsidies. - GVA of Various Sectors - Data not provided; typically includes agriculture (~15%), industry (~30%), services (~55%). - From GVA to GDP - Formula: - GVA (Basic Price) + Indirect Taxes – Subsidies = GDP (Current Market Price) - Example (LPG Cylinders): - GVA: - ₹600 - Indirect Taxes (CGST + SGST): ₹100 - Subsidies (PAHAL Scheme): - (–)₹200 - GDP @ Current Market Price: ₹600 + ₹100 – ₹200 = ₹500 - Adjusted with inflation (base year 2011) for GVA/GDP at Constant Prices. - GVA & GDP: Growth Rates @Current vs Constant Price - GVA: - Producer/supply-side perspective. - GDP: - Consumer/demand-side perspective (includes taxes/subsidies). - Since 2018, RBI uses GDP for economic analysis (not GVA). - GDP Misc Topics → Discrepancy - Discrepancies: - Errors in data collection or estimation (e.g., ₹6 lakh crore in 2022-23). - Explained in video (not detailed in text). - GDP Calculation Method → Income (WIPR) - Formula: - GDP = Wages (W) + Interest (I) + Profits (P) + Rent (R) - Result: - GDP at Current Factor Cost. - GDP Calculation Method → Income (CSO Real Life) - NSO Formula: - Compensation (Employee salary + employer’s social security contributions, e.g., EPFO/ESIC) - Operating Surplus and Mixed Income (family-run farms/enterprises where income/profit hard to separate) - Consumption of Fixed Assets (depreciation) - Total = GVA at Factor Cost - GDP → Growth Rate & Deflator - Growth Rate Formula: - [(GDP Present Year – Last Year) / Last Year] × 100 - Inflation Impact: - Use base year (2011) to convert current prices to constant prices. - GDP Deflator Formula: - (Nominal GDP @ Current Prices / Real GDP @ Constant Prices) × 100 - Example (ES22, 2019): -

- GDP Misc Topics → 2015 Calculation Reform - Compliance with UN System of National Accounts (SNA-2008). - Changes: - Base year changed from 2004 to 2011. - Updated data collection/classification for: - Crop and livestock data, handicraft industries. - Meat value calculation. - Services by local bodies (municipal bus, school, water, sanitation). - Informal sector (e.g., domestic maids). - Sand extraction, construction, mining. - Company data: - From Annual Survey of Industries (ASI)/Index of Industrial Production (IIP) to Ministry of Corporate Affairs’ balance sheets. - Financial services: - Improved data capture with RBI, SEBI, IRDAI, PFRDA. - Private coaching, hotel-tourism: - Use service-tax data for cross-checking. - GDP Misc Topics → Backseries Controversy - Outdated topic, removed for prelims. - GDP Misc Topics → Changing Base Years to 2017 & 18 - MoSPI (2018-Feb) proposed: - GDP & IIP: - From 2011 to 2017-18. - CPI: - From 2012 to 2018-19. - Reason: - Accommodate economic changes (GST, Demonetization, RERA). - GDP → Growth Rate → Economic Cycle - Phases: - Expansion/Prosperity/Boom: - Rising GDP. - Recession: - Negative growth for two consecutive quarters (e.g., USA 2007-09, subprime crisis). - Depression: - Severe, prolonged recession (e.g., USA 1929-39, stock market crash). - Recovery: - From recession/depression to prosperity. - Technical Recession: - Negative GDP growth for two consecutive quarters. - Recessionary Phase: - GDP growth lower than previous quarter. - Expansionary Phase: - GDP growth higher than previous quarter. - Post-Corona: V-Shaped Recovery for India - V-Shaped: - Sharp decline followed by quick recovery (e.g., USA 1918-20 Spanish Flu: –3.5% to 7.5%). - U-Shaped: - Slow recovery. - W-Shaped: - Recovery, decline, then recovery again. - K-Shaped: - Some sectors recover (e.g., e-learning, e-commerce), others lag (e.g., tourism, restaurants). - ES21 Projection: V-shaped recovery due to: - Mass vaccination boosting contact-sensitive sectors (trade, hotels, transport, tourism). - Unlocking pent-up demand. - Low base effect. - Low Base Effect in GDP Growth - Smaller denominator (previous year’s GDP) inflates % growth. - Example: - 2021 GDP growth ~9% due to low base from Corona 2020 (vs. usual 6-7%). - Misc. Terms: Animal Spirit - John Maynard Keynes: - Investors/consumers driven by psychological urges, not rational analysis. - 2019 RBI Report: - Weak domestic demand, animal spirit not reviving, causing slowdown. - Misc. Terms: Pent-Up Demand - Postponed shopping during recession; surges during recovery or festivals. - 2020 Diwali: - Surge in online/offline shopping due to discounts, but critics argue it’s temporary. - Misc. Terms: Lipstick Effect / Little Luxuries - During slowdown, people buy small luxuries (e.g., lipstick) for psychological thrill, not expensive items. - Misc. Terms: Hysteresis - Economic effects persist after cause is removed (e.g., reduced spending post-Corona due to lockdown/job-loss fears). - Misc. Terms: Doom Loop - One negative condition creates another, amplifying the first (e.g., Pakistan’s lack of funds → no schemes → poor manufacturing → low taxes → lack of funds). - Misc. Terms: Financial Contagion - Financial disruptions spread across countries/sectors (e.g., Silicon Valley Bank collapse → Indian startups → IT sector → banks/share market). - Misc. Terms: Goldilocks Scenario - Ideal economic growth: - Not too high (causing inflation) nor too low (causing slowdown). - Misc. Terms: Headwinds & Tailwinds - Headwinds: - Challenges (e.g., inflation, global slowdown, oil prices). - Tailwinds: - Opportunities (e.g., young population, favorable monsoon). - GDP Growth Rate & 5 Trillion Economy - World Bank-ICP’s GDP Series (PPP) - Outdated topic, removed. - Budget-2019: $5 Trillion Economy - GDP (Current Prices): - 2014-15: - $1.85 trillion - 2018-19: - $2.70 trillion - 2019-20: - $2.90 trillion - Target: - $5 trillion by 31/3/2025, $7 trillion (CEA Nageswaran). - ES19: - Blueprint for $5 trillion economy. - Counterview (C. Rangarajan): - Unachievable by 2025, requires 9-10% annual growth (current: 5-6%). - Note: - $5 trillion target still valid for Mains answers, as government hasn’t officially abandoned it. - GDP Growth Rate Before Corona - Growth Rate Decline (Pre-Corona) - Causes: - Protectionism (China, USA), US-Iran tensions → reduced global trade. - Sharp decline in automobile purchases (worsened by Bharat-6 norms’ higher costs). - Slow investment due to Twin Balance Sheet Syndrome (TBS), IL&FS-NBFC crisis. - Demonetization, GST: - Short-term harm, long-term benefit (per ES20). - Negative GDP Growth (Post-Independence) - Occurred 4 times: -
