- GDP → $5 Trillion → How to Achieve: ES Strategy - Savings: - Income excess of consumption (private: households/businesses; public: government). - Investment: - Domestic savings + foreign capital in physical assets (machines, buildings, roads, unsold inventory). - Gross Fixed Capital Formation (GFCF): Investment – disposal of assets; ignores depreciation, land purchases. - Capital Output Ratio - Capital needed per unit of output. - Example: - USA: - $3 lakh plant → 2 lakh bottles → Ratio = 1.5 (better). - India: - $3 lakh plant → 1 lakh bottles → Ratio = 3 (worse). - High ratio in India: Reason for subdued growth. - Incremental Capital Output Ratio (ICOR) - Additional capital needed for additional output. - India: - 3.8 (2016) → 4.9 (2018) → 6.9 (2019). - Higher ICOR = less efficient production. - Investment More Important Than Savings - ES18: - To achieve 9% growth, prioritize investment → GFCF increase → automatic growth and savings increase. - Strategies: - Resolve TBS, promote Make in India, Startup India, reform tax/labor/environment/FDI laws. - Savings mobilization (PMJDY, pension, gold bonds, demonetization) important but not urgent. - Capital Intensity Ratio (CIR) - Accounting: - Total assets ÷ total sales (capital needed for ₹1 sales). - Macroeconomics: - Total capital employed ÷ total labor employed (capital- vs. labor-intensive production). - Paradox of Savings / Paradox of Thrift - John Maynard Keynes (1936): Individual saving → reduced demand → GDP/job loss → less savings nationally. - Counterargument: - Savings → bank loans → R&D/innovation → future demand (long-term benefit). - Income & Savings: Misc. Terms: Chinese Atma-Nirbhar / Dual Circulation - China’s post-Corona strategy: - Boost local production with foreign tech/investment (details not important). - GDP Growth → ES Observations - Frontloaded Economic Stimulus (USA/EU) - Economic Stimulus: - Temporary measures (tax cuts, subsidies, cheap loans, transfers) to revive economy. - Frontloading: - Large funds delivered early (e.g., 3-3-1-1 vs. 2-2-2-2). - Overheating: - Unsustainable growth causing inflation post-stimulus withdrawal (per ES23). - 4 Challenges to GDP (CEA V. Anantha Nageswaran, 2024) - Challenge #1: Onshoring and Friendshoring - Friendshoring: - Supply chains focus on allies (e.g., USA-Taiwan/S. Korea for semiconductors); bad for India’s PLI scheme. - Onshoring: - Relocating supply chains to home country (e.g., Tesla from China to USA); bad for India’s Tesla factory goals. - Home-shoring: - Work-from-home to reduce costs (e.g., Infosys). - Impact: - Slowdown in hyper-globalization, geo-economic fragmentation. - Challenges #2–4: Energy, AI, Skill - Energy: - Balancing security and growth (coal use vs. climate activism; solar/wind subsidies reduce funds for other sectors). - AI: - 40% global jobs at risk (IMF). - Skill: - Shortage of talented/skilled workers. - GDP → GNP to NNP to Per Capita Income - Primary Income: - Wages, interest, profit, rent. - Secondary Income: - Gifts, donations, remittances (ignored in GNP). - Gross National Product (GNP): GDP + Net primary income from abroad (residents’ income from overseas – non-residents’ income from India). - Net National Product (NNP): GNP – Depreciation. - NNP at Factor Cost (National Income): NNP (Market Price) – Indirect Taxes + Subsidies. - Per Capita Income: - NNP ÷ Population. - Data: -

- Budget-2023: - Per capita income doubled to ₹1.97 lakh since 2014 (MoSPI data differs). - SBI Research: - Per capita income to reach ₹14.9 lakh by 2046-47. - Net Domestic Product (NDP) - NDP = GDP – Depreciation. - Depreciation % set by Ministry of Commerce. - Misc. Concepts - Gross National Income (GNI): GDP + Net receipts (wages, interest, profit, rent, taxes, subsidies) from abroad. - National Disposable Income: - NNP + Other current transfers (remittances, gifts, donations). - Personal Income: - Complex formula, not important. - Personal Disposable Income: - Personal Income – Personal taxes – Non-tax payments (fines). - National Income Accounting: - NCERT Class 12 chapter covering these topics. - Depreciation of Fixed Assets - Fixed Assets: - Used in business for >1 year (e.g., machines, buildings, computers). - Depreciation: - Decline in fixed asset value. - Factors Causing Depreciation - Wear and tear from use or time. - Obsolescence (new models). - Natural phenomena (weather, moisture). - Accidents (fire, earthquake, floods). - Features - Permanent, gradual shrinkage in asset value. - Deducted before taxable income (e.g., Profit ₹50,000 – Depreciation ₹10,000 = Taxable ₹40,000). - Non-cash expense (no cash outflow). - Helps ascertain true profit/loss. - Depletion and Amortization - Depletion: - Like depreciation, for natural resources (e.g., mines). - Amortization: - Like depreciation, for intangible assets (e.g., patents, copyrights). - Types of Nations: High Income, Low Income - World Bank Classification (2020, per capita GNI): - High Income: - ≥$12,696 (e.g., Israel, USA). - Upper-Middle Income: - $4,096–$12,695 (e.g., China). - Lower-Middle Income: - $1,046–$4,095 (e.g., India, $1,928 in 2020). - Low Income: - ≤$1,045. - IBRD: - Extra surcharge on loans for high-income countries (since 2018). - 2022: - India’s WTO complaint against China for fewer trade concessions as upper-middle-income country. - Types of Nations: Advanced Economies (AE) - IMF Definition: - High per capita income. - Export diversification (not single-item reliant, e.g., Kuwait’s oil). - High integration with global financial system (OECD members pre-1990s, e.g., USA, UK, Germany). - Types of Nations: - EMDEs - Emerging Market and Developing Economies (non-AE). - Subgroups: - Low Income Countries (LIC): e.g., Afghanistan, Nepal. - Emerging Market Economies (EM): e.g., India, China, Brazil. - Bangladesh Transition from LDC to Developing Country - UN ECOSOC (CDP) Criteria for LDC: - Per Capita GNI: - ≤$1,230.' - Economic & Environmental Vulnerability Index (EVI): Population in low coastal zones, disaster victims, unstable agriculture/exports. - Human Assets Index (HAI): Undernourishment, mortality, school enrollment, literacy. - 2021-Nov: - Bangladesh, Nepal, Laos to upgrade to Developing Country by 2026. - Negative Outcomes: - Loss of duty-free-quota-free WTO access. - Tighter WTO norms (agriculture subsidies, IPR). - No interest-free loans from World Bank/multilateral banks. - Reduced aid/donations. - Stricter climate/pollution norms. - Positive Outcomes: - Signals large consumer market → increased FDI → jobs, GDP. - Bangladesh Per Capita GDP Higher Than India - Outdated topic, removed. - Bhutan Graduates from LDC (2023) - Exits LDC list in Dec 2023 (similar to Bangladesh case). - India as a Developed Country - PM Modi (2022): - Goal to be developed by 2047 (100 years of independence). - Features: - High GDP, per capita GNI, standard of living, HDI. - Strategy: - Recycle points from Pillars 4-5-6. - GDP & Per Capita Income → Criticism / Limitations - GDP Issues: - Unorganized sector: - Incomplete production data capture. - Tax evasion: - Businesses underreport production to NSO. - Parallel economy: - Black money/cash transactions. - Qualitative/Negative Externalities Ignored: - Coal-based power increases GDP but ignores pollution. - Green Accounting/Green GDP (Peter Wood, 1980s): Includes environmental costs. - Uttarakhand (2021): - First state to include Gross Environment Product (GEP) in GSDP (forest, air, water, soil quality). - Non-Market Activities Ignored: - e.g., domestic work by mothers. - Opportunity Cost Ignored: - e.g., child laborer’s ₹50,000 firecracker output vs. potential ₹5,00,000 as doctor/engineer. - Inequality Ignored: - GDP doesn’t reflect income distribution. - Alternatives: - Gross Happiness Index, Physical Quality of Life Index, HDI (Pillar 6). - Economic Growth vs. Economic Development - Growth: - Quantitative (GDP increase). - Development: - Qualitative (HDI, poverty reduction, etc.). - Chart explanation in video. - Pillar 4E: Economic Indicators - Inflation and Production - Definition: - Economic indicators are statistical measures that assess the health, performance, and trends of an economy, providing critical insights into inflation, production, and consumption patterns for policymaking and economic analysis. - Context: - In India, indicators like the Consumer Price Index (CPI), Wholesale Price Index (WPI), and Index of Industrial Production (IIP) are essential for UPSC examinations, reflecting the Reserve Bank of India’s (RBI) inflation targeting, industrial performance, and economic policy effectiveness, particularly in the post-COVID recovery context. - Significance for India: - These indicators guide RBI’s monetary policy, government fiscal strategies, and reforms aimed at sustainable growth, financial inclusion, and stability in a globalizing economy, supporting India’s vision of becoming a developed nation by 2047. - Inflation: Concepts and Dynamics - Definition: - Inflation is the sustained increase in the general price level of goods and services over time, reducing purchasing power. Deflation is the persistent decline in prices, often signaling economic stagnation or recession. - Inflationary and Deflationary Gaps: - Inflationary Gap: - Occurs when aggregate demand (AD = Consumption + Investment + Government Spending + Net Exports) exceeds aggregate supply at full employment, leading to price increases. - Causes: - Increased money supply (e.g., RBI printing money). - Higher propensity to consume (e.g., increased disposable income from schemes like MNREGA or PM-KISAN). - Increased investment or government expenditure. - Rising net exports due to global demand. - High economic growth driving excessive demand. - Deflationary Gap: - Occurs when aggregate demand falls below aggregate supply, causing price declines. - Causes: - Reduced money supply (e.g., tight monetary policy). - Increased propensity to save or delayed purchases expecting further price drops. - Decreased investment or government spending (e.g., fiscal consolidation). - Reduced net exports due to global economic slowdown. - Economic depression or recession lowering demand. - Inflationary and Deflationary Spirals: - Inflationary Spiral: - Rising prices lead workers to demand higher wages, increasing production costs, which firms pass on as higher prices, further fueling inflation. - Deflationary Spiral: - Falling prices reduce firm profits, leading to lower production, wage cuts, or layoffs, reducing demand and further lowering prices. - Combating Inflation and Deflation - Combating Inflation: - RBI’s Monetary Policy: - Tight or hawkish policy: Increasing interest rates (e.g., repo rate) to make loans costlier, reducing money supply and demand. - Issuing inflation-indexed bonds or sovereign gold bonds to absorb excess liquidity. - Government Measures: - Increase direct taxes to reduce disposable income. - Curtail fiscal deficits to limit public spending. - Reduce subsidies that increase money supply without boosting production. - Implement Essential Commodities Act, stock limits, or minimum export prices to control prices. - Use schemes like FCI’s Open Market Sale or Operation Greens for price stabilization. - Combating Deflation: - RBI’s Monetary Policy: - Easy or dovish policy: Lowering interest rates to make loans cheaper, encouraging spending and investment. - Government Measures: - Provide tax deductions, exemptions, or subsidies to consumers to boost consumption (e.g., GST cuts on consumer goods). - Increase public expenditure on infrastructure (e.g., highways, dams) to stimulate demand in industries like steel and cement. - Neutral and Natural Rate of Interest - Definition: - The neutral rate of interest (or natural rate) is the theoretical interest rate at which monetary policy neither stimulates nor restricts economic growth, balancing aggregate demand and supply at full employment. - Significance: - Guides RBI in setting policy rates to achieve stable inflation (2-6% as per RBI Act) without causing overheating or slowdown. - NAIRU and Phillips Curve: - Non-Accelerating Inflation Rate of Unemployment (NAIRU): - The unemployment rate below which inflation rises due to increased consumer demand from employed individuals. - Phillips Curve: - Short-term: - Shows an inverse relationship between inflation and unemployment (downward sloping), where lower unemployment increases demand, pushing prices up. - Long-term: - Vertical, indicating no trade-off between inflation and unemployment, as unemployment stabilizes at NAIRU regardless of inflation levels (e.g., 3% unemployment with varying inflation rates of 0%, 4%, 8%, or 12%). - Inflation: Types Based on Causation - Demand-Pull Inflation: - Occurs when excessive demand (“too much money chasing too few goods”) outstrips supply, often due to schemes like MNREGA, Pay Commission, or Universal Basic Income increasing disposable income. - Monetary Inflation: - Results from excessive money supply, often due to RBI monetizing fiscal deficits (e.g., printing money to finance government debt). - Cost-Push Inflation: - Arises from increased input costs, such as: - High crude oil prices increasing transport costs. - Wage hikes from trade or labor union actions. - Natural disasters reducing agricultural output (e.g., lower potato production raising chip prices). - Profit-Push Inflation: - Caused by cartels or monopolists deliberately reducing supply or hiking prices for profit (e.g., OPEC oil production cuts). - Built-In Inflation: - Linked to wage-price spirals, where rising prices prompt wage demands, increasing costs and further raising prices. - Repressed Inflation: - Occurs when government imposes price controls or rationing (e.g., during wars), but prices surge once controls are lifted due to pent-up demand. - Stagflation: - Combines high inflation, high unemployment, and low growth, leading to a stagnant economy. - Skewflation: - Episodic price rises in specific commodities (e.g., pulses, onions) while general inflation remains stable. - Structural Inflation: - Embedded in the economic system, requiring policy overhaul to address (e.g., MSP hikes for wheat but not pulses, causing pulse shortages). - Shrinkflation: - Companies reduce product size while maintaining prices (e.g., Vim Soap from 155 gm to 135 gm for ₹10). - Taxflation: - Price increases due to higher indirect taxes (e.g., excise or VAT on petrol/diesel). - Black Money-Induced Inflation: - Tax evasion increases disposable income, boosting lavish spending and driving prices (e.g., real estate). - Black Marketing and Hoarding: - Traders artificially reduce supply, causing price spikes. - Credit Inflation: - Cheap loans from banks increase demand, pushing prices up. - Inflation: Types Based on Speed/Quantum - Creeping Inflation: - Moderate, ~4% per annum, considered safe for job creation and growth. - Walking/Trotting Inflation: - Above 4%, transitioning to double-digit rates. - Running Inflation: - Double-digit inflation, significantly impacting purchasing power. - Galloping/Hyperinflation: - Extremely high rates (20%–10,000%+), rendering money nearly worthless (e.g., post-Versailles Germany, modern Venezuela, Zimbabwe, Iran). - Runaway Inflation and Depreciation: - Runaway Inflation: - Uncontrollable, rapid price increases (e.g., hyperinflation scenarios). - Runaway Depreciation: - Rapid decline in local currency value (e.g., Pakistani rupee: $1 = 175 PKR in 2022 to 300 PKR in 2023). - Inflation: Base Effect - Definition: - The base effect refers to the impact of the previous year’s price level (denominator) on the calculated inflation rate, which may exaggerate or understate inflation. - Example: - Onion prices: - ₹100 (2010), ₹110 (2011), ₹120 (2012) show a ₹10 annual increase. - Inflation rate: - 10% for 2011 (110/100), but 9.09% for 2012 (120/110), despite consistent ₹10 rise, due to the higher base. - Effects of Inflation and Deflation - On Individuals and Groups: -
Group During Inflation During Deflation
Businessmen/Borrowers Gain due to faster-rising product prices compared to input costs, increasing profits. Face losses as product prices fall faster than production costs, leading to layoffs.
Fixed-Income Groups/Lenders Suffer as real purchasing power declines due to reduced real interest rates. Benefit from increased purchasing power, but risk job losses per Phillips Curve.
Currency Exchange Rate Rupee weakens as purchasing power falls, reducing foreign demand for Indian goods. Rupee strengthens, boosting export competitiveness.
- Inflating Away Debt: - Governments or central banks may deliberately induce inflation (e.g., via quantitative easing) to reduce the real value of debt, as borrowers repay less in purchasing power terms. - Inflation Impact on Exports: - High inflation weakens the rupee, reducing export competitiveness as foreign buyers get less value (e.g., onion prices rising from ₹50 to ₹100 per kg with exchange rate shifts). - Inflation and Production Indices - Laspeyres, Paasche, and Fisher Indices: - Laspeyres Index: - Uses a fixed basket of goods with base-year weights to calculate CPI, WPI, and IIP, measuring price/production changes against a base year. - Paasche Index: - Uses current-year quantities to calculate what today’s goods would cost at base-year prices. - Fisher Index: - Geometric mean of Laspeyres and Paasche indices for a balanced measure. - Consumer Price Index (CPI): - Measures retail price changes for a basket of goods and services, base year 2012, by NSO, MoSPI. - Components (All India, weights): - Food & Beverages: - 45.86% - Services (Transport, Communication, Health, Education, Recreation): 20.62% - Housing: - 10.07% - Fuel & Light: - 6.84% - Clothing & Footwear: - 6.53% - Miscellaneous (Personal Care, Household Goods): 7.69% - CPI Variations: - Rural: - No housing weight, higher food weight (54.18%). - Urban: - Includes housing, lower food weight. - CPI-Industrial Workers (CPI-IW): - Base year 2016, by Labour Bureau, monitors prices for industrial workers. - CPI-Rural/Agricultural Labourers: - Base year 1986 (proposed change to 2019), by Labour Bureau. - Consumer Food Price Index (CFPI): - Tracks food prices (cereals, meat, fish, eggs, milk, oils, fruits, vegetables, pulses, sugar, spices), excluding non-alcoholic beverages and prepared meals. - Wholesale Price Index (WPI): - Measures wholesale price changes, base year 2011, by Economic Advisor, DPIIT. - Components (weights): - Manufactured Products: - ~64% - Primary Articles (Unprocessed Food, Crude Petroleum, Minerals): ~23% - Fuel & Power: - ~13% - CPI vs. WPI Divergence: - CPI includes indirect taxes and services, WPI excludes them. - CPI gives higher weight to food (~46%) than WPI (~19% for primary articles). - Example: - April-July 2020, WPI was negative, while CPI inflation exceeded 6% due to food price volatility. - Index of Industrial Production (IIP) - Definition: - A monthly index by NSO, base year 2011, using Laspeyres formula, measuring production across 407 item groups in mining, manufacturing, and electricity. - Classification by Use (Weights): - Primary Goods: - 34% (ores, minerals, crude oil, electricity). - Capital Goods: - 8% (machinery, boilers, vehicles). - Infrastructure/Construction Goods: - 12% (cement, cables, paints). - Intermediate Goods: - 17% (yarn, steel tubes, fasteners). - Consumer Durables: - 13% (TVs, cars, jewelry). - Consumer Non-Durables: - 15% (food, beverages, cigarettes). - Sector-Based Weights: - Manufacturing: - 77.63% - Mining: - 14.37% - Electricity: - 7.99% - Trends: - 2018-2019: - IIP declined due to NPA issues, ILFS-NBFC crisis, protectionism, and reduced demand in automobiles and real estate. - 2020: - IIP hit a low in April due to COVID lockdown, later recovered. - 2021: - IIP surged 22% in March due to base effect. - 2024: - Economic Survey notes healthy IIP growth. - Index of Eight Core Industries - Definition: - A monthly index by EA-DPIIT, base year 2011, focusing on eight core industries with 40.27% weight in IIP. - Components (Descending Weight): - Refinery Products, Electricity, Steel, Coal, Crude Oil, Natural Gas, Cement, Fertilizers. - Other Economic Indices - Producer Price Index (PPI): - Measures price changes from sellers’ perspective, covering goods and services, unlike WPI (goods only). - Experimental Service Price Index: - By EA-DPIIT, covers railway, port, air, postal, telecom, banking, and insurance services. - Banking Business Service Price Index: - By RBI, tracks fees for NEFT, RTGS, card transactions, and DEMAT accounts, base year 2011. - Inflation Expectation Survey: - RBI’s quarterly survey of ~5,000 households across 18 cities on expected inflation. - Business Inflation Expectations Survey: - By IIM Ahmedabad, assesses business expectations on price trends. - Housing Inflation: - National Housing Bank’s RESIDEX (HPI, base year 2017) tracks residential house prices. - RBI’s Home Price Index monitors housing market trends. - Causes: - Post-COVID cheap loans and investment demand increased housing prices. - Household Consumption Expenditure Survey (2022-23) - Overview: - Conducted by NSO, MoSPI, released in February 2024, covering Monthly Per Capita Consumption Expenditure (MPCE) from August 2022 to July 2023. - MPCE Without Imputation: -
Period Rural (Current Prices) Urban (Current Prices) Rural (2011-12 Prices) Urban (2011-12 Prices)

- High-Frequency Indicators (HFIs) - Definition: - HFIs are frequently updated economic data providing real-time insights into economic activity, unlike slower indicators like annual GDP. - Examples (Economic Survey 2021-22): - Inflation: - Retail CPI. - Financial: - UPI/ATM transactions, currency in circulation, SENSEX, NIFTY, G-Sec yields. - Taxation: - Monthly GST, E-way bills. - Rural/Agro: - APMC mandi arrivals, tractor sales, MNREGA work demand. - Production: - IIP, power consumption, vehicle sales. - Transport: - Railway, port, airway traffic, road toll collection. - Global Trade: - FDI, FPI, crude oil prices, Baltic Dry Index, forex reserves. - Pros and Cons: - Pros: - Enable rapid policy responses and targeted interventions. - Cons: - High noise-to-signal ratio (e.g., market fluctuations due to rumors may not reflect economic fundamentals). - Thalinomics (Economic Survey 2020) - Definition: - Thalinomics estimates the cost of a typical Indian thali (food platter) to assess food affordability across regions. - Trends: - 2015-2018: - Thali prices decreased for both vegetarian and non-vegetarian options across India. - 2019: - Prices increased, but affordability improved for poor households, saving families of five ~₹10,000 annually. - 2020 (June-December): -

Urban Vegetarian Andaman & Nicobar (₹40) Madhya Pradesh (₹24)
Rural Vegetarian Andaman & Nicobar (₹39) Uttar Pradesh (₹23)
Urban Non-Vegetarian Mizoram (₹52) Haryana (₹28)
Rural Non-Vegetarian Arunachal Pradesh (₹49) Chandigarh (₹30)
- Significance: - Reflects success of Modi-era schemes (e.g., PM-KISAN, FCI operations) in enhancing food production and affordability. - Inflation in Other Countries - Economic Survey 2024: - India’s inflation remained moderate compared to many global economies, reflecting effective monetary and fiscal policies. - Pillar 5A1: Infrastructure - Mining and Basic Industries - Definition: - Infrastructure refers to the set of basic facilities that enable an economy to function and grow, including energy, irrigation, roads, railways, and telecommunications. - Characteristics of Infrastructure: - Natural Monopoly: - Often exhibits monopoly characteristics (e.g., railways, pre-LPG aviation, and telecom). - High Sunk Costs: - Investments with low resale value (e.g., airport airstrips). - Non-Tradable Output: - Cannot be relocated (e.g., roads, bridges, airports). - Intangible Nature: - Some elements like spectrum or electricity are intangible. - Non-Rival Consumption: - Usage by one does not limit availability for others (e.g., roads, streetlights). - Price Exclusion Difficulty: - Hard to deny access to non-payers (e.g., rural roads). - Positive Externalities: - Generates benefits like increased business for local economies (e.g., new railway stations boost nearby commerce). - Sectors with Infrastructure Status (Finance Ministry - Dept. of Economic Affairs): - Transport & Logistics: - Roads, bridges, ports, shipyards, inland waterways, airports, railways, tunnels, transport infrastructure. - Energy: - Electricity, oil, gas. - Water & Sanitation: - Water supply, treatment, sewage, solid waste management, irrigation. - Communication: - Telecommunications. - Social & Commercial Infrastructure: Hospitals, educational institutions, sports infrastructure, tourism (hotels, ropeways), industrial/food/textile parks, SEZs, cold storage, soil-testing labs, affordable housing. - Benefits of Infrastructure Status: - Tax benefits, subsidized public land leases, faster environmental/FDI approvals. - RBI relaxes External Commercial Borrowing (ECB) norms, debt restructuring (e.g., 5/25 rule), and Priority Sector Lending (PSL) norms. - SEBI relaxes REITs/InvITs norms for easier capital mobilization. - IRDAI/PFRDA mandates minimum investment in infrastructure by insurance/pension companies. - Easier funding from World Bank and multilateral banks. - Budget 2022: - Infrastructure status granted to data centers, energy storage systems, grid-scale battery systems, and EV charging infrastructure. - Infrastructure: Mining (खनन) / Basic Industries - Basic Industries: - Supply raw materials for other goods (e.g., iron, steel, copper, aluminum, chemicals). - Capital Goods Industries: - Produce goods used in manufacturing (e.g., textile machinery, conveyor belts, mining equipment). - Heavy Industries: - Manufacture large/heavy products (e.g., shipbuilding, bulldozers, industrial machinery, transformers). - Reference: - Ministries and departments differ as per forms of government organizations (see unacademy.com/lesson/mrunals-yearbook-ministries-and-departments). - [Yearbook] Ministry of Heavy Industries - Departments: - Department of Heavy Industry. - Department of Public Enterprises: Manages Ratna status allocation and Public Enterprises Survey (shifted to Finance Ministry in 2021, see Pillar 2A). - Attached/Subordinate/Statutory: - Not MCQ-worthy. - Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs): - National Automotive Testing and R&D Infrastructure Project (NATRiP): Implements FAME-India for electric vehicle adoption. - Bharat Heavy Electricals Ltd. (BHEL). - Cement Corporation of India Ltd. (1965, approved for strategic disinvestment 2019). - Hindustan Newsprint Ltd., Scooters India Ltd., Bharat Pumps and Compressors Ltd., Andrew Yule (tea plantations), Braithwaite, Burn & Jessop Construction, Hindustan Salts (salt, bromine, magnesium chloride), Rajasthan Electronics Ltd. (joint venture for solar panels). - Notable Schemes: - Faster Adoption and Manufacturing of Electric Vehicles (FAME-India). - National Programme on Advanced Chemistry Cell (ACC) Battery Storage. - Productivity Linked Incentive (PLI) for automobile and auto components. - [Yearbook] Ministry of Steel (इस्पात मंत्रालय) - Departments: - None. - Attached/Subordinate/Statutory: - Not MCQ-worthy. - CPSEs: - Steel Authority of India Ltd. (SAIL). - Rashtriya Ispat Nigam Ltd. (RINL). - National Mineral Development Corporation (NMDC, iron ore). - Salem Steel Plant (Tamil Nadu), Bhadravati Steel Plant (Karnataka), Ferro Scrap Nigam Ltd. (approved for disinvestment 2019). - E-Governance: - Steel Import Monitoring System (SIMS) portal. - Targets (National Steel Policy 2017): - Increase per capita steel consumption from 74 kg to 160 kg by 2031. - Reduce coking coal imports from 85% to 65% by 2030-31. - 100% indigenous high-grade automobile steel production. - Rankings (Yearbook 2024): - Crude Steel Production: - #1 China (54%), #2 India (6%), #3 Japan. - Steel Consumption: - #1 China (49%), #2 USA, #3 India (6%). - Steel: Purvodaya Initiative (2020) - Focus: - Eastern states (Odisha, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Chhattisgarh, Northern Andhra Pradesh) with 80% of India’s iron reserves. - Objective: - Establish new steel plants and transport infrastructure, coordinated by Steel Ministry with central/state governments and private companies. - [Yearbook] Ministry of Chemicals & Fertilizers - Departments: - Chemicals and Petrochemicals. - Fertilizers. - Pharmaceuticals. - Attached/Subordinate/Statutory: - Fertilizers Industry Coordination Committee (FICC). - National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA, see Pillar 6). - Autonomous Bodies: - Multi-State Cooperative Societies: - IFFCO, KRIBHCO. - Bureau of Pharma PSUs of India (BPPI): Supplies affordable medicines to PM Jan Aushadhi Kendras. - National Institute of Pharmaceutical Education and Research (NIPER). - Central Institute of Plastics Engineering & Technology (CIPET, Ranchi). - CPSEs: - Hindustan Insecticide Ltd. (HIL): Manufactures DDT for mosquito control in National Vector Borne Disease Control Program. - Indian Drugs and Pharmaceuticals, Bengal Chemicals and Pharmaceuticals, Hindustan Antibiotics, Karnataka Antibiotics & Pharma, Hindustan Fluorocarbon Ltd., Madras Fertilizer, Brahmaputra Valley Fertiliser, Aravali Gypsum (approved for disinvestment 2019). - Notable Schemes: - Plastic parks for the plastic industry. - Petroleum, Chemical, and Petrochemical Investment Regions (PCPIRs): Andhra Pradesh (Vishakhapatnam), Gujarat (Dahej), Odisha (Paradeep), Tamil Nadu (Cuddalore, Nagapattinam). - Pradhan Mantri Bhartiya Janaushadhi Pariyojana for affordable medicines. - [Yearbook] Ministry of Petroleum & Natural Gas - Departments: - None. - Attached/Subordinate: - Directorate General of Hydrocarbons: Regulates upstream activities (oil/gas exploration and production, 2018 statutory status proposal rejected). - Statutory: - Petroleum and Natural Gas Regulatory Board (2006): Regulates downstream activities (pipelines, fuel marketing). - CPSEs: - Bharat Petroleum Corp Ltd., Hindustan Petroleum Corp Ltd. (approved for disinvestment 2019). - Engineers India Ltd.: - Consultancy for petroleum refineries. - Gas Authority of India, Indian Oil Corporation, Oil India, ONGC, ONGC Videsh Ltd. (foreign projects: Sakhalin-Russia, Al-Furat-Syria, Greater Nile-Sudan, San Cristobal-Venezuela). - Indian Strategic Petroleum Reserve Ltd. (ISPRL): Stores crude oil in Vishakhapatnam, Mangaluru, Padur (see Pillar 3A). - Dutch Disease & Resource Curse (Economic Survey 2016-17) - Dutch Disease: - Discovery of natural gas in the Netherlands led to foreign currency inflows, strengthening local currency, reducing non-energy exports (e.g., agriculture, textiles), causing food shortages, hyperinflation, and riots. - Resource Curse/Paradox of Plenty: Despite large oil reserves, countries like Venezuela face economic crises due to Dutch Disease effects. In India, Chhattisgarh and Jharkhand’s mineral wealth fuels mining mafia, Naxalism, corruption, and poverty. - Crude Oil Prices, Petrol/Diesel Taxes, Oil Bonds, NELP-HELP Policies - Reference: - See Pillar 2A2 (Indirect Taxes) and Pillar 3A (Import-Export). - [Yearbook] Ministry of Mines (खनन मंत्रालय) - Departments/Statutory/Attached/Subordinate: - National Mineral Exploration Trust: Funds mineral exploration. - Geological Survey of India (1851): Focuses on coal, landslide, and glacial disaster research. - Indian Bureau of Mines (1948): Regulates mining activities. - CPSEs: - National Aluminium Company Ltd. (NALCO, Bhubaneswar). - Hindustan Copper Ltd. (HCL, Kolkata). - Mineral Exploration Corporation Ltd. (MECL, Nagpur). - Autonomous Bodies: - National Institute of Rock Mechanics (Kolar Gold Fields, Karnataka). - National Institute of Miners’ Health (Karnataka, merged with ICMR-NIOH, Ahmedabad, 2020). - Statutory: - District Mineral Foundations (DMF) in mining districts for local welfare. - Mineral Products in India (धातु और खनिज उत्पाद) - Categories: - Hydrocarbon Energy Minerals: - Coal, lignite, petroleum, natural gas (4 types). - Atomic Minerals: - Ilmenite, rutile, zircon, uranium, monazite (5 types). - Metallic Minerals: - 10 types. - Non-Metallic Minerals: - 21 types. - Minor Minerals: - 55 types (Total: 95 types). - Regulation: - Major Minerals (Union List): Atomic minerals, bauxite, iron, coal, petroleum, natural gas. - Minor Minerals (State List): Sand, mica, marble, granite, agate, chalk, gypsum, shale. - National Mineral Policy (NMP) 2019 - Replaces NMP 2008, under Ministry of Mines. - Targets (Non-Fuel/Non-Coal Minerals): - Allow transfer of mining leases for mergers/acquisitions. - Grant ‘industry’ status to mining for tax/scheme benefits. - Harmonize taxes/royalty rates with global benchmarks. - Enhance FDI (100% allowed in exploration) via ease of doing business. - Promote R&D, skilling, and environmental conservation. - Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 2015 - Replaces MMDR Act 1957 for ease of doing business. - Key Provisions: - Mining leases granted via auction, not discretionary allotment. - Lease duration: - 50 years, followed by re-auction (no renewal). - National Mineral Exploration Trust: Funded by mining companies for exploration. - District Mineral Foundations (DMF): Not-for-profit trusts in mining districts, funded by companies for local welfare, with state-prescribed guidelines. - Higher penalties/jail terms for illegal mining. - MMDR Amendment Bill/Act, 2021 - Excludes coal and atomic minerals. - Changes: - Before: - Mines reserved for captive use (e.g., Tata’s iron ore only for its steel plant). - After: - No captive use restrictions; companies can sell minerals to others. - Before: - States conducted minor mineral auctions, often delayed. - After: - Union sets auction timelines; if states fail, Union conducts auctions. - Before: - Lease expires if no mining for 2 years. - After: - Up to 3-year extension (e.g., for delays due to COVID, labor, disasters). - Royalty Rates for Critical Minerals Reduced (2023) - Before (12% Royalty on Average Sales Price): - Lithium, Niobium, Rare Earth Elements (REE). - After (October 2023): - Lithium: - 3% (used in batteries for mobiles, laptops, EVs, pacemakers). - Niobium: - 3% (superconducting, used in jet engines, rockets, pipelines, MRI scanners). - REE: - 1% (17 minerals like scandium, yttrium, cerium for catalysts, magnets, alloys, electronics, EVs, wind turbines, LEDs). - Note: - Sales prices based on London Metal Exchange (LME). - Benefits: - Improved profitability, attracting investment/FDI. - Cheaper EV batteries, aiding pollution control and net-zero emissions by 2070. - Reduced reliance on imported minerals, lowering current account deficit, stabilizing currency (see Pillar 3B). - MMDR Amendment, 2023 - Private Sector in Atomic Mineral Mining: - Before: - Six atomic minerals (beryl/beryllium, lithium, niobium, titanium, tantalum, zirconium) restricted to government entities. - After: - Delisted from atomic minerals list, allowing private sector exploration/mining. - New Mining Licenses: - Before: - Reconnaissance (survey), prospecting (exploration), mining, composite (prospecting + mining) licenses. - After: - Added exploration license for reconnaissance/prospecting of specified minerals. - Specified Minerals and Licensing: - Minerals: - Gold, silver, copper, cobalt, nickel, lead, potash, rock phosphate, beryl/beryllium, lithium, niobium, titanium, tantalum, zirconium. - Licenses: - Exploration (reconnaissance/prospecting): - State government, with Union-prescribed auction terms. - Mining and Composite Licenses: Union government. - Reconnaissance - Sub-Surface Methods: - Before: - Limited to aerial, geophysical, geochemical surveys, geological mapping; sub-surface activities (trenching, drilling, excavation) prohibited. - After: - Sub-surface methods allowed. - Offshore Areas Mineral (Development and Regulation) Amendment, 2023 - Amends 2002 Act for offshore mining. - Changes: - Before: - 30-year license, renewable for 20 years (prone to bribery). - After: - 50-year license for ease of doing business. - Before: - Licenses via administrative discretion (prone to cronyism). - After: - Competitive bidding/auction. - Before: - No restriction on atomic mineral mining. - After: - Only government companies can mine atomic minerals (uranium, monazite, thorium). - Before: - No statutory trust. - After: - Offshore Areas Mineral Trust, funded by companies for research, environmental conservation, and disaster management. - Before: - Lower penalties for illegal mining. - After: - Increased penalties/jail terms. - National Critical Mineral Mission (2025): - Funding: - ₹16,300 crore (government) + ₹18,000 crore (PSUs) = ₹34,300 crore over 7 years. - Objectives: - Enhance exploration/recycling of critical minerals, fast-track mining project approvals, acquire foreign mineral assets (e.g., lithium in Argentina’s Catamarca). - Critical Minerals from Tailings: - Tailings: - Byproducts after primary mineral processing (e.g., cobalt from copper ore tailings). - Budget 2025: - Encourages extraction of critical minerals from tailings. - Mining: Coal (कोयला) - Global Coal Reserves: - #1 USA, #2 Russia, #3 China, #4 Australia, #5 India. - India: - 2nd largest coal producer but imports >₹1.5 lakh crore annually due to high demand. - Uses: - Electricity, steel, cement, paper, brick kilns. - Coal Types: - Peat: - 40% carbon, high moisture, smoky, inferior. - Lignite/Brown Coal: - 40-60% carbon, in Tamil Nadu (Neyveli), Gujarat, Rajasthan. - Bituminous/Black Coal: - 60-80% carbon, releases bitumen, used for coking/gas/steam coal, in Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Madhya Pradesh, Odisha. - Anthracite/Hard Coal: - 80-90% carbon, low moisture, high energy, short blue flame. - [Yearbook] Coal Ministry (कोयला मंत्रालय): - Attached/Subordinate: - Coal Controller’s Organization: - Collects data, monitors quality, hears objections to coal-bearing area notifications. - CPSEs: - Coal India Ltd. (CIL): Kolkata, Maharatna, world’s largest coal producer. - Neyveli Lignite Corporation (Tamil Nadu). - Singareni Collieries Company Ltd.: Telangana (51%), Union (49%). - Statutory: - Coal Mines Provident Fund Organization (C-CARES portal). - Coal Mining: Nationalization & Entry of Private Sector - 1973: - Coal Mines Nationalization Act: Coal India and CPSEs took over private coal companies for thermal power and industrial supply. - 1993: - Private captive mining allowed for steel, cement, aluminum (led to scams, e.g., UPA-era allocations to ministers’ relatives). - 2014: - Supreme Court canceled coal block allocations. - 2015: - Coal Mines (Special Provisions) Act: Allows commercial coal mining for private/public entities, ending Coal India’s monopoly (captive mining still permitted for existing rights). - Mineral Laws (Amendment) Ordinance/Act, 2020 - Amends MMDR Act 1957 and Coal Mines (Special Provisions) Act 2015. - Changes: - Before: Only iron, steel, power, coal companies could bid for coal mining. - After: Any India-registered company can bid, encouraging competition/FDI. - Before: Prior mining experience required. - After: No experience needed. - Before: Separate prospecting and mining licenses. - After: Composite prospecting-cum-mining lease. - Before: Fixed payment per tonne of coal. - After: Revenue-sharing model (minimum 4% revenue share, higher bids win). - Before: Captive miners restricted to own use. - After: Can sell up to 50% of production. - Coal Selling: Shakti Policy (2017) - Facilitates coal allocation to power plants and industries. - National Coal Index: - Tracks coal price changes (domestic/imported) against base year 2017-18. - Apps: - Coal Mitra App (Power Ministry): Facilitates coal buying/selling. - UTTAM App (Coal Ministry): Monitors coal quality from mines. - Mining: Atma-Nirbhar (खनन) - PM Garib Kalyan: - DMF funds used for COVID-19 testing/infrastructure. - Mineral Index: - Proposed for various minerals (details pending). - Joint Auction: - Bauxite and coal blocks to reduce electricity costs for aluminum smelting. - Coal Gasification/Liquefaction, Coal Bed Methane: Promotes gas-based economy. - Commercial Mining: - Allowed via revenue-sharing model. - Coal Energy: Economic Survey Suggestions/Observations - Carbon Imperialism: - First-world nations push energy consumption norms on third-world countries to sell nuclear fuel/technology and deflect global warming blame. India’s GHG contribution <10%, per capita emissions <2 tons. - Coal Necessity: - Wind/solar power non-dispatchable, nuclear fuel challenges, land constraints for solar, unemployment risks if coal plants close. - Budget 2020: - Close old, high-emission thermal plants, repurpose land. - Budget 2022: - Co-fire 5-7% biomass pellets in thermal plants for farmer income and reduced stubble burning. - Budget 2022: - Promote coal gasification and coal-to-chemicals (formaldehyde, ethylene, propylene, acetic acid). - Interim Budget 2024: - Target 100 MT coal gasification/liquefaction capacity by 2030 to reduce natural gas, methanol, ammonia imports. - ES22 (World Bank): - Clean energy requires copper, aluminum, iron, manganese, nickel, lithium, graphite; India lacks sufficient reserves. - Energy Transition in First-World Nations - 1700s: - Wood to coal transition due to industrialization, causing forest loss. - 1946: - Oil and gas overtook coal as primary energy sources. - 1970s: - Yom Kippur War oil embargo led France to nuclear transition. - 2022: - EU’s REPowerEU plan to reduce Russian gas reliance post-Ukraine war. - 2023: - US approved largest oil drilling project in Alaska. - 2026: - AI data centers to consume 6% of US electricity. - Economic Survey 2025: Energy/Climate Change - India: - 7th most vulnerable to climate change. - 2024 UNFCCC Summit (Baku, Azerbaijan): ‘Finance COP’ for New Collective Quantified Goal (NCQG) on climate finance; first-world contributions inadequate. - Vertical Gardens: - Reduce carbon, enhance biodiversity, improve air quality, mitigate urban heat islands. - Europe: - Gas plants used due to insufficient wind turbine output. - Solar Panels: - Recycling difficult/expensive at end of lifecycle. - Vegetarianism: - Reduces carbon footprint by up to 2.1 tons. - Mining: Miscellaneous Schemes, Apps, Portals, Issues - Note: - Not all details required for memorization; included to address FOMO from current affairs. - Illegal Mining: - Harms environment, deprives government of royalty. - Mining Surveillance System (MSS): Satellite-based monitoring by Indian Bureau of Mines. - Khan Prahari App: - Reports illegal coal mining. - cVIGIL App: - Election Commission’s app for model code violations. - TAMRA App/Portal (2017): - Facilitates online mining auction bidding. - PRAKASH Portal (2019): - Connects coal companies, railways, thermal plants for supply chain efficiency. - Satyabhama Portal (2020): - Mining Ministry’s portal for mining-related research. - CIMS/AIMS: - Copper/Aluminium Import Monitoring Systems. - Pollution: - Red Mud: - Bauxite-to-aluminum waste, used in cement/ceramics. - Fly Ash: - Thermal plant pollutant, used in cement, bricks, tiles, roads; monitored via ASH TRACK App. - Lakshya Portal (2021) - Boss: - Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas. - Purpose: - Lists items imported by oil/gas companies to encourage domestic manufacturing for Atma-Nirbhar Bharat. - Pradhan Mantri Khanij Kshetra Kalyan Yojana (2015): - Uses DMF funds to complement schemes for drinking water, health, sanitation, education, skill development, women/child care. - Star Rating of Mines (2016): Indian Bureau of Mines rates mines (0-5 stars) based on social, economic, and environmental impact. - Pillar 5A2: Infrastructure - Energy, Electricity, and Cooking - Overview: - Electricity is critical for modern life, powering irrigation pumps, mobile phones, agricultural growth, and digital connectivity. - Historical Context: - Electricity supply began in Darjeeling (1897) and Shivasamudram hydropower station (1902, Karnataka). Pre-independence, power supply was primarily private and urban-centric. - Significance: - Increased energy access drives economic growth and human development. India aims to quadruple per capita energy consumption to improve Human Development Index (HDI). - Data (Yearbook 2023): - India’s per capita energy consumption is ~1/3rd of the global average. - India, with ~18% of the world’s population, consumes ~6% of global energy. - India is the 3rd largest energy consumer globally (after USA, China), 3rd largest crude oil importer, and 4th largest LNG importer. - Basic information - Electricity Generation by Ownership: - Union-Owned: - 25% - State-Owned: - 26% - Private Sector: - 49% - Total: - 100% - [Yearbook] Ministry of Power: - Departments: - None (no MCQ-worthy departments). - Statutory Bodies: - Joint Electricity Regulatory Commission (JERC): For UTs like J&K, Ladakh, Goa, Manipur, Mizoram. - Central Electricity Authority (CEA): Sets standards for electrical plants and lines. - Central & State Electricity Regulatory Commissions (CERC/SERC): Fix electricity tariffs. - Appellate Tribunal for Electricity (APTEL): Handles appeals against CERC/SERC decisions. - Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE): Promotes energy efficiency. - Damodar Valley Corporation (DVC): Manages power and water in Damodar Valley. - Bhakra Beas Management Board: Manages Bhakra-Nangal and Beas projects. - Autonomous Bodies: - Central Power Research Institute: Conducts power research. - National Power Training Institute: Trains power sector professionals. - Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs): - National Thermal Power Corporation (NTPC): Thermal power generation. - National Hydroelectric Power Corporation (NHPC): Hydropower generation. - SJVN Ltd.: - Satluj hydropower (GoI: 62%, Himachal: 27%, others: 11%). - Power Finance Corporation (PFC): Finances power projects. - Power Grid Corporation of India (POWERGRID): Manages national grid. - Power System Operation Corporation (POSOCO): Operates power systems. - Energy Efficiency Services Ltd. (EESL): Joint venture (NTPC, PFC, REC, POWERGRID) for UJALA LED bulbs. - THDC India Ltd.: - Tehri hydropower (GoI: 75%, UP: 25%, approved for disinvestment 2019). - Rural Electrification Corporation (REC): Supports rural electrification (DDUGJY). - North Eastern Electric Power Corporation (NEEPCO): Power generation in Northeast. - National Electricity Distribution Company: - Context: - PM Modi’s 24x7 power goal by 2022 was hindered by NPA/debt issues in state and private distribution companies (DISCOMs). - Formation (2019): - 50:50 joint venture between NTPC and POWERGRID. - Objective: - Expand electricity distribution on a pan-India basis to address DISCOM inefficiencies. - Indian Energy Exchange (IEX): - Private sector company facilitating electricity trading. - Note: - Limited exam relevance due to poor cost-benefit ratio for current affairs (CA) preparation. - Electricity: One Nation-One Grid: - Initial Setup: - Five regional grids (Northern, Eastern, Western, North Eastern, Southern) interconnected, but surplus electricity was limited to regional trading. - Objective: - Integrate all regional grids into a single national grid for seamless transfer of surplus electricity to deficit regions. - Mechanism: - Trading via power exchanges like Power Exchange of India (PXIL) and Indian Energy Exchange (IEX). - Boss: - Ministry of Power, implemented by POWERGRID. - Grid: Green Energy Corridor Project: - Objective: - Enable renewable energy flow into the national grid, allowing states like Rajasthan (solar) and Tamil Nadu (wind) to sell surplus electricity. - Phase-II (2022): - Union provides 33% subsidy on project costs. - Grid: GREEN Grids / OSOWOG: - Proposed (2018): - By India at International Solar Alliance (HQ: Gurugram). - Launched (2021): - By PM Modi and UK PM Boris Johnson at COP26 Glasgow as One Sun One World One Grid (OSOWOG). - Objective: - Connect renewable energy grids across borders, enabling countries to access solar energy post-sunset via time zone differences. - Electricity: Power Ministry’s Apps/Portals: - Examples: - Garv, Deep, Tarang, National Power Portal (NPP). - Purpose: - Monitor electricity data (generation, distribution, consumption). - Electricity: Integrated Power Development Scheme (IPDS, 2014): - Boss: - Ministry of Power (Central Sector Scheme, 100% Union-funded). - Target: - Strengthen urban power infrastructure. - Implementation: - Financial assistance to DISCOMs for improving distribution networks. - Installation of ICT-enabled smart meters for billing. - Solar panel installation in areas not feasible for grid connection. - Electricity: Prepaid Smart Meters: - Features: - Internet-enabled meters allow remote electricity supply based on prepaid balance, reducing theft via meter tampering. - Budget 2020: - Plan to replace conventional meters with prepaid smart meters within 3 years. - Electricity: NPA Resolution - UDAY (2015): - Objective: - Address DISCOMs’ non-performing assets (NPAs) and debt. - Mechanism: - States take over DISCOM debts, improve operational efficiency. - Incentives: - Union provides additional funding for DDUGJY, IPDS, and MNRE schemes. - Outcome (2019-20): - First phase completed, but failed to fully resolve DISCOM issues. - UDAY 2.0: - Proposed by Power Minister with enhanced features, but no progress yet. - Electricity Reforms in Atma-Nirbhar: - Note: - Outdated/low-profile topic, removed from study material. - Electricity (Amendment) Bill 2022: - Context: - Electricity is on the Concurrent List; Union law prevails in conflicts. - Responsibilities: - Union: - Electricity generation, transmission. - States: - Electricity distribution. - Objective: - Amend Electricity Act 2003 to improve efficiency, but controversial and faded from focus. - Electricity (Rights of Consumers) Rules, 2020: - Boss: - Ministry of Power (under Electricity Act 2003). - Requirements: - DISCOMs must provide 24/7 electricity, grievance redressal, and compensation mechanisms. - Exception: - Agricultural consumers may have reduced supply hours to prevent groundwater over-exploitation. - Benefit: - Addresses DISCOM monopolies, ensuring consumer rights where alternatives are unavailable. - Time-of-Day (ToD) Tariff (2023): - Boss: - Ministry of Power (under Electricity (Rights of Consumers) Amendment Rules, 2023). - Mechanism: Varies electricity prices by time: - Normal sunny hours: - 20% below normal price. - Peak hours (e.g., evening): 1.10-1.20x normal price (varies by consumer type). - Analogy: - Similar to surge pricing in taxis during high-demand periods. - Faster Connection Rules (Feb 2024): - Boss: - Ministry of Power (under Electricity (Rights of Consumers) Rules). - Features: - Separate electricity connections for EV charging. - Reduced time for new connections. - Simplified rules for rooftop solar installations. - “Prosumers”: - Consumers producing electricity via rooftop solar. - Mandatory additional meter installation for billing disputes. - Electricity: Deen Dayal Upadhyaya Gram Jyoti Yojana (DDUGJY, 2015): - Boss: - Ministry of Power, implemented by REC (Central Sector Scheme, 100% Union-funded). - Target: - 24x7 metered electricity for rural households by 2022. - Features: - Separate feeder lines for rural households and agricultural use. - Strengthen sub-transmission and distribution networks to reduce losses. - Install electricity meters. - Benefit: - Reduces kerosene use, pollution, and import/subsidy bills. - Predecessor: - Rajiv Gandhi Grameen Vidyutikaran Yojana (Manmohan Singh). - Electricity: PM Sahaj Bijli Har Ghar Yojana (Saubhagya, 2017): - Boss: - Ministry of Power, implemented by REC (Central Sector Scheme). - Target: - Electrify all un-electrified rural and urban households. - Implementation: - Identify beneficiaries using SECC-2011 data. - Free metered electricity connections. - Solar cells, DC battery packs, and LED lights for remote households. - Revamped Distribution Sector Scheme (RDSS, June 2021): - Boss: - Ministry of Power (funding: >₹3 lakh crore). - Umbrella Scheme: - Subsumes DDUGJY, Saubhagya, IPDS, and PMDP (J&K, Ladakh). - Features: - Separate agricultural feeder lines. - Solarization of feeder lines under KUSUM (farmers sell excess solar power). - AI-monitored smart meters for non-agricultural users. - Modernize state-level distribution infrastructure. - Extra funding for special category states (e.g., J&K, Ladakh, Andaman, Lakshadweep). - DISCOMs need ≥60% performance score for funding. - Outcome (ES22): - 96% of Indian households electrified. - Electricity: Energy Efficiency: - Definition: - Using less energy for the same output (e.g., LED vs. incandescent bulbs). - Perform, Achieve and Trade (PAT) Mechanism: - Boss: - Ministry of Power, implemented by Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE) under National Mission for Enhanced Energy Efficiency (NMEEE, part of NAPCC 2008). - Target: - 8 energy-intensive industries (Thermal Power, Aluminium, Cement, Fertilizer, Iron-Steel, Pulp-Paper, Textiles, Chlor-Alkali). - Mechanism: - Industries must reduce energy consumption as per assigned quotas or face penalties. - Incentives: - Overachievers earn Energy Saving Certificates (ESCerts) via BEE’s PATNET portal, tradable to underachieving firms (similar to Priority Sector Lending Certificates). - Regulator: - Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (CERC) sets ESCert prices. - Green Credit Programme (Budget 2023): - Notified under Environment (Protection) Act, 1986. - Objective: - Promote environmentally beneficial activities (e.g., water saving, waste management) through voluntary participation. - Trading Mechanisms: RPO, PAT, CCTS, GCP: - Renewable Purchase Obligation (RPO, 2014): - Ministry: - Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE). - Objective: - Mandates electricity companies to source a percentage of electricity from renewables. - Legal Basis: - Electricity Act, 2003 (compulsory). - Perform, Achieve and Trade (PAT, 2012): - Ministry: - Ministry of Power. - Objective: - Reduce energy use in large industries. - Legal Basis: - Energy Conservation Act, 2001 (compulsory). - Carbon Credit and Trading Scheme (CCTS, June 2023): - Ministry: - Ministry of Power. - Objective: - Replace PAT, reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. - Legal Basis: - Energy Conservation Act, 2001 (2022 Amendment, compulsory). - Green Credit Programme (GCP, Oct 2023): - Ministry: - Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change. - Objective: - Encourage voluntary environmental actions (e.g., water management, waste management). - Legal Basis: - Mission-LiFE (voluntary). - Difference between GCP and CCTS: - Compulsory: - CCTS: - Legally required for specified industries (Energy Conservation Act). - GCP: - Voluntary under Mission-LiFE. - Ministry: - CCTS: - Ministry of Power. - GCP: - Ministry of Environment. - Regulator/Administrator: - CCTS: - BEE and National Steering Committee (Power Secretary). - GCP: - Indian Council of Forestry Research and Education (Environment Ministry). - Objective: - CCTS: - Reduce GHG emissions. - GCP: - Broader environmental goals (e.g., tree plantation, sustainable agriculture, air pollution reduction). - Certificate: - CCTS: - 1 Carbon Credit = 1 ton of CO2 equivalent (tCO2e). - GCP: - Credit value determined by administrator. - Electricity: National LED Programme: - Boss: - Ministry of Power, implemented by Energy Efficiency Services Ltd. (EESL). - Components: - Unnat Jeevan by Affordable LEDs and Appliances for All (UJALA): Subsidized LED bulbs for households (previously Domestic Efficient Lighting Program, DELP). - Street Lighting National Program: EESL replaces halogen streetlights with LEDs at no cost. - Electricity: Gram Ujala Programme: - Boss: - Ministry of Power, implemented by EESL’s Convergence Energy Services Ltd. (CESL). - Mechanism: - Villagers exchange working incandescent bulbs and pay ₹10 for LED bulbs (3-year warranty, max 5 bulbs per villager). - Benefits: - 12W LED bulb equals 100W incandescent bulb, reducing CO2 emissions. - Longer lifespan, lower energy bills, and reduced waste. - Electricity: Miscellaneous Energy Efficiency Schemes: - ESCO Company (Budget 2022): Promote energy efficiency in large commercial buildings. - Atal Jyoti Yojana (AJAY): Free solar LED streetlights in special category states, Assam, Bihar, Jharkhand, Odisha, Uttar Pradesh, aspirational districts, Andaman & Nicobar, Lakshadweep (75% MNRE, 25% MPLADS funding). - SAATHI: - Ministry of Power and Textiles funds EESL to provide energy-efficient equipment to small/medium powerlooms. - Star Label: - BEE’s labeling for energy-efficient appliances (see Pillar 4B). - Smart Electricity Meters: - EESL assists DISCOMs with IT-enabled meters for remote monitoring, reducing theft. - FCI Ethanol (2019): - Ethanol production from surplus rice/maize with Food Corporation of India (see Pillar 4A). - UNNATEE: - BEE’s 2017-2031 strategy for national energy efficiency. - SIDHIEE: - Power Ministry’s portal for energy efficiency best practices in MSMEs. - Eco-Niwas Samhita: - BEE’s energy conservation standards for residential buildings. - Building Energy Efficiency Programme (BEEP): EESL’s initiative for commercial buildings. - Energy Index Global Reports: - World Energy Investment Report (IEA): - 2021: - Top energy consumers: - 1) China, 2) USA, 3) EU, 4) India.' - By 2040: - India projected to surpass EU as 3rd largest. - Global Energy Transition Index (World Economic Forum, Geneva): - Measures CO2/pollution in energy production and commitment to reduction. - 2023 Ranking: - 1) Sweden, 2) Denmark, 3) Norway, 67) India (improving rank). - World Energy Transitions Outlook (IRENA, Abu Dhabi): - Highlights global renewable energy trends. - India Energy Outlook Report (IEA, Paris): - 2021: - India as 4th largest energy consumer. - By 2030: - India to become 3rd largest, with fuel import bill tripling in 20 years. - State Energy Efficiency Index: By BEE and Alliance for an Energy Efficient Economy (AEEE). - Infrastructure: Renewable Energy: - Context: - Under UNFCCC Paris Accord (2015), India’s Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) include: - By 2030: - Reduce emission intensity of GDP by 33-35% from 2005 levels. - By 2030: - 40% of installed power capacity from non-fossil fuel sources. - Target (2022): - 175 GW renewable capacity (100 GW solar, 60 GW wind, 10 GW biomass, 5 GW small hydro). - PM Modi’s Panchamrit @ COP-26 Glasgow (2021): - Announced at UNFCCC COP-26 Summit, UK, with Lifestyle for Environment (LiFE) proposal. - Updated NDCs (2022): - By 2030: - 500 GW renewable energy capacity (not in NDC). - By 2030: - 50% of energy from non-fossil fuels (included in NDC). - By 2030: - Reduce emission intensity by 45% from 2005 levels (included in NDC). - By 2070: - Net-zero emissions (not in NDC). - By 2030: - Reduce 1 billion tonnes of projected carbon emissions (not in NDC). - Carbon sink of 2.5-3 billion tonnes via afforestation (included in NDC). - Budget 2022: - 280 GW solar capacity by 2030, with Production Linked Incentive (PLI) for solar cell manufacturing (see Pillar 4B). - [Yearbook] Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE): - Departments/Statutory Bodies: - None MCQ-worthy. - Autonomous Bodies: - National Institute of Solar Energy (NISE, Gurugram): Developed Solar Atlas of India. - National Institute of Wind Energy (NIWE, Chennai): Developed Wind Atlas of India. - Sardar Swaran Singh National Institute of Renewable Energy (SSS NIRE, Kapurthala, Punjab). - National Institute of Bio Energy (NIBE, Kapurthala, Punjab). - CPSEs: - Indian Renewable Energy Development Agency (IREDA, Delhi). - Solar Energy Corporation of India (SECI, Delhi): Set up India’s largest Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) in Rajnandgaon, Chhattisgarh. - Portals: - India Renewable Idea Exchange (IRIX) Portal. - Akshay Urja Portal and Magazine. - Renewable: KUSUM (2019): - Full Name: - Kisan Urja Suraksha evam Utthaan Mahabhiyan. - Boss: - MNRE. - Components: - Install solar pump tube wells for irrigation (reduces diesel use). - Farmers/panchayats/cooperatives install up to 2 MW renewable plants on barren/cultivable land. - Sell excess electricity to DISCOMs (prices set by SERC). - Funding: - Union (30%), State (30%), Bank Loan (30%), Farmer (10%). - Benefit: - Reduces diesel/thermal electricity use, cuts 27 million tonnes CO2 annually, increases farmer income. - Renewable: Jawaharlal Nehru National Solar Mission (2009-10): - Part of NAPCC 2008 (Manmohan Singh). - Targets: - Original (Manmohan): - 20,000 MW by 2022. - Modi: - 100 GW by 2022. - Budget 2022: - 280 GW by 2030. - Boss: - MNRE. - Initiatives: - SRISTI: - Subsidies for rooftop solar equipment. - Tax-free solar bonds. - Rooftop solar in government complexes. - State building bye-laws mandating rooftop solar in large private buildings. - Solar parks on wastelands. - Net-metering for residential/commercial solar power sales to DISCOMs. - Surya Mitra: - 90-day skill development for solar equipment installation/repair. - ARUN Mobile App: - Assists rooftop solar installation. - Solar City Initiative (2012-17): 60 cities to replace 10% conventional energy with solar. - Amending Electricity Act for RPO and Renewable Generation Obligation (RGO). - Renewable: Renewable Purchase Obligation (RPO): - Applicable: - DISCOMs, large electricity consumers, captive power plants. - Requirement: - Purchase a minimum percentage of electricity from renewable sources (set by MNRE). - Quotas: - 2014 (11.5%), 2018 (17%), 2019 (17.5%), 2022 (21%), with internal solar/non-solar and Hydropower Purchase Obligation (HPO) quotas. - Pricing: - Set by CERC (interstate) or SERC (intrastate). - Related: - Renewable Generation Obligation (RGO) mandates coal-based thermal plants to generate/procure a percentage of renewable energy. - Renewable: World’s Largest Hybrid Renewable Energy Park (Khavda): - Location: - Kutch, Gujarat (near Indo-Pakistan border). - Capacity: - 30,000 MW (solar + wind) over 72,600 hectares. - Operators: - Adani Green, Gujarat State Electricity Company, etc. - Renewable/Energy Efficiency Rankings/Portals: - SARAL Index: - By MNRE, Shakti Sustainable Energy Foundation, ASSOCHAM, Ernst & Young; ranks states for rooftop solar attractiveness. - SAATHEE Portal: - Power Ministry’s portal to monitor state-level energy efficiency. - PM Surya Ghar Muft Bijli Yojana (Interim Budget 2024): - Boss: - MNRE. - Loan: - Interest Rate: - Repo + 0.5% (currently 7%). - Collateral: - Not required. - Subsidy: - Up to 2 kW: 60% (₹30,000 for 1 kW, ₹60,000 for 2 kW). - 2-3 kW: - 40% (₹78,000 for 3 kW). - Above 3 kW: - No subsidy. - Eligibility: - Indian citizen. - Owns a house with a suitable roof for solar panels. - Valid electricity connection. - No prior solar panel subsidy availed. - Benefits: - Saves electricity bills. - Earns income by selling surplus power to DISCOMs. - Example: - 3 kW panel with 300 units/month usage saves ~₹15,000/year. - Energy: E20 Blending (Fossil Fuel Reduction): - Context: - Dr. Rakesh Sarwal Committee (2021) roadmap for ethanol blending (2020-2025). - Targets: - E10 (10% ethanol in petrol): Achieved by 2022. - E20 (20% ethanol in petrol): By 2025, reduces CO emissions by 30-50%, hydrocarbons by 20%. - Support: - R&D funding for E20-compliant vehicle engines. - Tax/subsidy for E20-compliant vehicles. - Divert surplus sugarcane/rice for ethanol; promote maize/non-food crops for future sustainability. - Loan interest subsidies for ethanol distilleries. - Ultimate Goal: - E100 (100% ethanol vehicles). - Benefits: - Saves ₹30,000 crore in fuel imports annually, enhances energy security, reduces emissions, uses damaged grains, boosts farmer income, creates jobs. - Biogas Blending in Natural Gas: - Boss: - Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas. - Process: - Biogas from anaerobic decomposition (agriculture residue, cattle dung, municipal waste) is purified (remove CO2, H2S) to produce Compressed Biogas (CBG). - Blending Targets: - 2024-25: - Voluntary. - 2025-26: - 1%. - 2026-27: - 3%. - 2027-28: - 4%. - Applications: - Blend CBG with CNG (vehicles) or PNG (cooking), delivered via city gas distribution pipelines. - Benefits: - Increases biogas use in cooking/transport. - Reduces LNG imports, saves forex, promotes circular economy. - Enhances logistics efficiency, reduces air pollution from LPG cylinder transport. - Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF): - Definition: - Liquid fuel for commercial aviation, produced from food waste, fats, green/municipal waste, and non-food crops blended with jet fuel. - Benefit: - Reduces CO2 emissions by up to 80%. - Targets (Petroleum & Natural Gas Ministry): - 2027: - 1% SAF blending (international flights). - 2028: - 2% SAF blending (international flights). - Energy: Green, Grey, Blue Hydrogen: - Green Hydrogen: - Production: - Electrolysis of water using renewable energy (solar/wind). - Emissions: - Zero. - Cost: - High (expected to decrease). - Blue Hydrogen: - Production: - Steam Methane Reforming (SMR) with carbon capture and storage (CCS). - Emissions: - Low. - Cost: - Moderate. - Grey Hydrogen: - Production: - SMR without CCS. - Emissions: - High. - Cost: - Low. - SMR Process: - CH4 + H2O → CO + 3H2 (synthesis gas/syngas). - Energy: National Hydrogen Mission (Budget 2021, PM Modi’s August 2021 Speech): - Historical Context: - Ancient Indus Valley Civilization prioritized sanitation with integrated systems in town planning. However, by 2012, over 50% of Indians practiced open defecation due to neglect by policymakers. - Significance: - Access to clean water and sanitation is critical for public health, dignity (especially for women), and environmental sustainability. - Related Reference: - Pillar 4A (Agriculture) for irrigation and drinking water schemes. - Infrastructure: Sanitation - Swachh Bharat Mission (SBM, 2014) - Introduction: - Launched on October 2, 2014, by PM Narendra Modi, restructured from Nirmal Bharat Abhiyan (2012, PM Manmohan Singh). - Boss: - Originally Ministry of Drinking Water & Sanitation, now under Ministry of Jal Shakti. - Funding: - Core scheme (not 100% Union-funded; 60:40 or 90:10 Union-State ratio) with Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) contributions. - Recognition: - PM Modi received the Global Gatekeeper Award (2019) from the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation for SBM. - Objective: - Achieve a clean and open defecation-free (ODF) India by promoting sanitation, waste management, and behavioral change. - Phases: - Phase 1 (2014-2019): - Focused on toilet construction, ODF status, and awareness. - Phase 2 (2020-2025): - Reinforces ODF status, emphasizes waste management and sustainability. - Target of Swachhta Diwas (October 2, 2019) - Gandhi’s 150th Birth Anniversary: - Open Defecation Free (ODF) India. - Eradication of manual scavenging. - Improved Municipal Solid Waste Management (MSWM). - Outcome: - Approximately 90 million toilets constructed by 2019, per government data.[](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swachh_Bharat_Mission) - SBM - How to Achieve Targets: - Construction: - Financial assistance for building individual household toilets, community toilets, bathing houses, and public toilets at bus stations, schools, and temporary construction sites. - Solid Waste Management: - Funding for trucks, garbage disposal units, and infrastructure. - Awareness Campaigns: - Information, Education, and Communication (IEC) initiatives via Swachhta Doots, social media, posters, and advertisements. - Darwaza Band Campaign: - Promotes toilet use to prevent open defecation. - Research and Development: - Innovations in sanitation technologies. - Mobile Applications: - Platforms for reporting unclean areas and public grievances. - Citizen Engagement: - Encourages large-scale participation through community clean-ups and sustainable practices.[](https://www.mygov.in/campaigns/swachh-bharat) - SBM - Who Implements the Scheme: - Rural Areas: - Department of Drinking Water & Sanitation, Ministry of Jal Shakti. - Urban Areas: - Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs (MoHUA). - SBM Gramin Phase 2 (2020-2025): - Objective: - Ensure sustained toilet use and expand waste management. - Features: - Plastic waste management. - Animal and biodegradable solid waste management. - Greywater management (used domestic water, excluding toilet wastewater). - Fecal sludge management. - Progress (2023): - 50% of villages achieved ODF Plus status, with Telangana at 100% ODF Plus.[](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swachh_Bharat_Mission) - SBM Village Types: - Aspiring: - Sustains ODF status + arrangements for either solid or liquid waste management. - Rising: - Sustains ODF status + arrangements for both solid and liquid waste management. - Model (ODF Plus): - Rising category + visual cleanliness (minimal litter, stagnant wastewater, no plastic waste dumps) + displays ODF Plus IEC messages. - SBM Urban 2.0 (Budget 2021): - Timeline: - 2021-2026. - Funding: - Over ₹1 lakh crore. - Features: - Management of fecal sludge and wastewater. - Garbage segregation. - Reduction in single-use plastics. - Decreased air pollution from construction and demolition activities. - Bioremediation of dumpsites. - Emphasis on circular economy principles. - SBM Protocols: - Note: - Specific protocols not detailed in raw text, but typically include guidelines for ODF verification, waste management standards, and citizen engagement strategies. - Big Cities (3-10 lakh): Noida, Chandigarh. - Million Plus (>10 lakh): Navi Mumbai, Indore, Surat. - Infrastructure: Sanitation - Swachhta Udyami Yojana (2014): - Boss: - Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment, implemented by National Safai Karamcharis Finance and Development Corporation. -
