Developer: - Central Ground Water Authority. - Objective: - Manage groundwater resources, monitor usage, and ensure sustainability. - FloodWatch India App (v2.0): - Developer: - Central Water Commission. - Objective: - Provide real-time flood forecasts and warnings. - Pillar 5B1: Infrastructure - Transport (Inland Waterways, Shipping & Ports) - Overview: - Transport infrastructure, including inland waterways and ports, is critical for economic growth, trade, and connectivity. - Economic Survey 2025: - India’s navigable waterway length is approximately 14,850 km, with 26 operational waterways spanning over 4,800 km. - Significance: - Inland Waterways Transport (IWT) and ports facilitate low-carbon, cost-effective cargo movement, reducing road/rail congestion. - Infrastructure: Transport - Inland Waterways - Benefits of Inland Waterways Transport (IWT): - Lower CO2 emissions and fuel consumption per tonne of cargo compared to rail/road. - Minimal land acquisition required compared to rail/road infrastructure. - Eases traffic congestion on road/rail networks. - Inland Waterways - Inland Waterway Authority of India (IWAI): - Boss: - Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways. - Status: - Statutory body established under the Inland Waterways Authority of India Act, 1985. - Functions: - Develops and regulates inland waterways for navigation and transport. - Inland Waterways - National Waterways: - Legal Basis: - 7th Schedule (Union List); Parliament can legislate on inland waterways. - National Waterways Act, 2016: Declared 111 national waterways, including 5 pre-existing ones. - Key National Waterways (Operational): - NW-1: - Ganga-Bhagirathi-Hooghly River System (Haldia-Allahabad, 1,620 km, UP/Bihar/Jharkhand/WB). - NW-2: - Brahmaputra River (Dhubri-Sadiya, 891 km, Assam). - NW-3: - West Coast, Champakara, and Udyogmandal Canals (205 km, Kerala). - NW-4: - Krishna, Godavari, and Canals (2,890 km when completed, TN/Andhra/Telangana). - NW-5: - Mahanadi Delta Rivers and Canals (588 km, Odisha/WB). - NW-40: - Ghagra/Saryu River (354 km, UP; planned for Ramayan Cruise Tour, Ayodhya). - Others: - NW-68 (Mandovi, Goa), NW-111 (Zuari, Goa), NW-97 (Sundarbans). - Note: - Over 20 waterways are currently operational, per Economic Survey 2025. - Inland Waterways - Jal Marg Vikas Project (2014): - Objective: - Develop infrastructure for commercial navigation on NW-1 (Varanasi-Haldia stretch of Ganga). - Challenges: - Low depth upstream of Farakka, limiting large vessel navigation. - Features: - Construction of navigational locks and infrastructure. - Roll on-Roll off (Ro-Ro) ferries. - Digital tools: - River Information System (RIS) and Vessel Traffic Management System (VTMS). - Multi-modal terminal at Varanasi (inaugurated November 2018 by PM Modi, received cargo ship MV Rabindranath Tagore from Kolkata). - Funding: - Central Sector Scheme (100% Union-funded) with World Bank (IBRD) loans and Public-Private Partnership (PPP). - Completion: - Targeted for March 2023, aimed at transforming Ganga into “Arth Ganga” (River of Wealth). - Additional: - Varanasi designated as India’s first freight village for cargo operations. - Arth-Ganga (August 2022): - Objective: - Promote sustainable economic development along the Ganga beyond cleaning. - Six Pillars: 1. Zero Budget Natural Farming: Chemical-free farming within 10 km of Ganga, promoting cow dung fertilizers via GOBARdhan scheme. 2. Sludge and Wastewater Management: Recycling for irrigation and industrial use. 3. Cultural Heritage: Boat tourism, adventure sports, and yoga activities. 4. Livelihood Opportunities: Local markets for products, medicinal plants, and Ayurveda. 5. Local Administration Improvement. 6. Public Participation Enhancement. - MV Ganga Vilas - Longest River Luxury Cruise: - Overview: - World’s longest river cruise, covering 3,200 km in 51 days across 27 rivers. - Route: - Varanasi (UP) to Dibrugarh (Assam) via Bangladesh. - Coverage: - 50 tourist spots, including world heritage sites, national parks, river ghats, and cities (Patna, Sahibganj, Kolkata, Dhaka, Guwahati). - Operator: - Antara Luxury River Cruises (Kolkata-based private company). - Ticket Price: - ₹25,000/day onwards. - Inland Vessels Act, 2021: - Note: - Outdated/low-profile topic, removed from study material due to limited exam relevance. - Harit Nauka Initiative: - Objective: - Promote green fuels/technology in inland waterway vessels. - Milestone (February 2024): - PM Modi launched India’s first hydrogen cell-powered inland waterway vessel, manufactured by Cochin Shipyard. - Green Hydrogen Hub: - V.O. Chidambaranar Port (Tuticorin) designated as India’s first Green Hydrogen Hub Port. - Jalvahak Scheme (2025): - Boss: - Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways. - Feature: - 35% subsidy on cargo transportation costs via NW-1 (Ganga), NW-2 (Brahmaputra), and NW-16 (Barak). - Infrastructure: Transport - Shipping & Ports - Context: - India’s coastline: - ~7,517 km. - Trade: - ~95% of trade by volume and 68% by value transported via sea. - Alang-Sosiya (Gujarat): - World’s largest ship recycling yard, operational since 1983. - [Yearbook] Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways: - Old Name: - Ministry of Shipping (renamed in 2020). - Statutory Bodies: - Inland Waterway Authority of India (IWAI). - Tariff Authority for Major Ports (TAMP): Sets fees for major ports. - Indian Maritime University (IMU, Chennai): Established via IMU Act, 2008, for maritime education, training, and research. - Directorate General of Shipping (Mumbai): National Authority for Ship Recycling under Recycling of Ships Act, 2019 (office in Gandhinagar, Gujarat). - Directorate General of Lighthouses and Lightships. - Minor Ports Survey Organisation. - Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs): - Shipping Corporation of India (Mumbai, approved for disinvestment in 2019). - Dredging Corporation of India Ltd. - Kamarajar Port Ltd. (Ennore, Tamil Nadu). - Cochin Shipyard Ltd. (Cochin). - Central Inland Water Transport Corporation Ltd. - Hooghly Dock & Port Engineers Ltd. - Sethusamudram Corporation Ltd. - Global Cooperation: - International Maritime Organization (IMO, London): UN agency for shipping regulation. - Hong Kong International Convention (2009, ratified by India in 2019): Safe and environmentally sound ship recycling. - UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS, 1982, Jamaica): Regulates maritime activities; notable for 2012 Enrica Lexie case (Italian marines killed Indian fishermen off Kerala). - Polar Code (IMO): - Safety guidelines for ships in polar waters (e.g., ice removal equipment, thermal clothing). - Miscellaneous: - Ropax Service: - Roll on-Roll off cum passenger ferry service launched in March 2020 (Mumbai-Mandwa, Maharashtra). - Types of Ports - Classification Method #1: Major and Minor Ports: - Legal Basis: - Indian Ports Act, 1908. - Major Ports: - 12 operational, regulated by Union Government (Union List, 7th Schedule). - Minor Ports: - Over 200, regulated by State Governments (Concurrent List). - Note: - Government reports list 12 operational major ports, though new ports (e.g., Galathea Bay) are notified. - List of Major Ports in India (A: Artificial, N: Natural Harbor): - West Coast (6): - Jawaharlal Nehru Port (Nhava Sheva, Maharashtra, N, 1989): Largest container port (per NCERT), satellite to Mumbai Port. - Mumbai Port (Maharashtra, N): Largest oil terminal in India. - Deendayal Port (Kandla, Gujarat, N): Tidal port, first Special Economic Zone (SEZ) in India/Asia, developed post-Partition. - Mormugao Port (Goa, N): Tidal port at Zuari estuary, exports iron ore to Japan. - New Mangalore Port (Karnataka, A): Deep-water, all-weather port (1974-75). - Cochin Port (Kerala, N): Willingdon Island, developed during British Raj, known as Queen of the Arabian Sea. - East Coast (6): - Kolkata Port (West Bengal, N): Oldest major port, riverine port on Hooghly River with Kolkata and Haldia docks; requires constant dredging due to silt. - Vishakhapatnam Port (Andhra Pradesh, N): Land-locked harbor, Eastern Naval Command base. - Paradeep Port (Odisha, A): Manmade lagoon in Mahanadi Delta, Union-owned since 1965. - V.O. Chidambaranar Port (Tuticorin, Tamil Nadu, N): Gulf of Mannar. - Chennai Port (Tamil Nadu, A): All-weather port (1875), less suitable for large ships due to shallow waters. - Kamarajar Port (Ennore, Tamil Nadu, A): Corporate port under Companies Act, primarily for thermal coal for Tamil Nadu Electricity Board. - Additional Developments: - 2010: - Port Blair (Andaman & Nicobar) announced as a major port. - 2016: - New major ports announced: Sagar (West Bengal), Duggirajupatnam (Andhra Pradesh), Vadhavan (Maharashtra), Enayam (Tamil Nadu). - 2020: - Vadhavan Port (Maharashtra) to be developed via Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV) with Jawaharlal Nehru Port Trust (JNPT) holding ≥50% shares. - 2024: - Galathea Bay (Great Nicobar, Bay of Bengal) notified as the 13th major port. - Budget 2020: - Plan to corporatize at least one major port and list its shares on stock exchanges. - Note: - For state PSC exams, assume 12 operational major ports unless options specify otherwise. - Vizhinjam International Seaport (Kerala, Under Construction): - Overview: - India’s first deep-water transshipment port, developed by Adani Group. - Significance: - Addresses lack of mega-ports for ultra-large container ships; currently, 75% of India’s transshipment cargo is handled at Colombo, Singapore, and Klang (Malaysia). - Minor Port - Mundra, Gujarat: - Overview: - India’s first greenfield Public-Private Partnership (PPP) port, operated by Adani Ports and Special Economic Zone Ltd. (APSEZL). - Model: - Build, Own, Operate, and Transfer (BOOT); Adani operates for 30 years before transferring to Gujarat government. - Status: - Largest privately owned port in India. - Types of Ports - Classification Method #2: - Dry Ports: - Inland terminals connected to seaports by rail/road (e.g., Patna, Bihar; Hazira, Gujarat; 20+ under development since 2018). - Industrial Ports: - Handle bulk cargo (grain, sugar, ore, oil, chemicals). - Commercial Ports: - Handle general cargo and passengers. - Comprehensive Ports: - Combine industrial and commercial facilities. - Packet Stations: - Ferry ports for short-distance passenger/mail transport (e.g., Dover, England; Calais, France). - Inland Ports: - Located away from sea via rivers/canals (e.g., Kolkata, Memphis, Rhine, Manchester). - Out Ports: - Deep-water ports built away from main ports for large ships (e.g., Piraeus for Athens, Greece). - Ports of Call: - Anchor points for refueling, watering, and food supplies (e.g., Aden, Honolulu, Singapore). - Entrepot Ports: - Collection centers for goods from various countries for export (e.g., Singapore, Rotterdam, Copenhagen). - Naval Ports: - For warship repair/construction (e.g., Kochi, Karwar). - Major Port Authorities Bill, 2020: - Note: - Technical topic, removed from study material due to low exam relevance. - Ports - Challenges in India: - Neglected Infrastructure: - Aging fleets, manpower shortages, and lack of world-class ports; large ships unload at Sri Lanka for transshipment to India. - Congestion and Delays: - High turnaround times, excessive paperwork, slow customs clearance/inspection. - Connectivity Issues: - Inadequate road/rail links to hinterland. - Major Port Inefficiencies: - Labor union issues and politicization of Boards of Directors; minor ports (privately owned) are more efficient. - Land and Environmental Issues: Challenges in land acquisition and environmental clearances for new ports. - Underdeveloped Shipbuilding: - Domestic shipping companies rely on costly foreign ships due to weak domestic industry. - History: - Proposed by PM Vajpayee (2003), ignored by Manmohan Singh, revived by PM Modi (2015). - Boss: - Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways. - Funding: - Central Sector Scheme (0% state funding), implemented via Sagarmala Development Company Ltd. (2016) through Special Purpose Vehicles (SPVs) with state/private participation. - Objectives: - Develop/improve ports and encourage coastal shipping. - Establish Coastal Economic Zones (CEZs) for manufacturing and employment. - Enhance hinterland connectivity via rail, road, and inland water transport. - Skill development for coastal communities. - Related Initiatives: - SAGAR-SETU: - Mobile app to improve Ease of Doing Business. - Harit Sagar: - Vision for zero carbon emissions from ports. - Sagar Manthan: - Incorrectly noted as a fish production mission (not relevant to Shipping Ministry). - Costa Serena: - First international cruise liner in India. - Infrastructure: Transport - Blue Economy Policy 2021: - Boss: - Ministry of Earth Sciences (MoES). - Objective: - Sustainable use of ocean resources for job creation and GDP growth, aligning with UN SDG #14 (Life Below Water). - Context: - India’s coastline: - ~7,500 km, 12 major ports, 9 coastal states, 1,300+ islands, 2 million sq.km Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ). - Resources: - Living (algae, fish, prawns) and non-living (oil, gas, polymetallic nodules). - Features: - Fisheries and marine food processing. - Deep-sea mining and offshore energy. - Research and skill development. - Interim Budget 2024: - Blue Economy 2.0 focuses on coastal aquaculture and mariculture (see Pillar 4A). - Related: - Sethusamudram Project (1997) to create a shipping canal between Palk Bay and Gulf of Mannar; pending in Supreme Court due to marine biodiversity and Ram Sethu concerns. - Infrastructure: Transport - Maritime Vision 2030: - Objective: - Enhance ships, ports, exports, and create 7-10 lakh jobs. - Note: - Overlaps with Blue Economy Policy; low-priority technical details. - Infrastructure: Transport - Multi-Modal Transportation of Goods Bill, 2019: - Definition: - Multimodal transport uses multiple modes (rail, road, sea) for goods movement. - Original Act (1993): - Governs registration and liability for cargo delays/damage. - 2019 Proposal: - Replace 1993 Act with updated provisions (technical, low exam relevance). - Pillar 5B2: Infrastructure - Transport (Roads) - Overview: - Importance: - A robust road network is essential for economic growth, connecting remote areas, opening backward regions, and facilitating access to markets, trade, and investment. - Data: - India has the world’s second-largest road network (64 lakh km) after the USA (66 lakh km). National Highways (NH) constitute 2% of the total network (146,195 km) but carry 40% of road freight traffic (Economic Survey 2025). - Economic Contribution: - Road transport generates the highest Gross Value Added (GVA) within transport services. - [Yearbook] Ministry of Road Transport & Highways: - Statutory Bodies: - National Highways Authority of India (NHAI): Manages national highways. - Central Public Sector Enterprise (CPSE): - National Highways and Infrastructure Development Corporation (NHIDCL). - Autonomous Bodies: - Indian Academy of Highway Engineers (IAHE): Training for highway engineers. - Indian Road Congress (IRC): Organizes conferences on road construction, maintenance, and development. - Number Plates: - 2019: - ‘LA’ number plates for vehicles registered in Ladakh UT. - 2021: - ‘BH’ series for Defense personnel, government employees, and private companies with offices in 4+ states/UTs. - Green Number Plates: - Notified for electric vehicles. - E-Governance Initiatives: - Vahan Portal: - Vehicle registration, taxation, permits, and fitness services. - Sarathi Portal: - Driving licenses, learner licenses, and driving school services. - mParivahan App: - Combines features of Vahan and Sarathi portals. - Integrated Road Accident Database (iRAD): Developed with IIT Madras and National Informatics Centre (NIC) for accident data analysis. - Bhoomi-Rashi Portal: - Facilitates land acquisition for highways. - Data Lake and Project Management Software: NHAI’s digital platform for paperless decision-making and dispute resolution in highway construction. - Infrastructure: Transport - Road Types: - National Highways: - Responsibility: - Union Government (NHAI). - Connects: - State capitals, major cities, ports. - State Highways: - Responsibility: - State Government (Public Works Department - PWD). - Connects: - State capital to district headquarters. - District Roads: - Responsibility: - Zila Parishad. - Connects: - District headquarters to tehsils and blocks. - Village Roads: - Responsibility: - Gram Panchayat. - Connects: - Villages to neighboring towns. - Expressways: - Responsibility: - Public-Private Partnership (PPP) or Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV), often under NHAI. - Features: - Six- to eight-lane high-class highways (e.g., Ahmedabad-Vadodara Expressway by NHAI and IRB Infrastructure Developers). - Associated Organizations: - NHAI, State PWD, Border Roads Organisation (BRO, under Ministry of Defence). - Road Length Hierarchy (largest to smallest): Other roads > State highways > National highways > Expressways. - Transport - National Highways Authority of India (NHAI, 1988): - Status: - Statutory body under Ministry of Road Transport and Highways. - Funding Sources: - Road and Infrastructure Cess on petrol/diesel (Central Road and Infrastructure Fund, non-lapsable, 2000). - External assistance (World Bank, ADB, Japan Bank for International Cooperation). - Market borrowings and PPP. - 2019: - NHAI established Infrastructure Investment Trust (InvITs) for fundraising (see Pillar 1C). - GATI Portal (2020): - Monitors highway construction progress, allows contractors to file complaints (e.g., against delays or corruption). - NHAI Functions: - Develop, maintain, and manage national highways. - Collect fees (tolls) on national highways. - Regulate vehicle size/weight on highways. - Provide consultancy and construction services in India and abroad. - Conduct research on highway development. - Transport - National Highways Development Programme (NHDP, 1998): - Launched by: - PM Atal Bihari Vajpayee. - Components: - Golden Quadrilateral (GQ): - Connects Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai, Kolkata. - North-South Corridor: - Connects Srinagar to Kanyakumari. - East-West Corridor: - Connects Silchar to Porbandar. - Related Term: - Diamond Quadrilateral (High-Speed Railways connecting major metros). - Transport - Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana (PMGSY, 2000): - Boss: - Ministry of Rural Development. - Funding: - Centrally Sponsored Core Scheme (60:40 for general states, 90:10 for special category states). - Objective: - Construct all-weather single-lane roads for unconnected rural habitations. - Targets (by 2019): - Habitations with ≥500 population (plains, per 2001 Census). - Habitations with ≥250 population (special category states, tribal districts, desert areas). - Habitations with 100-249 population in Naxal/Left-Wing Extremism (LWE) areas by 2020. - Phases: - PMGSY-II (2013): - Repair existing rural roads and construct new ones. - PMGSY-III (2019-2025): - Upgrade 1,25,000 km of roads, including bridges, connecting agricultural markets, schools, and hospitals. - Technology: - Uses green technologies (waste plastic, cold mix) to reduce carbon footprint. - Monitoring: - eMARG portal (scheme progress), Meri-Sadak App (citizen feedback). - Benefits (World Bank Study, 2019): Increased school enrollment, institutional deliveries, and vaccination rates in rural areas. - Transport - Bharatmala Pariyojana (2017): - Boss: - Ministry of Road Transport and Highways (NHAI). - Funding: - Cess, PPP, SPV. - Objective: - Upgrade and expand highways from NHDP, focusing on coastal areas, economic corridors, and border regions (for troop movement and trade with Nepal, Bhutan, Bangladesh, Myanmar). - Phase 1: - Upgrade 24,800 km of national highways by 2022. - Transport - Green National Highways Corridor Project (2016): - Objective: - Develop eco-friendly national highways. - Coverage: - Rajasthan, Himachal Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh, Andhra Pradesh. - Transport - E-Toll Collection via FASTag (2017): - Reference: - Pillar 1A-1 (Digital Payments). - Features: - RFID-based toll collection to reduce delays at toll plazas. - Satellite-Based Toll Collection: - Transition from FASTag: - Before: - Vehicles slow down at toll plazas for RFID scanning (~50 seconds). - After: - GPS-based system using Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) tracks distance traveled, deducts tolls directly from bank accounts. - Benefits: - Zero wait time at toll plazas. - Pay only for distance traveled (e.g., 80 km instead of full 180 km). - Eliminates need for FASTag recharges. - Status (March 2025): - Postponed due to security and privacy concerns. - Transport - NoWAIT@Railway Crossing: Setu Bharatam: - Boss: - Ministry of Road Transport and Highways. - Funding: - Central Sector Scheme (100% Union-funded). - Objective: - Eliminate railway level crossings on national highways by constructing Railway Over Bridges (ROB) or Railway Under Bridges (RUB). - Deadline: - 2019. - Benefits: - Reduced traffic congestion, fewer accidents, and lower staffing needs for railway crossings. - Transport - Char Dham Mahamarg Vikas Pariyojana: - Boss: - Ministry of Road Transport and Highways. - Objective: - Build/renovate roads connecting four pilgrimage sites in Uttarakhand: Gangotri, Yamunotri, Kedarnath, Badrinath. - Transport - Fossil Fuel Reduction: Electric Vehicles (EVs): - Definition: EVs are propelled by rechargeable batteries, classified as: - Battery Electric Vehicles (BEVs): Fully electric. - Hybrid Electric Vehicles (HEVs): Run on both battery and petrol/diesel. - Context: - Transport sector is India’s second-largest CO2 emitter after industry. EVs reduce emissions and oil imports. - Data: - EV market share in India <1% (vs. 2% in China, 40% in Norway). - EVs in India - Steps to Promote: - 100% FDI via automatic route in the automobile sector. - National Electric Mobility Mission Plan (NEMMP, 2013): Promotes electric and hybrid vehicles. - FAME Scheme (2015, Ministry of Heavy Industries): - Phase I: - Initial promotion of EV adoption. - Phase II (2019-2024): - Targets 2,700 charging stations (3x3 km grid in cities, every 25 km on highways), electrifies public transport, reduces GST on EVs to 5%. - Budget 2019: - Income tax deduction on EV loans. - Green Number Plates: - For EVs. - E-AMRIT Portal: - Launched at COP26 (2021, Glasgow) by NITI Aayog and UK Government to promote EV awareness. - Phased Manufacturing Program (PMP): - Objective: - Provide tax benefits for manufacturing EVs, components, and other electronics (e.g., smart watches, touchscreens). - Boss: - Ministries of Heavy Industries (EVs) and Electronics (other devices). - Note: - Low-profile scheme, less exam-relevant compared to RODTEP/PLI/FAME. - 100% EV Adoption - NITI vs. Highway Ministry: - 2017: - NITI Aayog proposed 40% private transport to be electric by 2030. - 2019 (June): - NITI proposed only EVs to be sold post-2030. - 2019 (August): Union Minister Nitin Gadkari clarified: - No ban on petrol/diesel vehicles. - No deadline for automakers to switch to EVs. - NITI Aayog lacks authority to set EV deadlines. - Economic Survey 2019 - EVs: Charging Challenges: - Comparison: - Norway leads EV adoption (40% market share) due to tax incentives, toll waivers, and free parking. - Challenges in India: - Limited EV battery range requires widespread charging stations. - Charging time varies (30 minutes to 8 hours), necessitating universal standards. - Need for GPS-based apps/maps to locate charging stations. - High temperatures reduce battery life, requiring R&D for heat-resistant batteries. - Lithium supply: - China dominates global supply; India needs to secure resources. - Implication: - Without charging infrastructure, consumers prefer internal combustion engine (ICE) vehicles. - EV - Lithium: Khanij Bidesh India Ltd (KABIL, 2019): - Established by: - NALCO, Hindustan Copper, Mineral Exploration Ltd. - Objective: - Acquire strategic minerals (e.g., lithium, cobalt) globally. - Milestone: - 2020, acquired a lithium mine in Argentina. - EV New Policy (March 2024): - Boss: - Ministry of Commerce (handles import-export policies, Pillar 3). - Objective: - Promote EV manufacturing in India with tax relief on imports. - EV Policy Conditions: - Minimum Investment: - ₹4,150 crore (USD 500 million), no upper limit. - Factory Setup: - Within 3 years. - Domestic Value Addition (DVA): 25% by year 3, 50% by year 5. - EV Policy - Tax Relief on Imported EV Cars: - Before: - 60-100% customs duty based on price/engine model. - After: - 15% customs duty for 5 years if manufacturer (e.g., Tesla) commits to investment and factory setup with bank guarantee. - EV Policy - Quota System on Import Duty Relief: - Annual Limit: - 8,000 imported cars per company. - Total Limit (5 years): 40,000 cars per company. - Price Threshold: - Imported cars must cost >$35,000 (~₹30 lakh). - Additional Condition: - $800 million investment for full 40,000-car quota. - Note: - Technical details have poor cost-benefit for exam preparation. - PM E-DRIVE Scheme (2024): - Full Name: - PM Electric Drive Revolution in Innovative Vehicle Enhancement. - Boss: - Ministry of Heavy Industries. - Replaces: - FAME Scheme and Electric Mobility Promotion Scheme (EMPS). - Features: - Subsidies for e-two-wheelers (up to ₹10,000), e-three-wheelers, e-ambulances, e-trucks, and emerging EVs. - E-Vouchers: - Linked to Aadhaar and mobile number for subsidies. - Funding for public charging stations. - Criticism: - No subsidies for e-cars (four-wheelers). - Electric Vehicle: Miscellaneous Updates (2023-24): - Induction/Wireless Charging on Golden Quadrilateral: - Concept: - Inductive (wireless) charging via electrified roads. - Scope: - Planned for 6,000 km of Golden Quadrilateral (Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai, Kolkata). - Note: - Details pending; Germany uses overhead power lines for e-highways. - PM-eBus Sewa Scheme (2023): - Objective: - Operate 10,000 electric buses via PPP model. - Boss: - Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs. - Gigacasting: - Normal Car: - Underbody made of multiple parts. - Gigacasting: - Single die-cast underbody (e.g., Tesla’s method). - EV Conclusion: - Importance: - EVs are key for sustainable mobility, reducing GHG emissions, and boosting employment/export earnings. - Priority: - Address charging infrastructure, R&D, and mineral supply chains. - Fossil Fuel Emission - Bharat Stage (BS) Norms: - Boss: - Ministry of Environment, Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB). - Progression: - BS-IV: - Mandatory from April 2017; sales banned from April 2020. - BS-V: - Skipped in favor of BS-VI. - BS-VI: - Mandatory from April 2020; reduces sulphur and nitrogen oxide emissions. - Impact: - BS-IV vehicles have lower resale value; BS-VI compliance increased costs, contributing to 2019 auto sales decline. - Corporate Average Fuel Efficiency (CAFE) Norms: Introduced by Department of Heavy Industry (2017) to reduce CO2 emissions from passenger vehicles. - Decarbonizing Transport in India (June 2020): - Project: - 5-year initiative by NITI Aayog and OECD’s International Transport Forum. - Goal: - Reduce transport sector’s 13% contribution to India’s CO2 emissions. - Vehicle Scrappage Policy (Budget 2021): - Official Name: - Voluntary Vehicle-Fleet Modernisation Programme. - Boss: - Ministry of Road Transport and Highways (amends Motor Vehicles Act). - Targets: - Commercial vehicles (e.g., taxis, trucks) >15 years. - Personal vehicles (e.g., bikes, cars) >20 years. - Exemptions: - Vintage/museum vehicles >50 years (not for daily use). - Process: - Vehicles failing fitness tests after specified age are seized/destroyed. - Voluntary scrapping at authorized centers yields a certificate for 4-6% discount on new vehicle purchase (transferable). - Exemptions: - Registration fees and state road tax relaxations. - Scrapping centers linked to National Police database to track stolen/criminal vehicles. - Budget 2023: - Loans to states for replacing old vehicles and ambulances. - Benefits: - Cleaner emissions, fuel efficiency, improved safety (e.g., airbags), 35,000 jobs, ₹10,000 crore GDP boost. - India to Produce Reference Fuels: - Definition: - High-standard petrol/diesel for vehicle/engine calibration. - Milestone: - 2023, Indian Oil Company began production at Paradip and Panipat refineries (previously imported). - Budget 2022 on Road Transport/EVs: - Expand National Highways by 25,000 km in 2022-23. - Battery Swapping Policy: - Addresses space shortages for charging stations. - Promote public transport in urban areas. - Special Mobility Zones: - Zero fossil-fuel policy with EV focus. - Bharat New Car Assessment Program (NCAP, 2022): - Boss: - Ministry of Road Transport and Highways. - Launched: - April 1, 2023. - Objective: - Award star ratings to M1 category vehicles (≤8 seats + driver) based on crash test performance. - Benefit: - Helps consumers choose safer vehicles. - Motor Vehicle Amendment Act, 2019: - Context: - ~1.5 lakh annual road accident deaths prompted amendments to Motor Vehicles Act, 1988. - Key Provisions: - Steep penalties (e.g., drunk driving fine increased from ₹2,000 to ₹10,000). - Penalties for road contractors/engineers for faulty infrastructure causing accidents. - Aadhaar mandatory for driving licenses and vehicle registration. - Good Samaritan Protection: - No harassment in civil/criminal cases; identity disclosure to police/doctors not mandatory. - Penalties for vehicle companies for sub-standard components; government can order recalls. - Simplified registration for vehicles modified for persons with disabilities (Divyang). - Motor Vehicle Accident Fund: Mandatory insurance for road users. - Technical reforms in third-party insurance and claims. - Legal Basis: - Concurrent List (Entry 35); Union law prevails, but states can revise penalties (some reduced fines). - Truck Drivers Eye Checkup - Project Abhay: - Objective: - Conduct eye checkups for truck drivers. - Partners: - IIT Delhi, Ministry of Road Transport and Highways. - Motor Vehicle Amendment Act, 2019 - Gig Drivers: - Guidelines for cab aggregators (e.g., Ola, Uber): - Provide health and term life insurance for drivers. - Norms on surge pricing linked to Wholesale Price Index (WPI, see Pillar 4C). - Data storage on Indian servers. - Driver training and gender sensitization. - Humsafar Policy for Highway Amenities (2024): - Boss: - Ministry of Road Transport and Highways. - Objective: - Develop Way Side Amenities (WSA) with fuel stations, food courts, restaurants, dhabas, retail stores, hygienic toilets, drinking water, first aid/medical rooms, and emergency helipads. - Transport - Bridges, Tunnels, and Miscellaneous: - Integrated Road Accident Database (iRAD): By IIT Madras and NIC for accident data. - Indian Bridge Management System (IBMS): Monitors 50,000+ bridges on National Highways to facilitate repairs and divert heavy vehicles. - Dhola-Sadiya Bridge: - India’s longest road bridge (9.15 km) over Lohit River, connecting Dhola (Assam) to Sadiya (Arunachal, inaugurated 2017). - Dhubri-Phulbari Bridge: - 19.3 km road bridge over Brahmaputra, connecting Dhubri (Assam) to Phulbari (Meghalaya); approved 2019, completion by 2026-27 (will become India’s longest). - Difo Bridge: - Over Difo River, Arunachal Pradesh. - River Ropeway: - India’s longest (2 km) over Brahmaputra, connecting Kachari Ghat, Guwahati, Assam. - SARDP-NE: - Special Accelerated Road Development Programme for Northeast roads. - Sela Tunnel: - Arunachal Pradesh, through Sela Pass; reduces distance to China border via Tawang by 10 km (altitude: 13,000+ feet). - Mavala Machine: - India’s largest tunnel boring machine for Mumbai’s first undersea road tunnel (South Mumbai to Worli). - Longest Road Tunnels in India: - Atal Road Tunnel: - Length: - 9.02 km. - Objective: - Longest high-altitude tunnel, reduces travel time between Leh and Manali by 4 hours. - Dr. Syama Prasad Mookerjee (Chenani-Nashri) Tunnel: - Length: - 9.34 km. - Objective: - Longest road tunnel in India, reduces travel time between Jammu and Srinagar by 2 hours. - MCQs: - Atal Tunnel (IES-2021): - Question: - Which is NOT correct about the Atal Tunnel? - Answer: - (a) It is the highest altitude tunnel in the world (not true; other tunnels, e.g., in Peru, are higher). - India’s Longest Road Tunnel (CDS-2023-II): - Question: - Which is India’s longest road tunnel? - Status: - Implemented by Bangladesh, India, Nepal; Bhutan yet to ratify. - International North-South Transport Corridor (INSTC, 2000): - Members: - India, Iran, Russia, Turkey, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, Armenia, Belarus, Tajikistan, Kyrgyzstan, Oman, Ukraine, Syria (Observer: Bulgaria). - Objective: - Multimodal (ship, rail, road) cargo transport, connecting Afghanistan via Chabahar port. - Ashgabat Agreement (2011): - Members: - Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan, Iran, Oman, Pakistan (2016), India (2018). - Proposed by: - US President Joe Biden at G7 Summit for post-COVID infrastructure development. - Blue Dot Network (2019): - Proposed by: - USA, Japan, Australia (India not joined). - Objective: - Certify infrastructure projects for quality, transparency, sustainability to attract private investment. - New Eurasia Land Bridge Economic Corridor. 2. China-Mongolia-Russia Economic Corridor. 3. China-Central Asia-West Asia Economic Corridor. 4. China-Indochina Peninsula Economic Corridor. 5. China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC): Passes through Gilgit-Baltistan (Indian territory occupied by Pakistan). - Status: - India has not joined; partner nations face debt repayment issues, prompting China to consider loan restructuring. - Pillar 5B3: Transport and Infrastructure - Definition: - Transport infrastructure encompasses the physical and organizational systems facilitating the movement of people, goods, and services, including railways, aviation, and tourism-related facilities, critical for economic growth, connectivity, and regional development in India. - Context: - India’s transport sector, managed by ministries like Railways, Civil Aviation, and Tourism, is undergoing modernization to enhance efficiency, safety, and sustainability, aligning with initiatives like Atmanirbhar Bharat and Gati Shakti for integrated infrastructure development. - Significance for India: - Robust transport infrastructure supports India’s economic ambitions by improving trade logistics, fostering tourism, and enhancing regional connectivity, particularly in underserved areas like the Northeast, while addressing environmental and safety challenges. - Railways - Definition: - Indian Railways, the fourth-largest rail network globally, spans over 68,000 route-km, serving as a lifeline for passenger and freight transport, with significant modernization efforts to enhance efficiency, safety, and sustainability. - Historical Context: - Established in 1853 with the first Mumbai-Thane line (34 km) under Governor General Dalhousie, Indian Railways has evolved significantly, merging its budget with the general budget in 2017 under PM Modi, streamlining financial planning. - Organizational Structure: - Ministry of Railways oversees: - Railway Board (statutory body under the Indian Railway Board Act, 1905). - Subordinate offices: - Railway Recruitment Boards, Railway Staff College (Vadodara), Indian Railway Engineering Institute (Pune), Research Design and Standards Organisation (RDSO, Lucknow). - Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs): IRCON (construction), IRFC (finance), IRCTC (catering/tourism), Konkan Railway Corporation, Rail Vikas Nigam Ltd., RailTel (communication), Dedicated Freight Corridor Corp., CONCOR (approved for privatization in 2019). - Zonal Headquarters: - Indian Railways operates 18 zones, with headquarters including: - Central (Mumbai), Eastern (Kolkata), Northern (New Delhi), Southern (Chennai), South Coast (Visakhapatnam, 2025). - 18th Zone: - South Coast Railway (2025), carved from East Coast and South Central zones, headquartered in Visakhapatnam, per the Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act, 2014. - Key Concepts: - Cross Subsidization: - Passenger fares kept low to ensure affordability, offset by higher freight charges, impacting operational revenue. - Operating Ratio: - Ratio of operating expenses to revenues; 2017: 98.4% (1.6% surplus), 2018: 96.2%, targeted at 95% in Budget 2019. - Modified Economic Internal Rate of Return (MEIRR): - Pre-2019: - Projects required minimum 12% profit. - Post-2019: - Projects approved with 2-3% profit for remote connectivity, pollution reduction, or traffic decongestion, with NITI Aayog consultation for projects over ₹500 crore. - Challenges: - Cross-subsidization strains finances, compromising sanitation, service quality, and safety. - Over two-thirds of cargo transported by trucks, which are slower, costlier, and more polluting than rail. - Excessive stoppages for political reasons reduce train speeds. - Modernization Efforts: - Personnel Reforms (Unification of Services): - Pre-2019: - Eight services (e.g., Indian Railway Service of Engineers, Traffic, Accounts) recruited via UPSC exams, causing coordination issues. - Post-2019: - Merged into Indian Railways Management Service (IRMS) for improved efficiency; Indian Railway Medical Service renamed to Indian Railway Health Service (IRHS). - Controversy: - Officers fear seniority loss; non-engineers managing technical roles criticized as irrational. - Organizational Reforms: - Railway Board restructured (2019) with a CEO and four functional members, plus independent experts in industry, finance, and economics. - Private Train Operators: -
Before After (Post-2019)
- Indian Railways solely operated trains, collected fares. - Affluent passengers preferred airlines for speed and comfort. - Private operators run trains on select routes, using their own trains and staff, with market-linked fares. - Government provides tracks, signaling, and timetable; operators share revenue. - Premium trains (e.g., Vande Bharat, Tejas) introduced, but limited government funds necessitate private investment.
- Benefits: - Improved services (no hawkers, hygienic facilities), faster journeys (minimum 60 kmph, fewer stops). - 2006: - Private container trains allowed. - 2019: - Lucknow-Delhi Tejas Express (IRCTC-operated) launched as a semi-private trial. - 2020: - Proposal for 150 private trains on 100 routes under Design, Build, Finance, Operate (DBFO) model, with 35-year concessions.
- Pre-2019 Modernization: - Project Unigauge (1990s): - Converted tracks to broad gauge (1,676 mm) for uniformity. - Project Saksham (2018): - Employee training program. - Mission Avataran (2016): - Focused on speed, safety, and profitability. - Yatri Mitra Sewa (2016): Wheelchair and porter services for differently-abled passengers. - Rail Drishti Portal: - For customer complaints and train information. - Fare Reforms: - Rail Development Authority (2017, non-statutory) suggests fares, efficiency standards, and technological upgrades, but Railway Board retains final authority. - Tatkal Tickets: - For emergency bookings. - Flexi-Fare/Dynamic Pricing (2016): - Increased fares by percentage as seats filled on premium trains (Rajdhani, Shatabdi, Duronto); phased out by 2018 due to high costs. - Green Initiatives: - Solar/wind energy at stations, green curtains, bio-toilets (DRDO-developed, using anaerobic bacteria), 5% biodiesel blending. - Green Corridors: - Trains with bio-toilets to prevent excreta discharge. - Electric Traction (100% by 2022): Replaced diesel/coal engines, despite high costs (₹1 lakh crore) and topography challenges in J&K and Northeast. - Greenwashing Criticism: - Electric traction uses coal-based electricity, reducing environmental benefits. - National Rail Plan (NRP) 2030: - Increase freight share to 45%, average speed to 50 kmph, 100% electrification, 160 kmph on key routes (Delhi-Howrah, Delhi-Mumbai), new freight and high-speed corridors, and station upgrades. - Safety Initiatives: - Rashtriya Rail Sanraksha Kosh (2017): Funds safety projects like Train Collision Avoidance System. - 182 Helpline, RPGRAMS, Rail Madad App, Rail Drishti dashboard for grievances and operations. - NINA-UAV drones for track/station surveillance. - Railways Protection Force (RPF) Initiatives (2019): - Commando for Railway Security (CORAS): Combats terrorism/naxalism. - Operation Thirst: - Tackles unauthorized water sales. - Meri Saheli: - Enhances women’s security. - Rail Types: -
