Tejas Express Luxury with TVs, semi-private (IRCTC). 2016
Gatimaan Semi-high-speed, 160 kmph, electric. 2016
UDAY Double-decker AC trains in South India. 2018
Vande Bharat Express High-speed, made in Chennai, 75 trains by 2023. 2019
Shramik Special For migrant workers during COVID-19 (2020). 2020
Bharat Gaurav Theme-based tourist trains leased to private operators. 2021
- Dedicated Freight Corridor (DFC, 2006): - 2,800 km for cargo: Eastern (Ludhiana-Dankuni), Western (Dadri-JNPT Mumbai). - Increases cargo speed to 60 kmph from 20 kmph. - Regional Rapid Transit System (RRTS, NAMO BHARAT): - Connects Delhi with Panipat, Meerut, and Alwar, managed by NCRTC under MoHUA. - Metro Rail: - Mass Rapid Transit System (MRTS) for urban commuters, operational in Delhi, Mumbai, Kolkata, Chennai. - Challenges: - High capital costs, land acquisition issues, long cost-recovery periods. - Metro Rail Policy (2017): - MoHUA oversees; projects approved after cost-benefit analysis. - Funding: - 50:50 Union-State joint ventures or PPP with Viability Gap Funding. - Metrolite/Metro Neo (2021): Cheaper metro systems for smaller cities (e.g., Nashik, Jammu). -
Type Cost per km (₹ crore)
Conventional Metro 222
Metrolite 140
Metro Neo 71
- Kolkata Underwater Metro (Hooghly River): India’s first, with Howrah as the deepest station (30+ meters). - Kochi Water Metro (2023): Connects 10 islands via electric hybrid boats. - Indo-Bangladesh Rail Links: - Akhaura-Agartala (12 km): - Funded by DoNER (India) and MEA (Bangladesh), with Nischintapur as immigration/customs station. - Others: - Maitree Express (Kolkata-Dhaka, 2008), Mitali Express (Siliguri-Dhaka, 2021). - Budget Initiatives: - 2022: - 400 Vande Bharat trains, Kavach safety technology, One Station-One Product, PM GatiShakti cargo terminals, open-source transport software (ULIP). - 2023: - ₹2.4 lakh crore for railways, net-zero carbon by 2030. - 2024 (Interim): - Three economic corridors (energy/mineral/cement, port connectivity, high-traffic density), 40,000 bogies to Vande Bharat standards. - Hyperloop: - Proposed by Elon Musk, vacuum-tube transport for high-speed travel (e.g., Mumbai-Pune, 150 km in 25 minutes). - Avishkar Hyperloop (IIT-Madras) under development. - Aviation - Definition: - The aviation sector, under the Ministry of Civil Aviation, facilitates passenger and cargo transport, regional connectivity, and economic growth through airports, airlines, and regulatory frameworks. - Organizational Structure: - Ministry of Civil Aviation oversees: - Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA): Registers aircraft, licenses pilots, implements Chicago Convention. - Airports Authority of India (AAI, 1994): Manages 130+ airports, some via PPP (e.g., GMR for Delhi, Adani for Ahmedabad). - Airports Economic Regulatory Authority (AERA, 2008): Regulates airport fees and quality. - Commission of Railway Safety: Under aviation ministry’s administrative control. - CPSEs: - Air India (sold to Tata, 2021), Pawan Hans (planned privatization), Hotel Corporation of India. - Autonomous Bodies: - Indira Gandhi Rashtriya Uran Akademi, Rajiv Gandhi National Aviation University (Fursatganj, UP). - Civil Aviation Policy (2016): - Enhances regional connectivity, affordability, and Maintenance, Repair, and Overhaul (MRO) operations for Northeast and small towns. - UDAN (Ude Desh ka Aam Nagrik, 2017): - Regional Connectivity Scheme caps airfares at ₹2,500/hour for select routes. - Funded by Viability Gap Funding (Union), state contributions (10-20%), and ₹5,000 levy on major city flights. - UDAN 3.0 (2018): - Added tourist/Northeast routes, seaplanes at water aerodromes (e.g., Statue of Unity, Gujarat). - NABH Nirman (2018): - Plans 100 new airports by 2033 (₹4 lakh crore, mostly PPP), plus upgrades to existing airports. - Budget 2023: - 50 additional airports, heliports, and water aerodromes. - No-Frills Airports: - Basic safety/security features for small towns/Northeast, reducing operational costs. - Jamnagar Airport (2024): - Temporarily declared international for 10 days for Anant Ambani’s wedding, hosting global dignitaries. - Flexible Use of Airspace (FUA): - Allocates airspace dynamically for civil/military use, reducing fuel consumption and congestion. - Challenges: - High Aviation Turbine Fuel (ATF) taxes (50% of airline revenues). - Predatory pricing by airlines (e.g., AirDeccan, SpiceJet) risks monopolies or financial collapse. - Safety issues due to inadequate maintenance from high costs. - Air India’s losses led to privatization (Tata, ₹18,000 crore, 2021); Jet Airways shut down (2019). - Airfare Price Ceiling (2020): - Sets minimum/maximum fares (e.g., ₹3,500-₹10,000 for Delhi-Mumbai) to protect consumers and curb predatory pricing. - User Development Fee (UDF): - Added to air tickets for airport infrastructure, approved by AERA. - DigiYatra (2019): - Facial recognition for paperless airport passage, managed by Digi Yatra Foundation (AAI and private airports). - GAGAN GPS (2015): - GPS augmentation by AAI and ISRO for aviation accuracy. - Drone Regulation (2018): - Airspace classified: - Red (no-fly), Yellow (controlled), Green (automatic permission). - Digital Sky Platform for registration and flight permissions; NPNT (No Permission, No Takeoff) mechanism. - GARUD Portal (2020): - Fast-tracks permissions for COVID-related drone operations. - Budget 2022: - Kisan Drones for agriculture, Drone Shakti (Drone-as-a-Service), ITI training, import bans (except R&D/defense), sunrise sector benefits. - Challenges: - Drone misuse (e.g., Houthi attacks in Saudi/UAE, 2019-2022; US drone strike, 2020) requires strict oversight. - Lifeline UDAN (2020): - Ensured medical supply delivery (PPE, test kits) during COVID-19. - Air Bubble Agreements: - Temporary pacts (e.g., with Sri Lanka) for passenger flights during COVID-19 suspensions. - Operation Ganga (2022): - Evacuated Indians from Ukraine and neighboring countries (Romania, Hungary, Poland, Slovakia). - Air Taxis (2025): - Electric Vertical Takeoff and Landing (eVTOL) aircraft trials to reduce traffic congestion. - Tourism and Museum Infrastructure - Definition: - Tourism and museum infrastructure supports cultural, economic, and educational growth by promoting heritage, pilgrimage, and modern tourism, contributing to GDP and employment. - Significance: - Contributes 5% to GDP, supports 7 crore+ jobs (ES25), but was heavily impacted by COVID-19. - World Economic Forum’s Travel & Tourism Competitiveness Index: India improved from 64th (2014) to 34th (2019). - Organizational Structure: - Ministry of Tourism: - Subordinate Bodies: - Indian Institute of Tourism and Travel Management, National Institute of Watersports, National Council for Hotel Management, Institutes of Hotel Management. - CPSE: - India Tourism Development Corporation (approved for privatization, 2019). - E-Governance: - NIDHI for hospitality sector data. - Ministry of Culture: - Subordinate Bodies: - Archaeological Survey of India, National Archives, National Museum (Delhi), National Library (Kolkata). - Autonomous Bodies: - Lalit Kala Akademi, Sahitya Akademi, Sangeet Natak Akademi, Central Institute of Buddhist Studies, Jallianwala Bagh Memorial Trust. - Budget 2020: - Indian Institute of Heritage and Conservation (deemed university, location TBD). - PRASAD and HRIDAY (2014): - Central Sector Schemes (100% Union-funded) to enhance tourism infrastructure. - PRASAD: - Pilgrimage Rejuvenation and Spiritual Augmentation Drive, expanded to 20+ cities. - HRIDAY: - National Heritage City Development, covers 12 cities (e.g., Varanasi, Amritsar). - Swadesh Darshan (2015): - Develops tourism circuits (e.g., reception centers, waste management, parking) where private investment is limited. - E-Visa System: - Introduced (2014), renamed (2016) with sub-categories: e-Tourist, e-Business, e-Medical, e-Conference, e-Medical Attendant. - Atmanirbhar Initiatives and Budget 2022: - Stranded in India Portal: Assisted foreigners during COVID-19. - Dekho Apna Desh: - Promotes domestic tourism via virtual campaigns. - Parvatmala: - National Ropeways Development Programme via PPP. - Dharamshala Declaration (2022): - Aims for $1 trillion tourism revenue by 2047, promoting medical, film, and youth tourism. - Museum Infrastructure (Budget 2020): - Onsite Archaeological Museums: - Rakhigarhi (Haryana), Hastinapur (UP), Shivsagar (Assam), Dholavira (Gujarat), Adichanallur (Tamil Nadu). - Maritime Heritage Museum: - Lothal (Gujarat, Harappan site). - Indian Museum (Kolkata): - Oldest, under renovation. - Museum on Numismatics and Trade: Old Mint, Kolkata. - Tribal Museum: - Ranchi (Jharkhand). - Bharat Ranbhoomi Darshan App (2025): - Promotes battlefield tourism (1962, 1971, 1999 Kargil, Siachen, Galwan 2020), under Ministries of Defence, Tourism, and Army. - Bharat SHRI Digital Museum (Budget 2023): - Stores one lakh ancient inscriptions digitally. - Budget 2025: - Revamped Shipbuilding Financial Assistance Policy, Maritime Development Fund (₹25,000 crore, 49% Union, 51% private/ports). - Modified UDAN for 120 new destinations, 4 crore passengers in 10 years. - Bihar: - Greenfield airports, Brownfield airport at Bihta. - Promotes Medical Tourism and Heal in India. - Pillar 5C1: Urban Infrastructure - Introduction: - Urban infrastructure encompasses the physical and organizational systems that support urban areas, including transportation, water supply, sanitation, housing, and digital connectivity. In India, urban areas house over 31% of the population (Census 2011) and contribute 63% to GDP, projected to reach 40% and 75% by 2030, respectively, necessitating robust infrastructure development. - Urban development is a State subject under the Constitution (Seventy-Fourth Amendment) Act, 1992, which mandates states to delegate functions to Urban Local Bodies (ULBs). The Union Government, through the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs (MoHUA), plays a coordinating and monitoring role to ensure effective implementation of urban schemes. - Census Definitions of Urban Areas - Definition: - Urban areas, as per Census 2011, are classified based on governance and demographic criteria to distinguish them from rural areas, ensuring standardized urban planning and resource allocation. - Types of Urban Areas: - Statutory Towns: - Areas governed by a municipality, corporation, cantonment board, or notified town area committee, with a minimum population of 4,000. - Census Towns: - Areas without municipal governance but meeting specific criteria: minimum population of 5,000, population density of at least 400 per square kilometer, and at least 75% of male workers engaged in non-agricultural occupations. - Urban Area Classifications by Population: -
Class Population Range
Class I (Metro/Mega City) 1,00,000 and above (Metro: 40 lakh+, Mega: 1 crore+)
Class II (Semi-Urban) 50,000 - 99,999
Class III 20,000 - 49,999
Class IV 10,000 - 19,999
Class V 5,000 - 9,999
Class VI Less than 5,000
- Metropolitan Area: - Defined under the Constitution (74th Amendment) Act, 1992, as an area with a population of 10 lakh or more, comprising one or more districts, facilitating coordinated urban governance. - Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs (MoHUA) - Overview: - Established in 2017 by merging the Ministry of Urban Development and Housing with the Ministry of Urban Poverty Alleviation, MoHUA oversees urban infrastructure, housing, and urban poverty alleviation initiatives. - Organizational Structure: - Attached Offices: - Central Public Works Department (CPWD): Manages construction and maintenance of central government buildings. - National Buildings Organisation (NBO): Conducts research and data collection on housing and urban development. - Land & Development Office (L&DO): Manages central government land and property disputes via portals like E-SAMPADA (for allocation) and E-DHARTI (for property registration in Delhi). - Statutory Bodies: - Delhi Development Authority, Rajghat Samadhi Committee, Delhi Urban Arts Commission, Capital Region Planning Board. - Autonomous Bodies: - National Institute of Urban Affairs, Building Materials & Technology Promotion Council (BMTPC), Central Government Employees Welfare Housing Organisation, National Cooperative Housing Federation of India (NCHFI). - Subordinate Offices: - Town & Country Planning Organisation, Government of India Stationery Office, Department of Publication (for printing gazettes). - Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs): - Housing and Urban Development Corporation Ltd. (HUDCO), National Buildings Construction Corporation Ltd., Hindustan Prefab Ltd. (approved for strategic disinvestment in 2019). - E-Governance Initiatives: - mHariyali App (2019): - Encourages public participation in tree planting with geotagged photo uploads to promote urban greenery. - Urban Missions - Overview: - Launched in 2015, Urban Rejuvenation Missions include Atal Mission for Rejuvenation and Urban Transformation (AMRUT), Smart Cities Mission, and Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana (Urban), aimed at improving urban infrastructure and living standards. - Atal Mission for Rejuvenation and Urban Transformation (AMRUT) - Introduction: - Launched in 2015 as a successor to the Jawaharlal Nehru National Urban Renewal Mission (JNNURM), AMRUT targets 500 cities with populations above 1 lakh to enhance basic infrastructure. It is a Centrally Sponsored Scheme with a validity from 2015 to March 2022. - Objectives: - Improve public transport, water supply, sewerage, storm-water drains, green spaces, and parks to ensure sustainable urban living. - Funding Structure: -
City Type Union:State Funding Ratio
Cities with population > 1 million 50:50
Cities with population ≤ 1 million 80:20
North East and Himalayan States 90:10
- Components: - Basic Services for Urban Poor (BSUP): Provides essential services like water and sanitation to urban poor. - Integrated Housing and Slum Development Programme (IHSDP): Focuses on slum redevelopment and housing for economically weaker sections. - Reforms: - Allocate 25% of municipal budget for urban poor. - Implement a 7-Point Charter for land tenure, affordable housing, water, sanitation, education, health, and social security for the poor. - Reserve 25% of land in all housing projects (public and private) for slum improvement. - AMRUT 2.0 (2021): - Launched in October 2021, aims to make 4,700 urban local bodies water-secure by ensuring 100% water and sewerage connectivity to all households. - Emphasizes a circular economy for water management using advanced global technologies. - Smart Cities Mission - Introduction: - Launched in 2015 for 100 cities, the mission aims to develop sustainable and technologically advanced urban areas. Cities are selected based on state-submitted plans, with quotas proportional to state population and statutory towns. - Implementation: - Each city establishes a Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV) to manage an Integrated Command and Control Centre (ICCC). The mission, initially set for five years, was extended until March 2025, when it expired without clear plans for SPV funding continuity. - Sister City Project (2020): - Pairs top-performing cities (e.g., Ahmedabad) with underperforming ones (e.g., Chandigarh) to share best practices and improve project implementation. - Cities Coalition for Circularity (C-3): - A MoHUA-led multi-nation alliance for city-to-city collaboration and private sector partnerships to promote sustainable urban development through a digital knowledge exchange platform. - Urban Challenge Fund (Budget 2025): - A ₹1 lakh crore fund to support projects under “Cities as Growth Hubs” and “Water and Sanitation,” providing up to 25% project funding. - TULIP Internship (2020): - The Urban Learning Internship Programme, a joint initiative by MoHUA and AICTE, aims to provide 1 crore internships by 2025 in fields like urban planning, water supply, waste management, and municipal finance. Internships last 8 weeks to 1 year, with stipends funded from AMRUT or Smart Cities budgets. - Sugamya Bharat Abhiyan (2014) - Introduction: - Initiated by the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment (Divyangjan Department), this campaign aims to create an accessible environment for persons with disabilities under the Accessible India Campaign. - Features: - Includes ramps, wheelchair-accessible toilets, Braille symbols, auditory signals in lifts, and disabled-friendly websites in public buildings, railways, and airports. - Auditors assess compliance with the Persons with Disabilities Act, with grants provided for necessary modifications. - Awareness campaigns via IEC and mobile apps enhance public engagement. - Housing for All - Introduction: - Launched in 2015, Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana (PMAY) consolidates earlier schemes like Indira Awas Yojana (1985) and Rajiv Rinn Yojana (2008) to provide housing for all by 2022, a target not fully achieved as per 2023 reports. - Components: - PMAY (Urban): - Administered by MoHUA, it includes: - Financial assistance of ₹1.5 lakh for individuals owning land to build or renovate homes. - Subsidies for builders reserving 35% apartments for Economically Weaker Sections (EWS). - Slum redevelopment to improve living conditions. - Credit-Linked Subsidy Scheme (CLSS): Offers 3-4% interest subsidies on loans for EWS, Low Income Groups (LIG), and Middle Income Groups (MIG, income up to ₹18 lakh), tracked via the CLAP portal. - PMAY (Rural): - Administered by the Ministry of Rural Development, it provides: - ₹1.2 lakh (plains) or ₹1.3 lakh (hilly areas) for home construction, plus up to ₹70,000 in bank loans. - Convergence with schemes for electricity, LPG, drinking water, and toilets. - Skill programs for rural masons and a minimum house size of 25 square meters. - Reservation Targets: - 60% houses for SC/ST (national target, varies by state). - 5% houses for persons with disabilities, prioritizing women. - Sub-Initiatives: - Affordable Rental Housing Complexes (AHRC, 2020): - Under PMAY-U, provides affordable rental housing for urban migrants by offering builders vacant government land, concessional loans, and tax relief to construct complexes for 25-year rentals, reducing travel and congestion. - Angikaar Campaign: - Promotes community mobilization for water, energy conservation, waste management, sanitation, and hygiene under PMAY-U. - Light House Project (LHP): - Implemented in six states (Gujarat, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Tripura, Uttar Pradesh) to adopt cost-effective, sustainable, and disaster-resilient construction technologies. - National Urban Housing Fund (2018): - Managed by BMTPC, it aims to raise ₹60,000 crore through extra-budgetary resources to finance PMAY-U without increasing fiscal deficit. - SWAMIH Investment Fund: - Managed by SBICAP Ventures Ltd., it provides loans to complete stalled affordable and middle-income housing projects. - National Housing Bank (NHB) Concessional Refinancing: - Offers 0.25-0.30% loan concessions for housing loans to women, rural areas, SC/ST, aspirational districts, North-East, third gender, J&K, Ladakh, and 1% for green housing. - PM-UDAY (Delhi): - Grants ownership rights to residents of 1,731 unauthorized colonies in Delhi. - JAGA Mission (Odisha): - Awarded the UN-Habitat World Habitat Award 2023, it provides land ownership titles to urban slum dwellers, along with infrastructure like roads, streetlights, and water-sanitation, with 30 square meters of land free and additional land at state-determined prices. - Global Housing Technology Challenge: - Encourages private sector proposals for disaster-resilient, eco-friendly, and cost-effective construction technologies, piloted in select cities. - Miscellaneous Urban Infrastructure Initiatives - Floor Space Index (FSI): - Regulates maximum construction on a given land area, determined by municipal or state authorities. Higher FSI allows more floors, accommodating more residents. - Nagar Van (2020): - Initiated by the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change to develop 200 urban forests across India over five years, enhancing urban greenery and air quality. - Central Vista Redevelopment: - Led by MoHUA and CPWD, this ₹20,000 crore project redevelops iconic buildings in New Delhi (e.g., Rashtrapati Bhawan, Parliament House) to address structural safety and centralize government offices, reducing travel and pollution. Targeted completion was 2021-24, delayed due to funding and legal issues. - Ghost Shopping Malls: - Malls with over 40% unoccupied shops, totaling 13 million square feet in 2023, due to shifts to online shopping and failure to adapt to market demands. - Quality of Life Indices: - Ease of Living Index (EoLI, 2020): Ranks million-plus cities (e.g., Bengaluru, Pune) based on living standards. - Municipal Performance Index (MPI, 2020): Ranks cities (e.g., Indore, Surat) on governance and service delivery. - India Urban Data Exchange (IUDX): A MoHUA and IISc Bangalore portal for open-source urban data for researchers and startups. - Global Smart City Index (2023): Ranks cities like Zurich and Oslo highly, with Indian cities lagging due to pollution and poor water-sanitation. - Global Liveability Index (2021): Ranks Auckland as the most liveable city, with Indian cities unranked due to urban challenges. - World Smart City Award (2022): India won in the innovation category at the Smart City Expo World Congress in Barcelona. - Budget 2023 - Urban Infrastructure - Sustainable Cities of Tomorrow: - Focuses on transit-oriented development, increasing urban land affordability, and ensuring opportunities for all, with details pending. - Urban Infrastructure Development Fund (UIDF): - Managed by the National Housing Bank, it aims to develop infrastructure in Tier 2 and Tier 3 cities using funds from priority sector lending shortfalls (refer to Pillar 1A2 for details). - Pillar 5C2: Rural Infrastructure - Introduction: - Rural infrastructure encompasses systems like roads, water supply, housing, and digital connectivity that support economic and social development in rural areas. With over 65% of India’s population residing in rural areas (Census 2011), robust infrastructure is critical for reducing urban-rural disparities, enhancing livelihoods, and curbing migration to urban centers. - Managed primarily by the Ministry of Rural Development (MoRD) and the Ministry of Panchayati Raj, rural infrastructure development aligns with Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) for inclusive growth and poverty alleviation. - Ministry of Rural Development (MoRD) - Overview: - The MoRD is responsible for planning and implementing schemes to enhance rural livelihoods, infrastructure, and governance, addressing challenges like poverty, unemployment, and inadequate amenities. - Organizational Structure: - Departments: - Department of Rural Development: Oversees schemes like MGNREGS, NRLM, and PMAY-G. - Department of Land Resources: Manages land reforms, surveys, and digitization initiatives. - Autonomous Bodies: - National Institute of Rural Development and Panchayati Raj (NIRDPR): Headquartered in Hyderabad with an office in Guwahati, it focuses on training and research for rural development. - Council for Advancement of People’s Action and Rural Technology (CAPART): Chaired by the Union Minister for Rural Development, it coordinates with NGOs for rural technology and development. - E-Governance Initiatives: - Yuktdhara Portal: - Developed with ISRO, it aids rural planning through geospatial data. - Integrated Land Information Management System (ILIMS): Streamlines land record management. - Unique Land Parcel Identification Number (ULPIN): Assigns a 14-digit alpha-numeric ID to each land parcel for ownership clarity. - National Generic Document Registration System (NGDRS): Facilitates legal documentation for property transactions. - e-Court Linkage: - Integrates land records with judicial systems for dispute resolution. - Transliteration of Land Records: Converts records into 22 scheduled languages with CDAC-Pune’s assistance to break linguistic barriers. - Committees: - DISHA (District Development Coordination and Monitoring Committees): Comprises MPs, MLAs, and District Magistrates to ensure effective scheme implementation. - Major Schemes of MoRD - Overview: - MoRD implements schemes to provide employment, housing, connectivity, and social security, fostering sustainable rural development. - Key Schemes: - Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme (MGNREGS): Provides 100 days of wage employment (refer to Pillar 6). - National Rural Livelihoods Mission (NRLM): Promotes self-employment and skill development (refer to Pillar 6). - Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana-Grameen (PMAY-G): Provides housing for rural poor (refer to Pillar 5C1.4). - Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana (PMGSY): Enhances rural road connectivity. - National Social Assistance Programme (NSAP): Offers social pensions (refer to Pillar 1D). - Shyama Prasad Mukherjee Rurban Mission: Develops village clusters with urban amenities. - Watershed Development Component of Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchayee Yojana: Improves water management for agriculture. - Shyama Prasad Mukherjee Rurban Mission (2016) - Introduction: - Launched in 2016, this mission reimagines the PURA (Providing Urban Amenities in Rural Areas) concept proposed by Dr. A.P.J. Abdul Kalam. It is a Centrally Sponsored Scheme under MoRD, with shared funding between Union and States. - Objectives: - Develops clusters of 15-20 villages with urban amenities like electricity, water, roads, agri-processing centers, tourism facilities, and skill development hubs to enhance economic opportunities and reduce urban migration. - Benefits: - Improves ease of living, creates local employment, and reduces urban congestion by decentralizing development. - Rashtriya Gram Swaraj Abhiyan (RGSA, 2018) - Introduction: - A restructured scheme under the Ministry of Panchayati Raj, RGSA consolidates earlier programs like Backward Region Grant Fund, Rajiv Gandhi Panchayat Shasaktikaran Abhiyan, and Rashtriya Gram Swaraj Yojana to strengthen Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs). - Objectives: - Enhances PRI capacity through funding for e-governance, panchayat building renovations, and training for elected representatives and officials to achieve SDG goals. - Funding: - A Centrally Sponsored Scheme with shared Union-State funding. - Components: - e-GramSwaraj Portal: - Facilitates preparation and monitoring of Gram Panchayat Development Plans (GPDPs). - PRIASoft: - Tracks receipts and expenditures of PRIs at Zilla, Block, and Village levels. - Sabki Yojana Sabka Vikas: An awareness campaign to involve villagers in GPDP formulation. - National Panchayati Raj Day: - Celebrated annually on April 24 since 2010, marking the enforcement of the 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992, which empowered PRIs. - Land Assets Registration - SVAMITVA Scheme (2020) - Introduction: - Launched by the Ministry of Panchayati Raj on a pilot basis in six states, it uses drone technology for land surveys to clarify property rights in rural inhabited areas. - Objectives: - Facilitates land revenue collection, bank loan approvals, and dispute resolution. - Enhances GPDP quality through accurate land data. - Progress: - By December 2024, 57 lakh SVAMITVA property cards were distributed. - NAKSHA - Introduction: - A city survey initiative under the Digital India Land Records Modernization Programme (DILRMP), managed by the Department of Land Resources (MoRD). - Purpose: - Digitizes urban land records to improve property management and urban planning. - Unique Land Parcel Identification Number (ULPIN, Budget 2022) - Introduction: - A 14-digit alpha-numeric ID for each land parcel, linked to the owner’s Aadhaar, creating the world’s largest land ownership database. - Benefits: -
Benefit Description
Faster Dispute Resolution Resolves land disputes (2/3rd of civil cases in India) with an average pendency of 20 years.
Interstate Boundary Clarity Addresses disputes in villages at interstate boundaries.
Farmer Identification Supports subsidy and crop insurance distribution.
Loan Collateral Verification Enables banks/NBFCs to verify land assets for loans.
Infrastructure Planning Aids in designing rural infrastructure projects.
Land Acquisition Streamlines acquisition for infrastructure projects.
- Transliteration: - Land records are transliterated into 22 scheduled languages to ensure accessibility across linguistic regions. - Case Studies - Bihar: - Introduced dynamic village maps that update with changes in land ownership, reducing legal disputes. - Karnataka: - Bhoomi Project: - Digitizes all land records. - Dishaank App: - Enables citizens to access land ownership information from the Bhoomi database. - Budget 2024 Announcements - Rural Land Reforms: - 50-year interest-free loans to states for: (1) Assigning ULPIN (Bhu-Aadhaar) to all lands, (2) Digitizing cadastral maps, (3) Surveying map sub-divisions per current ownership, (4) Establishing land registries, (5) Linking to farmers’ registries. - Urban Land Reforms: - Digitization of urban land records with GIS mapping and an IT-based system for property record administration and tax management. - Model Panchayat Citizens Charter Framework (2021) - Introduction: - Developed by the Ministry of Panchayati Raj and NIRDPR, it provides a template for panchayats to create charters outlining services, timelines, and grievance redressal mechanisms. - Service Timelines: - 3 days: - Issuing birth, marriage, death certificates; repairing streetlights. - 7 days: - Repairing public toilets. - 15 days: - Issuing MGNREGA job cards; enrolling in skill development programs. - 30 days: - Repairing village roads; fixing Wi-Fi connectivity. - Grievance Redressal: - Citizens can escalate complaints to the panchayat secretary/Patwari, Pradhan/Sarpanch, or Block Development Officer. - Benefits: - Enhances transparency, accountability, and governance at the grassroots, aligning with SDG Goal 16 for effective and inclusive institutions. - Members of Parliament Local Area Development Scheme (MPLADS, 1993) - Introduction: - A Central Sector Scheme, fully funded by the Union, managed by the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI). - Features: - Each MP can recommend development works worth ₹5 crore annually in their constituency (Rajya Sabha MPs: any district in their state; Nominated MPs: any district in India). - MPs recommend works, while district authorities (DM/Collector) sanction, execute, and complete them. - Funding Allocations: - 15% for SC-inhabited areas, 7.5% for ST-inhabited areas. - Up to ₹20 lakh/year for persons with disabilities (e.g., tricycles, hearing aids). - Up to ₹25 lakh/year for works anywhere in India during disasters or to promote national unity. - Funds are non-lapsable, carrying forward to the next year if unused. - Suspension (2020-2021): - Suspended for 2020-21 and 2021-22 to redirect funds for COVID-19 response, with MP salaries cut by 30%. Restored in December 2021 with ₹2 crore for 2021-22 and ₹5 crore annually from 2022. - Adarsh Gram Yojanas - Saansad Adarsh Gram Yojana (SAGY, 2014-2024): - Managed by MoRD, MPs adopt villages to develop through existing schemes, encouraging community initiatives like libraries, tree planting, and celebrating girl child births. - Pradhan Mantri Adarsh Gram Yojana (PMAGY, 2009): - Managed by the Ministry of Social Justice, it targets villages with over 50% SC population, achieving “Adarsh Gram” status by meeting targets like 100% literacy, vaccination, and ODF status. - Pradhan Mantri Adi Adarsh Gram Yojana (2021-2026): - Managed by the Ministry of Tribal Affairs, it targets 36,000+ villages with at least 50% ST population, providing ₹20 lakh per village for eight sectors: road and telecom connectivity, schools, anganwadis, health sub-centers, drinking water, drainage, and waste management. - SAMARTH Campaign (2023) - Introduction: - A MoRD initiative to promote digital transactions in villages, particularly among women, through Women Bank Business Correspondent agents (BC Sakhis). - Objective: - Enhances financial inclusion and digital literacy in rural areas. - Border Area Development Programme (BADP) - Introduction: - A 100% Union-funded program under the Ministry of Home Affairs (Department of Border Management), covering 17 states/UTs within 50 km of international borders. - Eligible States/UTs: - Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Bihar, Gujarat, Himachal Pradesh, Jammu & Kashmir, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, Punjab, Rajasthan, Sikkim, Tripura, Uttar Pradesh, Uttarakhand, West Bengal. - Objectives: - Funds infrastructure like roads, bridges, schools, and hospitals to enhance security and living standards. - Related Event: - Seemant Vikasotsav (Dhordo, Kutch): Sensitizes border populations about their role in national security and development. - Vibrant Villages Programme (2023): - Targets northern border villages in Arunachal Pradesh, Sikkim, Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh, and Ladakh for infrastructure, housing, tourism, renewable energy, and access to Doordarshan/educational channels. - Budget 2022 Announcements: - PM-DevINE: - Funds infrastructure in Northeast through the North-Eastern Council. - Aspirational Blocks Programme: - Focuses on backward blocks in 112 Aspirational Districts for health, nutrition, financial inclusion, and infrastructure. - Budget 2024 Announcements: - Andhra Pradesh: - ₹15,000 crore for the new capital city, Polavaram Irrigation Project, industrial nodes at Kopparthy and Orvakal, and grants for Rayalaseema, Prakasam, and North Coastal Andhra. - Bihar: - Industrial node at Gaya on the Amritsar-Kolkata Industrial Corridor, Kosi-Mechi river linking, and Purvodaya initiative for eastern states (Bihar, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Odisha, Andhra Pradesh). - Temple Tourism (Bihar): - Development of Vishnupad and Mahabodhi Temple Corridors and Rajgir’s religious sites for Hindus, Buddhists, and Jains. - Disaster, Security, and Strategic Infrastructure - Ministry of Home Affairs - Departments: - Department of Border Management: Oversees border infrastructure and security. - Department of Internal Security: Manages internal law and order. - Department of Jammu, Kashmir & Ladakh Affairs: Handles regional administration. - Department of Official Language: Promotes official language policies. - Department of States: - Coordinates with state governments. - Department of Home: - Notifies appointments of PM and Ministers. - Attached/Subordinate Offices: - Registrar General & Census Commissioner: Conducts Census and SECC. - Security Forces: - Assam Rifles, BSF, CRPF, SSB, CISF, ITBP, NSG. - Statutory Bodies: - National Investigation Agency (NIA). - National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA): Manages disaster response and awards like Subhash Chandra Bose Aapda Prabandhan Puraskar. - National Human Rights Commission (NHRC). - Land Ports Authority of India: Manages border infrastructure, including Kartarpur Sahib Corridor. - Autonomous Bodies: - Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel National Police Academy (SVNPA, Hyderabad): Trains IPS officers. - National Crime Records Bureau (NCRB). - National Foundation for Communal Harmony (NFCH). - International Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure (CDRI). - E-Governance: - Crime and Criminal Tracking Network and Systems (CCTNS, 2009): Maintains a criminal database. - National Intelligence Grid (NATGRID, 2011): Facilitates intelligence sharing for counter-terrorism. - Additional Responsibilities: - Administers Padma Awards and legislative matters related to the Passport Act and Citizenship. - International Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure (CDRI, 2019) - Introduction: - Announced at the 2019 UN Climate Action Summit, headquartered in Delhi, registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1860. - Objective: - Promotes international knowledge exchange for disaster and climate-resilient infrastructure, aligning with Sendai Framework targets. - Ministry of Defence - Departments: - Department of Defence: - Oversees Armed Forces, Coast Guard, Border Roads Organisation, and NCC. - Department of Defence Production: Manages defence manufacturing. - Department of Defence Research and Development: Focuses on R&D. - Department of Ex-Servicemen Welfare: Supports retired personnel. - Department of Military Affairs: Led by the Chief of Defence Staff (first: Late General Bipin Rawat). - Attached Offices: - DG Defence Estate, DG Defence Accounts. - Autonomous Bodies: - Indian Military Academy (IMA, Dehradun), Sainik Schools, Institute for Defence Studies and Analyses (IDSA). - Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs): - Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL), Bharat Electronics, Bharat Dynamics, Garden Reach Shipbuilders, Goa Shipyard, Hindustan Shipyard, Mazagon Dock Shipbuilders, Mishra Dhatu Nigam Limited (MIDHANI), Bharat Earth Movers (approved for disinvestment in 2019). - Committees: - Defence Acquisition Council (DAC, 2001): Fast-tracks armament procurement. - Portals: - Srijan Portal (2020): - Promotes indigenization by showcasing import-dependent defence items for domestic production. - iDEX (2018): - Supports Innovations for Defence Excellence. - e-Chhawani Portal: - Facilitates e-governance for cantonment boards. - Operations: - Operation Samudra Setu: - Navy-led repatriation of Indian citizens during crises. - Ordnance Factory Board (OFB) Restructuring - Pre-2021: - OFB, under the Department of Defence Production, operated 41 ordnance factories as a departmental undertaking, producing ₹12,000 crore worth of equipment annually with 76,000 workers, facing issues of overstaffing and low output. - Post-2021 (October): - OFB was corporatized into seven government companies under the Companies Act, becoming Defence Public Sector Undertakings (DPSUs) to improve efficiency through mergers, privatization, or voluntary retirement schemes. - Essential Defence Services Act: - Passed to prevent strikes by ordnance factory workers, with penalties of up to 1 year in jail, ₹10,000 fine, or both. - Defence Production and Export Promotion Policy (2020) - Objectives: - Reduces import dependence and targets $5 billion in defence exports by 2025 through “Make in India” initiatives. - Measures: - Supports domestic R&D, IPR protection, FDI, ease of doing business, training subsidies, and MSME/startup support. - Ministry of External Affairs - Responsibilities: - Organizes Pravasi Bharatiya Diwas (refer to Pillar 3A). - Attached Offices: - Foreign Service Institute, Delhi. - Autonomous Bodies: - India Centre for Migration (ICM), India Development Foundation of Overseas Indians, Indian Council for Cultural Relations (Delhi). - Portals: - Madad Portal: - Handles consular grievances. - Passport India Portal: - Manages passport services. - Kailash Mansarovar Yatra Portal: Facilitates pilgrimage registration. - e-Sanad: - Verifies documents for Indian citizens abroad. - Pillar 5C3: Infrastructure - Communication/IT and Space - Introduction: - India is the second-largest telecommunications market globally, with over 1.18 billion telephone subscribers, 84% teledensity, and 941 million broadband users (Economic Survey 2025). Communication and IT infrastructure, including telecom, digital services, and space technology, are pivotal for economic growth, digital inclusion, and national security. - Managed by the Ministry of Communications, Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY), Ministry of Information and Broadcasting, and Department of Space, these sectors align with Digital India and Atmanirbhar Bharat initiatives. - Ministry of Communications - Overview: - Comprises two departments: - Department of Telecommunications (DoT) and Department of Posts (refer to Pillar 1D for postal services). - Organizational Structure: - Statutory Bodies: - Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI, 1997): Regulates telecom, internet, and DTH/cable TV sectors under the TRAI Act, 1997. - Telecom Disputes Settlement and Appellate Tribunal (TDSAT): Handles appeals against TRAI decisions. - Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs): - Bharat Sanchar Nigam Limited (BSNL, 2000): Provides telecom services nationwide; proposed merger with MTNL (Pillar 2). - Mahanagar Telephone Nigam Limited (MTNL, 1986): Operates in Delhi and Mumbai. - Bharat Broadband Network Limited (BBNL, 2012): Implements BharatNet for rural broadband; planned merger with BSNL. - Telecommunications Consultants India (TCIL, 1978): Provides telecom consultancy. - Indian Telephone Industries (ITI, 1948, Bengaluru): Manufactures telecom equipment. - India Post Payments Bank (IPPB): Refer to Pillar 1B1. - Hemisphere Properties India: - Manages surplus land from VSNL privatization (2002). - Attached/Subordinate Offices: - Digital Bharat Nidhi Fund (formerly Universal Service Obligation Fund, USOF): Supports rural telecom connectivity. - Telecommunication Engineering Center: - Sets technical standards. - Autonomous Bodies: - Centre for Development of Telematics (C-DOT): Develops indigenous telecom technologies to reduce foreign dependency. - Digital Bharat Nidhi Fund (Replaces USOF, 2024) - Introduction: - Replaced USOF (2003), which utilized only 72% of its funds due to inefficiencies. - Funding: - Financed by 5% Universal Service Levy on telecom companies’ Adjusted Gross Revenue (AGR), deposited into the Consolidated Fund of India. - Objectives: -
Objective Description
Rural Connectivity Extends telecom services to rural, remote, and Naxal-affected areas.
Affordability Ensures affordable telecom services for women, persons with disabilities, and weaker sections.
Innovation Supports telecom startups, manufacturing, and R&D.
- Legal Basis: - Telecommunications Act, 2023; managed by DoT. - Fraud Prevention Bodies (2021) - Digital Intelligence Unit (DIU): Combats unsolicited commercial communications (e.g., telemarketing, SMS spam). - Telecom Analytics for Fraud Management and Consumer Protection (TAFCOP): Addresses digital frauds involving mobile calls and SMS. - Digital Communications Commission (DCC) - Introduction: - Established as Telecom Commission (1989), renamed DCC in 2018. - Structure: - Chaired by DoT Secretary (IAS); NITI Aayog CEO as a part-time member. - Functions: - Finalizes policies, budgets, and spectrum auctions for ministerial/Cabinet approval. - Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) - Overview: - Drives Digital India, e-governance, and IT innovation, focusing on cybersecurity, data protection, and digital infrastructure. - Organizational Structure: - Attached Offices: - National Informatics Centre (NIC, 1976): Develops government websites, software, and ICT services; established Centre of Excellence in Blockchain Technology (Bengaluru, 2020). - Statutory Bodies (Under IT Act, 2000): - Controller of Certifying Authorities (CCA): Manages digital signatures and cyber appellate processes. - Computer Emergency Response Team-India (CERT-In): Issues Cyber Vulnerability Assessment (CVA) numbers for new cyber threats. - Unique Identification Authority of India (UIDAI, 2009, under Aadhaar Act, 2016): Manages Aadhaar; listed as an attached office in some contexts. - CPSEs (Section-8, Not-for-Profit): - National Informatics Centre Services Inc. (NICSI): Supports NIC’s ICT services. - Digital India Corporation: - Promotes grassroots ICT innovations. - MyGov.in: - Facilitates citizen-government interaction. - National Internet Exchange of India (NIXI): Connects Internet Service Providers. - National e-Governance Division (NeGD): Supports e-governance initiatives. - Autonomous Bodies: - Centre for Development of Advanced Computing (C-DAC): Develops “E-Sangam” for inter-departmental data sharing. - Centre for Materials for Electronics Technology (C-MET): Focuses on electronic materials. - Education & Research in Computer Networking (ERNET): Enhances IT education. - National Institute of Electronics and Information Technology (NIELIT): Provides IT training. - Society for Applied Microwave Electronics Engineering and Research (SAMEER, 1984): Conducts R&D in microwave technology. - Software Technology Parks of India (STPI): Promotes IT exports. - Bhaskaracharya National Institute for Space Applications and Geo-informatics (BISAG): Supports geospatial applications. - Semi-Conductor Laboratory (SCL): - Advances semiconductor research. - Applications: - UMANG (Unified Mobile Application for New-Age Governance, 2017): Delivers services like exam center location, doctor appointments, and EPFO complaints. - Private Sector Initiative: - Data Security Council of India: A NASSCOM-led not-for-profit body for data protection. - Communication-Related Regulators, Apps, and Portals - Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) - Introduction: - A statutory body under the Ministry of Communications, established under TRAI Act, 1997; appeals go to TDSAT. - Functions: - Regulates telecom, internet, and DTH/cable TV operators. - Consumer Protection Initiatives: - Do Not Disturb (DND) Registry: Prevents telemarketing calls/SMS. - SMS Scrubbing Guidelines: - Verifies SMS content to curb spam. - Call Drop Reduction: - Issues directives to improve call quality. - MySpeed App: - Measures 3G/4G speeds for consumer feedback. - Net Neutrality: - Ensures equal treatment of internet traffic. - DTH/Cable Freedom: - Allows customers to choose channels with fixed pricing. - Telecommunication Consumers Education and Protection Fund (TCEPF, 2007): Deposits unclaimed consumer funds (e.g., excess charges, security deposits). - Central Equipment Identity Register (CEIR) Portal - Managed by DoT, it allows reporting of stolen/lost mobile phones. - Process: - File FIR, upload details with International Mobile Equipment Identity (IMEI) number; government blocks IMEI, rendering the device unusable. - Emergency Response Support System (ERSS, 2019) - Managed by the Ministry of Home Affairs; launched pan-India in February 2019. - Features: - Dial 112 to connect to Emergency Response Centres, redirecting to police (100), fire (101), health (108), or women’s safety (1090). - Panic Button: - Long-press ‘5’ or ‘9’ on phones or use the ‘112 India’ app’s ‘shout’ feature for volunteer assistance. - Calling Name Presentation (CNAP) Service - Proposed by TRAI to display caller ID, reducing spam and scam calls. - Anti-Fraud Initiatives: Sanchar Saathi, Chakshu, and DIP - Managed by Ministry of Communications. - Sanchar Saathi Portal: - Reports stolen/lost mobiles for blocking and tracing. - Chakshu Facility: - Allows reporting of fraudulent calls/SMS/WhatsApp (e.g., impersonation scams). - Digital Intelligence Platform (DIP): Notifies banks, police, and telecom companies for action on reported frauds. - Telecom Sector Overview - Teledensity: - 84% (98% mobile, 2% landline); over 750 million internet users, with 300 million still on 2G speeds (2020 data). - Growth: - Consumer internet connections grew from 1995, with 50% of 750 million connections added in the last four years, reflecting Digital India’s impact. - Challenges: - Slow transition to higher-speed networks (4G/5G) in rural areas. - Adjusted Gross Revenue (AGR) - Introduction: - Post-1990s LPG reforms, private telecom companies paid license and spectrum fees based on AGR. - Dispute: - DoT included non-telecom revenue (e.g., rent, interest) in AGR; telecom companies contested this. - 2019 Supreme Court Ruling: Upheld DoT’s definition, mandating payment of AGR dues, interest, and penalties. - Dues (2019 Estimates): -
Company AGR Dues (₹ Crore)
Reliance Jio 62,000
Vodafone-Idea (Vi) 58,000
Bharti Airtel 43,000
- Implications: - Non-payment risks company insolvency (e.g., Vodafone-Idea), leading to bank NPAs, job losses, and reduced investor confidence. - Potential duopoly (Jio + Airtel) could harm consumers. - AGR Dues Relief Package (September 2021) - Reforms: -
Before After (2021 Reforms)
Immediate AGR payment required Four-year moratorium (from 1/10/2021); payments in installments post-moratorium with interest.
AGR included non-telecom revenue Non-telecom revenue excluded from AGR.
Spectrum Usage Charge (SUC) levied SUC removed with technical conditions.
Spectrum rights for 20 years Extended to 30 years.
FDI up to 49% (automatic), 50-100% with approval 100% FDI via automatic route (except from neighboring countries).
- Impact: - Eases financial burden on telecom companies, preventing market consolidation. - AGR Interest Payment: Vodafone-Idea (Vi) - Vi opted for a 4-year moratorium on ₹58,000 crore dues, incurring ₹16,000 crore interest. - Payment Options: - Cash or equity; in 2025, Vi transferred shares worth ₹36,950 crore to the Union, resulting in 49% government ownership. - 2G Spectrum Scam - Background: - During UPA-1, licenses and 2G spectrum were allocated on a “first-come, first-serve” basis, leading to allegations of corruption. - Shell companies acquired licenses and spectrum, reselling them at high profits without operating telecom services. - Key Figures: - A. Raja and Kanimozhi (DMK) were arrested but acquitted in 2017. - Post-Scam Reforms (2012): - Supreme Court declared the allocation illegal. - Introduced Unified License (for voice and data) and separate spectrum auctions by DoT. - Telecommunications Act, 2023 - Replaces: - Indian Telegraph Act, 1885 - Wireless Telegraphy Act, 1933 - Telegraph Wires (Unlawful Possession) Act, 1950 - Functions/Subjects Covered: -
Subject Coverage
Spectrum Allocation/Auction Yes
Wireless Networks and Internet Services Yes
OTT Services No (Under Ministry of Information and Broadcasting)
Internet-Based Apps (e.g., WhatsApp, Telegram) No (Under MeitY)
- Allocation of Spectrum: - Pre-2012: - Administrative allocation (alleged corruption). - 2012: - Supreme Court mandated auctions. - 2023 Act: - Allows both administrative allocation (for 19 purposes like national security, defense, disaster management, metro rails, satellite broadband) and auctions for commercial services. - Government Takeover of Private Networks: -
Purpose Authority
National security, war, foreign relations Union Government
Disaster, public emergency, law and order Union or State Governments
Message interception, service suspension Union or State Governments (journalists/media exempted unless national security is involved)
- Government can mandate telecom services to transmit public interest messages (e.g., disaster warnings). - Ease of Doing Business: -
Before After
Multiple licenses/registrations Single authorization process
TRAI controls tariffs, dispute resolution No changes
Spectrum sharing/trading required approval Relaxed rules
Unclear provisions Government can reallocate unutilized spectrum
- Miscellaneous Provisions: - Do Not Disturb Register: Prevents unsolicited spam messages. - Telecom networks not classified as taxable assets, reducing capital gains tax on sales. - Biometric verification mandatory for SIM cards and internet connections. - Dispute Resolution: - Adjudicating officer, committee of appeals, and TDSAT. - Penalties: - Unauthorized telecom services face up to 3 years imprisonment or ₹2 crore fine. - Limitations/Criticisms: - Lack of clarity on AGR definition. - Allows mass surveillance and internet shutdowns, risking user privacy. - Mandatory decryption of communications may target opposition leaders, activists, or journalists. - Biometric verification raises privacy concerns. - Conclusion: - A progressive step to modernize telecom regulations, promote innovation, and ease business operations, aligning with Digital India goals. - Digital India Programme - Introduction: - Launched in 2014 by restructuring the National e-Governance Plan (2006), managed by MeitY as a Central Sector Scheme (100% Union-funded). - Nine Pillars: -
Pillar Description
Broadband Highways BharatNet: Connects 2.5 lakh+ Gram Panchayats with broadband (target completion by 2025 via PPP). National Broadband Mission: Universal village broadband by 2022. Ghar Tak Fiber (Bihar, 2020). PM-WANI (2020). Budget 2025: Broadband for all government schools and health centers. National Knowledge Network (NKN): High-speed internet for institutions.
Universal Access to Mobile Connectivity USOF funds mobile towers in rural/remote/Naxal areas. Budget 2022: 5% USOF funds for R&D.
Public Internet Access Common Service Centres (CSCs) in 2.5 lakh+ Gram Panchayats; 1.5 lakh post offices offer similar services.
e-Governance Develops apps/portals (e.g., PFMS, Bharatkosh, Sandesh, MeghRaj, SWAN) to enhance efficiency and reduce corruption.
e-Kranti Electronic delivery of services via portals for taxes, passports, and company registration.
Information for All MyGov.in, Data.gov.in, E-taal, and online courses (e.g., IGNOU, mKisan) for transparency and accessibility.
Electronics Manufacturing Refer to Pillar 4 (National Policy on Electronics).
IT for Jobs Subsidies for BPOs in Northeast; computer courses in villages and ITIs.
Early Harvest Programmes Biometric attendance, Khoyapaya portal, Pencil portal, e-books, weather alerts, Cyber Swachhta Kendra, Saathi Chatbot.
- PM-WANI Public Wi-Fi (2020) - Managed by DoT; provides public Wi-Fi via Public Data Offices (PDOs) like kirana shops or CSCs. - Benefits: - Reduces ISP dominance, eliminates license fees for PDOs, and lowers roaming charges. - DigiLocker - Managed by MeitY; Aadhaar-linked cloud storage for documents (e.g., driving license, voter ID). - Features: - eSign facility, document sharing with authorities. Budget 2023: Expanded document categories and Entity DigiLocker for organizations. - MyScheme - e-Marketplace portal listing 180+ Union and State schemes, reducing search efforts for eligibility and application. - Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI) as a New Factor of Production (Interim Budget 2024) - Adds DPI to traditional factors (land, labor, capital, entrepreneurship). - Economic Survey 2023 Examples: -
Portal/App Utility
Bhashini (MeitY) AI-based translation into Indian languages.
OpenForge (MeitY) Shares open-source software codes (e.g., Aarogya Setu).
ONDC (DPIIT) Facilitates e-commerce (Pillar 4B).
OCEN (MeitY) Connects borrowers and lenders.
e-Sanchit, ICEGATE, TurantCustoms (CBIC) Customs clearance and import-export.
UPI (NPCI) Unique payment infrastructure (Pillar 1A1).
UMANG (MeitY) Access to government services (e.g., EPFO, passports).
GST Portal, E-Way Bill (GSTN) GST compliance (Pillar 2A2).
TReDS MSME short-term loans via factoring (Pillar 1C).
National Single Sign-On Unified login for government services.
S3 Waas NIC’s platform for secure government websites.
- Vision: - Achieve a $1 trillion digital economy by 2025. - India Stack - A set of open APIs and digital public goods for app and portal development, accessible globally. - Three Layers: -
Layer Components Owner/Regulator
Identity Aadhaar, e-KYC, eSign, DigiLocker UIDAI, Ministry of Communications, MeitY
Payments UPI, Aadhaar-Enabled Payment Service National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI)
Data Account Aggregator RBI-regulated NBFCs
- Data Marketplaces and Non-Personal Data (NPD) - Data Marketplaces: - Platforms for buying/selling/exchanging non-personal data (e.g., aggregate exam results for targeted advertising). - Regulation: - Opaque in India; governed by MeitY’s National Data Governance Framework Policy and Kris Gopalakrishnan Committee recommendations. - Critical Information Infrastructure - Managed by National Critical Information Infrastructure Protection Centre (NCIIPC, New Delhi) under IT Act, 2000, reporting to PMO via National Technical Research Organisation. - Critical Sectors: - Power, energy, banking, financial services (excludes irrigation, education). - NeSDA Way Forward Report (Since 2019) - Published annually by Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances (Ministry of Personnel). - Assesses States/UTs’ progress in e-governance. - Data Empowerment and Protection Architecture (DEPA) - Proposed by NITI Aayog to protect personal data, privacy, and cybersecurity. - Principles: - User control over data, adoption of EU’s GDPR best practices, reduction of unauthorized data sharing and fake news. - IT/Telecom Training Schemes -
Scheme Target Boss
Pandit Deen Dayal Upadhayay Sanchar Kaushal Vikas Pratisthan Youth for telecom jobs DoT
Pradhan Mantri Gramin Digital Saksharta Abhiyan (PMGDISHA) Villagers for computer training MeitY
Future Skill PRIME Youth for blockchain, AI, VR, 3D printing MeitY and NASSCOM
- 5G Revolution in India - Overview: - 5G offers 2-20 Gbps speeds (vs. 4G’s 6-7 Mbps), low latency, and network slicing for applications like IoT, tele-surgery, and Industry 4.0. - By October 2024, 5G services were launched in all States/UTs (ES25). - Frequency Bands: -
Band Coverage Max Speed
Low Frequency Largest 100 Mbps
Mid Band Medium Moderate
High Band Smallest 20 Gbps
- Challenges and Opportunities: - Challenges: - China’s 5G expansion in neighboring countries (e.g., Nepal) poses strategic risks. - 5G signals deteriorate faster, requiring more towers. - Potential interference with aircraft altimeters. - 300 million users still on 2G speeds. - Opportunities: - Enhances e-learning, e-medicine, and e-judiciary. - Boosts Make in India and employment through device upgrades. - A.J. Paul Raj Committee: Provided a roadmap for 5G rollout by 2020. - Spectrum Auction: - 8300 MHz at ₹5 lakh crore reserve price; affordability issues for Airtel and Vi may lead to Jio monopoly. - 5G Hackathon (2020) - Organized by DoT with NITI Aayog, MeitY, MSME, IITs, and industry; offered ₹2.5 crore in prizes for innovative 5G solutions. - 5G Trials (2021-2022) - Conducted by Airtel, Jio, Vi, and MTNL in frequency bands: 3.2-3.67 GHz, 24.25-28.5 GHz, 800 MHz, 900 MHz, 1800 MHz, 2500 MHz. - Launched in eight cities by October 2022. - NEST Division (MEA) - New, Emerging, and Strategic Technologies division collaborates with foreign nations on 5G, AI, and other technologies. - Right of Way for 5G - Indian Telegraph (Right of Way) Amendment Rules, 2022, facilitate faster 5G tower deployment by easing permissions for infrastructure installation. - Bharat 6G Alliance (B6GA, 2023) - Managed by DoT; aims to develop 6G technology with government, private sector, and universities, targeting 10% of global 6G intellectual property rights by 2029-30. - Private Initiatives for Internet -
Initiative Description
Starlink (Elon Musk) Plans 12,000 satellites by 2027 for global high-speed internet.
OneWeb (Airtel) Satellite-based broadband services.
Kuiper (Amazon) Satellite internet project.
Aquila (Facebook) Abandoned (2018) solar-powered drone project for remote internet.
Project Loon (Google) Used helium balloons for remote internet connectivity; discontinued.
- IT Rankings: -
Index Publisher Details
Digital Quality of Life Index Surf Shark Measures internet speed, affordability, cybersecurity; India ranks high in affordability but low in speed/reliability.
Global Cybersecurity Index ITU (UN) India ranked 10th in 2021, ahead of China and Pakistan.
e-Government Development Index UN DESA Monitors e-governance progress; India ranked 105th in 2022.
Network Readiness Index World Economic Forum Assesses digital readiness with private/university support.
- Ministry of Information and Broadcasting - Organizational Structure: - Attached Offices: - Press Information Bureau (PIB): Disseminates government information. - Publications Division: - Publishes government literature. - Directorate of Photo Division: Manages visual archives. - New Media Wing and Electronic Media Monitoring Centre: Monitors digital content. - National Film Archives of India: Merged with NFDC. - Directorate of Film Festivals: Merged with NFDC. - Statutory Bodies: - Press Council of India (PCI): Addresses press ethics violations. - Press Registrar General of India (PRGI, formerly RNI): Registers newspapers/periodicals. - Central Board of Film Certification (CBFC): Certifies films. - Prasar Bharati: - Operates All India Radio (1936), Doordarshan (1959), and DD Free Dish (largest free DTH platform). Motto: Bahujan Hitaya, Bahujan Sukhaya. - CPSEs: - National Film Development Corporation (NFDC): Supports film production. - Broadcast Engineering Consultants India Limited (BECIL, 1995): Provides broadcast solutions. - Indian Institute for Immersive Creators (IIIC, 2024, Mumbai): Section-8 company for animation, VFX, and gaming. - Autonomous Bodies: - Film and Television Institute of India (FTII, Pune, 1960): Trains filmmakers. - Satyajit Ray Film and Television Institute, Kolkata: Focuses on film education. - Indian Institute of Mass Communication (1965): Trains media professionals. - Children’s Film Society of India: Merged with NFDC. - Activities: - Operates Doordarshan Arunprabha (24x7 channel for Arunachal Pradesh). - Manages National Film Awards, Dadasaheb Phalke Award, International Film Festival of India (with Goa), and Himalayan Film Festival (with Ladakh). - SAMVAD Dashboard: - Analyzes news for decision-making. - Employment News/Rozgar Samachar: - Weekly journal since 1976. - Central Board of Film Certification (CBFC) - Established under Cinematograph Act, 1952; issues certificates: - Unrestricted (U) - Parental Guidance: - UA 7+, UA 13+, UA 16+ (revised in 2023) - Adult (A) - Specialized (S) for specific audiences (e.g., medical documentaries) - Controversies: - Excessive censorship by former chairman Pahlaj Nihalani (e.g., removing smoking/kissing scenes). - Abolition of Film Certification Appellate Tribunal (2021); appeals now go to High Courts. - Approval issues for films like Aadipurush and OMG2. - Allegations of bribery by CBFC officers. - Cinematograph (Amendment) Bill, 2023 -
Before After
U/A for children under 12 Three categories: UA 7+, UA 13+, UA 16+ (recommendatory)
Lenient piracy penalties Minimum 3 months jail, ₹3 lakh fine, up to 3 years jail or 5% of film production cost
Censor certificate valid for 10 years Lifetime validity
- Press Council of India (PCI) - Established under Press Council Act, 1978; addresses complaints against press ethics violations (e.g., yellow journalism) and protects press freedom. - Composition: - Chairman, journalists, MPs, and nominees from UGC, Bar Council, and Sahitya Academy. - Other Media Regulators: - Print and Digital Media Association (PADMA, 2022): Self-regulates digital news under IT Rules, 2021. - News Broadcasters Association (NBA, 2008): Self-regulates news channels. - Broadcasting Content Complaints Council (BCCC, 2011): Self-regulates entertainment channels. - OTT Platforms: - Shifted to Ministry of Information and Broadcasting (2020); TRAI lacks regulatory power (TDSAT, 2023). - Media-Related Laws: - Drugs and Magic Remedies Act, 1954: Prohibits ads for certain medical conditions. - Indecent Representation of Women (Prohibition) Act, 1986: Bans inappropriate depictions. - Cable Television Networks (Regulation) Act, 1995: Prohibits sports-gambling ads. - Television Rating Point (TRP): Managed by Broadcast Audience Research Council (BARC); faced data manipulation controversies. - Press Sewa Portal (2024) - Managed by Ministry of Information and Broadcasting for newspaper/periodical registration under Press and Registration of Periodicals Act, 2023. - Navigate Bharat Portal (2024) - Provides access to authentic government videos (e.g., press releases, scheme announcements). - Sahyog Portal - Enables government notices to social media companies for content removal under IT Act, 2000; controversial due to Twitter/X’s non-participation. - Space Technology Infrastructure - Managed by Department of Space (DoS, Bengaluru) and Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO). - CPSEs: - Antrix Corporation: - Assists foreign nations/companies in satellite launches. - NewSpace India Limited (NSIL, 2019): Produces launch vehicles and collaborates with private sector. - Atmanirbhar Bharat in Space - Indian National Space Promotion and Authorization Centre (IN-SPACe, 2020): Independent agency under ISRO to facilitate private sector use of space infrastructure for satellites and space tourism. - Economic Survey 2021 Data: -
Metric India USA China
Space Program Spending $1.8 billion 10x India 6x India
Satellites Launched (2019-20) 5-7 19 34
- India’s share: - 2% of global space economy; only 75 of 60,000+ startups focus on space technology. - Geospatial Data and Cartography (Economic Survey 2022) - Cartography: - Graphical representation of geographical areas (e.g., maps, charts). - Geospatial Data: - Location-based information (e.g., delivery tracking, traffic maps). - Applications: - Tracks development (e.g., airports increased from 60+ in 2016 to 130 in 2021). - Monitors highways, bank branches, metros, and night-time luminosity (indicating urbanization and electricity access). - Tracks crop sowing cycles and stubble burning. - Supports SDG goals, scheme implementation, property tax assessment, deforestation monitoring, and disaster management. - ISRO Portals - Bhuvan Platform: - Monitors infrastructure under MGNREGA and PMKSY’s watershed component. - NyayaVikas Portal: - Monitors 2,840 judicial projects in collaboration with the Department of Justice. - Pillar 5C4: Infrastructure - Investment Models - Introduction: - Infrastructure projects require substantial capital investment, which the government alone cannot finance due to fiscal deficit constraints and the need for technical expertise, management skills, and professionalism often lacking in traditional bureaucratic systems. - Investment models include Public-Private Partnerships (PPP), non-PPP models (e.g., Engineering, Procurement, and Construction [EPC], Outsourcing, Government-Owned Contractor-Operated [GOCO]), or hybrid approaches like the Hybrid Annuity Model (HAM) for highway development. - Public-Private Partnership (PPP) - Definition: - A long-term contract between a public sector entity (Union/State/Local Body/PSU) and a private sector company to develop public infrastructure (e.g., highways, ports) or provide public utility services (e.g., electricity, water, transport). - Unlike privatization, where ownership is fully transferred to the private sector, PPP involves shared ownership, risks, and rewards. - Types of PPP Projects: - Greenfield: - New infrastructure projects (e.g., GMR Group building Hyderabad International Airport). - Brownfield: - Upgrading existing infrastructure (e.g., private companies modernizing Delhi and Mumbai airports). - PPP Implementation: - Joint Venture (JV): - Government and private sector form a company with shared equity (e.g., 50:50 ownership). - Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV): A dedicated company created for a specific project, with equity from public and private sectors. - Concession/Lease/License: - Government grants legal rights to a private company (concessionaire) to design, finance, construct, operate, and maintain infrastructure assets. - PPP Major Types (Economic Survey 2023) -
PPP Model Description Payment Mechanism Risk Bearer (if Revenue Falls)
Design-Build-Finance-Operate-Transfer (DBFOT) Private entity designs, builds, finances, operates, and transfers the asset after the concession period. User fees or government payments. Private entity or shared.
Rehabilitate-Operate-Transfer (ROT) Private entity rehabilitates existing infrastructure, operates it, and transfers it back. User fees or government payments. Private entity or shared.
Hybrid Annuity Model (HAM) Government funds 40% during construction; private entity finances 60%, operates, and recovers costs via annuities. Government pays fixed annuities + interest. Government bears revenue risk.
Toll-Operate-Transfer (TOT) Private entity operates and collects tolls on existing infrastructure, then transfers it back. Tolls collected from users. Private entity.
Build-Operate-Transfer (BOT) - Toll Private entity builds, operates, and collects tolls, then transfers the asset. User tolls. Private entity.
Build-Operate-Transfer (BOT) - Annuity Private entity builds and operates; government pays fixed amounts. Government pays fixed annuities. Government.
- PPP Joint Venture (Theory) - Definition: - A collaboration where two or more entities pool resources and expertise to achieve a specific goal. - Legal Framework: - No separate laws for JVs in India; registered under Companies Act, 2013, Partnership Act, 1932, or Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008 (refer to Pillar 1C2). - Types: -
Type Description Example Ownership
Contractual Joint Venture Temporary agreement to collaborate on a project without creating a new entity. Dharma Productions and Excel Entertainment collaborating on a movie (e.g., Dharma handles shooting, Excel handles VFX). No shared ownership; parties exercise control via contract.
Equity-Based Joint Venture New company created with shared equity. Hero-Honda or Hyderabad International Airport Company. Ownership based on shareholding.

(iDeCK), National Institute of Urban Affairs (NIUA). - Purpose: - Analyzes infrastructure development trends, challenges, and opportunities in India. - Miscellaneous General Knowledge - Sustainable Investments in Infrastructure and Innovation (S3i) Initiative - Boss: - United Nations Office for Project Services (UNOPS, Copenhagen, Denmark). - Launched: - 2019-21 (exact year varies by source). - Focus Areas: - Affordable housing, renewable energy, health infrastructure. - Status: - Discontinued in February 2023 due to mismanagement. - Stability and Growth Pact of EU - Established: - 2014. - Purpose: - Guidelines for EU member states to: - Control fiscal deficits. - Implement structural reforms. - Invest in job creation and GDP growth. - Asian Development Bank (ADB) Commitment - Commitment: - $25 billion over five years to support PM Gati Shakti, social development, and climate action initiatives in India. - Pillar 6A1: Demography, Health, and Hunger - Introduction: - Demography studies population dynamics, including size, growth, and structure, which are critical for economic development, social upliftment, and policy planning. Health and hunger are closely linked to demographic indicators, influencing productivity, life expectancy, and quality of life. - Managed by the Ministry of Home Affairs (Census), Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (health policies), and other agencies like NITI Aayog for health and demographic indices. - Population Census - Overview: - First conducted in 1872 under Lord Mayo; systematic decadal census began in 1881 under Lord Ripon. - Constitutional Basis: - Union List, Entry 69; governed by Census Act, 1948. - Administered by: - Registrar General and Census Commissioner under the Ministry of Home Affairs; district-level operations overseen by District Magistrates (IAS). - Post-Independence: - Conducted every 10 years; 2011 was the 7th Census of independent India. - Data Collection (Until 2011): -
Period SC/ST Data OBC Data
Until 1931 Collected & Published Collected & Published
1941 Collected & Published Not Collected
1951-2011 Collected & Published Collected but Not Published
- Census 2021 (Postponed) - Funding: - ₹8,700 crore allocated by Union Cabinet in December 2019. - Data Points: - Housing conditions, amenities/assets, demography, religion, SC/ST, language, literacy, economic activity, migration, fertility. - Innovation: - First-time use of a mobile app for data collection. - Phases: - House Listing and Housing Census: April to September 2020. - Population Enumeration: - February 9 to February 28, 2021. - National Population Register (NPR): Updated concurrently (except in Assam) under Citizenship Act, 1955. - Status: - Postponed due to COVID-19; rescheduled for 2024-25. - Demand for OBC Caste Census - Background: - Mandal Commission (1979) estimated OBC population at 52%. Socio-Economic Caste Census (SECC) 2011 collected caste data but not released publicly. - Need: - Lack of OBC population, education, and income data hinders effective policy-making for OBC welfare. - Demand: - Political groups advocate including OBC enumeration in the next census. - Government Response (2021): - No caste-wise enumeration except for SC/ST in Census (Lok Sabha statement). - State Initiatives (2023-25): - Bihar, Karnataka, and others began state-level caste censuses. - Caste Census Inclusion (April 2025) - Announcement: - Modi government decided to include caste enumeration in the 2025 Census. - Rationale: - Census is a Union subject (Article 246, Seventh Schedule, Item 69). - State-level caste surveys lack transparency and are politically motivated, risking social fabric. - Centralized caste enumeration in the main census ensures credibility and avoids political bias. - Demographic Transition (Census Perspective) -
Phase Period Birth Rate Death Rate Remarks
Stagnant Population 1901-1921 High High Population declined (-0.31%) in 1921 due to WW1, droughts, epidemics, Spanish Flu. 1921 known as the "Great Demographic Divide."
Steady Growth 1921-1951 High Medium Mortality-induced growth due to declining death rates.
Rapid High Growth 1951-1981 High Low Fertility-induced growth due to agricultural revolution (reduced famines), medical advancements (contained epidemics), and increased life expectancy.
High Growth with Slowing 1981-2011 Medium to Low Lower Birth rate declined due to family planning, nuclear families, and high living costs.
- Demographic Transition (Theoretical Perspective) - Significance: - Population change reflects economic development, social upliftment, and cultural/historical context. - Stages: -
Stage Birth Rate Death Rate Period in India Remarks
High Stationary High High Up to 1920 Stable population.
Early Expanding High Medium 1921-1951 Population growth due to declining mortality.
Late Expanding Medium Low 1971 onwards India currently in this phase.
Low Stationary Lower Lower ~2026 onwards Most developed countries; India expected to enter soon.
Declining Lowest (below Death Rate) Lowest Not yet Population shrinks (e.g., Japan).
- Population Ageing and Inverted Population Pyramid - Definition: - Increasing proportion of elderly (65+) in the population due to declining birth rates and rising life expectancy. - Example: - Japan, with a shrinking working-age population and high elderly dependency. - Implications: - Increased healthcare costs, pension burdens, and reduced workforce. - Pro-Natalist Policy (2024) - Definition: - Government policies encouraging higher birth/fertility rates. - Examples (2024): - Andhra Pradesh CM Chandrababu Naidu and Tamil Nadu CM M.K. Stalin urged citizens to have more children. - Rationale: - States with larger populations secure more parliamentary seats. - Higher population increases tax devolution under Finance Commission formulas. - Malthusian Theory of Population Growth - Proposed by: - Thomas Robert Malthus (1798). - Theory: - Population grows geometrically (exponential), while food production grows arithmetically (linear). - Natural equilibrium achieved through "Positive Checks" (e.g., famines, epidemics, earthquakes) or "Preventative Checks" (e.g., family planning, celibacy, late marriages). - Family Planning - Definition: - Spacing or preventing births to control population growth and improve women’s health. - Methods: - Awareness campaigns. - Free contraceptives. - Tax disincentives for large families (e.g., China’s former one-child policy tax). - Sikkim: Incentives for Government Employees (2023) - Context: - Sikkim, India’s least populous state (~7 lakh), has the lowest Total Fertility Rate (TFR) of 1.1. - Policy: - From January 1, 2023, state government employees receive a bonus salary for having a second or third child to boost population growth. - Assam: Two-Child Policy - Policy: - From January 1, 2021, individuals with more than two children are ineligible for Assam state government jobs. - Demographic Indicators (Census 2011 and Economic Survey) -
Indicator Definition 2011 Data/Recent Data
Population Density Number of people per square kilometer. 382 (2011).
Natural Growth Births minus Deaths. -
Actual Growth Births minus Deaths plus In-Migration minus Out-Migration. -
Decadal Population Growth Rate (Latest Census - Previous Census) / Previous Census. 17.7% (2001-2011).
Birth Rate Live births per 1,000 population. ~20 (2018, SRS).
Death Rate Deaths per 1,000 population. ~6 (2018, SRS).
Crude Birth Rate (CBR) (Live births × 1,000) / Mid-year population. -
Crude Death Rate (CDR) (Deaths × 1,000) / Mid-year population. -
Population Growth Rate Birth Rate minus Death Rate. Positive: Population increasing; Near zero: Stabilized or replacement level.
Fertility Rate Live births per 1,000 women (15-49 years). -
Total Fertility Rate (TFR) Hypothetical number of children a woman would have over her reproductive years. 2.2 (2015) to 2.0 (2019, ES22); Target: 2.1 (Replacement level).
Infant Mortality Rate (IMR) Infant deaths (<1 year) per 1,000 live births. 34 (2016); 32 (2018, SRS).
Child Mortality Rate (CMR) Child deaths (<5 years) per 1,000 live births. ~50 (2016); SDG-2030 Target: 11.
Maternal Mortality Ratio (MMR) Women dying in childbirth per 1 lakh live births. ~130 (2016); SDG-2030 Target: 70.
Life Expectancy Average years a person is expected to live. Females: 70; Males: 67 (ES22); Urban: 72.6; Rural: 68.0; Highest: Kerala, Delhi (75); Lowest: Chhattisgarh (65).
Sex Ratio Females per 1,000 males. 943 (2011); Child Sex Ratio: 919 (2011, down from 927 in 2001).
Doctor-Patient Ratio Doctors per 1,000 people. 1:834 (ES23, includes Allopathic and AYUSH); WHO recommends 1:1,000.
Age Pyramid Distribution of population across age groups. Reflects proportion of working-age vs. dependent population.
Dependency Ratio (Population <15 and >64) / Population (15-64). Lower ratio indicates demographic dividend.
- Additional Notes (ES22): - TFR Decline: - Achieved through contraceptives, family planning, and girls’ education. - Sex Ratio at Birth: Improved in most states (2019-21 vs. 2015-16), except Himachal Pradesh, Bihar, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Odisha, Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Meghalaya, Goa, and Nagaland. - Global Sex Ratio: - ~102 males per 100 females; Asia has a lower sex ratio (more males). - Healthcare Expenditure (ES25) - Source: - National Health Accounts (2021-22, Ministry of Health). -

Share of GDP 3.8%

- Demographic Dividend - Definition: - A period when the dependency ratio declines, and the working-age population (15-64) is proportionately larger, boosting economic productivity. - Temporality: - Temporary, as the working-age population eventually ages into dependency. - Silver Dividend - Definition: - Economic and social benefits from active senior citizens contributing to economic, social, and familial roles. - Examples: - Elderly participation in workforce, community activities, or caregiving. - Census 2011: Migration and Occupation - Migration: - Definition: - A person settled in a place different from their previous residence (permanent, temporary, or seasonal). - Types: - Rural-to-Rural, Rural-to-Urban, Urban-to-Urban, Urban-to-Rural (e.g., reverse migration during COVID-19 lockdowns). - Immigrants: - People moving into a new place. - Emigrants: - People moving out of a place. - Statistics: - 37% of Indians are internal migrants; 70% are female, primarily due to marriage (70% for females, 28% for males due to work/employment). - Factors: -
Push Factors Pull Factors
Lack of jobs, low salaries, or business opportunities Availability of jobs, better salaries, or business opportunities
Lack of basic amenities (water, shelter, hospitals) Presence of amenities
Disasters, floods, famines Absence of disasters
Crime, war, lack of safety Safe, peaceful society
