Cultivators Own or work on agricultural land.
Agricultural Labourers Work on others’ agricultural land for wages.
Household Industry Workers Engaged in small-scale household industries.
Other Workers Non-agricultural workers (e.g., services, manufacturing).
- Demographic Indicators: Reports - NITI Aayog Healthy States, Progressive India (Health Index) - Published: - Since 2017; latest for 2019-20 (released December 2021). - Measures: - 24 indicators across three pillars: Health Outcomes, Governance and Information, Key Inputs/Processes. - Rankings: - Top-3 States: - Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Telangana. - Bottom-3 States: - Madhya Pradesh, Bihar, Uttar Pradesh (lowest). - Note: - West Bengal did not participate. - Sub-Categories: - Larger states, smaller states, Union Territories. - National Family Health Survey (NFHS) - Conducted by: - International Institute for Population Sciences (IIPS), Mumbai, under Ministry of Health. - Rounds: - 1992-93, 1998-99, 2005-06, 2015-16, 2019-21 (NFHS-5). - NFHS-5: - Phase 1: - Data for 22 States/UTs (December 2020). - Phase 2: - Data for remaining States/UTs (e.g., Uttar Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Punjab, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Jharkhand, Haryana, Chhattisgarh) (November 2021). - Key Findings: - Total Fertility Rate (TFR): Declined from 2.7 (2005) to 2.2 (2015) to 2.0 (2019); still >2.1 in Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, Jharkhand, Uttar Pradesh. - Improvements: - Increased contraceptive use, vaccinations, institutional births, breastfeeding, women’s bank accounts, and mobile phone access. - Challenges: - Child malnutrition persists; anaemia among children and women remains a concern. - Other Health Surveys -

- National Population Policy 2000 - Objectives: - Achieve TFR of 2.1 (replacement level) by 2010 (now targeted for 2025). - Stabilize population by 2045 (stable growth rate and age pyramid). - Promote family planning, contraceptives, safe abortions, HIV control, universal immunization, and mandatory birth/death registration. - Recommendations: - Freeze Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha seats based on 1971 Census until 2026 to discourage population growth for political gains. - Bodies Established: - National Commission on Population: Chaired by the Prime Minister, includes CMs, Union Ministers, NGOs, and experts (appears defunct). - Population Stabilization Fund (2005): Autonomous body chaired by Health Minister; promotes awareness, community participation, and fundraising. - Schemes: - Prerna Scheme: - Encourages delayed marriage, childbirth, and spacing; ASHA workers provide counseling and contraceptives. - Santushti Scheme: - Public-Private Partnership for sterilization services. - Global Reports and Rankings - World Population Prospects 2022 - Published by: - UN Department of Economic and Social Affairs (July 2022). - Key Findings: - India surpassed China as the world’s most populous nation in 2023 (142.86 crore). - Global population: - 8.5 billion (2030), 9.7 billion (2050), 10.4 billion (2100). - State of World Population Report - Published by: - United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA), New York. - Theme (2023): - “8 Billion Lives, Infinite Possibilities: The Case for Rights and Choices.” - Key Finding: - India became the most populous nation by mid-2023 (142.86 crore). - Pillar 6A2: Human Resource Development - Health - Definition: - Human resource development in health focuses on improving healthcare access, infrastructure, and outcomes to ensure healthy lives and promote well-being for all, aligning with Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 3, which targets reducing maternal and child mortality, combating communicable and non-communicable diseases, and enhancing healthcare systems by 2030. - Health Sector Overview - SDG Goal 3 Targets and India’s Progress: - Maternal Mortality Ratio (MMR): 130 per 1 lakh live births (baseline); target to reduce to 70 by 2030. Achieved in Kerala, Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu; Uttar Pradesh, Assam report over 200 deaths. - Under-5 Child Mortality Rate: 50 per 1000 live births; target to reduce to 11. Only Kerala has achieved (7). - Annual Reported TB Cases: 138 per 1 lakh population; target to eliminate by 2030. - Government Doctors, Nurses, Midwives: 221 per 1,00,000 population; target to increase to 550. Only Kerala has achieved (700). - Additional Goals: - Reduce road accidents, alcohol and tobacco abuse, mental illness, and eliminate HIV/AIDS, malaria, hepatitis, and other communicable diseases (no quantifiable targets set by India). - Ministry of Science and Technology - Departments: - Department of Science and Technology (DST): Oversees Survey of India (national mapping organization), National Atlas and Thematic Mapping Organisation (NATMO), Science and Engineering Research Board, Technology Development Board, National Innovation Foundation, and Indian Science Congress Association (Kolkata). - WHO Recommendation: - Minimum 5% of GDP for public healthcare. - CPSEs: - Hospital Services Consultancy Ltd (HSCC): Approved for privatization in 2019. - HLL Lifecare: - Approved for privatization in 2019. - World Health Organization (WHO) - Established: - 1948, headquartered in Geneva, Switzerland, as a UN specialized agency. - Governance: - Health Assembly (all member states) elects Director-General for a five-year term; decisions implemented by Executive Board. - Controversy: - Taiwan seeks observer status, opposed by China claiming Taiwan as its territory. - USA’s Exit from WHO (January 2025) - Reasons Cited by President Trump: - High membership fees for the USA. - WHO’s alleged mismanagement of COVID-19. - Perceived Chinese influence over WHO. - WHO’s advocacy for policies like sex-change/LGBT rights, abortion, and climate change, seen as conflicting with US interests. - CPSE: - Indian Medicine Pharmaceutical Corporation Ltd: Manufactures Ayurvedic and Unani medicines; owned by Union Government (98.01%) and Uttarakhand Government (1.99%); factory in Mohan, Almora, Uttarakhand; approved for privatization in 2019. - National Institute of Homoeopathy: Kolkata (Code: 3). - National Institute of Unani Medicine: Bengaluru (Code: 2). - National Institute of Siddha: Chennai (Code: 1). - Correct Code: - (c) 4, 3, 2, 1. - AYUSH Regulation - Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani, Sowa-Rigpa: Regulated by Indian Medicine Central Council Act, 1970, under NCISM, New Delhi. - Homoeopathy: - Regulated by Homoeopathy Central Council Act, 1973, under NCH, New Delhi. - Yoga and Naturopathy: - No governing body yet. - AYUSH: Yoga - Key Texts: - Charak Samhita and Sushruta Samhita (circa 2500 BC). - Definition by Panini: - Yoga means “Yujir” (union) or “Yuja” (samadhi, highest state of mind and knowledge). - International Yoga Day Themes: - 2021: - Yoga for Wellness. - 2022: - Yoga for Humanity. - 2023: - Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam (One Earth, One Family, One Future). - Event: - 9th International Yoga Day (June 21, 2023) led by PM Modi at UN Headquarters, New York. - AYUSH: Unani System - Origin: - Greece, integrating knowledge from Egypt, Arabia, Iran, China, Syria, and India. - Medicines: - Primarily herbal, with animal, marine, and mineral products. - Key Texts: - Al-Qanoon by Sheikh Abu-Ali Sina (Avicenna, 980-1037 AD); Al-Havi by Razi (850-923 AD). - Introduction to India: - Eighth century. - AYUSH: Siddha System - Origin: - Ancient Tamils/Dravidians, flourishing during Indus Valley Civilization (10000-4000 BC). - Key Terms: - Siddha: - Achievements. - Siddhars: - Practitioners who achieved medicinal perfection. - Vaathuvas: - 96 tools or principles of Siddha. - Focus: - Science of life, drugs, kayakalpam, anatomy, physiology, pathology, diagnostics, surgery, alchemy, astrology, atomic theory. - AYUSH: Homoeopathy - Founder: - Dr. Christian Friedrich Samuel Hahnemann (German physician). - Introduction to India: - 1810 by European missionaries. - Official Recognition: - 1948 by Constituent Assembly resolution. - Principle: - Similia Similibus Curentur (like cures like). - AYUSH: Sowa-Rigpa - History: - Over 2,500 years, practiced in Himalayan regions (Leh, Ladakh, Himachal Pradesh, Arunachal Pradesh, Sikkim, Darjeeling). - Efficacy: - Effective for chronic diseases like asthma, bronchitis, arthritis. - Philosophy: - Emphasizes five cosmological physical elements. - Health-Related Notable Policies - National Health Policy 2017 - Goals: - Increase public health expenditure to 2.5% of GDP by 2025. - Transform primary healthcare into Health and Wellness Centres. - Establish National Digital Health Authority (NDHA)/National eHealth Authority (NeHA) for telemedicine and remote diagnostics. - Promote generic drugs, affordable medical devices, Make in India, and AYUSH systems. - HIV/AIDS: - Achieve 90:90:90 target by 2020 (90% diagnosed, 90% treated, 90% virally suppressed); end AIDS by 2030 via HIV Prevention Act, 2017, preventing discrimination against HIV-positive individuals. - Observe World AIDS Day on December 1; National AIDS Control Organisation (NACO) as nodal body. - Reduce non-communicable diseases in a time-bound manner. - Five Pillars of Health Policy (Economic Survey 2025) - [Details not provided in raw text; placeholder for future inclusion]. - National Policy for Rare Diseases 2021 - Examples: - Spinal Muscular Atrophy, Lysosomal Storage Disorders, Cystic Fibrosis. - Classification: - Divides rare diseases into three groups. - Financial Support: - Up to Rs. 50 lakh through Rashtriya Arogya Nidhi. - Initiatives: - Encourages crowdfunding and donations; ICMR to maintain a rare disease database (e.g., Hemophilia, Thalassemia, Sickle Cell Anemia). - Cheap Medicine: NPPA Price Control - National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA): Established in 1997 under Department of Pharmaceuticals, Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers. - Powers: - Derived from Essential Commodities Act, 1955, and Drugs Prices Control Orders (DPCO) 1995, 2013; sets price ceilings on over 800 essential medicines. - Tools: - Pharma Sahi Daam: - App/portal for checking drug prices. - Pharma Jan Samadhan: - Web portal for filing complaints on drug pricing/availability. - Coronary Stents: - 2017 price ceilings to prevent profiteering by companies and hospitals. - Cheap Medicine: Pradhan Mantri Bhartiya Janaushadhi Pariyojana (PMBJP) - Administered by: - Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers via Bureau of Pharma PSUs of India (BPPI), registered under Societies Registration Act, 1860. - Objective: - NGOs/individuals open Jan Aushadhi Stores (JAS) to sell generic medicines at affordable prices, supplied by BPPI, located at district hospitals and public places. - Budget 2020: - Expand JAS to all districts by 2024. - Jan Aushadhi Diwas: - Celebrated annually on March 7. - Terminology: - Generic Drugs: - Non-proprietary drugs produced after patent expiry or compulsory licensing. - Fixed Dose Combinations (FDCs): Mixtures of two or more drugs; many banned (e.g., Corex, Saridon, D’Cold, Vicks Action 500) due to safety concerns. - Free Medicine: Free Drugs Service Initiative (FDSI, 2015) - Under National Health Mission (NHM), Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. - Objective: - Provides funds to states/UTs for free medicines in government hospitals and Primary Healthcare Centres (PHCs). - National Health Mission (NHM, 2005) - Administered by: - Ministry of Health and Family Welfare; Core Scheme (60:40 or 90:10 funding). - Objectives: - Reduce MMR to 100 per 1 lakh live births. - Reduce Infant Mortality Rate (IMR) to 25 per 1000 live births. - Reduce Total Fertility Rate (TFR) to 2.1. - Reduce anaemia in women aged 15–49. - Decrease household healthcare expenditure. - Focus on tuberculosis, leprosy, malaria; eliminate Kala-azar (target 2015, not fully achieved per WHO). - Sub-Missions: - National Rural Health Mission (2005): Enhances rural healthcare. - National Urban Health Mission (2013): Reduces healthcare expenditure for urban poor. - Mother and Child Healthcare - SDG Targets: - Reduce MMR to 70 per 1 lakh live births (from 130); reduce under-5 mortality to 11 per 1000 live births (from 50). - Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS, 1975) - Administered by: - Ministry of Women and Child Development; Core Scheme (60:40, 90:10). - Beneficiaries: - Children (0-6 years), pregnant and lactating mothers. - Components: - Anganwadi Services Scheme: - Nutrition and health services. - Pradhan Mantri Matru Vandana Yojana: Rs. 5,000 for childbirth. - SABLA: - Empowerment of adolescent girls (11-18 years). - POSHAN Abhiyaan: - Nutrition improvement. - National Creche Scheme: - Creches for working mothers. - Child Protection Scheme: - Supports children in difficult circumstances. - Benefits: - Reduces IMR, MMR, anaemia; provides immunization, health check-ups, pre-school education. - Mothers’ Health - Administered by: - NHM, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. - Key Initiatives: - Accredited Social Health Activists (ASHA): Provide Reproductive, Maternal, Newborn, Child, and Adolescent Health (RMNCH+A) services. - Interim-Budget 2024: - ASHA workers, Anganwadi workers, and helpers eligible for PM-JAY (Rs. 5 lakh health insurance). - Janani Suraksha Yojana (JSY) - Objective: - Reduce maternal and neonatal mortality by promoting institutional deliveries among Below Poverty Line (BPL) women. - Conditional Cash Transfers: - Low Performing States (LPS: Uttar Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Bihar, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Assam, Rajasthan, Odisha, Jammu and Kashmir): - Urban: - Rs. 1,000. - Rural: - Rs. 1,400. - High Performing States (HPS: Others): - Urban: - Rs. 600. - Rural: - Rs. 700. - ASHA Bonus: - Rs. 400–600 per beneficiary mother. - Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakram (JSSK) - Services: - Free normal/caesarean deliveries, food, medicines, and transport (dial 102) in public hospitals; covers sick infants up to 1 year. - Other Notable Schemes - Surakshit Matritva Aashwasan (SUMAN, 2019): Ensures dignified treatment; complaints via helpline/SMS/portal with zero tolerance for violations; reduces IMR, MMR. - Pradhan Mantri Surakshit Matritva Abhiyaan (2016): Free check-ups, iron folic acid, calcium tablets on the 9th of each month for antenatal care; private doctors volunteer. - Laqshya (2017): - Ensures sterilized delivery rooms with necessary equipment. - Mother’s Absolute Affection (MAA, 2016): Promotes breastfeeding for first six months to enhance child health. - Mission Parivar Vikas (2016): Targets high TFR states (Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Assam) for family planning; offers free contraceptives (Chhaya: non-hormonal, weekly; Antara: injectable, quarterly); aims to reduce TFR from 2.2 (2016) to 2.1 (2025). - Pradhan Mantri Matru Vandana Yojana (PMMVY, 2017) - Administered by: - Ministry of Women and Child Development; Core Scheme (60:40, 90:10). - History: - Renamed from Indira Gandhi Matritva Sahyog (2014). - Benefits: - Rs. 6,000 total (Rs. 1,000 + Rs. 2,000 + Rs. 2,000 via PMMVY; Rs. 1,000 via JSY for BPL women) for first child; Rs. 5,000 for second child if a girl, to support rest and breastfeeding, reducing MMR and IMR. - Eligibility: - Excludes women in government/PSU jobs or under 19 years. - Alignment: - Fulfills National Food Security Act (NFSA) 2013 requirement for Rs. 6,000 to pregnant/lactating mothers. - Paalan 1000 - Journey of the First 1000 Days - Administered by: - Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. - Objective: - Provides parental guidance via app for child’s physical, mental, emotional, cognitive, and social health in the first two years. - Kilkari Audio Training Messages - Objective: - Delivers 72 free weekly audio messages on pregnancy, childbirth, and childcare to mothers’ mobile phones. - ANMOL Tablet App - Objective: - Tablet-based app for health workers (Auxiliary Nurse Midwives) to streamline beneficiary registration and daily tasks. - Vaccination - Administered by: - Ministry of Health and Family Welfare with 100% funding, supported by WHO and UNICEF. - Universal Immunization Programme (UIP, 1985): - Vaccines: - BCG (TB, tubercular meningitis), Oral Polio Vaccine (India polio-free since 2014), Rotavirus (diarrhoea), Japanese Encephalitis (selected areas), Measles-Rubella (MR), Pentavalent (Diphtheria, Tetanus, Pertussis, Influenza Type B, Hepatitis B). - Coverage: - Only 65% of children covered by 2014. - Mission Indradhanush (2014) - Objective: - Achieve 100% immunization for children under 2 against seven diseases (diphtheria, whooping cough, tetanus, polio, tuberculosis, measles, hepatitis B). - Additional Vaccines: - Inactivated Polio Vaccine (IPV), Rotavirus, Measles-Rubella, Japanese Encephalitis (adults in Assam, Uttar Pradesh, West Bengal), Pneumococcal Conjugate Vaccine (PCV), Tetanus and Adult Diphtheria (Td). - Pregnant Women: - Vaccinated for selected diseases. - Intensified Mission Indradhanush (IMI, 2017): Targets 90% coverage for children under 2 and pregnant women by December 2018. - e-VIN: - Electronic Vaccine Network, supported by UNDP, monitors vaccine stocks. - Interim-Budget 2024: - Cervical cancer vaccination for girls aged 9-14 (linked to Human Papilloma Virus). - Intensified Mission Indradhanush (IMI) 3.0 (2021) & 4.0 (2022-23) - Focus: - Children and pregnant women who missed non-COVID vaccine doses during the pandemic; targets migrants and hard-to-reach areas. - Approach: - Staggered vaccination to reduce crowding. - Fully Immunized Child - Criteria - Vaccines by First Birthday: BCG, Oral Polio Vaccine (OPV), Pentavalent (Diphtheria, Tetanus, Pertussis, Hepatitis B, Haemophilus influenzae type B), Measles-Rubella. - Coverage: - 93% of children fully immunized (2023-24). - Adolescent Boys and Girls - Women and Child Development Ministry: - SAKSHAM: - Targets boys aged 11-18 for health, hygiene, nutrition, and vocational training. - SABLA (Rajiv Gandhi Scheme): Empowers adolescent girls (11-18) with health, hygiene, nutrition, adolescent reproductive and sexual health (ARSH), Iron-Folic Acid supplementation, and vocational skills. - Kishori Health Cards: - Track weight, height, BMI for girls aged 11-18. - Health Ministry: - Rashtriya Kishor Swasthya Karyakram: Targets boys aged 10-19 for similar objectives. - Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram (RBSK): Screens children aged 0-6 for birth defects, deficiencies, diseases, and developmental delays; provides annual check-ups for ages 6-18 in government schools. - Saksham Anganwadis (Budget 2022) - Objective: - Upgrade 2 lakh Anganwadi centres under ICDS with improved infrastructure, audio-visual aids, and clean energy for family planning, nutrition, and pre-school activities. - Ayushman Bharat National Health Protection Mission (AB-NHPM) - Definition: - A flagship healthcare initiative launched in 2018 to provide comprehensive health services and financial protection to India’s population, particularly the poor, through upgraded health facilities and insurance coverage. - Components: - Health and Wellness Centres (Ayushman Arogya Mandirs): - Upgrades Primary Health Centres (PHCs) into Health and Wellness Centres to deliver free drugs, diagnostic checkups, mother-child care, family planning, and treatment for non-communicable diseases (e.g., hypertension, diabetes, oral/breast/cervical cancers), communicable diseases (e.g., malaria, measles), mental health, ENT, ophthalmology, oral health, geriatric care, and palliative care (e.g., for HIV/AIDS, cancer). - Promotes yoga, wellness activities, and healthy lifestyles through initiatives like anti-tobacco campaigns, marathons, laughter clubs, and open gyms. - Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (PM-JAY): - Provides Rs. 5 lakh per poor family per year for health insurance, covering secondary and tertiary care, including 3 days of pre-hospitalization and 15 days of post-hospitalization expenses. - As of January 2023, enrolled 22 crore people, significantly reducing out-of-pocket healthcare costs for the poor. - Ayushman Bhav Campaign (2023): - An awareness and enrollment drive for Ayushman health insurance cards, generating Ayushman Bharat Health Account (ABHA) digital IDs, and raising awareness about government health schemes, tuberculosis, and sickle cell disease. - Components: - Ayushman Apke Dwar 3.0: Door-to-door beneficiary registration. - Ayushman Melas: - Health camps at Community Health Centres (CHCs). - Ayushman Sabhas: - Awareness events in villages and panchayats. - Duration: - September 17 to October 2, 2023 (Seva Pakhwada, aligned with Gandhi Jayanti). - Health Cess (2020): - A 5% cess on customs duty for imported medical devices to fund hospital construction under Ayushman Bharat in Public-Private Partnership (PPP) mode, particularly in Aspirational Districts (backward districts identified by NITI Aayog). - Pradhan Mantri Swasthya Suraksha Nidhi (PMSSN, 2021): - A non-lapsable fund under the Public Account, funded by a 4% Health and Education Cess on direct taxes (e.g., income tax, corporation tax). - Objectives: - Supports Ayushman Bharat schemes, including PM-JAY. - Funds Pradhan Mantri Swasthya Suraksha Yojana (PMSSY) for establishing AIIMS-like institutions and upgrading government medical colleges. - Supports National Health Mission (NHM) and health emergency responses (e.g., COVID-19). - PMSSY Objectives: - Correct regional imbalances in tertiary healthcare services. - Augment facilities for quality medical education. - National Health Mission (NHM) - Definition: - A comprehensive initiative to improve public health systems, focusing on both communicable and non-communicable diseases, maternal and child health, and rural healthcare access. - Components: - Communicable Diseases: - National Vector-Borne Disease Control Programme: Targets malaria, dengue, filaria, kala-azar, Japanese encephalitis, and chikungunya through mosquito prevention strategies like Indoor Residual Spraying (IRS), Long-Lasting Insecticidal Nets (LLIN), larvivorous fish, and bio-larvicides. - Leprosy Eradication Programme: - Aims to eliminate leprosy through early detection and treatment. - HIV/STD Programme: - Focuses on prevention, testing, and treatment. - Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme (IDSP): Monitors diseases like swine flu, Ebola, Nipah, Zika, and COVID-19. - TB Elimination (Target: - 2025): - National Tuberculosis Elimination Programme (NTEP) uses Directly Observed Treatment Short course (DOTS) strategy. - Pradhan Mantri TB Mukt Bharat Abhiyan (2022): Encourages community support through Nikshay Mitras (donors) via the NIKSHAY web portal, providing Rs. 500/month to TB patients for nutrition and vocational training. - SAANS Initiative (2019): - Social Awareness and Actions to Neutralize Pneumonia Successfully, reducing childhood pneumonia deaths. - Non-Communicable Diseases: - National Mental Health Programme (NMHP): Addresses mental health issues. - National Programme for Prevention and Control of Cancer, Diabetes, Cardiovascular Diseases, and Stroke (NPCDCS): Focuses on screening and management. - Blindness and Tobacco Control Programmes: Includes COTPA Act, 2003, mandating 85% health warnings on cigarette and tobacco packaging. - Fluorosis Prevention: - Targets excessive fluoride in drinking water (desirable limit: 1.0–1.5 mg/litre), linked to Anemia Mukt Bharat. - eDantSeva Portal: - Promotes oral health awareness. - Global Fund to Fight AIDS, TB, and Malaria (2002): - Headquartered in Geneva, supported by the UN and Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation. - Promotes 3-in-1 TLD pill (tenofovir, lamivudine, dolutegravir) for HIV treatment, recommended by WHO for its efficacy and low cost (<$45/year). - Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (ABDM, 2021) - Definition: - Launched on October 2021 (announced August 2020), ABDM aims to create a digital health ecosystem for seamless healthcare access and data management. - Features: - Managed by the National Health Authority (NHA), also responsible for PM-JAY. - Provides a 14-digit Unique Health ID (UHID) for citizens, linked to mobile numbers or Aadhaar (optional), storing records of diseases, diagnoses, reports, and medications. - Consent-based, voluntary, with opt-out and data deletion options; allows nominee access (e.g., for guardians). - Integrates with digital health services like digi-doctor, telemedicine, and e-pharmacy. - Budget 2022: - Plans digital registries for doctors, hospitals, and patient records. - Health Data Management Policy: - Covers patients, doctors, governments, insurance, pharma, and research bodies. - Ensures patient rights to remove data, correct errors, restrict disclosures, and request data copies. - Data sharing complies with applicable laws and international standards. - Includes awareness programs on data privacy. - E-Sanjeevani Telemedicine - Definition: - A telemedicine platform developed by the Centre for Development of Advanced Computing (C-DAC, Mohali) under the Ministry of Electronics and IT (MeitY). - Features: - Offers patient registration, audio-video consultations with doctors, and e-prescriptions. - Types: - Doctor-to-Doctor (eSanjeevani). - Patient-to-Doctor (eSanjeevani OPD). - PM Ayushman Bharat Health Infrastructure Mission (PM-ABHIM, 2021) - Definition: - Renamed from PM AtmaNirbhar Swasth Bharat Yojana, launched in 2021 to strengthen public health infrastructure (tenure: 2021–2026). - Features: - Centrally sponsored scheme with state contributions. - Aims to detect and cure new/emerging diseases, manage pandemics, and enhance primary, secondary, and tertiary healthcare systems. - Focuses on IT-enabled surveillance, public health labs, and National Centre for Disease Control. - 15th Finance Commission Grants (2021–2026): - Rs. 70,000 crore for local bodies. - Rs. 15,000 crore for critical care hospitals (e.g., ICU, ventilators, dialysis). - Rs. 13,000 crore for training allied healthcare workers (e.g., lab technicians, ASHA workers). - Rs. 2,000 crore for doctor training in district hospitals. - Recommendations: - Union and state governments to spend 2.5% of GDP on healthcare by 2025. - Propose All India Medical and Health Service under All-India Services Act, 1951, for UPSC recruitment to address doctor shortages. - Address concentration of medical colleges and super-specialty hospitals in western/southern India. - COVID-19 Response - Vaccination Timeline: - Jan 2021: - Health and frontline workers (e.g., policemen). - Apr 2021: - Citizens aged 45+. - May 2021: - Citizens aged 18+. - Jan 2022: - Teenagers aged 15–18. - Health Apps and Portals: - COVAX Network: - Led by WHO, GAVI, and CEPI to procure vaccines for member countries. - Controversy: - Alleged insufficient vaccine supply for poor nations; deals only with union governments, not states (e.g., Punjab denied). - CoWIN App/Portal: - Managed by NHA for vaccination slot registration and certificate downloads. - Supports non-Aadhaar IDs (e.g., voter ID, driving license). - Open-sourced in 2021 for global use. - COVAID Portal: - NITI Aayog portal for importing/donating COVID relief materials (e.g., oxygen cylinders, ventilators, Remdesivir). - Aarogya Setu (2020): - Uses Bluetooth and GPS to track COVID infections and contacts. - Developed by National Informatics Centre (NIC) with NITI Aayog and private IT experts. - Privacy concerns: - Data hacking/misuse risks. - AarogyaPath: - CSIR portal for real-time availability of masks, PPE, and critical healthcare supplies. - Suraksha Store Initiative: - Department of Consumer Affairs monitors health-safety guidelines at retail stores with tech startups Safejob and Seekify. - Corona Strategies: - R0 (Basic Reproduction Number): - R0 < 1: - Disease fades. - R0 = 1: - Disease persists without epidemic. - R0 > 1: - Epidemic possible. - R0 > 10/100: - Super-spreader event. - Mitigation vs. Suppression: -
Mitigation Suppression
- Slows pandemic spread (e.g., R0 from 100 to 2) using masks, social distancing, contact tracing, and partial lockdowns. - Reduces economic damage while cutting deaths by ~50%. - Stops/reverses spread (R0 < 1) via nationwide complete lockdowns. - Causes significant economic damage.
- Barbell Strategy: - Initial nationwide lockdown to save lives and flatten the epidemic curve, followed by gradual unlocking to save livelihoods, combined with social distancing, contact tracing, and vaccination. - Miscellaneous Health Schemes - Pradhan Mantri Swasthya Suraksha Yojana (PMSSY): - Central sector scheme to establish AIIMS-like institutions and upgrade government medical colleges to address regional healthcare imbalances. - Rashtriya Arogya Nidhi (RAN): - Provides financial aid for Below Poverty Line (BPL) patients with life-threatening diseases to access free treatment at super-specialty hospitals. - National Pharmacovigilance Programme: - Monitors adverse drug reactions and spurious/fake drugs. - Deworming: - Administers Albendazole tablets to children for intestinal worm infections, observed on National Deworming Day (Feb 10, Aug 10). - Atal Jai Anusandhan Biotech Missions (2019): - Sub-missions: - GARBH-ini: - Research on preterm birth causes. - IndCEPI: - Affordable vaccines for endemic diseases. - UNaTI: - Bio-fortified and protein-rich crops. - Antimicrobial Resistance: - Addresses drug-resistant infections. - Swachh Bharat: - Innovative technologies for sanitation. - National Ayush Mission (2014): - Promotes AYUSH (Ayurveda, Yoga, Unani, Siddha, Homoeopathy) through new colleges, hospitals, and medicinal plant cultivation. - PM Vrikshayush Yojana: - Supports cultivation and post-harvest management of medicinal plants. - e-AUSHADHI Portal: - Facilitates online licensing and information on AYUSH drugs, including cancelled/spurious drugs. - Yoga Initiatives: - BHUVAN-YOGA App (ISRO): - Tracks International Yoga Day participation. - Yoga Locator: - Identifies venues for International Yoga Day. - Important Days: - June 21: - International Yoga Day (since 2015, UNGA). - Jan 4: - Siddha Day (since 2018, Ayush Ministry). - Dec 1: - World AIDS Day. - Disease Elimination: - India eliminated polio, guinea worm disease, yaws, maternal, and neonatal tetanus (Economic Survey 2022). - MERA and TruNAT: - MERA: - ICMR’s Malaria Elimination Research Alliance. - TruNAT: - ICMR’s low-cost TB detection project. - AMRIT Outlets: - Affordable Medicines and Reliable Implants for Treatment, offering cancer/cardiovascular drugs and cardiac implants at 60–90% discounts. - SUGAM Portal: - CDSCO portal for drug approvals, clinical trial reports, and complaints. - U-Win Platform: - Records vaccinations for pregnant women and children up to 16 years under Mission Indradhanush. - Interim Budget 2024: - Cervical cancer vaccination for girls aged 9–14 (linked to Human Papillomavirus). - ASHA and Anganwadi workers/helpers eligible for PM-JAY Rs. 5 lakh insurance. - Budget 2025: - Day Care Cancer Centres in all district hospitals within three years. - Other Initiatives: - Drones for Medicine Delivery: ‘Medicines from the Sky’ (WEF, Telangana, Arunachal) and i-DRONE (ICMR, Northeast). - AI in Healthcare: - Rajasthan’s AI for silicosis detection; Uttarakhand’s eSwasthya Dham for Char Dham Yatra pilgrims. - Toxic Work Culture (Economic Survey 2025): Impacts mental health, low prelims relevance. - Ultra-Processed/Junk Food: - Linked to obesity, cardiovascular diseases, and mental health issues. - Suggestions: - Higher GST, stricter advertising, and labeling rules. - Hunger and Malnutrition - Definitions: - Hunger: - Distress from insufficient calorie/food intake. - Malnutrition: - Deficiency from insufficient calories and/or nutrients. - Food Security: - Availability of nutritious food at stable, affordable prices year-round. - Causes of Malnutrition: - Income Inequality: - Poor cannot afford nutrient-rich foods (e.g., milk, vegetables); ~21% of India’s population is Below Poverty Line (2011). - Gender Inequality: - Women eating last/least; >1/3rd of Indian women have low BMI. - Social Inequality: - Marginalized groups (SC/ST) lack economic opportunities for nutritious food. - Water-Sanitation Issues: - Open defecation causes intestinal worms and enteropathy. - Psychological Issues: - Disorders like anorexia nervosa, exacerbated by social media body image pressures. - Dietary Habits: - Vegetarian diets may lack protein, per Western research. - Food Security Pillars and India’s Efforts: -
Pillar India’s Efforts
Availability Union: MSP, fertilizer subsidies, PM-KISAN. States: Cheap canal water, electricity for farmers.
Affordability National Food Security Act (NFSA) provides subsidized grains to the poor.
Nutrition Poshan Abhiyaan, Mid-Day Meal, Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS) ensure nutritious food for children and women.
Stability Food Corporation of India (FCI) maintains buffer stocks for distribution during inflation or disasters.
- Ministry of Consumer Affairs, Food and Public Distribution - Departments: - Department of Consumer Affairs: Manages INGRAM portal for consumer complaints. - Department of Food and Public Distribution: Oversees food security schemes. - Attached/Subordinate Offices: - Directorate of Sugar and Vegetable Oils: Includes National Sugar Institute. - Indian Grain Storage Management & Research Institute. - Statutory Bodies: - Warehousing Development and Regulatory Authority (2007). - National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission. - Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS): Manages ISI and gold hallmarking. - Enforces Essential Commodities Act, 1955. - Commercial Undertakings: - Food Corporation of India (FCI, 1964): Procures, stores, and distributes food grains. - Central Warehousing Corporation (1962). - Central Railside Warehouse Company Limited. - Hindustan Vegetable Oils Corporation Limited. - National Food Security Act (NFSA, 2013) - Definition: - A legal framework to provide subsidized food grains to ~67% of India’s population (75% rural, 50% urban), converting food entitlements into legal rights. - Features: - Boss: - Department of Food and Public Distribution. - Union procures grains at Minimum Support Price (MSP) and sells to states at Central Issue Price (CIP, not exceeding MSP). - Food Subsidy: - FCI’s economic cost minus CIP. - States distribute grains via Fair Price Shops (FPS)/Public Distribution System (PDS). - Budget 2019: - Allocated >Rs. 1.5 lakh crore. - Beneficiary Categories: - Priority Households (PH): - 5 kg grains per person at Rs. 3/kg (rice), Rs. 2/kg (wheat), Rs. 1/kg (coarse grains). - Antyodaya Anna Yojana (AAY): 35 kg grains per family at same rates, regardless of family size. - 2023: - Grains made free (Jan–Dec) under PM Garib Kalyan Anna Yojana (PMGKAY). - Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT): States like Chandigarh, Puducherry, Dadra & Nagar Haveli provide cash for market purchases. - Food Security Allowance: - Paid if states fail to provide grains on time. - Women Empowerment: - Eldest woman (18+) is household head for ration cards. - Additional Benefits: - Pregnant/lactating mothers: - 600-calorie take-home ration, free Anganwadi meals, Rs. 6,000 maternity benefits (PM Matru Vandana Yojana). - Children (6–14): - Free hot meals or take-home rations in government schools (Mid-Day Meal Scheme). - One Nation One Ration Card (ONORC, 2019): - Enables inter-state and intra-state portability of PDS benefits. - Implemented nationwide by July 31, 2021 (per Supreme Court order). - Portals: - IMPDS: - Manages national-level portability. - Annavitran: - Displays sales data via e-Point of Sale (e-PoS) devices. - Food Distribution Reforms - GPS and RFID: - Tracks trucks transporting subsidized grains to prevent black-market diversion. - ePoS Devices: - Installed at FPS for systematic distribution tracking. - Aadhaar: - Removes duplicate/ghost beneficiaries. - Toll-Free Helpline: - Addresses grievances. - Jan Poshan Kendra: - Renames FPS to focus on nutrition-rich foods (50% inventory) and household items (50%). - FPS Sahay Loan App: - Provides collateral-free loans to FPS dealers. - Rice Fortification: - Adds micronutrients (iron, folic acid, vitamin B12) to rice under NFSA/PMGKAY/ICDS. - Central sector scheme, fully funded by Union, valid till Dec 2028. - PM Garib Kalyan Anna Yojana (PMGKAY): - Launched during COVID-19 (Apr 2020–Dec 2024, extended to 2029). - Provided 5 kg free grains (wheat/rice) + 1 kg pulses per month (2020 phases). - Merged with NFSA in Jan 2023, making 5 kg grains free. - Estimated cost: - Rs. 11.8 lakh crore over 5 years. - Bharat Atta (2023): - Subsidized wheat flour (Rs. 27.50/kg vs. Rs. 36/kg market rate) sold via mobile vans, NAFED outlets due to price hikes from Russia-Ukraine crisis, exports, and festival demand. - Other Initiatives: - Free LPG cylinders for PM-Ujjwala beneficiaries (3 months, 2020). - Non-NFSA migrants: - 5 kg grains + 1 kg chana per family for 2 months (2020). - Poshan Abhiyaan (National Nutrition Mission, 2018) - Definition: - A flagship program to achieve nutritional security by addressing malnutrition among children, women, and adolescents, launched with the motto “Sahi Poshan, Desh Roshan.” - Features: - Boss: - Ministry of Women and Child Development. - Core scheme with 60:40/90:10 funding (Union:States), half-funded by World Bank/MDBs. - Interventions: - Iron-folic acid tablets, nutritious food via Anganwadi/schools, convergence with women/child schemes, online monitoring, IEC awareness, e-learning, yoga. - Bharatiya Poshan Krishi Kosh: Database of crops across 128 agro-climatic zones for nutritional outcomes. - Poshan Anthem: - By Prasoon Joshi and Shankar Mahadevan. - Rashtriya Poshan Mah: - Celebrated annually in September. - Objectives and Targets: - Reduce stunting (0–6 years) from >35% to 25% by 2022. - Reduce stunting, undernutrition, low-birthweight by 2% annually (till 2020). - Reduce anemia in children (0–6), adolescent girls, women by 3% annually (till 2020). - Anemia Mukt Bharat (AMB) Strategy (2018): - 6x6x6 Approach: - Population Groups: - Children (6–59 months, 5–9 years), adolescents (10–19), pregnant/lactating women, women of reproductive age (15–49). - Interventions: - Iron-folic acid supplementation, deworming, delayed cord clamping (3 minutes post-delivery), digital anemia testing, fortified foods in government programs, addressing non-nutritional causes (malaria, hemoglobinopathies, fluorosis). - Institutional Mechanisms: - Inter-ministerial coordination, National AMB Unit, Centre of Excellence for Anemia, ministry convergence, supply chain strengthening, AMB Dashboard/Portal. - National Council on India’s Nutrition Challenges: - Chairman: - Vice Chairman, NITI Aayog. - Members: - NITI Aayog CEO, ministers (Women and Child, Drinking Water, Tribal Affairs, Rural Development), CMs of backward states, Health Ministry secretaries. - Mission Poshan 2.0 (2021): - Merges Poshan Abhiyaan and Supplementary Nutrition Scheme (ICDS sub-scheme). - Provides hot-cooked meals/take-home rations (rice, wheat, pulses, eggs, etc.) for children (6 months–6 years), pregnant/lactating mothers, and out-of-school adolescent girls (11–14). - Focuses on first 1,000 days (pregnancy to child’s second birthday). - Portals: - Poshan Tracker: - Monitors pregnant women, lactating mothers, children, adolescents. - Poshan Gyan: - Digital repository for nutrition knowledge, led by NITI Aayog with Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation. - Global Hunger Index (GHI) - Definition: - An annual report by Concern Worldwide (Ireland) and Welthungerhilfe (Germany), measuring hunger through four indicators: undernourishment, child wasting, child stunting, and child mortality (0–5 years). - India’s Rank: - 94th (2020), 101st (2021), 107th (2022), 111th (2023), 105th (2024). - 2024 Theme: - Gender justice for climate resilience and zero hunger. - NITI Aayog Critique: - Claims international survey methodologies are faulty; Indian surveys show improvement. - Other Reports: - World’s Children Report (UNICEF): Every second Indian child affected by malnutrition (2019). - Global Nutrition Report: - Profiles India with high anemia and stunting. - State of Food Security and Nutrition (FAO/WHO): Uses Food Insecurity Experience Scale. - Food Waste Index (UNEP): 50 kg food wasted per person annually in Indian homes. - Hunger Hotspots (FAO/WFP): - Identifies Ethiopia, Madagascar, Yemen, South Sudan, Nigeria. - One Health Approach - Definition: - An integrated approach recognizing interconnections between human, animal, and environmental health, particularly for zoonotic diseases (e.g., Nipah, Ebola, COVID-19). - Examples: - Nipah Virus: - Spread from jungle bats to pigs to humans due to environmental degradation. - Ebola: - Transmitted via monkey/antelope meat consumption. - COVID-19: - Linked to Wuhan’s wildlife meat market. - Advocacy: - Supported by FAO, World Organisation for Animal Health (OIE), WHO, UNEP. - Indian Department of Animal Husbandry organizes seminars/workshops. - Pillar 6B1: Human Resource Development - Education - Definition: - Education is the systematic process of acquiring knowledge, skills, values, and attitudes through structured instruction, typically in schools or universities, fostering individual and societal development. - Context: - Education is a cornerstone of human resource development, driving economic growth, social equity, and national progress. In India, education reforms aim to achieve universal access, improve quality, and align with global standards like SDG Goal 4, targeting inclusive and equitable education by 2030. - Significance for India: - India’s education system is pivotal for leveraging its demographic dividend, reducing poverty, and fostering innovation. Initiatives like NEP 2020 and digital platforms aim to enhance access, quality, and employability, aligning with Atmanirbhar Bharat and global competitiveness. - Education Statistics and Metrics - Definition: - Education metrics like literacy rate, Gross Enrolment Ratio (GER), and dropout rates measure access, participation, and retention, guiding policy interventions for equitable education. - Literacy Rate: - As per Census 2011, India’s literacy rate is 73%, with urban areas surpassing rural and males outpacing females. Literacy is defined as the ability of a person aged 7 or above to read and write with understanding in any language. - Adult Literacy Rate: - Measured for individuals aged 15 and above, focusing on functional literacy for economic and social participation. - Gross Enrolment Ratio (GER): - GER = (Number of students enrolled in a specific age group or standard) / (Total population in that age group). A GER of 97% indicates 3% of children are out of school, while GER >100% suggests underage admissions. - Economic Survey 2025 Data: - Primary GER: - 77.4% - Secondary GER: - 56.2% - Higher Secondary GER: - 14.1% - NEP 2020 Target: - Achieve 100% GER in school education by 2030. - Gender Parity Index (GPI): - GPI = Ratio of female to male students enrolled in a specific age or standard group. Budget 2020 notes higher GER for girls than boys at all levels (elementary, secondary, higher secondary), driven by schemes like Beti Bachao Beti Padhao. - School Dropout Data (Economic Survey 2025): - Dropout rate is the proportion of students discontinuing education between school years (e.g., enrolled in Class 9 but not continuing to Class 10). - Rates: - Primary (1.9%), Upper Primary (5.2%), Secondary (14.1%). - Factors Contributing to Dropouts: - Lack of interest due to traditional gender, societal, or occupational norms. - Girls engaged in domestic work or early marriage. - Financial constraints leading to child labor. - Inaccessible schools, unsuitable timings, or lack of transport. - Teacher absenteeism, poor teaching quality, or language barriers for tribal students. - Post-Class 8 dropout surge due to cessation of free mid-day meals and increased academic/family pressure. - Retention Rate (Economic Survey 2025): - Percentage of first-grade students expected to reach the last grade of their level: - Primary (I-V): - 85.4% - Elementary (I-VIII): - 78% - Secondary (I-X): - 63.8% - Higher Secondary (I-XII): - 45.6% - SDG Goal 4.1: Universal Primary and Secondary Education: - India’s Baseline (2025) vs. SDG Target 2030: - Enrollment ratio (Class 1-10): 75% → 100% - Dropout rate (Secondary): - 17% → 10% - Schools with Pupil-Teacher Ratio ≤30%: 70% → 100% - Learning outcomes (Maths, Language, Science): 57-67% score → Improved outcomes. - School, Student, and Teacher Data (Economic Survey 2025): - 2023-24: - 24.8 crore students, 14.72 lakh schools, 98 lakh teachers. -

- Educational Bodies and Institutions - Overview: - India’s education system is governed by multiple bodies under the Ministry of Education (formerly HRD), ensuring curriculum development, examinations, funding, and quality standards. - Key Bodies: - Department of School Education and Literacy: - Oversees primary and secondary education, focusing on access and quality. - Department of Higher Education: - Manages universities, colleges, and technical education institutions. - Statutory Bodies: - All India Council of Technical Education (AICTE, 1987): - Regulates technical education, runs schemes like Pragati, Saksham, Prerana, Samridhi, and Ishan Uday for scholarships and research funding for girls, SC/ST, PH, and Northeast students. - University Grants Commission (UGC, 1956): - Coordinates and funds higher education; to be replaced by Higher Education Commission of India (HECI) per NEP 2020. - Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs): - Higher Education Financing Agency (HEFA, 2016): - Non-profit company (91% Education Ministry, 9% Canara Bank), registered as a non-deposit-taking NBFC with RBI. Provides loans to IITs, IIMs, NITs, AIIMS, Kendriya Vidyalayas, and Navodaya Vidyalayas for infrastructure and equipment upgrades. - RISE-2022: - Budget 2018 allocated additional funds for HEFA to support infrastructure revitalization by 2022. - Educational Consultants of India Limited (EdCIL): - Provides consultancy services for educational projects. - Autonomous Bodies: - National Council of Educational Research and Training (NCERT, 1961): - Develops curricula, textbooks, and teacher training programs. Units include: - National Institute of Education (NIE), New Delhi - Central Institute of Education Technology (CIET), New Delhi - Pandit Sunder Lal Sharma Central Institute of Vocational Education, Bhopal - Regional Institutes of Education (RIEs): Ajmer, Bhopal, Bhubaneswar, Mysuru, Umiam (Meghalaya) - Central Board of Secondary Education (CBSE, 1929): - Conducts Class 10 and 12 board exams, Central Teachers Eligibility Test (CTET), admission tests for Navodaya Vidyalayas, National Achievement Survey, and SAFAL tests (Classes 3, 5, 8). - Sets quality standards for Kendriya Vidyalayas and Navodaya Vidyalayas. - National Institute of Open Schooling (NIOS, 1989): - Provides open schooling for pre-degree learners unable to attend physical schools. Levels: A (Class 3), B (Class 5), C (Class 8), Secondary (Class 10), Senior Secondary (Class 12). - Offers vocational courses (e.g., computer training, office secretary training) and life enrichment programs. Operates Radio Vahini FM 91.2 MHz for educational podcasts. - Kendriya Vidyalaya Sangathan (KVS): - Runs Kendriya Vidyalayas (since 1962) for government employees’ children (Class 1-12, in India and abroad). Launched Project Balvatika for ages 3-5. MP quota for admissions removed in 2022. Uses Shaala Darpan e-governance platform. - Navodaya Vidyalaya Samiti (NVS): - Manages Jawahar Navodaya Vidyalayas, free residential schools for talented rural children (Class 6-12), requiring entrance exams. Established under the Societies Registration Act, 1860, with states providing 30 acres of land. - National Testing Agency (NTA): - Conducts common entrance exams for higher education admissions. - National Council for Teacher Education (NCTE): - Regulates teacher education programs. - Indian Council of Historical Research (ICHR): - Promotes historical research. - National Book Trust (NBT) and National Bal Bhavan: - NBT promotes publishing; Bal Bhavan runs Bal Kendras for children’s activities. - National Institution of Industrial Engineering, Mumbai: - Focuses on industrial engineering education. - Advisory Body: - Central Advisory Board of Education (CABE, 1920): - Advises Union and State governments on education policy. Chaired by the Education Minister, includes Union/State ministers, MPs, and heads of educational bodies. - International Organization: - UNESCO (1946, Paris): - UN agency promoting education, science, and culture globally. - Miscellaneous: - Central Tibetan Schools Administration (CTSA, 1961): - Funds schools, hostels, and scholarships for Tibetan refugee children in Shimla, Dalhousie, Darjeeling, Kalimpong, Mussoorie, and Herbetpur. - Bharatiya Shiksha Board (2019): - Standardizes Vedic education (e.g., Acharyakulam, Vidya Bharati, Gurukuls) with new syllabi, exams, and certifications, addressing non-recognition by CBSE/State boards. - Notable Union-Funded Schools: - Kendriya Vidyalayas (KVS): - Established 1962, for government employees’ children (Class 1-12). Managed by KVS under the Societies Registration Act, using Shaala Darpan for e-governance. - Kasturba Gandhi Balika Vidyalaya (KGBV): - Residential girls’ schools (Class 5-12) for SC, ST, OBC, minorities, and BPL families. Reservations: 75% for SC/ST/OBC/minorities, 25% for BPL girls. - Eklavya Model Residential Schools: - Residential schools in high ST-population areas, managed by the Ministry of Tribal Affairs. - Jawahar Navodaya Vidyalayas: - Free residential schools (Class 6-12) for talented rural children, requiring entrance exams. Managed by NVS under the Societies Registration Act. - Seema Darshan: - Initiative by Education, Defence, and Home Ministries to take KVS/NVS students to border areas to foster patriotism through interactions with armed forces. - New Education Policy (NEP) 2020 - Introduction: - NEP 2020, based on the Dr. K. Kasturirangan Committee (2017-19), replaces the 1986 National Policy on Education, aiming for transformative reforms from pre-primary to higher education. - Historical Context: - 1948-49: - University Education Commission - 1952-53: - Secondary Education Commission - 1964-66: - Dr. D.S. Kothari Education Commission - 1968: - National Policy on Education - 1976: - 42nd Constitutional Amendment (Education moved to Concurrent List) - 1986: - National Policy on Education (modified 1992) - 2015-16: - T.S.R. Subramaniam Committee - Key Features: - Targets 100% GER from pre-school to secondary by 2030. - Promotes flexibility in academic streams, integrating vocational and academic education. - Enhances critical thinking, emotional intelligence, and 21st-century skills. - Primary Education Reforms: - National Mission on Foundational Literacy and Numeracy: - Ensures all Class 3 students achieve basic reading and math skills by 2025. - Flexible Streams: - Eliminates rigid separation between science, commerce, arts, curricular/extracurricular, and vocational/academic streams to promote holistic learning. - Counseling and Social Work: - Schools to employ counselors and social workers to address psychological issues, sexual harassment, bullying, and depression. - Open/Distance Learning: - Expanded through NIOS for Classes 3, 5, and 8, targeting 2 crore out-of-school children. - Curriculum Changes: - National Curricular Framework for School Education (NCFSE): - Developed by NCERT for Classes 1-12, focusing on core concepts and reducing rote learning. - Structure (5+3+3+4): - Foundational (5 years: - 3 years pre-primary, 2 years Classes 1-2) - Preparatory (3 years: - Classes 3-5) - Middle (3 years: - Classes 6-8) - Secondary (4 years: - Classes 9-12) - Emphasis on critical thinking, emotional intelligence, scientific temper, and 21st-century skills. - Early Childhood Care and Education (ECCE): - National Curricular and Pedagogical Framework for ECCE (NCPFECCE): - Developed by NCERT for up to Class 8, implemented by Ministries of Education, Women and Child Development, Health, and Tribal Affairs. - Programs: - Aadharshila (Birth to 3 years): - Focuses on holistic development, maternal mental health, and Garbh Sanskar (pregnancy practices). - Navchetana (3-6 years): - Emphasizes play-based learning for foundational skills. - Poshan bhi Padhai bhi (PBPB): - Trains Anganwadi workers on malnutrition, Aadharshila, and Navchetana to enhance early education and nutrition. - Peer Teaching and Student Champions: - Older/bright students mentor younger/weaker peers, as per SARTHAQ guidelines (Students’ and Teachers’ Holistic Advancement through Quality Education). - Social and Emotional Learning - Tim Tim Tare (TTT): - Launched in Tamil Nadu (2009), now expanding nationwide. - Based on WHO’s Life Skills Framework, TTT promotes soft skills like communication, empathy, critical thinking, etiquette, time management, and social well-being. - Language and Medium: - Mother tongue/regional language as medium of instruction up to Class 5, with efforts to extend to Class 8 and beyond. - Sanskrit offered at all levels; foreign languages at secondary level. - Three-language formula: - Students learn three languages, at least two native Indian (e.g., mother tongue + Hindi/Sanskrit + English/French). - No language imposed, addressing concerns about Hindi imposition in non-Hindi states. - New Organizations: - National Institute for Pali, Persian, and Prakrit - Indian Institute of Translation and Interpretation (IITI) - PM Schools for Rising India (PM SHRI, 2022): - Upgrades 14,000+ existing schools (2022-27) with advanced infrastructure (labs, smart classrooms, libraries, sports facilities). - Acts as role models for nearby schools; post-2027, states/UTs handle maintenance. - Vocational Education: - Introduced from Class 6 with internships, targeting 50% learner exposure by 2025. - Secondary schools collaborate with ITIs, polytechnics, and local industries; skill labs established. - Higher Education Reforms: - GER Target: - Increase from 26% (2018) to 50% (2035) by adding 3.5 crore seats. - Multi-disciplinary courses (e.g., philosophy and architecture) and college autonomy. - Vocational education integration for employability. - Academic Bank of Credits (ABC, 2021): - Digitally stores credits from multiple courses/institutions, enabling flexible degree completion. - National Credit Framework (NCrF, 2022): - Integrates educational and vocational training for seamless credit transfer. - Multiple Entry and Exit Points: - Allows flexible degree completion with certifications: - 1 year: - Certificate - 2 years: - Advanced Diploma - 3 years: - Bachelor’s Degree - 4 years: - Bachelor’s with Research - Example: - IITs offer BSc after 3 years, BTech after 4 years. - Flexible Degree Completion (UGC, 2024): - Accelerated Degree Programs (ADP): - Bright students complete degrees faster (e.g., 4-year degree in 3 years) by earning more credits per semester. Limited to top 10% of students. - Extended Degree Programs (EDP): - Weaker students complete degrees slower (e.g., 4-year degree in 5 years) with fewer subjects per semester. - Both treated as equivalent to standard degrees by UPSC/State PSCs. - Higher Education Commission of India (HECI): -
Before HECI After HECI
Multiple regulators (UGC, AICTE, NMC, Bar Council). Single umbrella body for higher education (excl. medical, legal).
Bribery in inspections/fund approvals. Faceless inspections using technology.
Different rules for public/private colleges. Uniform rules for all institutions.
HECI Verticals: - National Higher Education Regulatory Council (NHERC): Regulation - General Education Council (GEC): Standard setting - Higher Education Grants Council (HEGC): Funding - National Accreditation Council (NAC): Accreditation
- UGC Budget Cut (Interim-Budget 2024): - Allocation reduced from ₹5,000+ crore (2023) to ₹2,500 crore (2024) to transition to HECI. - Other Higher Education Organizations: - Multidisciplinary Education and Research Universities (MERUs): - Equivalent to IITs/IIMs, focusing on research and teaching-intensive courses. - National Research Foundation (NRF): - Apex body for research, established under NRF Act 2023. - University Definition Expansion: - Includes more institutions offering research and teaching-intensive courses. - Ministry Renaming: - HRD Ministry renamed to Ministry of Education per NEP 2020. - SARTHAQ: - Plan to implement NEP 2020, focusing on holistic advancement. - SATH-E (Outdated, 2017-20): - NITI Aayog’s roadmap for school education in Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh, Odisha. - Adult and Divyang Education: - Targets 100% adult literacy through life-enrichment programs. - National Book Promotion Policy to encourage reading and publishing. - Uniform Indian Sign Language (ISL) for hearing-impaired students. - Open, Distance, and E-Learning: - Expanded through NIOS for Classes 3, 5, 8. - Promotes MOOCs for online learning in regional languages. - Divyang-friendly educational software. - National Educational Technology Forum (NETF): - Facilitates technology use in learning, exams, and administration. - Student Assessment: - Holistic Progress Card (HPC): - Tracks progress via inputs from students, peers, parents, and teachers. - Assesses strengths (e.g., collaboration, creativity) and weaknesses (e.g., lack of attention). - Formative vs. Summative Assessment: -
Before After
Summative: End-of-semester exams testing factual knowledge. Formative: Ongoing assessments (oral questions, homework) for analytical thinking.
High-stake board exams focusing on memory. Low-stake board exams testing core concepts and application, with school assignments counted.
- Assessment Bodies: - PARAKH (Performance Assessment, Review, and Analysis of Knowledge for Holistic Development): - NCERT’s standard-setting body for assessments. - National Testing Agency (NTA): - Conducts common entrance exams for higher education. - School Assessment: - State School Standards Authority (SSSA): - Requires schools to disclose seats, facilities, fees, and board exam results for public oversight and accountability. - Teacher Recruitment and Training: - Minimum qualification by 2030: 4-year integrated B.Ed. - Frameworks by NCTE and NCERT: - National Curriculum Framework for Teacher Education (NCFTE) - National Professional Standards for Teachers (NPST) - Transparent recruitment, merit-based promotions, and operational freedom. - National Mission for Mentoring: - Engages senior/retired faculty to mentor college teachers. - NEP 2020 Funding: - Current public investment (Union + States): ~4.4% of GDP. - NEP Target: - Increase to 6% of GDP. - Expanded National Scholarship Portal for SC/ST/OBC, SEDGs (women, transgender). - Gender Inclusion Fund for girls’ education. - Special Education Zones for disadvantaged regions. - Encourages private college scholarships. - NEP 2020 Criticism: - Insufficient clarity on funding and fee regulation, risking privatization. - Inadequate focus on girls and weaker sections. - Unaddressed teacher demands for job security, salaries, and work conditions. - Limited attention to students’ emotional needs and competition-related stress. - Alleged Sanskrit promotion for political agendas. - Non-adoption of best practices from previous committees or foreign systems. - NEP 2020 Conclusion: - Aligns with SDG Goal 4 for inclusive, equitable education and lifelong learning. - Reforms aim to universalize education, leverage demographic dividends, and achieve sustainable development. - PRAGYATA Guidelines on Digital Education (2020): - Launched by the Ministry of Education during the COVID-19 lockdown, addressing 240 million children unable to attend school. - Types of Digital Education: - Synchronous: - Real-time (live) teaching. - Asynchronous: - Non-real-time (e.g., recorded programs, articles). - Eight Steps: - Plan, Review, Arrange, Guide, Yak (talk), Assign, Track, Appreciate. - Screen Time Recommendations: -
Class Level Screen Time (Synchronous)
Pre-Primary ≤30 minutes
Classes 1-8 ≤2 lectures (30-45 minutes each)
Classes 9-12 ≤4 lectures (30-45 minutes each)
- Teacher Guidelines: - Teach ≤2-3 hours online daily to ensure physical (back pain, eye strain) and mental well-being, cyber safety, and digital privacy. - Mid-Day Meal Scheme (MDM, 2001-2020): - Boss: - Ministry of Education. - Core Scheme (60:40, 90:10 funding by Union:States). - Provides free hot-cooked meals for 200 days/year to students in government/government-aided schools, madrassas, and maqtabs (up to Class 8). - Nutritional Standards: - Lower Primary (Classes 1-5): ≥450 calories, 12g protein. - Upper Primary (Classes 6-8): ≥700 calories, 20g protein. - Benefits: - Enhances nutritional security and class attendance for poor children. - Tithi Bhojan: - Community contributions (money/food/sweets) for celebrations (e.g., birthdays). Adopted as Sampriti Bhojan (Assam), Dham (Himachal Pradesh), Sneh Bhojan (Maharashtra), etc. - Challenges: - Siphoning of rations, unhygienic food preparation, resistance to Dalit cooks, poison/pesticide mixing, and lack of take-home rations during COVID-19 closures. - Food Security Allowance: - Provided if MDM is unavailable due to food/cook shortages. - PM Poshan Scheme (2021-2026): - Renamed from MDM, covering Classes 1-8 in government/government-aided schools. - Validity: - 2021-22 to 2025-26. - Excludes pre-school children (covered under ICDS/Mission Poshan). - Features: - School nutrition gardens for students to grow fruits/vegetables. - Cooking competitions to promote healthy eating. - Supplies from Farmer Producer Organizations (FPOs) and Self-Help Groups (SHGs). - Compulsory social audits by local communities and college students to ensure food quality. - Food Allotment: -

- Funding: - Per meal cost: - Balvatika/Primary (₹11.54), Upper Primary (₹16.74). - Union covers 100% food-grain and transport costs, linked to CPI-Rural Laborers. - Criticism: - NEP 2020’s breakfast recommendation not implemented. - Social audits not conducted in many states. - Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan (SSA, 2001): - Boss: - Ministry of Education. - Core Scheme (60:40, 90:10 funding). - Legal Framework: - 86th Constitutional Amendment (2002): - Article 21A: - Fundamental right to free and compulsory education (ages 6-14). - Article 51A(k): - Parental duty to ensure education. - Right to Education Act (2009): - Operationalizes Article 21A, including 25% EWS reservation in private schools. - Prarambhik Shiksha Kosh (2004): - Non-lapsable fund from education cess on direct taxes. - Features: - Funds school construction, free uniforms/textbooks, teacher recruitment, computer labs, and libraries to achieve universal education. - Subschemes: - Shagun Portal: - Monitors school quality under SSA. - Padhe Bharat Badhe Bharat (2014): - Enhances Class 1-2 education with ≥4 hours/day teaching in math/reading/writing, mentoring for weak students, minimum PTR (30:1), 200 school days, and 75% student/95% teacher attendance. - NIPUN Bharat (2021): - Improves foundational literacy and numeracy for Class 3 by 2026-27. - Rashtriya Avishkar Abhiyan (2015): - Promotes science, math, and technology (ages 6-18) via science melas and mentoring. - Vidyanjali: - Engages volunteers (NRIs, retired teachers, professionals) for teaching, mentoring, and providing resources (e.g., fans, water purifiers, digital devices). - Rashtriya Madhyamik Shiksha Abhiyan (RMSA, 2009): - Boss: - Ministry of Education. - Core Scheme (60:40, 90:10 funding). - Madhyamik and Uchchtar Shiksha Kosh (2007): - Non-lapsable fund from education cess. - Objective: - Achieve 100% retention up to Class 10 by 2020 (no dropouts). - Features: - Funds school infrastructure (libraries, labs, toilets, hostels), teacher recruitment, and salaries. - CBSE Syllabus Reduction (2020-21): - Reduced by 30% due to COVID-19, excluding topics like federalism, nationalism, and secularism (one-time measure, later re-added). - Samagra Shiksha Scheme (2018): - Boss: - Ministry of Education. - Core Scheme (60:40, 90:10 funding). - Merges SSA, RMSA, and Teacher Education into a single scheme (pre-school to Class 12). - Focus: - E-learning, skill development, funding, and stipends. - Subcomponents: - NISHTHA (2019): - Trains teachers/headmasters on gender rights, PH rights, and POCSO Act. - NISHTHA 2.0 (2021): - Online training for secondary teachers via DIKSHA. - NISHTHA 3.0: - Trains primary teachers for reading/math skills. - NISHTHA 4.0 (ECCE): - Trains master trainers for early childhood education. - Atal Tinkering Labs (ATL): - Research/innovation labs (Class 6-12) with ₹10 lakh funding for high-performing schools. - Salary and Grants: - Supports teacher salaries, Hindi teachers in non-Hindi states, library/sports grants. - Kasturba Gandhi Balika Vidyalaya (KGBV): - Residential girls’ schools with hostel facilities and self-defense training. - Free Textbooks: - Provided up to Class 8. - Rashtriya Avishkar Abhiyan: - Promotes science/math (ages 6-18). - e-Pathshala: - NCERT books in digital format. - Prashikshak: - Online teacher training portal (now merged into DIKSHA). - Pariksha Pe Charcha: - PM’s interaction with students, parents, and teachers to address exam stress. - GANIT Week: - Promotes math in CBSE schools, commemorating Srinivasa Ramanujan’s birth anniversary (22nd December, National Mathematics Day). - Madrassa Education: - Union Funding: - Up to ₹50 lakh for teaching formal subjects (Science, Math, Social Studies, Hindi, English). - NIOS affiliation enables board exams for Class 10-12 certifications, aiding college admissions and jobs. - Assam Madrassa Conversion (2021-23): - 1,281 madrassas converted to Middle English (ME) schools by 2023, following repeal of state funding laws for religious education. - Scholarships for Classes 9-12 - National Means-cum-Merit Scholarship Scheme (NMMSS): - Launched: - 2008, extended till 2025-26. - Boss: - Department of School Education and Literacy, Ministry of Education. - Beneficiaries: - Bright students in Classes 9-12 from families with annual income ≤ ₹3.5 lakh. - Selection: - State/UT governments conduct exams to identify eligible students. - Scholarship: - ₹1,000/month (₹12,000/year) for Classes 9-12. - Funding: - 100% by Union Government, disbursed via Public Financial Management System (PFMS) to Aadhaar-linked bank accounts through National Scholarship Portal (NSP). - National Scheme of Incentive to Girls for Secondary Education (NSIGSE): - Launched: - 2008. - Boss: - Department of School Education and Literacy, Ministry of Education. - Beneficiaries: - SC/ST girls in Classes 9-12. - All girls in Kasturba Gandhi Balika Vidyalayas (irrespective of caste). - Scholarship: ₹3,000 fixed deposit, withdrawable only if: - Student completes Classes 9-12. - Remains unmarried until age 18. - Funding: - 100% by Union Government, disbursed via PFMS to Aadhaar-linked accounts through NSP. - Criticism: - Allegations of fund discontinuation since 2018, though scheme remains active. - Rankings for School Education - Annual Status of Education Report (ASER): - Published by: - NGO Pratham. - Latest: - ASER 2022 (released January 2023). - Key Findings: - Government school enrollment increased from 65% (2018) to 73% (2022) due to unaffordable private school fees. - Only 20% of Class 3 students can read Class 2-level texts, highlighting learning gaps. - Other Notable Reports: - Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA): - Conducted by: - OECD, every 3 years, assessing 15-year-olds in reading, math, and science. - India’s Participation: - Poor performance in 2009 led to boycott in 2012, 2015, 2018; rejoined via 2019 agreement for 2021 tests. - National Achievement Survey (NAS): - Conducted by: - CBSE/NCERT under Ministry of Education. - Assesses students in Classes 3, 5, 8, and 10 to evaluate learning outcomes. - Purpose: - Counter ASER/PISA methodologies with government-led assessments. - School Education Quality Index (SEQI): - Published by: - NITI Aayog. - Evaluates school education quality across states/UTs. - Performance Grading Index (PGI): - Published by: - Ministry of Education for 2019-20. - Data Sources: - UDISE+, NAS, Mid-Day Meal Scheme. - Ranking: - 10 levels (Level 1 = highest). No state reached Level 1; Punjab scored highest, Meghalaya lowest. - World Bank’s Ending Learning Poverty Report: - Defines learning poverty as inability to read/understand simple text by age 10. - India: - 54.8% of 10-year-olds face learning poverty (Sweden: 2%). - Right to Education (RTE) Act and Amendments - RTE Act, 2009: - Provides free and compulsory education for children aged 6-14 under Article 21A. - Key Provision: - No child can be failed till Class 8 (No Detention Policy). - Continuous and Comprehensive Evaluation (CCE): Teachers assess students via assignments, essays, mentoring, and remedial classes. - Challenges: - CCE implemented superficially due to teacher workload (low salaries, contractual jobs, auxiliary duties like election work, Swachh Bharat patrolling). - Lax student performance led to poor ASER scores. - RTE Amendment, 2019: - Regular exams at Classes 5 and 8. - Failure leads to re-test within 2 months; if failed again, states may detain student for one year, ending the No Detention Policy. - RTE Amendments - 25% Quota: - Provision: - Private schools reserve 25% Class 1 seats for Economically Weaker Sections (EWS) and disadvantaged groups, with fee concessions subsidized by state governments. - State Rules to Avoid Quota: - Kerala (2011), Karnataka (2018), Maharashtra (2024): No quota if government school exists within 1 km of private school. - Bombay High Court (May 2024): Stayed Maharashtra’s rule, pending further hearing. - Other RTE Amendments: -
Year Provision
2012 Exempts madrassas, Vedic pathshalas, and religious training institutions from RTE Act.
2017 Technical amendments for teacher qualifications.
2019 Ends No Detention Policy; allows exams at Classes 5 and 8 with potential detention.
- CBSE Class 12 Result (2020-21): - COVID-19 led to cancellation of Class 12 board exams. - Marks calculated using 30:30:40 formula (30% Class 10, 30% Class 11, 40% Class 12 internal assessments). - National Testing Agency (NTA) - Established: - 2017, under Ministry of Education, registered under Societies Registration Act, 1860. - Funding: - Initial ₹25 crore; self-sustained via exam fees. - Structure: - Board of Governors: - Chaired by a noted educationist, includes members from institutes for which NTA conducts exams. - CEO/Director General: - Manages daily operations. - Exams Conducted: - Joint Entrance Examination (JEE) for engineering. - National Eligibility cum Entrance Test (NEET) for medical (replaced AIPMT, conducted twice yearly since 2019). - UGC National Eligibility Test (NET) for assistant professorship and research fellowships (twice yearly). - Graduate Pharmacy Aptitude Test (GPAT) for pharmacy. - Common Management Admission Test (CMAT) for management. - Hotel Management Joint Entrance Examination. - Entrance exams for 45 Central universities. - NEET Controversies: - Age limit criteria (maximum age limit removed in 2022). - Stringent security checks, wrong questions/translations, perceived bias against non-English medium students. - Opposition from Tamil Nadu government. - Higher Education: Colleges and Universities - Growth Since Independence: - 1947: - 20 universities, 500 colleges. - 2022: - Over 1,000 universities (50x increase), over 40,000 colleges (80x increase). - Rashtriya Uchchatar Shiksha Abhiyan (RUSA) / PM-USHA: - Boss: - Department of Higher Education, Ministry of Education. - Type: - Centrally Sponsored Scheme (Union + State funding). - Launched: - 2013 as RUSA; renamed PM Uchchatar Shiksha Abhiyan (PM-USHA) in 2024. - Features: - Funds new colleges, faculty recruitment, research grants, scholarships, market-linked courses, industry connections, internships, and e-learning, aligned with NEP 2020. - Coverage: - Government and government-aided institutions in States/UTs. - Higher Education Institutes (Economic Survey 2025): -

- Gross Enrolment Ratio (GER) in Higher Education: - 2014-15: - 23.7%. - 2021-22: - 28.4%. - NEP 2020 Target: - 50% by 2035 (adding 3.5 crore seats). - Higher Education Rankings: - Atal Ranking of Institutions on Innovation Achievements (ARIIA): - Ranks centrally funded technical institutions, state universities, private universities, and colleges in categories like innovation and technical/non-technical performance. - National Institutional Ranking Framework (NIRF): - Conducted annually since 2016 by Ministry of Education. - Categories: - Overall, universities, engineering, management, pharmacy, medical, architecture, law, dental, research. - Top Rank (2024): - IIT Madras (overall). - NIRF 2025: - Release stayed by Madras High Court (March 2025) due to PIL alleging baseless rankings based on unverified, emailed data. - National Assessment and Accreditation Council (NAAC): - Funded by UGC, rates colleges/universities from A++ to D. - Paramarsh Scheme: - Ministry of Education mentors institutions for NAAC accreditation. - Quacquarelli Symonds (QS) World University Rankings: - Top-200 Indian institutes: - IIT Bombay, IIT Delhi, IISc Bengaluru. - Institutions of Eminence (IoE): - Budget 2016: - Plan to develop 20 world-class institutions (10 public, 10 private) with ₹1,000 crore over 5 years. - Selection: - N. Gopalaswami Committee (2018) shortlisted 6 IoEs (3 public, 3 private), including Jio Institute (Reliance Foundation, Pune) as a greenfield project, sparking controversy. - Deemed-to-be Universities: - Granted by Ministry of Education based on UGC recommendations, allowing autonomy in courses, syllabus, admissions, and fees. - Issue: - Over 40 institutes blacklisted post-UPA era for deficient faculty/infrastructure. - 2017: - Supreme Court barred Deemed Universities from using “university” in names (e.g., Manipal University renamed Manipal Academy of Higher Education). - Central Sanskrit Universities: - Central Sanskrit Universities Act, 2020 converted three institutions into Central Universities: - Rashtriya Sanskrit Sansthan, New Delhi. - Shri Lal Bahadur Shastri Rashtriya Sanskrit Vidyapeeth, New Delhi. - Rashtriya Sanskrit Vidyapeeth, Tirupati. - Libraries for Children and Teenagers (Budget 2023): -
Digital Library Physical Libraries
National-level, device-agnostic (works on Android, Apple, Microsoft, etc.). At Panchayat and Municipal ward levels, funded by 50-year interest-free Union loans to states.

- Pillar 6B2: Human Resource Development - Skilling, Vocational Training, Recruitment - Definition and Significance: - Skill: - The ability to perform a task proficiently, enhancing employability and productivity. - Vocational Training: - Methods to improve skills for specific trades (e.g., auto repair, plumbing, carpentry, welding). - Demographic Dividend: - Economic growth potential when the working-age population (15-59 years) exceeds the dependent population (<15 or >65 years). India’s population: >65% below 35 years (Economic Survey 2025). - Dependency Ratio (Economic Survey 2025): -
Year Dependency Ratio
2011 64.6%
2021 55.7%
2026 (Projected) 54.3%
- Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS) 2017-18: Only 14% of the workforce (15-59 years) received formal training; most rely on self-learning, family, or on-the-job training. - Context: - By 2020, India’s average population age was 29 years (vs. USA: 40, EU: 46, Japan: 47). Over the next 20 years, India’s labor force is projected to grow by 32%, while developed nations’ decline by 4%. Skilling is critical to harness this demographic dividend. - Challenge: - Over 40% of India’s workforce is in agriculture (vs. <25% in advanced economies like USA: 4%, UK: 5%, France: 14%, Australia: 16%). Skilling is essential to shift workers to manufacturing and service sectors. - Yearbook: Recruitment and Training-Related Ministries - Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances & Pensions: - Departments: - Department of Personnel and Training (DoP&T). - Department of Pensions and Pensioners’ Welfare (DPPW): Manages Jeevan Pramaan digital life certificate with MEITY (Ref: Pillar 1D). - Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances (DARPG): - Celebrates Civil Services Day on April 21 since 2006. - Operates CPGRAMS portal for citizen complaints. - Publishes Good Governance Index (2019: Tamil Nadu > Maharashtra > Karnataka). - Attached/Subordinate Offices: - Lal Bahadur Shastri National Academy of Administration (LBSNAA): Trains IAS probationers. - Staff Selection Commission (SSC). - Institute of Secretariat Training and Management (ISTM). - Public Enterprises Selection Board (PESB). - Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI): Derives powers from Delhi Special Police Establishment Act, 1946. - Constitutional Body: - Union Public Service Commission (UPSC). - Statutory Bodies: - Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT, 1985). - Central Vigilance Commission (CVC): Established in the 1960s (Santhanam Committee), statutory status in 2003. - Central Information Commission (CIC): Under Right to Information Act, 2005. - Lokpal: - Established under Lokpal Act, 2013;
