Poverty - Definition: - Poverty is the lack of sufficient money to meet the minimum standard of living, including food, clothing, shelter, health, and education. - Poverty in India - Factors Responsible for Poverty in India: - Poor fiscal capacity due to tax evasion, leading to inadequate public healthcare, education, housing, water, and sanitation infrastructure. - Poor educational outcomes resulting in illiteracy and lack of vocational skills, causing unemployment, underemployment, and disguised unemployment (Ref: Pillar 4C). - Unhygienic slums leading to diseases, loss of wages, savings, and school days. - Lack of family planning increases birth rates, leading to child labor and reduced education opportunities. - Large families result in insufficient food, malnutrition, and limited mental/physical capacity for better economic opportunities. - Unprofitable agriculture due to monsoon vagaries and structural bottlenecks in APMC markets. - Low asset base (e.g., lack of land, milch animals, farm machinery, or bank deposits) reduces self-employment/business opportunities, perpetuating a vicious trap of low savings, low investment, and low income. - Lack of financial planning, with money wasted on tobacco, liquor, social rituals, and pilgrimages. - Lack of financial inclusion, leading to debt traps by informal moneylenders. - Majority of labor in the unorganized/informal sector, where minimum wages are not enforced. - Poor insurance density and lack of social security, pushing families into poverty if the breadwinner dies or becomes permanently disabled. - Social barriers faced by SC/ST/minorities in economic advancement in rural areas. - Low female labor force participation rate, weak enforcement of Maternity Benefits Act and Equal Wages Act, and gender inequality in education/nutrition, confining women to unpaid domestic work. - Misgovernance, terrorism, and secessionism in Special Category States, leading to underdeveloped infrastructure, industries, and tourism. - Corruption and leakages in poverty removal programs, with inadequate accountability by Finance Commission and planning machinery. - Delayed economic reforms compared to China, with India’s industrialists constrained by license, quota, and inspector raj, and archaic factory/labor laws hindering manufacturing job creation. - Vicious Circle of Poverty: - Supply Side: - Low income leads to low savings, low investment/capital, inability to start/expand businesses, and persistent poverty. - Demand Side: - Low income results in low demand for goods (e.g., mobiles, TVs, fridges), reducing company/factory investments, leading to fewer jobs and more poverty. - Implication: - Poor individuals lack money for quality food/education, reducing productivity and perpetuating low income. This cycle also explains low development in Least Developed Countries (LDCs). - Economics Nobel 2019 for Global Poverty Alleviation: - Awarded to Abhijit Banerjee (Mumbai-born, MIT, USA), Esther Duflo (France), and Michael Kremer (USA) for their experimental approach to alleviating global poverty. - Prize: - 9 million Swedish krona, shared equally. - Approach: - Divide poverty into smaller, manageable questions (e.g., improving educational outcomes via extra classes for weak students, enhancing child health through vaccination incentives like food grains for parents). - Economics Nobel 2024 for Importance of Institutions for Economic Growth: - Awarded to Daron Acemoglu, Simon Johnson, and James A. Robinson (USA) for highlighting the role of institutions and rule of law in economic growth. - Findings: - Inclusive Institutional Framework (e.g., democracy, law and order, property rights protection) in countries like USA and Canada, where European colonial masters settled permanently. - Extractive Institutional Framework (e.g., lack of rule of law, autocracy, concentrated power) in African and Asian countries, where Europeans did not settle due to malaria, heat, or large local populations, leading to exploitation and stunted growth. - Counterarguments: - Model does not fully explain China’s growth. - USA exploited African slaves and Native Americans. - Britain’s industrial revolution relied on labor exploitation, challenging the notion of an inclusive framework for all citizens. - Poverty Measurement/Estimation: - World Bank (Videshi Methods): - International Poverty Line (IPL): $2.15/day (PPP exchange rate, 2017). - Absolute Poverty: - A person spending less than $2.15/day is classified as poor, measured via Poverty Head Count Ratio (HCR). - 2011: - 21.2% of India’s population below IPL, the highest globally; by 2018, Nigeria surpassed India. - World Bank Goal: - Eliminate extreme poverty by 2030 (Reports: Poverty and Shared Prosperity 2016, 2018, 2020). - 2020 Report: - Noted COVID-19 could push 150 million into poverty by 2021; criticized India for lacking recent poverty data but praised Mumbai’s Dharavi slum community support during COVID. - Relative Poverty: - Households earning less than 60% of median income (e.g., UK standard). - World Bank Poverty Line Changed (September 2022): -

- Composite/Multidimensional Measurement of Poverty: - Uses a composite index aggregating multiple indicators into a single score, capturing broader wellbeing dimensions (health, education, living standards). - Examples: - UNDP’s Human Development Index (HDI, Ref: Pillar 6E), UNDP’s MPI, NITI’s MPI. - UNDP-MPI (2022 Report): - Measures poverty beyond income, focusing on deprivations in health, education, and living standards. - Prepared by UNDP and Oxford Poverty and Human Development Initiative (OPHI). - 10 Indicators (3 Dimensions): - Health: - Nutrition, child mortality. - Education: - Years of schooling, school attendance. - Living Standards: - Cooking fuel, sanitation, drinking water, electricity, housing, assets (e.g., radio, TV, bicycle). -

- Progress: - 41.5 crore people moved out of MPI poverty (2005-2021). - Global Ranking: - India (22.8 crore poor) ranks #1, followed by Nigeria. - Global MPI: - 19.1% (120 crore) people live in multidimensional poverty. - FAQ: Is MPI a Poverty Line? - MPI is not an absolute or relative poverty line but a composite measurement, providing a more refined picture of poverty by capturing multiple deprivations. - Videshi Methods - Inequality: - Gini Coefficient (Corrado Gini, 1912): - Measures income/wealth inequality (0 = perfect equality, 1 = perfect inequality). - Used by World Bank, Credit Suisse, etc. - Global Wealth Report (Credit Suisse): - India’s richest 10% own over 70% of wealth; over 70% of Indians have personal wealth below $10,000. - Inclusive Wealth Report (UN Environment): - Biennial report measuring economic sustainability and wellbeing (last report: 2018). - Global Social Mobility Report (World Economic Forum, 2019 onwards): - Measures access to health, education, technology, work opportunities, and social protection. - 2020 Ranking: - #1 Denmark, #76 India, #82 Ivory Coast. - World Inequality Report 2022 (World Inequality Lab, Paris): - Richest 10% globally own 60-80% of wealth; poorest 50% own less than 5%. - Women earn one-third of global labor income. - India: - Bottom 50% earn <₹55,000/year; top 10% earn >₹11 lakh/year. - Suggestion: - Higher taxes on the rich. - Oxfam Inequality Index (Commitment to Reducing Inequality, CRI): - Measures government efforts via social sector spending, progressive taxation, and labor rights. - 2018 Ranking: - #1 Denmark, #147 India, #157 Nigeria. - 2020 Report (WEF-Davos): - India’s 1% hold four times more wealth than 70% of the poor; a female domestic worker would need 22,277 years to earn a top tech CEO’s annual income. - Period Poverty: - Social taboos and hygiene issues around menstruation hinder women’s education and employment potential. - Issues: - Lack of sanitary products/separate toilets leads to school absenteeism; Chhaupadi practice in rural Nepal forces menstruating women into separate huts, risking infection/death. - Initiatives: - Scotland (2020) passed a law for free sanitary products; India applies 0% GST on sanitary napkins; Rajasthan’s Udaan scheme provides free sanitary napkins. - Deshi Methods (Below Poverty Line - BPL): - Alagh Committee (1979): - Defined BPL as adult daily calorie intake of 2100 (urban), 2400 (rural). - Lakdawalla Committee (1993): - Included calorie intake, clothing, and shelter. - Suresh Tendulkar Committee (2005-09): - Defined poverty line at monthly per capita expenditure (MPCE): ₹816 (rural, ~₹27/day), ₹1000 (urban, ~₹33/day). - Used all-India urban poverty line basket as a reference for both rural and urban estimates. - State-specific poverty lines adjusted using CPI inflation. - 2011-12: - 21.9% (all India), 25.7% (rural), 13.7% (urban) below poverty line. - Used by NITI Aayog and Modi government in official documents. - States with >21.9% poverty: Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Assam, Odisha, Bihar, Arunachal Pradesh, Manipur, Jharkhand, Dadra & Nagar Haveli, Chhattisgarh (highest). - C. Rangarajan Committee (2012-14): - Poverty line for a family of five: ₹4860/month (rural), ₹7035/month (urban). - Components: - Food: - Based on average calorie, fat, and protein requirements. - Normative Non-Food: - Clothing, housing, mobility, education. - Behavioral Non-Food: - Other expenses based on actual spending patterns. - SBI Research Paper (2024): -

- Application: - Excluded households ineligible for schemes; included households prioritized; deprivation-based households ranked by deprivation level for schemes like PM Awas Yojana, PM Ujjwala, PM Jan Arogya Yojana (₹5 lakh health insurance for 10 crore families). - Process: - Rural survey results verified at Gram Sabha; urban methodology differs slightly; caste census data not released. - Deshi Methods - NITI-MPI (2022-23): - First Indian MPI by NITI Aayog (November 2021), inspired by Alkire-Foster methodology. - Alkire-Foster Methodology: - Developed by Sabina Alkire and James Foster (OPHI). - Flexible technique for measuring poverty/wellbeing, similar to UNDP-MPI. - NITI-MPI Indicators: - 3 Dimensions (equal weight): Health, Education, Standard of Living. - 12 Indicators: -
Indicator Deprivation Criteria
Nutrition Any woman (15-49 years) or man (15-54 years) with BMI <18.5 kg/m²; or child under 5 with stunting/underweight (below -2 SD of reference population median).
Child-Adolescent Mortality Any child under 18 died in the household in the past 5 years.
Maternal Health Any woman (last 5 years) with <4 antenatal care visits or no skilled medical assistance during recent childbirth.
Years of Schooling No household member (10+ years) completed 6 years of schooling.
School Attendance Any school-aged child not attending school up to class completion age.
Cooking Fuel Household uses dung, agricultural crops, shrubs, wood, charcoal, or coal.
Sanitation Unimproved/no sanitation facility or improved but shared with other households.
Drinking Water No access to improved drinking water or safe water is ≥30-minute walk (round trip).
Housing Inadequate housing (natural floor or rudimentary roof/wall materials, e.g., mud, clay).
Electricity No electricity.
Assets Does not own >1 of: radio, TV, telephone, computer, animal cart, bicycle, motorbike, refrigerator; and does not own a car/truck.
Bank Accounts No household member has a bank/post office account.
- Data Source: - National Family Health Survey (NFHS). - NITI-MPI 2024 Report: - Poverty Reduction: - 24.82 crore people escaped multidimensional poverty (2013-14 to 2022-23), ~2.75 crore annually. - 2022-23: - 11.28% of Indians poor. - Projection: - India to reach single-digit poverty levels in 2024, ahead of SDG target to halve poverty by 2030. - Best Performing States (2024 Report): - Highest Poverty (2021): - Bihar (52%), Jharkhand (42%), Uttar Pradesh (38%), Madhya Pradesh (36%), Meghalaya (32%). - Lowest Poverty (2021): - Kerala (0.71%), Goa (3.76%), Sikkim (3.82%), Tamil Nadu (4.89%), Punjab (5.59%). - Most Progress (2013-14 to 2022-23): - Uttar Pradesh: - 5.94 crore escaped poverty. - Bihar: - 3.77 crore. - Madhya Pradesh: - 2.30 crore. - Rajasthan: - 1.87 crore. - Bare Necessities Index (BNI, Economic Survey 2021): - Concept: - Poverty as failure to achieve minimum basic needs (Amartya Sen), including food, housing, water, sanitation, electricity, clean cooking fuel. - BNI Structure: 5 dimensions, 26 indicators (notable ones listed): -
Dimension Indicators Implications Related Scheme
Water Source (e.g., tanker, river); distance from source; collection method (tap, pot). Distant water sources reduce daughters’ education due to water hauling. Jal Jeevan Mission (piped water).
Sanitation Toilet type (exclusive/community). Open defecation causes infections, diseases, higher IMR/MMR, reduced girls’ school attendance, malnutrition. Swachh Bharat Mission.
Housing House condition, wall/roof materials. Dilapidated housing increases vulnerability to crime, disasters, diseases. Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana.
Micro-Environment Drainage system; flies/mosquitoes issues and government response. Poor drainage increases diarrhea, jaundice, malaria risks. -
Other Facilities Electricity; cooking fuel (LPG, firewood, dung); kitchen/bathroom type. Wood/dung fuel causes indoor air pollution, affecting mother/child health; firewood collection reduces girls’ education and causes deforestation; electricity enables education and democratic awareness. Saubhagya (electricity), PM Ujjwala (LPG).
- Scoring: - Arithmetic mean, score range 0-1; higher score indicates better access to bare necessities. - Visualization: - Green, yellow, red colors on state maps to show access levels. - BNI Findings: - Highest Progress: - Kerala, Punjab, Haryana, Gujarat, Uttarakhand, Delhi, Goa, Mizoram, Sikkim. - Lowest Progress: - Odisha, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Tripura. - Urban areas score better than rural areas. - Schemes Praised: - Swachh Bharat Mission, National Rural Drinking Water Programme, PM Awas Yojana, Saubhagya, Ujjwala Yojana. - Progress: - BNI improved for all states from 2012 to 2018, with better infant mortality and health outcomes (NFHS data). - BNI Analysis - Conclusion/Significance: - Tracks SDG progress (Goal 6: water/sanitation; Goal 7: electricity/clean fuel). - Improves scheme implementation via real-time monitoring, geo-tagging, social audits, and DBT. - Enhances transparency, accountability, and good governance. - Poverty Removal in Rural Areas (Economic Survey 2023): - Rural Population: - 80% (1960), 70% (2007), 65% (2021). - Agriculture Dependency: - 47% of population (ES23). - Schemes Praised: - Insurance, pension, loans, financial inclusion (Ref: Pillar 1D, e.g., Jeevan Jyoti, Mudra, Vay Vandana, Shram Yogi Maan-Dhan). - Poverty Removal (SDG Goal 1 - End Poverty): - Target: - Halve BPL population by 2030 (2011 baseline: 21.9% to 10.95%). - Indicators and Targets: -
Indicator Baseline (2011) Target (2030)
BPL Population 21.9% 10.95%
Homeless Households (per 10,000) ~11 0

- Schemes: - NSOAP (pension/insurance for poor, Ref: Pillar 1D), PMJDY (Jan Dhan accounts). - Poverty Removal - MGNREGA (2005): - Act: - Enacted in 2005, launched in 2006 (200 districts), expanded nationwide in 2008 as Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme. - Boss: - Ministry of Rural Development (Centrally Sponsored Core Scheme, partial Union funding). - Structure: - Central Employment Guarantee Council (chaired by Rural Development Minister) advises on implementation. - Features: - Guarantees 100 days of unskilled manual labor to rural households volunteering for it. - Unemployment allowance if work not provided within 15 days. - Creates durable assets (e.g., ponds, wells, cattle sheds, granaries, vermicompost plants, anganwadi centers, school buildings). - No contractors/machinery allowed; ≥60% of district work linked to agriculture/allied activities. - Funding: - 60% wages, 40% materials; Union covers 100% wage cost, 75% material cost. - Data: - Over 5 crore households employed; >50% workers were women (2018-2022). - Social Audit: - Conducted by Gram Sabha every 6 months. - MGNREGA Wages: - Linked to Consumer Price Index (Agricultural Labour); proposed shift to CPI-Rural. - 2020 (COVID): - Wages increased from ₹182 to ₹202/day (₹2000 extra for 100 days). - State Variations (due to inflation differences): -
Area 2023-24 2024-25
Lowest Daily Wage ₹221 (MP, Chhattisgarh) ₹234 (Arunachal, Nagaland)
Highest Daily Wage ₹357 (Haryana) ₹374 (Haryana)
Uttar Pradesh ₹230 ₹237
Goa ₹322 ₹356
All India Average ₹261 ₹289
- 2025-26: - Wages hiked by 2-7%. - MGNREGA - DBT (Mixed Model): - Wages paid via Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) using: - Aadhaar-Based Payment System (ABPS, 95% workers, Aadhaar mandatory). - National Automated Clearing House (NACH, 5% workers, Aadhaar not required). - 2023: - Plan to phase out NACH, but operational issues led to continuation of mixed model. - 2024: - Controversy over shifting fully to ABPS. - MGNREGA Budget 2023: - Allocation reduced (₹86,000 crore in 2025) due to expected economic recovery post-COVID, assuming villagers would return to urban jobs. - Bare Foot Technicians (BFT, 2015): - Rural Development Ministry trains 10,000 young workers in basic civil engineering. - Benefits: - Skill upgradation for construction sector jobs; improved MGNREGA work planning, layout, measurement, and supervision. - MGNREGA Reforms/Apps/Portals: -
Name Usage
Yuktdhara Portal Plans MGNREGA assets using GIS and remote sensing (with ISRO).
GeoMGNREGA Portal Tracks assets via mobile-based photo geo-tagging.
SECURE Portal Online application for MGNREGA work preparation/approval.
NeFMS Portal & NREGASoft National Electronic Fund Management System for DBT of wages.
Project UNNATI Upgrades skills of MGNREGA workers (18-40 years) for alternative jobs/businesses, with stipends.
Amrit Sarovar Project Constructs/renovates ≥75 ponds per district.
Jaldoot App Monitors rural groundwater for MGNREGA project planning (Rural Development & Panchayati Raj Ministries).
Ombudsperson App Handles MGNREGA complaints.
Gram Samvaad Mobile App Provides village-level scheme fund allocation data, fostering debate on development.
JanMnREGA Tracks MGNREGA assets and collects feedback.
National Mobile Monitoring Software (NMMS) App Records worker attendance with geo-tagged photos.
- MGNREGA Problems/Suggested Reforms: - Shifted to Mains Handout. - PM Garib Kalyan Rojgar Abhiyaan (GKRA, 2020): - Launched in Bihar’s Telihar village to support returnee migrants. - Boss: - Rural Development Ministry, coordinating with ministries like Roads, Mines, Jal Shakti. - Coverage: - 6 states (Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, Jharkhand, Odisha). - Duration: - 125 days. - Activities: - Building panchayat bhavans, community toilets, rural mandis, roads, cattle sheds, anganwadi bhavans. - Rajasthan Indira Gandhi Shehri Rozgar Guarantee Yojana (2022): - Urban equivalent of MGNREGA, guaranteeing 100 days of work. - Activities: - Tree plantation, pond cleaning, garbage collection, stray animal management, environmental/water conservation, cleanliness, sanitation, property defacement prevention, heritage conservation. - Rajasthan Minimum Guaranteed Income Bill (2023): - Features: - 125 days of employment guarantee for all rural/urban families; minimum ₹1000/month pension for aged/disabled/single women, with 15% annual increase. - Controversy: - Financial strain on state, compounded by reverting to Old Pension Scheme (Ref: Pillar 1D). - National Livelihood Missions (Skill + Loan): - Evolution: - Integrated Rural Development Programme (IRDP) and TRYSEM (1970s) → Swarnjayanti Gram/Sahari Rozgar Yojana (1997-99) → National Rural Livelihood Mission (NRLM, 2011) and National Urban Livelihood Mission (NULM, 2013) → prefixed with Deen Dayal Antyodaya Yojana. - Structure: -
Scheme Deen Dayal Antyodaya Yojana: NULM Deen Dayal Antyodaya Yojana: NRLM
Boss Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs Ministry of Rural Development
Features 1. Skill training and loans (with interest subvention via PAISA Portal) for urban poor.
2. Develops vendor markets.
3. Shelters for homeless.		 1. Brings ≥1 woman from each poor household to Self-Help Groups (SHGs) for training and loans (e.g., candle/soap/handicraft businesses); 8 crore+ women in 81 lakh SHGs.
2. Trains rural men for self-employment or skilled wage employment.
- DAY-NRLM: Community Resource Persons (CRPs): - SHG members trained as Pashu Sakhi (animal husbandry), Krishi Sakhi, Bank Sakhi, Bima Sakhi, Poshan Sakhi (nutrition) to advise/help villagers. - DAY-NULM: NIPUN (2022): - Boss: - Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs. - Objective: - Skill training/upgradation for 1 lakh construction workers for domestic and international jobs. - Full Name: - National Initiative for Promoting Upskilling of Nirman Workers. - NRLM Lakhpati Didi: - Boss: - Ministry of Rural Development (DAY-NRLM). - Status: - 3 lakh SHGs with 9 crore women; 1 crore women earning ₹1 lakh/year (2023). - Target (Interim Budget 2024): 3 crore women earning ₹1 lakh/year. - DAY-NRLM/NULM Sub-Schemes: -
Sub-Scheme Features
SVEP (2015) Startup Village Entrepreneurship Programme: Training, loans, marketing assistance for villagers.
SHG Bank Loans Up to ₹3 lakh at 7% interest; government subsidizes 4.5%, reducing effective rate to 2.5%.
AGEY (2017) Aajeevika Grameen Express Yojana: Interest-free loans for SHGs to buy public transport vehicles.
SonChiraiya Brand logo for marketing urban SHG products (Urban Affairs Ministry).

- NRLM Institutions/Funds: - Institutions: - SHGs, livelihood collectives, producer cooperatives/companies, production hubs. - Training: - Via SHGs, federations, government, bankers, NGOs, CRPs. - Funds: - Community Investment Support Fund (CIF): Formed via SHGs to support poor families. - Vulnerability Reduction Fund (VRF): Part of CIF for interest-free loans to poor families. - National Special Fund Support: With state governments to reduce poverty and empower rural poor. - Infrastructure/Marketing: - Market research, intelligence, technology extension, backward/forward linkages, livelihoods collectives. - Support Structures: - National, state, district, sub-district levels with dedicated professionals. - Deen Dayal Upadhyaya Grameen Kaushalya Yojana (DDU-GKY): - Objective: - Free skill training for rural youth via public/private training organizations. - Timeline: - 1999: - Swarnjayanti Gram Swarozgar Yojana (SGSY) launched from IRDP. - 2010: - SGSY split into NRLM (SHGs) and Aajeevika Skills. - 2014 (25th September, Antyodaya Diwas): Aajeevika Skills renamed DDU-GKY. - Three-Tier Structure: - National Unit: - Policy, central investments, technical support (Ministry of Rural Development). - State Skills Missions: - State investments, implementation, monitoring. - Project Implementing Agencies (PIAs): Public/private partners for skill training and placements. - Funding Quota: - 50% for SC/ST, 33% for women, 15% for minorities, 3% for physically handicapped (PH). - Beneficiaries: - Rural youth (15-35 years, higher for SC/ST/women/PH) from: - MGNREGA worker families (≥15 days work). - Rashtriya Swasthya Bima Yojana (RSBY, now PM-JAY) households. - Antyodaya Anna Yojana cardholders. - BPL PDS cardholders. - NRLM-SHG households. - SECC-2011 auto-inclusion households. - Placement/Jobs: - Minimum 70% trainees must secure jobs with ≥₹6000/month or state minimum wage (whichever is higher). - Special Focus: - ROSHNI: - For Left-Wing Extremist areas (9 states), mandatory residential course, 40% women coverage. - Himayat: - For all youth in Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh, 100% central funding. - Poverty Removal - DISHA Committees (2016): - Boss: - Ministry of Rural Development. - Full Name: - District Development Coordination and Monitoring Committee. - Members: - Elected representatives (Parliament, state legislature, PRI, ULB). - Function: - Meets quarterly to assess scheme implementation; chaired by senior-most Lok Sabha MP, with DM/Collector as member secretary. - Mission Antyodaya (2017): - Boss: - Ministry of Rural Development. - Objective: - Implements schemes with greater vigilance/accountability via Gram Panchayats, NGOs, SHGs, ASHA workers. - Target: - ≥50,000 Gram Panchayats poverty-free by 2020. - RUDSETI (RSETI): - Full Name: - Rural Development and Self-Employment Training Institute. - Objective: - Trains unemployed rural youth (18-45 years) via a three-way partnership (Ministry of Rural Development, state governments, banks). - Requirement: - Banks must establish ≥1 RSETI per district. - Courses: - Papad/pickle/masala making, embroidery, fabric painting, costume jewelry, women’s tailoring, house aya, beauty parlor management. - Certification: - By Assessment and Certification Board. - SMILE 75: - Boss: - Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment. - Objective: - Makes 75 cities begging-free through rehabilitation, medical facilities, education, skill development, and economic opportunities. - Poverty Removal - Universal Basic Income (UBI): - Context (Interim Budget 2019): Government spends ~₹12 lakh crore on schemes, including ₹3.3 lakh crore on subsidies, but faces: - Inclusion Error: - ~40% food subsidies benefit non-poor families. - Exclusion Error: - ~40-60% needy families miss scheme benefits. - Leakage: - 20-36% PDS/MGNREGA funds lost to corruption. - Tendulkar Poverty Line (2011): Rural (≥₹816/month, ₹9800/year), Urban (≥₹1000/month, ₹12000/year) considered non-poor. - Economic Survey 2017: - Proposed UBI to transfer money directly to poor individuals’ bank accounts to enhance purchasing power. - Arguments for/against: - Shifted to Mains Handout. - DBT - E-Rupi: - Covered in Pillar 1A1 (Digital Payments). - Pillar 6D1: HRD/EDU Weaker Section - Minorities, SC/ST, OBC, EWS - Minorities - Minorities - Constitutional Protection - Constitution does not define "minority" but provides: - Article 25-28: - Right to freedom of religion. - Article 25(2): - Sikhs have the right to wear and carry kirpans. - Article 29(1): - Right to conserve distinct language, script, or culture. - Article 30(1): - Minorities’ right to establish and administer educational institutions. - Article 350B: - Commissioner for Linguistic Minorities. - Minorities - Legal Protection - 1955: - Durgah Khwaja Saheb Act empowers Union to administer Durgah of Khwaja Moin-ud-din Chishti at Ajmer. - 1992: - National Commission for Minorities Act, Section 2(c) recognizes six national minorities: Muslims, Christians, Buddhists, Sikhs, Zoroastrians (Parsis), Jains (added in 2014). - 1995: - Waqf Act establishes Waqf Councils at Union and State levels for managing donated Muslim properties. - 2002: - Haj Committee Act. - 2004: - Minority Educational Institutions Act. - Minorities - Census 2011 - Population Share: - Hindu (79.8%), Muslim (14.2%), Christian (2.3%), Sikh (1.7%), Buddhist (0.7%), Jain (0.4%), Parsis (0.06%), Animist & others (0.72%). - Decadal Growth Rate (2001-2011): Hindus (16.8%), Muslims (24.6%), Christians (15.5%), Sikhs (8.4%), Buddhists (6.1%), Jains (5.4%). - Jain Population Share: - Maharashtra (1.3%), Rajasthan (1.2%), Delhi (1.1%), Gujarat (1.0%). - Non-Hindu Majority Areas: - Muslims (J&K, Lakshadweep), Sikhs (Punjab). - Hindu Minority States/UTs: - Lakshadweep, Mizoram, Nagaland, Meghalaya, J&K, Arunachal, Manipur, Punjab (per PIL in Supreme Court). - Minorities - Religious Freedom Reports - United States Commission on International Religious Freedom (USCIRF) 2020 Report: Labeled India as a Country of Special Concern (CSC) due to communal violence. - India’s Ministry of External Affairs rejected the report, deeming it biased. - State Commission for Minorities - Statutory bodies in 18 states/UTs: Andhra Pradesh, Assam, Bihar, Chhattisgarh, Delhi, Jharkhand, Karnataka, Kerala, Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Manipur, Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Telangana, Uttarakhand, West Bengal, Punjab. - Example: - Rajasthan State Minorities Commission Act, 2001. - Linguistic Minorities - Constitutional Rights -
Article Provision
29, 30 Right to conserve distinct language, script, or culture; establish and administer educational institutions.
347 Official recognition of any language as specified by the President.
350 Right to submit complaints in any language used in Union/states.
350A Instruction in mother tongue at primary education stage for linguistic minority children.
350B Commissioner for Linguistic Minorities (est. 1957, HQ: Delhi, zonal offices: Belagavi, Chennai, Kolkata).
- Ministry of Minority Affairs - CPSE: - National Minorities Development & Finance Corporation (NMDFC), non-profit under Companies Act, 73% Union-owned, state/UT share proportional to minority population. Virasat: NMDFC loan scheme for craftsmen. - Autonomous: - Maulana Azad Education Foundation (MAEF), named after India’s first Education Minister. - Statutory: - National Commission for Minorities, Waqf Council, Haj Committee. - Constitutional: - Commissioner for Linguistic Minorities (Art 350B). - Minority Schemes - PM Janvikas Karykram (PMJVK, 2018) - Evolution: - 2005-06 Sachar Committee → 2005 PM’s 15-Point Programme → 2008 Multi-sectoral Development Programme (MsDP) → 2018 PMJVK. - Boss: - Ministry of Minority Affairs, Centrally Sponsored Scheme (60:40, 90:10 funding). - Coverage: - Village clusters with ≥25% minority population (earlier MsDP covered ≥50% minority areas, ~90 districts). - Focus: - Health (PHCs, Anganwadi centers), Education (schools, classrooms, labs), Skills (ITIs, Polytechnics), Community Halls, Marketsheds, Rural Housing, Water, Toilets. - Allocation: - 80% for health, education, skills; 33-40% for women-centric projects. - PMJVK Sub-component - CyberGram - Boss: - Ministry of Minority Affairs. - Objective: - Provide computer training to Madressa students. - Minority Scheme - Education/Exams -
Scheme Details
Nai Roshni Leadership development for minority women, training to interact with government and banks for assertiveness and confidence.
Nai Manzil For Madressa pass-outs and school dropouts (17-35 years), provides employable skills (e.g., computer, accounting) and NIOS certification for organized sector jobs; ≥30% seats for minority girls.
Naya Savera Central Sector Scheme, 100% Union-funded, free coaching for minority students for competitive exams (UPSC, SSC, State PCS).
Nai Udaan Financial support for minority students clearing prelims of UPSC, SSC, State PCS (gazetted posts), family income ≤₹6 lakh, max 2000 students annually, first-come-first-serve.
Padho Pardesh Education loan subsidy for minority students pursuing higher education overseas.
Maulana Azad National Fellowship Five-year financial assistance for M.Phil/Ph.D. for Buddhists, Christians, Jains, Muslims, Parsis, Sikhs; discontinued in 2022-23 due to overlap with other schemes.
Pre-matric Scholarship Earlier for Class 1-10, from 2022 only for Class 9-10.
- Minority Skilling - USTTAD - Full Name: - Upgrading Skills & Training in Traditional Arts/Crafts for Development. - Boss: - Ministry of Minority Affairs, Central Sector Scheme (100% Union-funded). - Beneficiaries: - Minority craftsmen (≥30 years, 10 years experience), trained with stipends to become master trainers (Ustads) to teach younger generations. - Examples: - Phulkari embroidery (Sikh), Kashmiri shawls/carpets, Aligarh handmade locks (Muslims), Thanka painting (Buddhist), Parsi Gara hand-embroidered sarees. - Related: - Hunar Haat (trade mela for craftsmen), Virasat (NMDFC credit scheme). - Minority Skilling - Seekho Aur Kamao (Learn & Earn) - Boss: - Ministry of Minority Affairs, Central Sector Scheme (100% Union-funded). - Beneficiaries: - Minority persons (min Class 5 pass, 14-45 years). - Training: - Modern trades (saloon, restaurant, computer data entry) or traditional crafts (carpets, handicrafts) with stipends; followed by placement/self-employment support. - Minority Skill/Culture - PM VIKAS (2022) - Full Name: - Pradhan Mantri Virasat Ka Samvardhan (earlier Pradhan Mantri Kaushal Ko Kaam Karykram). - Umbrella scheme covering Seekho Aur Kamao, USTTAD, Hamari Dharohar, Nai Roshni, Nai Manzil. - Boss: - Ministry of Minority Affairs. - Beneficiaries: - ≥33% women. - Minority Skilling - MANAS Academy - Boss: - Ministry of Minority Affairs via NMDFC and Maulana Azad National Academy for Skills (MANAS). - Functions: - Uses government scheme funds and donations to set up PPP training institutes, provide concessional loans for skill courses/businesses, and offer technical/marketing support. - Monitoring: - Online portal with Skill Ministry to oversee private training institutes. - Shahari Waqf Sampatti Vikas Yojana - Boss: - Ministry of Minority Affairs via Central Waqf Council. - Objective: - Interest-free loans up to ₹2 crore for constructing economically viable buildings (e.g., commercial complexes, marriage halls, hospitals, cold storage) on Waqf land. - Preserving Community/Culture/Pilgrimage -
Scheme Details
Jiyo Parsi (2013) Central Sector Scheme, encourages Parsi couples to have children to reverse population decline; supports infertility treatment, IVF, advocacy, counseling.
Hamari Dharohar Ministry of Minority Affairs with Culture Ministry, preserves minority culture, heritage, manuscripts.
- Pilgrim - Hajj Subsidy - 1932: - British India started subsidized sea transport for Hajj pilgrims. - Modern Era: - Civil Aviation Ministry provided subsidies to Air India for cheap transport/meals. - 2012: - Supreme Court ordered phasing out Hajj subsidy, redirecting funds to Muslim education/social development. - 2018: - Subsidy canceled based on Afzal Amanullah Committee (2017) report. - Pilgrim - Hajj Mehram - Earlier: - Muslim women required a Mehram (husband, son, or male first blood relation) for Hajj. - Post-2017: - PM Modi allowed women ≥45 years to travel without Mehram in groups of ≥4, per Afzal Amanullah Committee. - App: - E-MASIHA health app for Hajj pilgrims. - Scheduled Tribes (ST) - ST - Constitutional Protection - Article 23: - Abolishes human trafficking and bonded labor. - Article 164: - Tribal Welfare Minister in Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh, Odisha (Bihar excluded via 94th Amendment, 2006). - Articles 330, 332: - SC/ST reservation in Lok Sabha and Vidhan Sabha. - Articles 243D, 243T: - Reservation in PRI and ULB. - Article 338A: - National Commission for ST (bifurcated from NCSC via 89th Amendment, 2003). - 2021: - Constitution (Scheduled Tribes) Order (Amendment) Bill updates tribe names in Arunachal Pradesh. - 5th & 6th Schedules: Special provisions for tribal areas (Ref: Laxmikanth). - ST - Legal Protection - 1955: - Protection of Civil Rights Act. - 1976: - Bonded Labour System Abolition Act. - 1989: - Prevention of Atrocities Act for SC/ST. - 1996: - Panchayats Extension to Scheduled Areas Act (PESA). - 2006: - Scheduled Tribes & Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act. - ST - Census 2011 - Population: - 8.6% of India’s population. - Sex Ratio: - 990 (better than national 943). - Literacy: - 59% (below national 73%). - ST Share (%): - Lakshadweep > Mizoram > Nagaland > Meghalaya > Dadra & Nagar Haveli. - Absolute Numbers: - Madhya Pradesh > Maharashtra > Odisha > Jharkhand > Gujarat > Rajasthan. - No ST notified in Punjab, Haryana, Chandigarh, Delhi, Puducherry. - Ministry of Tribal Affairs - Cooperative/Autonomous: - TRIFED (1987): - Tribal Cooperative Marketing Development Federation, under Multi-State Cooperative Societies Act, markets Minor Forest Produce (MFP) under TRIBES INDIA; 2020 launched TRIFOOD for mahua drink, amla/jamun juice. - National Education Society for Tribal Students (NESTS), autonomous under Society Registration Act. - CPSE: - National Scheduled Tribes Finance & Development Corporation, non-profit under Companies Act. - Constitutional: - National Commission for ST (Art 338A). - E-Governance: - Swasthya Portal: - Health/nutrition info for tribals. - GOAL: - Leadership development for ST students. - ALEKH: - Newsletter for tribal communities. - Shramshakthi Portal: - For migrant workers. - ADIGRAMS Portal: - Monitors funds/schemes. - Adiprashikshan Portal: - Training/capacity building. - Days: - 15th Nov (Janjatiya Gaurav Divas, Birsa Munda’s birthday, from 2021); 9th Aug (World Tribal Day). - ST - Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups (PVTGs) - 1960s: - Dhebar Commission identified tribes with pre-agricultural technology, isolation, low literacy, declining/stagnant population (earlier called Primitive Tribal Groups, now PVTGs). - Current: - 75 PVTGs across 18 states and Andaman-Nicobar. - Examples: -

- Pradhan Mantri Janjatiya Unnat Gram Abhiyan (2024-Sep) - Centrally Sponsored Scheme for tribal-majority villages and aspirational districts. - Saturation approach to cover every ST family. - Focus: - Socio-economic improvement via schemes like PM Awas, PMJAY, Jal Jeevan Mission, PM Ujjwala. - Tourism Ministry funds tribal homestays. - Faster land title clearances under Forest Rights Act. - AIIMS to research sickle cell anemia (genetic blood disorder affecting red blood cells). - ST - Tribal Sub Plan (1974) - Strategy for rapid socio-economic development of STs. - Union ministries allocate funds to states proportional to ST population for infrastructure (e.g., schools, roads, hospitals). - Continues despite abolition of Planning Commission and plan/non-plan budget merger. - ST - Vanbandhu Kalyan Yojana (2014) - Boss: - Ministry of Tribal Affairs. - Focus: - Better implementation of existing schemes, additional funds for schools, hospitals, roads, irrigation, housing in tribal areas. - Emphasis: - Sickle cell anemia, tribal cultural heritage, sports promotion. - ST - Van Dhan Yojana - Boss: - Ministry of Tribal Affairs via TRIFED. - Establishes Van Dhan Vikas Kendras in forested tribal districts. - Forms SHGs for non-timber forest produce (e.g., tamarind, mahua, chironji). - Provides training, finance, and marketing linkages for value addition and sales. - ST - MSP for Minor Forest Produce - Boss: - Ministry of Tribal Affairs via TRIFED’s Pricing Cell. - MSP for items like chironji, tamarind, wild honey, mahua seeds, karanj seeds, baheda, shikakai pods, guggul, arjuna bark. - Seasons: -
Season Notable MFPs
Jan-Mar Lac, mahua flower, tamarind
Apr-Jun Tendu leaves, sal seeds, chironji

- Scheduled Castes (SC) - SC - Constitutional Protection - Article 17: - Abolishes untouchability. - Article 23: - Abolishes human trafficking and bonded labor. - Article 25(2)(b): - Ensures entry to Hindu temples. - Articles 330, 332: - SC/ST reservation in Lok Sabha and Vidhan Sabha. - Articles 243D, 243T: - Reservation in PRI and ULB. - Article 338: - National Commission for Scheduled Castes (NCSC). - SC - Legal Protection - 1955: - Protection of Civil Rights Act. - 1976: - Bonded Labour System Abolition Act. - 1989: - Prevention of Atrocities Act for SC/ST. - 2006: - Central Educational Institutions Reservation in Admission Act. - 2013: - Prohibition of Employment as Manual Scavengers & Rehabilitation Act. - SC - Census 2011 - Population: - 16.6% of India’s population (1,200+ SCs). - SC Share (%): - Punjab > West Bengal > Himachal > Uttar Pradesh > Haryana. - Absolute Numbers: - Uttar Pradesh > West Bengal > Bihar > Tamil Nadu > Andhra Pradesh > Maharashtra. - No SC notified in Nagaland, Andaman & Nicobar, Lakshadweep. - SC Sub-categorisation - Madiga in Telangana (2023) - Madiga community: - ≥50% of Telangana’s SC population. - Issue: - Madigas allege Mala community corners most SC reservation benefits, demand sub-quota. - SC Sub-categorisation - Article 341 (2024) - Article 341: - Parliament solely authorizes inclusion/exclusion from SC list; states have recommendatory role. - Past Attempts: - Punjab, Bihar, Tamil Nadu tried SC sub-categorization laws. - 2005: - Attorney General supported sub-categorization with data justification. - NCSC Opposition: - Prioritize existing scheme benefits for all SCs. - 2023: - PM Modi met Madiga activists in Hyderabad, promised action. - 2024: - Karnataka (Congress) requested Union to amend Article 341(3) for sub-quota. - Aug 2024: - Supreme Court ruled states can sub-classify SCs for preferential treatment in employment/education. - Aug 2024: - Union Government stated no plans for SC/ST sub-categorization, citing no creamy layer provision in Constitution. - Oct 2024: - Haryana BJP CM supported SC sub-categorization. - Ministry of Social Justice & Empowerment - Departments: - Social Justice & Empowerment, Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities (renamed from derogatory term). - Constitutional: - NCSC (Art 338), National Commission for Backward Classes (NCBC, Art 338B, 102nd Amendment, 2018; earlier statutory body, 1993). - Statutory: - Rehabilitation Council of India (1992), National Council for Transgender Persons (2019). - Non-statutory: - National Commission for Safai Karamcharis (NCSK, Act expired 2004), National Commission for Denotified, Nomadic & Semi-Nomadic Tribes (2003, reconstituted 2005, 2015 under Bhiku Ramji Idate). - Autonomous: - Development & Welfare Board for DNTs (2019), Dr. Ambedkar Foundation, Babu Jagjivan Ram National Foundation, National Institute of Social Defence (Delhi). - CPSE: - National Scheduled Castes Finance & Development Corporation (NSFDC), corporations for Backward Classes, Safai Karamcharis, Artificial Limbs Manufacturing Corporation (ALIMCO). - Days: - 26th Nov (Constitution Day, from 2015), 14th Apr (Ambedkar’s birthday). - Committees: - Justice G. Rohini (OBC sub-categorization), Justice K.G. Balakrishnan (SC reservation for converts to non-Hindu/Buddhist/Sikh religions). - Ministry of Law & Justice - Departments: - Legal Affairs, Legislative, Justice. - Executive: - Law Commission of India (non-statutory, non-constitutional, 22nd Commission 2020). - Statutory: - National Legal Services Authority (NALSA), State Legal Services Authority (SALSA) for free legal aid, Bar Council of India, Delimitation Commission. - Constitutional: - Election Commission. - Apps: - Nyay Bandhu (connects poor with pro bono advocates), Tele-Law (legal aid for rural/poor). - Index: - Rule of Law Index by World Justice Project (#1 Denmark, #79 India), focuses on government openness, rights, justice, anti-corruption. - SC Welfare Schemes - Part of Centrally Sponsored Schemes, Umbrella Program for SC Development (not 100% Union-funded). -

Standup India Bank loans (₹10 lakh–₹1 crore) for SC/ST and women entrepreneurs, 7-year tenure, under FinMin’s Dept of Financial Services.

- SC Welfare - Pradhan Mantri Anusuchit Jaati Abhyuday Yojana (PM-AJAY) - Merges three schemes: - PM Adarsh Gram Yojana, Special Central Assistance to SC Sub Plan, Babu Jagjivan Ram Chatrawas Yojana. - Components: 1. Develop SC-dominated villages into Adarsh Grams. 2. Grants for skill development, business loans, infrastructure (e.g., SC women cooperatives). 3. Hostels for SC students in schools/colleges. - Skill Development - PM Daksha - Full Name: - Pradhan Mantri Dakshta Aur Kushalta Sampann Hitgrahi. - Free skill training for SCs, OBCs, EBCs, DNTs, sanitation workers, waste pickers (18-45 years). - Implemented via NSFDC, NBCFDC, NSKFDC under Social Justice Ministry. - DNT - SEED (Scheme for Economic Empowerment of DNTs) - Context: - 1871 Criminal Tribes Act (repealed 1952), DNTs categorized as SC/ST/OBC or none. - 2008: - Renke Commission for DNT development. - 2019: - Development & Welfare Board for DNTs (autonomous). - 2022: - SEED Scheme by Social Justice Ministry with four components: 1. Free coaching for competitive exams (Civil Services, NEET, IIT, MBA). 2. Health insurance via PMJAY. 3. Employment/livelihood support. 4. Housing via PMAY. - DNT - Nanaji Deshmukh Scheme - Provides hostel facilities for DNT students. - Weaker Section - OBC & EWS - OBC Sub-categorization - Ref: - Pillar 6A (Census, demand for OBC caste census). - EWS Reservation - 2019: - 103rd Constitutional Amendment provides 10% reservation for Economically Weaker Sections (EWS) among unreserved categories (non-SC/ST/OBC). - Gujarat: - First state to implement EWS quota. - Boss: - Ministry of Social Justice & Empowerment. - PM-YASASVI - Full Name: - PM Young Achievers Scholarship Award Scheme for Vibrant India. - Provides scholarships for Class 9-12 students from OBC, EBC, and DNT communities. - Pillar 6D2: HRD/EDU Weaker Section - Women & Children - 66 Introduction - Women constitute nearly half of India’s population but lag behind men in socio-economic indicators despite over 70 years of independence. - UNDP Gender Inequality Index: Female Labour Force Participation Rate (LFPR) <30%, parliamentary seats <15%. - World Economic Forum’s Global Gender Gap Report highlights persistent gender disparities. - Women - Constitutional Provisions -

14 Equality before law.

15(3) Special provisions for women & children.

23 Prohibits forced labour & human trafficking.
39(d) Equal pay for equal work for men & women.

44 State to endeavour for Uniform Civil Code.

47 Raise nutrition levels & standard of living.
51A(e) Duty to renounce practices derogatory to women’s dignity.
243 1/3rd reservation for women in PRI/ULBs (some states like Gujarat, Bihar, Madhya Pradesh have 50%).
106th Amendment, 2023 33% reservation for women in Lok Sabha, State Legislative Assemblies, and Delhi Vidhan Sabha for 15 years.
- Legal Provisions - 1860: - Indian Penal Code (IPC) - Sections 376 (Rape), 498A (Dowry Torture), 509 (Sexual Harassment); Section 497 (Adultery) removed by Supreme Court in 2018. - 1952: - Cinematograph Act - Censor Board prohibits glorification of violence against women; OTT platforms (e.g., Netflix) unregulated, Supreme Court directed Union to regulate in 2019. - 1956: - Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act, amended 1986. - 1961: - Dowry Prohibition Act, amended 1986. - 1961: - Maternity Benefit Act. - 1971: - Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act. - 1976: - Equal Remuneration Act. - 1986: - Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act. - 1987: - Sati (Prevention) Act. - 1990: - National Commission for Women Act. - 1992: - Infant Milk Substitutes, Feeding Bottles & Infant Food Act. - 1994: - Pre-Conception & Pre-Natal Diagnostic Techniques (PCPNDT) Act - Prohibits sex selection. - 2000: - Juvenile Justice (Care & Protection of Children) Act, amended 2015. - 2005: - Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act. - 2005: - Commission for Protection of Child Rights Act. - 2006: - Prohibition of Child Marriage Act (replaced 1929 Act). - 2012: - Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act. - 2013: - Prevention of Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (POSH) Act; linked to 1997 Vishakha Guidelines. - 2019: - Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act - Bans Triple Talaq; 1st August celebrated as Muslim Women Rights Day. - Global Cooperation: Beijing+25 - 1995: - UN World Conference on Women, Beijing - Beijing Declaration. - 2010: - UN Women established (HQ: New York). - 2020: - Beijing+25 review by UN Women to assess progress. - Census 2011 - Sex Ratio (higher than national 943): Kerala > Puducherry > Tamil Nadu > Andhra Pradesh > Chhattisgarh. - Lowest Sex Ratio: - Daman-Diu < Dadra-Nagar Haveli < Chandigarh < Delhi < Andaman < Haryana < J&K < Sikkim < Punjab. - Ministry of Women & Child Development - Statutory Bodies: - National Commission for Women (NCW). - National Commission for Protection of Child Rights (NCPCR). - Central Adoption Resource Agency (CARA): Autonomous, later statutory under Juvenile Justice Act 2015. - Autonomous Bodies: - National Institute of Public Cooperation & Child Development (NIPCCD): Trains ICDS functionaries (HQ: Delhi). - Rashtriya Mahila Kosh (RMK): Loans to NGOs/MFIs for women (shut down 2023). - Central Social Welfare Board: Technical/financial aid to NGOs (shut down 2023). - Food and Nutrition Board: Checks ICDS food quality (shut down 2023). - International: - UNICEF (1946, HQ: - New York). - Policies: - 2001 National Policy for Women Empowerment; 2016 draft policy. - Days: - 8th March - International Women’s Day; Nari Shakti Puraskar Awards named after Rani Rudramma Devi, Rani Gaidinliu Zeliang, Mata Jijabai, Kannagi Devi, Devi Ahilya Bai Holkar. - Son-Meta Preference - PCPNDT Act enforcement reduced sex-selective abortions. - Couples produce children until desired number of sons, termed “Son Meta-Preference” (Economic Survey 2017-18). - Result: - 21 million+ “unwanted girls” in India. - Son-Meta Preference: Why Bad - Neglect of girls/women in food/health leads to anaemia, malnutrition. - Forced childbirth for sons increases Maternal Mortality Ratio (MMR). - Early marriage of daughters (seen as burden) leads to child marriages, early pregnancies, high MMR, low LFPR. - Economic Survey 2017-18: - Economic development (e.g., Punjab’s high GSDP) not antidote to gender inequality. - Impacts India’s ranking in UNDP GII and WEF Global Gender Gap Report. - Jaya Jaitley Task Force - 1929 Sharda Act: - Minimum marriage age for girls 15, raised to 18 in 1978. - 2020: - Budget announced task force to re-examine marriage/motherhood age for nutrition, education, career, MMR, TFR. - 2020: - Jaya Jaitley Task Force set up by Ministry of Women and Child Development. - 2021: - Prohibition of Child Marriage (Amendment) Bill proposed raising girls’ marriage age to 21. - Nobel 2023 - Claudia Goldin - Research on female LFPR: Non-linear, U-shaped relation with economic growth. - LFPR falls initially, rises with education, birth control, and service sector growth. - UNDP Gender Inequality Index (GII) - Measures inequality in: - Reproductive Health: - Maternal Mortality Ratio (India: 103/100,000; Denmark: 5), Adolescent Birth Rate (India: 14/1,000; Denmark: 1). - Empowerment: - Female secondary education enrollment (India: 43%; Denmark: 91%). - Labour Market: - Parliamentary seats (India: 13%; Denmark: 35%), LFPR (India: 44%; Denmark: 59%). - GII Score/Rank (2023): - India (0.403, #102); Denmark (0.003, #1). - WEF Global Gender Gap Report - Annual since 2006, measures gender gap in: - Economic Opportunity: - LFPR, wage equality, managerial roles (India: #142, 2024). - Educational Attainment: - Literacy, enrollment (India: - #112, 2024). - Health & Survival: - Life expectancy, sex ratio (India: #142, 2024). - Political Empowerment: - Women in parliament/ministerial roles (India: #65, 2024). - Overall Rank: - India #129 (2024), Iceland #1 (13 years). - Note: - 2023, India included women’s representation in local bodies. - OECD Social Institutions & Gender Index (SIGI) - Since 2007, measures discrimination at home/society. - Classifies nations from very low to very high discrimination; no ranking due to cost-benefit. - UNDP Gender Social Norms Index (GSNI) - Started 2020, measures social beliefs obstructing gender equality in politics, work, education. - 90% globally, 98% in India hold biases (e.g., men as better leaders). - Impacts: - Political, educational, economic empowerment, physical integrity. - No ranking due to cost-benefit. - SDG Goal #5: Gender Equality & Empowerment -

- Drug Addicts - 1985: - Narcotic Drugs & Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act - Punishes peddlers, rehabilitates addicts. - Weaker Section - LGBT - 2018: - Supreme Court decriminalized consensual homosexual acts (IPC Section 377). - 2019: - Akhil Bhartiya Kinnar Siksha Seva Trust announced India’s first transgender university in Fazilnagar, UP. - 2020: - Manipur’s Khudol initiative provided food/medicine to LGBTQI+ & HIV community during Covid, recognized by UN. - National Council for Transgender Persons - 2016: - Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Bill, enacted 2019 - Prohibits discrimination in education/employment/residence. - National Council for Transgender Persons (NCPT): Statutory, chaired by Social Justice Minister, includes ministry/NHRC/NCW/state/NGO representatives, 5 transgender members (3-year tenure). - SMILE Scheme - Boss: - Social Justice Ministry. - Support for Marginalized Individuals for Livelihood and Enterprise. - Sub-schemes: - Welfare of Transgender Persons, Rehabilitation of Beggars. - Pillar 6E1: Human Development - Introduction - Human development measures the richness of human life, not just economic wealth. - Three foundations: - Live a healthy and creative life. - Be knowledgeable. - Achieve a decent standard of living. - Four pillars: - Equity, Sustainability, Productivity, Empowerment. - Four approaches (NCERT): -
Approach Description
Income Approach Oldest; higher income equates to higher human development.
Welfare Approach People as passive recipients; requires government expenditure on education, health, social services.
Basic Needs Approach Proposed by International Labour Organisation (ILO); focuses on six needs: health, education, food, water supply, sanitation, housing.
Capability Approach By Amartya Sen; emphasizes building human capabilities in health, education, resource access (e.g., jobs, loans).
- Social Capital - NCERT classification of social resources: -
Type Description Examples
Economic Capital Material assets and income. Money for college admission.
Cultural/Educational Capital Educational qualifications and status. Degrees, certifications.
Social Capital Networks of contacts and social associations. Connections aiding access to advice, jobs.
- Social Overhead Capital - Includes transportation, education, healthcare, water, electricity utilities. - Essential for long-term economic growth and human development. - Economic Survey 2023: - Acknowledged significant government investment in social overhead capital. - UNDP Human Development Report - Published annually by UNDP (New York, under ECOSOC) since 1990, based on formula by Mahbub ul Haq (Pakistan) and Amartya Sen (India). - Mahbub ul Haq pioneered the human development concept. - Themes: -
Year Theme
2020-Dec Next frontier: Human development and the Anthropocene.
2021 No report published.
2022-Sep Uncertain times, unsettled lives: Shaping our future in a transforming world (covers 2021-22).
2023-24 Breaking the gridlock: Reimagining cooperation in a polarized world (ranks for 2022).
2025-May A matter of choice: People and possibilities in the age of AI (ranks for 2023).
- Provides five indices: - Human Development Index (HDI, 1990). - Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI, 2010). - Gender Inequality Index (GII, 2010). - Gender Development Index (GDI, 2014). - Planetary Pressures-adjusted HDI (PHDI, 2020). - UNDP Human Development Index (HDI) - Geometric average of three dimensions: -
Dimension Indicator India Iceland

- HDI score (0–1): - India (0.685), Iceland (0.972). - Nations ranked and grouped: - Very High Human Development. - High Human Development. - Medium Human Development (India). - Low Human Development. - India’s HDI Ranks Across Years -

- UNDP Inequality Adjusted HDI - Adjusts HDI for inequality in health, education, income. - India: - HDI (0.644), Inequality-adjusted HDI (0.444; lower score indicates more inequality). - Ranking not emphasized due to low exam relevance. - UNDP Gender Development Index (GDI) - Ratio of Female HDI to Male HDI. - Nations grouped (1–5), not ranked; India in Group 5 (with Niger, Chad). - GDI >1 possible if female indicators (life expectancy, education, income) surpass males (e.g., Estonia, Latvia due to male dropouts, early deaths). - UNDP Planetary Pressures-adjusted HDI (PHDI) - Started 2020, adjusts HDI for carbon dioxide emissions, material footprint per capita. - Scores (2024): - Iceland (HDI: 0.972, PHDI: 0.735), India (HDI: 0.685, PHDI: 0.656). - Ranking not emphasized due to low exam relevance. - UNSDSN World Happiness Report - Annual since 2012 by UN Sustainable Development Solutions Network. - Scores (0–10) based on income, freedom, life expectancy, social support, generosity, corruption. - Rankings: -
Year Most Happy India Most Unhappy
2023 Finland 126/137 Afghanistan
2024 Finland (7th time) 126/143 Afghanistan
- China, Pakistan, Nepal, Bhutan, Sri Lanka, Bangladesh rank happier than India. - World Bank Human Capital Index - Launched 2018, measures health and education for next-generation productivity. - Components: - Child survival rate (under-5 mortality). - Expected years of schooling. - Health (under-5 stunting, adult survival rate). - India rejected the report, citing faulty methodology. - Human Development Misc. Indicators -
Indicator Details
Gross National Happiness Index (GNHI) Coined 1972 by Bhutan’s fourth king; measures sustainable development, environmental conservation, culture, governance.
Physical Quality of Life Index (PQLI) Mid-1970s by Morris D Morris; scores (1–100) on life expectancy, infant mortality, literacy rate.
Human Poverty Index Developed 1997 by UNDP; replaced by Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI).

- PRITHvi VIgyan Scheme (2024) - Boss: - Ministry of Earth Sciences. - Addresses five Earth components: atmosphere, hydrosphere, geosphere, cryosphere, biosphere. - Sub-schemes: - ACROSS: - Atmosphere & Climate Research-Modelling Observing Systems & Services. - O-SMART: - Ocean Services, Modelling Application, Resources and Technology. - PACER: - Polar Science and Cryosphere Research. - SAGE: - Seismology and Geosciences. - REACHOUT: - Research, Education, Training and Outreach. - Sustainable Development: Meaning - 1980s: - UN Brundtland Commission’s ‘Our Common Future’ Report defined sustainable development as meeting present needs without compromising future generations’ ability to meet theirs. - 1992: - Earth Summit, Rio, Brazil; 2012: Rio+20 Summit announced SDGs for post-2015 era after MDG expiry. -
Period Goals Number of Goals Targets
2000-2015 Millennium Development Goals (MDG) 8 18
2015-2030 Sustainable Development Goals (SDG) 17 169
- SDG India’s Implementation/Monitoring - NITI Aayog tasked with monitoring SDG implementation, coordinating with Union ministries, states, academia, civil society. - 2018: - NITI’s Baseline SDG India Index Report outlined baseline vs. 2030 targets, state progress. - NITI’s SDG India Index: Overall Scoring - Scores (0–100) classify states/UTs: -
Category Score 2018 Examples 2023 Examples
Aspirant 0–49 Assam, Bihar, UP None
Performer 50–64 Remaining states/UTs Bihar, Jharkhand, Nagaland, Meghalaya
Front Runner 65–99 Himachal, Kerala, TN, Chandigarh, Puducherry Uttarakhand (79), Kerala (79), Tamil Nadu (78)
Achiever 100 None None
- 2021 Report: - Monitored 13 goals (2018) to 17 goals (2023). - SDG Goal #3 (Health) Targets: - Reduce MMR: - 130 (baseline) to 70 (2030); Kerala achieved. - Eliminate TB by 2030: No state achieved. - Reduce under-5 mortality: - 50 (baseline) to 11 (2030); Kerala, Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu achieved. - Increase doctors/nurses/midwives per 1,00,000: 221 (baseline) to 550 (2030); Kerala achieved. - Categorization: - Achiever (none), Front Runners (Kerala, TN, Puducherry), Performers (Bihar, UP, MP, Odisha). - NITI SDG Urban India Index - Launched 2021-22, ranks urban areas. - Top 10: - Shimla, Coimbatore, Chandigarh, Thiruvananthapuram, Kochi, Panaji, Pune, Tiruchirappalli, Ahmedabad, Nagpur. - Bottom 10: - Dhanbad, Meerut, Itanagar, Guwahati, Patna, Jodhpur, Kohima, Agra, Kolkata, Faridabad. - Developed with Indo-German Development Cooperation. - NITI’s VNR Review to UN - 2020: - India’s second Voluntary National Review (VNR) to UN SDG forum. - Theme: - “Taking SDGs from Global to Local.” - SDG Goals vs India’s Notable Schemes -
Goal Description Notable Schemes
Goal 1 End poverty MGNREGA, National Livelihood Missions, PMJJBY, PMJSBY, NSAP (pension for elderly, widows, PH in BPL), PMJAY (health insurance).
Goal 2 End hunger, food security, nutrition, sustainable agriculture Green Revolution (Krishonnati Yojana, National Mission for Sustainable Agriculture, National Food Security Mission), Food Security Act, POSHAN Abhiyaan, PM Poshan (Mid-day Meal).
Goal 3 Healthy lives, well-being National Health Mission (rural/urban), Ayushman Bharat (PHC transformation, PMJAY), Intensified Mission Indradhanush, PM Matru Vandana Yojana, Janani Suraksha Yojana, Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakram.
Goal 4 Inclusive, equitable education, lifelong learning Samagra Shiksha (merges SSA, RMSA, Teacher Education), SWAYAM (online learning).
Goal 5 Gender equality, women/girls empowerment Gender Budget Statement (2005), Beti Bachao Beti Padhao, Sukanya Samriddhi Yojana, PM Ujjwala Yojana, MSME procurement quota for women, Standup India loans.
Goal 6 Water, sanitation Swachh Bharat Mission, National Rural Drinking Water Programme.
Goal 7 Affordable, sustainable energy PAHAL (LPG subsidy), PM Ujjwala Yojana, Saubhagya (electricity connections), Revamped Distribution Sector Scheme, National Solar Mission, Green Energy Corridor, National Bio-fuels Policy (20% ethanol, 5% biodiesel by 2030), PM Ji-Van Yojana, GOBAR-DHAN, UJALA/Gram Ujala LED, International Solar Alliance (World Solar Bank, One Sun One World One Grid, First World Solar Technology Summit 2020).
Goal 8 Sustainable economic growth, employment Make in India, Startup India, Skill India (PM Kaushal Vikas Yojana), Mudra/Standup India loans, PMEGP (credit-linked subsidy for micro-enterprises).
Goal 9 Resilient infrastructure, sustainable industrialization, innovation PM Awas Yojana, PM Gram Sadak Yojana, Bharat Mala, Sagar Mala, Digital India, Smart City, AMRUT.
Goal 10 Reduce inequality within/among countries MGNREGA, DDU-GKY, Standup India, PMJDY, Rurban Mission, technical/financial assistance to neighboring/least developed countries.
Goal 11 Inclusive, safe, resilient, sustainable cities Smart City, AMRUT, Rurban Mission, PM Awas Yojana, Swachh Bharat Mission.
Goal 12 Sustainable consumption/production Targets: Reduce emissions intensity of GDP by 45% by 2030 (from 2005); reduce per capita fertilizer/fuel/plastic waste. SEBI’s BRSR (mandatory for top-1000 listed companies from 2022). Mission LIFE (jute bags, energy conservation).
Goal 13 Combat climate change 4th Biennial Update Report (2025): Energy (75.66%), agriculture (13.72%), industrial processes (8.06%), waste (2.56%) emissions. Targets: Zero deaths in extreme weather, 40% renewable electricity, LED adoption. NAPCC (8 missions), National Air Quality Monitoring Programme, NAFCC (NABARD), CCAP (NCAP by IIT-Bombay, LTEO).
Goal 14 Sustainable use of oceans/seas/marine resources Marine protected areas, Coastal Regulation Zone, National Oil Spill Disaster Contingency Plan. NITI ranks only coastal states (Odisha, Andhra, Karnataka, Gujarat, Maharashtra, Kerala, Goa, WB, TN).
Goal 15 Protect terrestrial ecosystems, forests, combat desertification, land degradation, biodiversity loss NAPCC (Green India Mission, Himalayan Ecosystem Mission), Project Tiger/Elephant. Targets: Increase forest cover from 21.54% to 33%, carbon sink of 2.5–3 billion tons CO2 by 2030. Mangrove Alliance for Climate (COP-27, 2022), 30x30 initiative, Mission LIFE: Ek Ped Maa Ke Naam (2024).
- Water: Mission Amrit Sarovar - Launched: - 24 April 2022 (National Panchayati Raj Day). - Target: - Construct/rejuvenate 50,000 ponds by 15 August 2023. - Specs: - 1-acre pond area, 10,000 cubic meter water capacity. - Funding: - MGNREGA, PM Krishi Sinchayi Yojana. - Boss: - Rural Development Ministry. - Water: JALDOOT App (2022) - Developed by: - Ministries of Rural Development, Panchayati Raj. - Purpose: - Capture village well water levels with geo-tagged photos. - Benefit: - Systematic groundwater data collection. - Environment: Amrit Dharohar & MISHTI (Budget 2023) -
Scheme Details Duration
MISHTI Mangrove Initiative for Shoreline Habitats & Tangible Incomes; mangrove plantation on 540 sq. km across 11 states, 2 UTs; funds from MGNREGA, CAMPA. 5 years
Amrit Dharohar Promotes wetland eco-tourism, income generation for locals. 3 years
- Boss: - Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change. - NITI’s Grow Portal for Agroforestry (2024) - Greening and Restoration of Wasteland with Agroforestry. - Uses remote sensing, GIS to assess agroforestry suitability across districts. - Develops Agroforestry Suitability Index (ASI). - Benefits: - Reduces wood imports, carbon sequestration, optimizes arable land use. - SDG Goal 16 Onwards - Goal 16: - Promote peaceful, inclusive societies, access to justice, effective institutions. - Targets (2030): - Reduce murders: - 2.4 to 1.2 per 1 lakh population. - Reduce corruption crimes: - 34 to 17 per 1 crore population. - Increase courts: - 12 to 34 per 10 lakh persons. - 100% Aadhaar coverage. - Actions: - Increased funding, criminal law amendments. - Bail Money for Poor Prisoners - Financial support for poor prisoners unable to afford bail/penalties. - Union government funds states; technical guidelines pending. - Goal 17: Partnership - Strengthen implementation, global partnerships for sustainable development. - India’s efforts: - Joined International Solar Alliance, Paris Climate Deal, founding member of European Commission’s International Platform on Sustainable Finance (2019). - NITI’s 2021 SDG Index: Qualitative assessment, no quantitative targets due to measurement challenges (e.g., respecting policy space). - SDG 17: Global Cooperation - UN Summit for Future (2024-Sep) - Location: - UN Headquarters, New York. - Adopted ‘Pact for the Future’: - Global Digital Compact for AI and digital technologies. - Declaration on Future Generations. - SDG 17: Global Cooperation - Global Alliance Against Hunger and Poverty - Launched: - G20 Leaders Summit, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. - Supports poor countries via technical assistance, financial support to eradicate hunger and poverty.
